Inside the world’s first solar ambulance transforming remote healthcare even when the sun goes down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:07 UTC
14:00:07 KST

Solar ambulance Stella Juva could transform access to healthcare in regions that lack reliable infrastructure, electricity and fuel.
The world’s first solar-powered ambulance has officially taken to the road, in what has been described as an “important first step towards the future of sustainable healthcare”.
Students from Solar Team Eindhoven at Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands have developed Stella Juva – a road-legal ambulance that operates as an electric vehicle (EV) powered by fully integrated solar panels.
Energy generated from the sun is stored in a 50 kWh battery, allowing the ambulance to safely keep driving and deliver healthcare in remote areas – which often lack reliable infrastructure, electricity and fuel options – even when the sun has gone down.
Unlike traditional ambulances that pick patients up and transport them to a hospital, Stella Juva brings healthcare directly to people in need.
“When a healthcare professional arrives at a dispensary, they are able to extend solar panels from the side of the ambulance,” Yarno Basten of Solar Team Eindhoven tells Euronews Earth.
“This helps generate extra energy and provide shade for delivering healthcare. While stationary, the ambulance generates more solar energy than the medical equipment uses. This means that healthcare workers can keep using medical equipment at all times.”
World’s first solar ambulance takes to the road
During its first practical test, in collaboration with the international health organisation Amref Health Africa, Sella Juva covered more than 800km driving around various field locations in the Narok region of Kenya.
At one point, the team spent six hours travelling on challenging roads to reach a remote field location in Mosiro.
“During the end challenge in Kenya, the solar ambulance tackled rough off-road terrain,” Basten says. “During this off-roading, the toelink broke down, which connects the front wheels to the steering mechanism.
“Luckily, this part was designed as the first part to break. Within just half an hour, the team was able to exchange it with a new piece, so that Stella Juva was able to finish her journey.”
An ‘energy independent’ ambulance
Stella Juva is equipped with medical equipment that is urgently needed by health organisations in remote locations, such as an X-ray machine, ultrasound, Automated External Defibrillator (AED) and cooling equipment for vaccines.
During a two-day test, the solar ambulance proved that it could have provided medical care to approximately 200 people.
While stationary, Stella Juva generated more solar energy than it consumed while using all of the medical equipment simultaneously. Researchers say that this shows the ambulance can operate in an “energy independent manner”, allowing healthcare workers to keep using medical equipment at all times.
“It is really great for the team to see the potential of Stella Juva in practice,” says team manager Mathijs van Gerven. “Not only to drive sustainably, but also to be able to provide fully independent care. Especially in remote areas where energy is often scarce, this can make all the difference.”
‘The potential impact could be enormous’
“In Narok, long distances and unreliable electricity still make quality healthcare difficult to access,” says Geoffrey Sadera, a project lead of maternal and child health at Amref Health Africa.
“Stella Juva can bring not only health workers to remote communities, but also the power and medical equipment needed to examine and diagnose people on the spot.”
For example, during a single outreach, Stella Juva could provide an ultrasound scan for up to 40 pregnant women. This could be a literal life-saver in Narok and nearby counties, which face high levels of maternal and child mortality.
“If we could deploy Stella Juva in these areas, the potential impact could be enormous: we could identify risks earlier, intervene sooner and ultimately save lives,” Sadera says.
Following the successful test, the research team hopes that its impressive results will inspire companies, social organisations and governments to tackle societal challenges. It says they are open to parties who want to explore scaling up the invention.

====================================================================================================

On Lithuania’s border, Europe is chipping away at refugee rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

People began entering the EU from Belarus in the summer of 2021. They were soon routinely subjected to pushbacks – and that has continued ever since. Swedish journalist Thord Eriksson travelled to Lithuania, where the interior minister wants border guards to be allowed to open fire on people crossing the border.
The gravel road runs between rolling fields before disappearing into dense forest. It could have been out in the countryside somewhere in the Stockholm region, if it weren’t for the fence. It glints in the August sun, topped with thick coils of razor wire. With only a few gaps, the four-metre-high structure runs the entire 1,250-kilometre stretch that separates the EU from Belarus, from Latvia in the north to Poland in the south, with Lithuania in between.
It has been three days since right-wing populists across Europe like Italy’s neo-fascist prime minister Giorgia Meloni, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, and AfD chair Alice Weidel in Germany held up Spain as a threat to the EU and to freedom of movement.
Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk held up his own country’s border regime – essentially identical to Lithuania’s – as a model, saying Spain must follow Poland’s example if Schengen is to survive.
Exactly what Tusk’s example means in practice is not something the countries along the border are eager to show. No one – not even journalists or aid organisations – is allowed near the fence without a permit. In Lithuania the restricted zone is five kilometres wide, in Latvia two kilometres, and in Poland up to four kilometres. Anyone who defies the ban risks a fine.
“You’d better take over, they tend to be more cooperative when a woman is driving,” says Mantautas Šulskus, braking his worn Mitsubishi to a stop.
He is the field coordinator of the organisation Sienos Grupė, the Border Group, which he also helped found in 2021 in response to the humanitarian crisis. Now he swaps places with 24-year-old volunteer Vaiva Vinskaitė, a graphic designer who describes herself as a full-time refugee activist.
The purpose of the trip into the restricted zone is to see the places associated with 32-year-old Samrin from Sri Lanka, one of the border’s victims.
“There are cameras everywhere, so there’s no doubt the border guards already know we’re in the area.” After a while Vaiva parks by the roadside and we walk across a field to a steep slope above the river Neris.
It was on the riverbank below that Samrin was found dead in August 2022. Five days earlier, Lithuanian border guards had subjected him to a so-called pushback, forcing him out of the country and into Belarus.
Lithuania was the first country along the Belarus border to see people entering from its eastern neighbour, in the summer of 2021. They came through the forests and crossed a border then marked only by posts stuck in the ground. The same development soon followed in Latvia and Poland. There was talk of instrumentalised migration, invasion and hybrid war – the same terms now being used about those who entered Ceuta.
It is speculated that the incident in the Spanish exclave was staged by Morocco. The parallels were easier to see in 2021: Alexander Lukashenko, who has ruled Belarus with an iron grip for nearly three decades, had already threatened to let migrants through to the border. The trigger was the sanctions the EU imposed after the country’s rigged 2020 presidential election and the brutal violence inflicted on those who dared to protest.
The method was simple: start granting visas to people who would not normally be granted them. From the capital, Minsk, to Lithuania – the nearest stretch of the EU border – was then just a 150-kilometre trip. A border guard has told Politico what happened to those who, for whatever reason, changed their minds and wanted to go back to Minsk:
“If they chose to return, they were detained by the Belarusian side and treated like animals. Anyone who tried to return was dragged back to the border – and they were beaten.”
The situation initially drew extensive media attention. Reporting teams from around the world travelled to Lithuania, Latvia and Poland. Since then, media interest has faded, not least after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but people are still making it across the border.
According to official statistics, Lithuania has so far this year forced nearly 1,100 people to return to Belarus, and since 2021 the total has reached just over 25,000. The figures should be treated with caution, however, since most people have made several attempts to enter Lithuania and are therefore counted more than once. The “invasion” is consequently smaller than Lithuania, Latvia and Poland make it out to be.
Since 2021, the three countries have described their actions as self-defence against an outside attack. But it is not Lukashenko who feels the resistance – it is the people who have seized the chance to avoid the deadly crossing of the Mediterranean in order to enter the EU.
Among Šulskus and others critical of the country’s pushbacks, the name Ylva Johansson carries a particular weight, he explains. In 2021, the former Swedish Social Democratic minister and member of parliament was the EU’s commissioner for home affairs, which included responsibility for migration. And since Lithuania was the first to notice the border crossings, that is where she travelled in early August of that year.
“It doesn’t seem to be people in need of protection, but rather other kinds of migrants,” she told TT news agency.
Until then, people who made it into the country had been stopped and placed in accommodation centres that were often makeshift and full, but they at least had a roof over their heads, food, and had their asylum claims investigated. After that, the practice that still applies today became established: anyone who crosses the border is forced straight back out and given no opportunity to seek asylum.
“People may not remember Ylva Johansson’s name, but they do remember that the EU commissioner was here and that she was convinced pushbacks were an option. That’s when they began,” says Šulskus.
The day before the trip into the restricted zone, I visit a border station just south of Vilnius. It is located in Šalčininkai District, where a strip of Lithuanian territory juts into Belarus and is surrounded by the neighbouring country on every side except the northwest. This is where the first border crossings began to be noticed, according to Žydrūnas Vaikasas, the station’s chief, a solidly built man with a hard stare.
“First came Chechens, and after a few days groups started showing up from countries like Afghanistan, Pakistan and India.”
Five years ago there were cameras and patrolling border guards. Since then the fence has been built and more modern technical equipment installed – an essentially impenetrable structure, according to Vaikasas.
Earlier this summer Lithuania got a new interior minister, Social Democrat Martynas Katelynas, who previously belonged to the country’s nationalist National Alliance party. Since taking office he has said that border guards should have the right to shoot at people trying to enter the country. Vaikasas declined to comment on the proposal.
“But of course we follow whatever legislation is decided,” he says, with translation help from non-commissioned officer Vytautas Makauskas. Like his boss, he was dressed in military green, but he also carried a Glock 19 in a holster.
Since 2021, border guards have mainly received military training, Vaikasas said. In late July, Lithuanian media reported the discovery of a tunnel dug from the Belarusian side – a new way of entering the country that the border chief seemed to take in stride. Sensors along the border pick up the vibrations caused by digging.
“That’s how we know that an attempt like that is going on somewhere near here right now. We just haven’t found it yet, but we will.”
Later it turns out that the tunnel was actually found on the same day as my visit.
Another tunnel discovered this past spring had been the way into Lithuania for several people.
“There were 37 of them, from Afghanistan, but they were caught and forced to return”, Vaikasas said.
These pushbacks sounded self-evident when Vaikasas spoke about them. He insisted firmly that the border patrols have the law on their side.
That’s only partly true.
The pushbacks that have been carried out routinely since 2021 were formalised in 2023 through a law passed by Lithuania’s parliament – similar decisions have also been made in Poland and Latvia. Under international law, however, it is not clear-cut that people seeking protection can be sent away without their situation being assessed. The decision was accordingly criticised by, among others, Amnesty, which described the law as a green light for torture.
UNHCR has also criticised Lithuania’s pushbacks. “We do not think that people should be used as pawns in a political chess game,” Annika Sandlund, head of the UN refugee agency for the Nordics and the Baltics, told the Lithuanian news agency BNS late last year. She stressed that those affected have a right to individual asylum processes – even if they have been exploited by Lukashenko and are alleged to be part of a planned hybrid attack.
“That does not mean they are not refugees. It is a separate determination that looks at the situation in your country of origin, not how you arrived.”
The European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg has had three open cases since 2021 and 2022 concerning the conduct of Lithuania, Latvia and Poland respectively. The case concerning Lithuania involves four Cubans who in 2021 felt forced to leave their home country after taking part in a protest against the government. They travelled to Moscow and on to Belarus, and in March 2022 crossed into Lithuania for the first time. Over the course of a week they made repeated further attempts, but were forced back each time, sometimes at gunpoint, they claim.
The four were eventually let into the country, allowed to seek asylum – and granted refugee status.
There is no clearer illustration of the problem with forcing people to leave a country without investigating their grounds for staying. Lithuania, Latvia and Poland have nonetheless argued before the European Court for their right to carry out pushbacks. Other countries, including Norway, Finland and Denmark, have submitted written filings backing that position.
Sweden, by contrast, has kept a low profile, but backed a statement this past winter arguing that the European Convention on Human Rights should not fully apply to people coming over from Belarus, on the grounds that they should be regarded as part of a hybrid attack. The statement, signed on Sweden’s behalf by Minister for Justice Gunnar Strömmer, called among other things for a restricted application of Article 3 of the Convention: “No one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.”
The written statement was addressed directly to the European Court, which is expected to rule before long in the three cases concerning the Belarus border. The message was clear: states’ interests should take precedence over individuals’ human rights.
I asked border guard station chief Vaikasas how he thinks about the risk that people turned away, like the Cubans, have legitimate asylum claims. No danger, he assured me – it is assessed right at the border, so genuine refugees are not at risk of being pushed back.
The claim that border guards, on the spot, carry out individual assessments of complex personal accounts and geopolitical circumstances is of course not plausible. When I pointed that out, he fetched a binder and quickly showed me a form filled in by an Ahmad from Pakistan who had been at the border and had no identity documents.
According to the head of the border station, everyone who is stopped fills in one of these forms. He insisted forcefully that this is sufficient basis for deciding whether someone should be forced out of the country.
“We do everything the law requires us to do.”
Those who are forced back end up in limbo, since on the Belarusian side they are just as unwelcome as in Lithuania, Latvia and Poland. There are cases of people getting stuck in the border zone for long stretches of time, and in winter having to sleep outdoors. From the summer of 2021 to March 2024, a total of 116 deaths were confirmed along the three countries’ border stretches, though the true number is most likely far higher. Many are never found.
Samrin could have been one of them. He is buried near Vilnius airport – the tail fins of planes rise above the treetops at the edge of the field where his grave lies. The fact that he rests beneath a stone bearing his name is thanks to his wife, Sanooja.
The first thing he did after eight days of trying to get into the country was call her to say he was unharmed. Then came a draining silence. Sanooja understood something had happened, but she didn’t know that her husband had been reported by the manager of the hotel in Vilnius where he had checked in, and that he had then been forced out of the country again.
She called border guards, police, and organisations such as UNHCR and the Red Cross, but nowhere could she get information about what had happened to Samrin.
After four and a half months, she was contacted by Sri Lanka’s foreign ministry, which had received information from Interpol that he was dead. His body had been in Lithuania the whole time, after being found by the river.
Sanooja decided the remains would not be taken back to Sri Lanka. That wasn’t only because it would have been expensive. Other reasons weighed even more heavily.
“As Muslims, we believe that even dead bodies can feel pain. I felt broken that he was in the mortuary, feeling the cold for four and a half months,” she explained to journalists who have documented deaths at the border.
Instead he was laid to rest in the section of the cemetery marked out as Muslim, with graves facing Mecca, while the surrounding Catholic graves run east–west. Sienos Grupė raised money for a headstone.
Lithuanian border guard service put no resources into investigating deaths and keep no statistics on bodies that are found. Unmarked graves simply appear, and it falls to activists like Mantautas and Vaiva to do their best to piece together who is buried there.
Right next to Samrin’s grave are two such graves, with no name or marker – just mounds of earth surrounded by weeds. Vinskaitė searches an app to try to find details, but comes up empty. Everything remains unclear.
But one thing is beyond doubt: The border claims victims.
At least every other month, people contact Sienos Grupė asking about missing relatives, says Šulskus.
“The fact that pushbacks are used means people risk dying. The danger is just as great now as it was before.”
Migration as a political pressure tool
Using migration as a political pressure tool is not new. Since the UN Refugee Convention was adopted in 1951, the method has been used on average once a year, according to American researcher Kelly M. Greenhill, author of the book Weapons of Mass Migration: Forced Displacement, Coercion and Foreign Policy.
How the phenomenon is described and responded to has changed, however. The previously little-used term “instrumentalised migration” truly took hold in 2021, when it was used by Belarus’s neighbours Lithuania, Latvia and Poland. Both the rhetoric and a tacit acceptance of pushbacks and suspended asylum rights spread quickly to other parts of the EU, not least the European Commission.
Earlier this summer, the EU’s regulation on addressing crisis and force majeure situations in the field of migration and asylum came into force. It treats instrumentalisation as a crisis that justifies extraordinary measures. Pushbacks, however, are not explicitly named in the legal text as such a measure.
Rhetorically, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen took a major step when, in a statement at the end of 2024, she not only spoke of instrumentalisation at the EU’s border with Belarus as a threat, but also about “weaponisation” of migration.
In an analysis from Germany’s Hertie School, migration researchers conclude that the alleged crisis, and the methods it is said to justify, are generally undermining the rights of migrants and refugees across Europe.
The article was originally published by the Swedish outlet Dagens ETC on August 12, 2026.
Thord Eriksson is a journalist and author writing a book about the situation at the EU’s border with Belarus.

AFL introduces contract training limits in bid to curb concussions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:56:54 UTC
13:56:54 KST

The AFL is set to introduce weekly limits to contact training in both the men's and women's competitions from 2027.
All clubs will be required to audit contact training and provide vision of sessions to the AFL upon request.
Measures start from a total limit of 120 minutes per week, including 60 minutes of high-intensity contact training.
The AFL will introduce limits on contact training for the 2027 men's and women's season in a bid to reduce concussion and head trauma.
All 18 clubs will be required to audit contact training and provide training vision to the AFL on request as part of regulations announced on Monday.
The measures dictate limits for the upcoming men's pre-season, with in-season training and an AFLW framework to be later introduced.
Set by week, measures start from a total limit of 120 minutes, which includes 60 minutes of high-intensity contact training.
From week five of pre-season, the standard limit will be a total of 160 minutes and 120 minutes of high-intensity training.
Clubs will not be allowed to put players through high-intensity contact training on consecutive days, with teams recommended to use these high-intensity drills sparingly across all contact levels.
Consulting across disciplines from coaches to club doctors and data analysts, the contact training limits follow the 2023 recommendations from the Victorian coroner's investigation into the death of former Richmond player Shane Tuck.
Tuck died by suicide in July 2020 and was subsequently diagnosed with the degenerative brain condition chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).
A separate consultation process will commence in September to develop similar limits with adjustments for the AFLW.
These measures are not mandated for community football, with the league preparing the next release of its local football concussion guidelines.
Concussion and head trauma is one of the most pressing issues facing the AFL.
The training framework comes after the AFL last month fined Geelong $140,000 over Jake Kolodjashnij's concussion waiver.
In 2024, Geelong struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij whereby he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action in the future.
Multiple players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern and premiership Magpie Nathan Murphy, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.
There is also a multi-million-dollar concussion class action case against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.

Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has slowed to its lowest level since May, with an average of 10 commodity ships transiting the waterway per day over the past 10 days, Reuters reports, citing shipping data by Kpler.
 
 
 The 10-day moving average was 10 on Sunday, down from more than 15 on Friday and nearly 13 on Saturday. Only two vessels passed through the strait on Saturday, while six went through on Sunday. 
 
 
 Kpler data showed that one very large crude carrier and three bulk carriers entered the strait on Sunday, while no very large crude carriers (VLCCs) have exited since Wednesday.
 
 
 Separately, LSEG data showed that a tanker carrying refined products from a Saudi port attempted to leave the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday but turned back, Reuters reported.
 
 
 The slowdown comes amid heightened maritime tensions following a new round of US and Iranian attacks on tankers. The UK’s Maritime Trade Operations Agency says 27 projectile attack incidents have damaged vessels operating in and around the strait since July 6.

Germany’s far-right AfD wins a historic 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt but falls three seats short of a governing majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:43:09 UTC
13:43:09 KST

- i24NEWS
- International

- Germany: Far-Right AfD falls just three seats short of solo majority in strongest-ever regional performance
Germany: Far-Right AfD falls just three seats short of solo majority in strongest-ever regional performance
Germany’s far-right AfD wins a historic 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt but falls three seats short of a governing majority
The far-right Alternative for Germany party surged to a historic victory in Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt, securing its strongest-ever regional performance but falling just short of the absolute majority required to form the country’s first far-right state government since World War II.
Final results show the party, known as the AfD, winning 39 seats in the 83-member regional parliament. The tally leaves the nationalist movement three seats shy of the 42 needed to govern alone in the eastern state.
Despite the shortfall, the result represents a massive electoral shift, with the party capturing nearly 44% of the popular vote and doubling its previous standing in the state.
The Christian Democratic Union, which previously led the state coalition, suffered severe losses, slumping to roughly 17% of the vote. Because all established mainstream parties have repeatedly pledged to maintain a strict "firewall" against coalitions with the far right, the election outcome plunges Saxony-Anhalt into profound political fragmentation and uncertainty.
The triumph of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, where its local chapter is officially designated as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, has sent shockwaves through Germany’s Jewish communities and drawn close scrutiny from Israel.
For Jewish leaders in Germany and observers in Jerusalem, the AfD's rise raises acute safety and historical concerns.
'The policy of AFD when it comes to Israel is the same as the German radical left- catastrophic,' expert on German-Israel relations Melody Sucharewicz told i24NEWS.
The Central Council of Jews in Germany has consistently warned that the party harbors xenophobia, historical revisionism, and antisemitic undercurrents that threaten Jewish life.
Prominent leaders within the party have routinely sought to downplay Nazi-era atrocities, downplayed Germany's Holocaust remembrance culture, and pushed nationalist platforms that alienate minority populations.
Officials in Jerusalem have historically maintained a policy of official non-engagement with far-right European parties with roots or elements tied to revisionist stances on the Holocaust.
The expansion of the AfD’s political footprint in state capitals tests the stability of Germany’s post-war democratic consensus, which has long served as a bedrock of strong German-Israeli bilateral relations and a guarantor of protection for local Jewish institutions.
As political leaders in Magdeburg begin arduous negotiations to explore alternative governing alliances, the election shows a deepening political divide between eastern and western Germany.
While the AfD’s victory demonstrates its formidable grass-roots strength, the remaining political parties now face the challenge of cobbling together a broad coalition to keep the far right out of power.

Germany’s right-wing AfD wins Saxony-Anhalt election with record 43.8% vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:40:47 UTC
13:40:47 KST

Ayhan Simsek
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Germany’s right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt with a record 43.8% of the vote but fell short of a majority to govern alone, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) slumped to a historic low of 17.2%, according to preliminary official results.
The state election authority said all ballots had been counted. The AfD more than doubled its 20.8% result from 2021 and posted its strongest showing in any German state election. It won 39 of 83 seats in the Magdeburg parliament, three short of the 42 needed for an outright majority. With all other major parties ruling out a coalition with the AfD, the outcome pointed to political uncertainty and long talks on forming a government.
Turnout was 77.8%, up from 60.3% in 2021 and the highest in the state since German reunification.
“We have achieved exactly what we set out to achieve. We have made history in this country,” AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund told public television.
He said cooperation was possible “only with those who support the AfD’s demand for a clear change in policy,” whether that came “through a parliamentary group or through individual deputies.” Asked what would happen if no partner emerged, he said: “If necessary, there will just be new elections.”
The Social Democrats (SPD) finished third with 9.3%, one of their weakest showings in the eastern state. The Greens followed with 8.9% and the socialist Left Party with 8.6%. The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) passed the 5% threshold with 5.3% and entered the new parliament. The Free Democrats, junior partners in the outgoing government, missed the threshold with 2.6%.
Merz’s CDU took 15 seats, down from 40 in 2021. The Greens, the Social Democrats and the Left Party won eight seats each, and the left-wing populist BSW won five. The other parties together hold 44 seats.
The numbers offer no clear path to a governing majority. A coalition of the CDU, SPD and Greens would hold 31 seats. Adding the Left Party would lift that bloc to 39, still short of 42. The AfD could reach a majority only with BSW support. The BSW could back an AfD candidate, support a CDU-backed contender or abstain. In a third ballot for state premier, only a plurality is required.
Party leaders are expected to set out their positions this week, with initial exploratory coalition talks likely to begin in the coming days.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has classified the AfD’s regional branch as a proven right-wing extremist organization, saying parts of the party promote a racist, ethnic understanding of national identity that is incompatible with the country’s democratic constitutional order. Mainstream parties have cited that assessment in maintaining a refusal to govern with the AfD.

Wildfires, heatwaves threaten to undermine air quality: UN weather agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:39:00 UTC
13:39:00 KST

Wildfires, heatwaves threaten to undermine air quality: UN weather agency
- Wildfires and heatwaves driven by climate change are increasing air pollution, making it harder to meet global air quality goals, the UN's World Meteorological Organization warned.
- Wildfire smoke raises harmful pollutants like PM2.5 and ground-level ozone, linked to respiratory and heart diseases, even in regions with otherwise clean air.
- The report urges better monitoring of pollutants such as black carbon and microplastics and highlights that extreme fire-smoke events have tripled since the 1990s, causing many deaths.
AI generated
GENEVA – Pollution from increasingly intense wildfires and heatwaves could undermine global efforts to improve air quality and protect human health, the United Nations’ weather agency said on Sept 7, warning that climate change is making it harder to meet international air quality goals.
In its annual report on air quality and the climate, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said air pollution and climate change are closely linked and should be tackled through coordinated policies rather than in isolation.
It warned that meeting the World Health Organization’s air quality guidelines will become more difficult because extreme wildfires are more likely to occur in the future.
Wildfires are becoming a growing source of harmful air pollution even as regulations have reduced emissions from industry and transport in many developed countries, the WMO said in its report.
“No matter how clean your city or your region is... if you have a lot of pollution brought about by wildfires, that has the potential to negatively impact air quality in those regions as well,” Lorenzo Labrador, scientific officer at the WMO, told Reuters.
The report highlights the growing impact of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, and ground-level ozone, pollutants linked to respiratory and cardiovascular diseases.
It also calls for improved monitoring of pollutants and aerosols, including black carbon and microplastics, which it said remain poorly tracked despite their widespread presence in the atmosphere.
The year 2026 has been marked by extreme heat and destructive wildfires across parts of Europe, including Spain, France and Greece. The WMO has said that extreme heat is becoming more frequent, intense and longer-lasting as the planet warms.
The new report said PM2.5 concentrations in 2025 were above long-term averages in northern Canada, parts of Russia and western-central Africa due to heightened fire activity, while north-western Spain was a hot spot following exceptional late-summer fires.
A study cited in the report found that extreme fire-smoke events have tripled globally since the 1990s and may have contributed to nearly 100,000 additional deaths annually between 2010 and 2018.
Particulate matter from wildfires is particularly harmful because it comes with a host of toxic chemicals, Labrador said, adding that inhalation causes bodywide inflammation that can lead to pulmonary disease. REUTERS

Country diary: A dreadful den of murder and thievery – or is it? | Merryn Glover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:30:24 UTC
13:30:24 KST

The word “cave” is full of possibility. It speaks of darkness, secrets, treasures and escapees, all of which can be found in the stories of Raitts Cave, which lies in a field near the hamlet of Lynchat, Inverness-shire.
Its Gaelic name is An Uaimh Mhor, “the great cave”, and one legend claims it was built by giants, the females hollowing out the earth and carrying the soil in their aprons to dump in the River Spey, while the males cut its massive stone slabs from the hills above. Because, in fact, it is not a natural cave, but a subterranean passage, shaped like a horseshoe and lined with stone.
Another tale attributes it to the 11 strapping sons of a local freebooter from the powerful 13th-century Clan Cumming (or MacNiven), who used it to stash their loot and hide from the law (or the laird, who tricked them by disguising himself as a beggar). Justice, or vengeance, eventually caught up with them, and the brothers were hauled out and executed at the cave’s entrance.
Or, it could have been the hiding place of escaping Jacobites after Culloden, who were burned alive inside. Or indeed a shelter for persecuted worshippers.
The identities of the builders, the hiders and the avengers and their various fates change with each version of the story, but the evidence is scant. Officially, archaeologists first excavated the site in 1835, and called it an erd house – “earth shelter” – and later a souterrain, an underground space constructed by humans. At some point, the central roof was removed, giving access to steps and a narrow tunnel on one side, and a large covered chamber at the other.
Further digs have dated it to the late iron age (100-400 AD) and the conclusion is that it was a storeroom, probably for food, serving a roundhouse above. Bother. What about all the magic and calamity? I hearten myself that the academic’s mundane deductions do not rule out other thrilling escapades, and I explore the cave in the vivid company of giantesses, thieves, fugitives and murderers – who are, of course, much more fun in folklore than reality.

North Korea commissions nuclear-capable naval destroyer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:30:11 UTC
13:30:11 KST

Aamir Latif
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
North Korea has commissioned its new naval destroyer Kang Kon as part of efforts to bolster its fleet with nuclear-capable vessels, state media reported Monday.
The commissioning ceremony, held Sunday in the eastern port city of Wonsan, was attended by North Korean Leader Kim Jong Un, who called the 5,000-ton vessel "essentially an offensive destroyer" and part of "the state nuclear counteraction system," according to the Korean Central News Agency.
He was accompanied by his wife, Ri Sol-ju, and daughter Ju-ae.
The Kang Kon's commissioning came a day before the start of a joint military drill between the US, Japan and South Korea which Pyongyang has long denounced as a “war rehearsal.”
"The new-generation destroyer should deal a deadly retaliatory blow at the enemies, as it is a force involved in the state nuclear counteraction system," Kim added.
Kim stressed the need to develop the country's navy into "a nuclear armed force" in order to carry out maritime defense and war deterrence activities "more clearly."
The Kang Kon has been commissioned into North Korean navy's East Sea Fleet.
The destroyer was commissioned less than three months after the North commissioned its first 5,000-ton destroyer, the Choe Hyon, into the West Sea Fleet.
Early this year, Pyongyang unveiled plans to build two large warships of more than 5,000 tons over the next five years, including 10,000-ton-class warships.

Illegal call center case: Kravchenko explains visa and house allegations involving his family
Kravchenko published the statement on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
"It is clear from the conversations that the earlier allegations by anti-corruption authorities about my involvement in receiving and laundering money from illegal call centers have no factual basis. Conversations are simply conversations, just as a photo of a safe containing money is merely a photo of a safe containing money and has nothing to do with either me or the Prosecutor General's Office. According to the lawyers, it is a photograph from another criminal case," Kravchenko said.
According to him, his family's expenses for travel and household needs were incurred strictly within the law and were covered by declared income, with no violations.
Regarding a U.S. visa and the purchase of a laptop, Kravchenko said that his wife had prepared the documents and obtained the visa herself, and that she does not have a new laptop.
As for the 280-square-meter house where his family lives under a rental agreement, Kravchenko said they had chosen it back in the winter, but it needed some finishing work and equipment to be set up. He said that discussions about the work of contractors, the alarm system and household appliances took place in this context.
"We moved into the house on May 1, 2026. My permanent place of residence will be declared in accordance with the law," Kravchenko said.
He stressed that holding public office does not exempt anyone from scrutiny, "but neither does it eliminate the requirement to substantiate allegations with facts."
As reported, on September 4, the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office and the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine said that, as part of Operation Carthage, they had exposed a criminal organization led by the head of a Prosecutor General's Office department that systematically collected bribes from fraudulent call centers and laundered the proceeds.
According to investigators, the PGO official formed the group in mid-2025, involving current prosecutors and close associates who were not officially affiliated with the office. The group imposed payments in exchange for allowing shadow call centers to operate without interference. The centers allegedly defrauded Ukrainian and foreign citizens on a large scale.
On September 6, the High Anti-Corruption Court ordered Serhii Kropyva, deputy head of the Department of International Cooperation, who is accused of shielding fraudulent call centers, to be held in custody with bail set at UAH 120 million as an alternative to detention.

Australians could opt out of social media algorithms under proposed law
The government’s digital duty of care bill forces big tech to offer chronological feeds but the opposition raises doubts over enforcement
2-MIN READ2-MIN
Australians could be given the option of opting out of powerful social media algorithms under new legislation cracking down on big tech, a minister said on Monday.
The draft law requiring a “digital duty of care” is expected to be introduced to Australia’s parliament this week.
It would require firms like Meta Platforms to give users the option of turning off algorithms that tailor recommendations to their personal taste.
“A lot of Australians appreciate the algorithm, both for the enjoyment they get out of it or the utility they get out of it,” Communications Minister Anika Wells told national broadcaster ABC.
“A lot of Australians will want to choose the algorithm – but we think that big tech should offer them the choice in the first place, and they should respect that choice,” she said
“We should give Australians more choice over what they should see on their feeds.”

WELLINGTON, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's governing National Party has extended its lead over the opposition Labor Party in a new poll released on Monday, as support for both major parties declined and smaller parties gained ground.
National fell 2 percentage points to 29 percent in the September Taxpayers' Union-Curia Poll, while Labor dropped 1.9 points to 25.9 percent, its lowest result since July 2024.
The poll projected National to win 39 seats in parliament, one fewer than in August, while Labor was projected to take 35 seats, also down one. The Greens and ACT recorded the biggest gains among the major parties.

National leader Christopher Luxon remained ahead of Labor leader Chris Hipkins as preferred prime minister, according to the poll, which surveyed 1,000 adults from Sept. 1 to 3 and has a maximum margin of error of 3.1 percentage points. ■

Japan's August foreign reserve assets drop by record 6 pct after yen interventions
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
12:18:31 CST
13:18:31 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Japan's foreign reserve assets totaled 1.21 trillion U.S. dollars at the end of August, down by 79.58 billion dollars from a month earlier, marking the largest percentage decline on record, the Finance Ministry said Monday.
The 6.18-percent drop was driven by a decline in the market value of government bonds held in the reserves amid rising interest rates, as well as a reduction following Tokyo's record foreign exchange intervention to support the yen, according to the ministry.
Between July 30 and Aug. 26, the ministry said Japan had spent a record 15.4 trillion yen (about 98.75 billion dollars) on dollar-selling, yen-buying interventions.
Foreign reserve assets fell for a fourth consecutive month in August, posting the largest declines in both percentage and dollar terms since comparable data became available in April 2000, ministry data showed. ■

MAGDEBURG, Germany, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- Saxony-Anhalt, a relatively small eastern German state with just over 2 million residents, rarely attracts global attention. But on Sunday, its capital Magdeburg became the center of a political storm after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a historic state election, securing around 44 percent of the vote.
The result marked an unprecedented setback for the ruling Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and put the AfD in a position to install its first-ever state governor.
The political divide was already visible on the streets of Magdeburg during the election weekend.
On Saturday afternoon, thousands of people gathered at Magdeburg's Domplatz under banners defending pluralism and democracy. Music filled the square, but the mood among many participants was one of quiet concern.
"If the cultural landscape here suffocates, I'll pack my bags," said Anja, an artist who traveled from nearby Leipzig.
She feared that an AfD-led administration could cut public funding for the arts and restrict space for independent expression.
Nearby, Matea, a local physical therapist, acknowledged the widespread frustration that has fueled support for the AfD, saying that she was deeply dissatisfied with the policies of the federal government. "Still, handing power to the AfD will only make things worse," she said.
Less than 2 km away, outside the AMO Kulturhaus, police vans formed a security perimeter around a sharply different scene.
The AfD's final campaign rally before the election drew a packed crowd, with some supporters standing outside on the pavement.
They applauded and chanted in support of the party's 35-year-old lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, whom they described as "a good fellow."
Bastian, 40, traveled across the country from North Rhine-Westphalia to attend the rally. The employee of an automotive parts supplier sees eastern Germany as the forefront of a broader national backlash.
"I look at the young apprentices at our plant and wonder whether their jobs will still exist in five years," he said. He cited economic stagnation and uncontrolled immigration as reasons why he wants to "bring back the old Germany."
By Sunday, these competing anxieties had converged quietly at polling stations.
Outside a downtown polling station, Lieas, a 20-year-old student of Syrian descent, was heading to cast his ballot for the Greens, hoping to help smaller parties cross the 5-percent electoral threshold and prevent the AfD from securing an outright majority.
"We have to vote strategically," he said, describing the election as "extremely important."
Lieas said his younger brother is preparing to move to Germany for university, and he had given him clear advice: avoid Saxony-Anhalt and consider other parts of the country.
"The atmosphere here is changing, and it is very worrying," he said. ■

Wildfires, heatwaves threaten global air quality and health, UN warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:16:48 UTC
13:16:48 KST

Wildfires, heatwaves threaten global air quality and health, UN warns
Wildfires and heatwaves are threatening global efforts to improve air quality and protect human health, the World Meteorological Organisation said on Monday. The UN agency warned that increasingly severe fires are raising exposure to toxic PM2.5 pollution, even as regulations have reduced industrial and transport emissions in Europe and North America.
Wildfires and heatwaves, which generate microscopic airborne pollutants, risk undermining international efforts to improve air quality, protect human health and safeguard nature, the World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) said on Monday.
The United Nations' weather and climate agency underlined the links between air pollution and climate change, which scientists say is leading to more frequent and more intense heatwaves and wildfires.
"Extreme wildfires are increasing, leading to big health consequences because of the high toxicity of smoke," the WMO said in a statement accompanying its latest annual Air Quality and Climate Bulletin.
"Whilst regulations in Europe and North America have reduced industrial and transport PM2.5 emissions, exposure to fire-related PM2.5 has increased."
Particulate matter PM2.5 is composed of microscopic particles and droplets of less than 2.5 micrometres in diameter, which is a health hazard because it can penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream.
It is emitted by fossil fuel-driven industrial activities, farming, domestic heating and transport, as well as by wildfires and dust storms.
The report said the world needs to better monitor air pollutants such as aerosol -- including black carbon and microplastics --, fine particles and ground-level ozone.
These pollutants "are not sufficiently monitored even though they are widespread and are potentially harmful to ecosystems", the WMO said.
"(We need) complementary and coordinated policies on air quality and climate because they cannot be dealt with in isolation."
Read moreFrance announces €1 billion aid for farmers after climate-hit summer
Toxic wildfire smoke
"Air quality and climate change can't be dealt with separately. If one worsens, the other does too," Lorenzo Labrador, from the WMO's Global Atmosphere Watch network of scientists, told AFP.
"In places where there are relatively powerful forest fires, we find a lot of fine particle pollution," he said.
Microparticles generated by burning vegetation are "much more toxic" than those emitted by other sources, even car exhaust, he stressed.
They damage the health of people and wildlife living far from the fire itself because they are carried by the wind, but their poisonous effect is not sufficiently taken into account in air quality assessments, Labrador said.
"Conventional risks models based on total PM2.5 concentrations may underestimate wildfire-attributable mortality by up to 93 percent," the WMO said.
One study cited in the WMO Bulletin says extreme fire-smoke events have tripled globally since the 1990s, contributing to nearly 100,000 additional deaths per year between 2010 and 2018, although this may be an underestimate.
Read moreTunisia water crisis deepens as temperatures approach 50°C
Ozone, microplastics
Another source of air pollution that carries major health risks is ground-level ozone, which accumulates when temperatures rise, atmospheric conditions stagnate and solar radiation is intense, as seen during recent heatwaves in China, Europe and the southeastern United States.
"This increased exposure to ozone pollution has the potential to lead to tens of thousands of additional premature deaths," particularly due to respiratory diseases, the WMO warned.
Another growing concern is aerosol particles, which can also travel to oceans and continents far from their source.
They can alter the way the atmosphere reflects sunlight, change the chemical properties of land and water, and pollute otherwise clean environments.
"One example is the deposition of black carbon -- or soot -- on snow and ice, which reduces the amount of sunlight reflected by these surfaces and in turn can hasten the melting process," the WMO explained.
Another example is microplastics, formed when plastics break down because of sunlight or other factors, and found virtually everywhere -- in the air, the soil and the oceans.
One simulation in the WMO Bulletin estimates there are "51 million tonnes for land and 22 million tonnes for the ocean -- which are in turn a source of microplastics for the atmosphere".
"As plastic production and, critically, mismanaged plastic waste, continues to increase," monitoring the airborne paths that carry microplastics from their source and dump them in remote environments will be "crucial", the report said.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

‘Iran-South Korea relations; a bridge that stands firm even in toughest days’

Unknown Publisher

‘Iran-South Korea relations; a bridge that stands firm even in toughest days’
Interview with Pooya Firoozi, First Vice Chairman of Iran-South Korea Chamber of Commerce
TEHRAN- Iran and South Korea have maintained economic and diplomatic ties for decades, navigating sanctions, geopolitical shifts, and regional turbulence. In an interview with Tehran Times, Pooya Firoozi, First Vice Chairman of the Iran-South Korea Chamber of Commerce, discusses how the joint chamber is working to preserve this vital bridge during the current circumstances—not by waiting for conditions to improve, but by actively preparing Iran for the future opportunities. From transferring South Korea's development know-how and publishing specialized reports to identifying new industrial capacities and fostering provincial partnerships, Firoozi outlines a forward-looking strategy that goes beyond humanitarian projects and aims to transform a fragile connection into a lasting corridor for trade, technology, investment, and human collaboration.
In this interview, while referring to the decades-long history of economic relations between the two countries, Firoozi emphasized that the joint chamber has not merely sufficed with efforts to maintain economic ties in the current difficult circumstances. Rather, by transferring South Korea's development experience, preparing specialized reports, identifying new operational capacities that can be implemented, and maintaining communication with government bodies, chambers of commerce, trade associations, and economic actors of both countries, it is preparing itself for a new phase in Iran-South Korea relations.
He believes that relations between the two countries should not be analyzed superficially or intermittently, and the joint chamber strives to preserve the "communication bridge" between the economic sectors of Iran and South Korea even in the most challenging conditions.
• Despite international sanctions, South Korea has continued its engagement with Iran through humanitarian and development projects, including establishing a vocational training center in Kurdistan, the "Kahak" rural wastewater project in Sistan-Baluchestan, and a school equipped with solar panels in Tehran. How can these projects be used to reopen broader trade routes?
These projects should not be regarded merely as humanitarian actions; rather, they are part of the capital of accumulated trust and history of cooperation between the two nations. In a situation where economic relations have been affected by sanctions and international restrictions, these very collaborations have helped maintain the connection between Iran and South Korea in human, educational, technical, environmental, and clean energy fields.
The Iran-South Korea Joint Chamber is also prepared to transform these experiences, which you mentioned, from the level of limited projects into broader economic cooperation at the appropriate time.
For instance, the vocational training center in Kurdistan can pave the way for broader cooperation in industrial skills training, technical knowledge transfer, and human resource development. The "Kahak" rural wastewater project can be serve as a basis for broader development projects involving cooperation between Iranian and Korean companies in the fields of water, wastewater, and the environment. Moreover, the experience of equipping a school in Tehran with solar panels can serve as a model for nationwide and larger renewable energy projects, especially in public sectors such as schools and universities across the country.
I believe there is readiness to define a cooperative economic development project for each of these experiences and, at the right time, connect Iranian and Korean companies to expand them.
Therefore, these projects should be viewed as small seeds of cooperation that can, under favorable conditions, grow into major economic projects, technology transfer, and joint ventures
• The Korean ambassador has emphasized that "changing external conditions is not within our control, but even within this framework, many things can be done." Beyond humanitarian projects, what is the joint chamber doing to maintain economic dialogue and prepare Iran?
Our approach in the current difficult and difficult circumstances is not merely to maintain trade relations; rather, we have tried, through research and analytical work, to utilize South Korea's valuable experiences during its own crisis periods to define a set of lessons for Iran.
South Korea itself is a country that faced many challenges after the war, resource scarcity, infrastructure problems, and serious economic challenges, yet it managed to become one of the world's major industrial and technological powers within a few decades. Therefore, South Korea's experiential lessons, especially in the current situation, are not merely historical anecdotes; they can provide a collection of practical lessons for Iran's future.
Accordingly, the Iran-South Korea Joint Chamber has in recent months sought to examine Korea's experience in various fields—including reconstruction and infrastructure development, industrialization, export development, financing, SME development, energy, technology, artificial intelligence, human resource training, crisis management, and regional development—and present it for application in Iran.
We continuously prepare and publish specialized and practical reports on South Korea's experience. These reports are not mere translations of news or introductions to Korea's economy; rather, they attempt to analyze Korea's experience and demonstrate which parts of that experience can be adapted and utilized in Iran's current conditions.
This collection of reports is a significant and distinctive effort in this regard, and fortunately, it has been very well received by government bodies, chambers of commerce, economic associations, universities, and Iranian experts.
In fact, in a situation where the extensive development of trade is limited and the transfer of capital, technology, and commodity exchange has become impossible, we have tried to partially compensate for the gap in relations by transferring "experience and knowledge."
This approach is very important to us because a joint chamber should not only be active when trade is booming. On the contrary, in difficult times, the chamber's duty is to preserve knowledge, connections, and experience and prepare the country's economic and business environment for the next phase.
On the other hand, the chamber's communication with Iranian and Korean companies, government bodies, chambers of commerce, and specialized associations remains intact. Thus, simultaneously with transferring Korea's experience, we are also identifying the capacities of both sides and preparing the grounds for future cooperation.
I and other members of the chamber's board of directors believe this is one of the most important duties of a joint chamber in the current situation: not waiting for conditions to change, but preparing Iran for the next phase and the return of economic stability starting from today.
• Emerging industries such as semiconductors, artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and renewable energy have been identified as new areas for cooperation. Is Iran's private sector ready to enter these fields?
Iran's private sector possesses considerable scientific, technical, and human capacity in many of these areas, and the joint chamber, due to its close connection with companies and specialized associations, has a good understanding of these capacities.
Of course, we must be realistic. South Korea is at a global level in fields like semiconductors, and Iran cannot yet enter cooperation from an equal footing in all areas. However, this very difference can create a basis for complementary cooperation.
In fields such as artificial intelligence, software, medical equipment, solar energy, biotechnology, robotics, water technology, and the environment, there are very good grounds for cooperation.
The joint chamber is prepared to identify Iranian companies with capacity and connect them with Korean companies appropriate to their field of activity.
We believe future cooperation should not be based merely on purchasing goods from Korea; it should move towards technology transfer, joint R&D, joint production, human resource training, and even joint exports to regional markets.
• The chairman of the Isfahan Chamber has noted that Korean companies typically prefer cooperation with Iranian government bodies. What is the chamber doing to increase trust in Iran's private sector?
This is understandable, because on one hand, a large portion of our economy is defined within the framework of the government and state-owned enterprise transactions, and on the other hand, Korean economic actors, like any economic actors entering a new market, seek stability, credibility, and risk reduction.
One of the most important capacities of the joint chamber lies precisely at this point.
Over years of activity, the joint chamber has established connections with government bodies, chambers of commerce, specialized associations, large and small companies, and economic actors of both Iran and Korea. Therefore, it can play the role of a professional intermediary between the two private sectors.
We can identify a suitable Iranian partner for a Korean company, especially in the SME sector, review its track record and capabilities, and facilitate initial negotiations.
Conversely, for Iranian companies, we provide an understanding of Korea's business environment, negotiation culture, regulations, and the expectations of Korean companies.
In fact, one of the special advantages of the joint chamber is that it knows both Iran's economic community and Korea's economic community.
This capacity is the result of years of specialized activity in the field of South Korea, and for this reason, the Iran-South Korea Joint Chamber possesses strong expertise and an extensive professional network—a capacity that may not exist to this degree among many other trade partners.
Our goal is to show Korean economic actors that Iran's private sector can not only be their trading partner but can also be a reliable partner in joint production, investment, technology transfer, and regional market development.
• In the meeting of chamber members with the Korean ambassador, emphasis was placed on expanding cultural cooperation and strengthening ties among economic actors. Do you have specific plans for the coming year?
We believe culture and economy are not separate from each other. Cultural understanding is the prerequisite for commercial understanding and for building trust among economic actors.
Relying on its long history of activity in the field of South Korea, the joint chamber has acquired special capacities in trade connections and human capital, including relationships with universities, researchers, translators, cultural activists, economic experts, companies, and institutions on both sides.
Therefore, our plan is not merely to hold a few cultural events. The main goal is to strengthen a sustainable network between Iran and South Korea.
Within this framework, we can develop specialized seminars on Korea's economy and culture, B2B meetings, academic programs, training courses, introducing Iran's industrial and trade opportunities to the Korean side, and the targeted participation of Iranian companies in specialized Korean exhibitions.
We also believe that the capacity of the younger generation and knowledge-based companies of both countries should be utilized more, so that Iran-Korea relations are not based solely on the relationships of past generations, and a new generation of economic and scientific actors from both countries enters this network.
• The Korean ambassador has visited several Iranian provinces and praised their industrial and tourism capacities. How does the chamber facilitate provincial connections?
This area is actually one of the country's very important capacities that can also create a roadmap for the chamber's strategy.
Iran is not just Tehran, and South Korea is not just Seoul. Iran's various provinces have diverse capacities in industry, agriculture, mining, energy, tourism, and technology.
The joint chamber, given its connections with provincial chambers and private sector associations, is prepared to connect the capacities identified by them in each province with the appropriate Korean counterpart.
We can use a province-to-province and company-to-company model.
For example, if a province has high capacity in solar energy, we should introduce it to a Korean company active in solar energy; if a province has advantages in medical equipment, food industries, steel, tourism, or technology, we should find the Korean counterpart active in that field.
This model is far more effective than holding general and non-targeted meetings.
The provincial visits of the esteemed South Korean ambassador are also a very good opportunity for this. When the ambassador visits the industrial and tourism capacities of Iran's various provinces, the chamber, alongside specialized associations and provincial chambers, can take this understanding one step further and transform it into direct connections between companies and specific projects.
• Looking five years ahead, what is your vision for Iran-South Korea economic relations, and what indicators would show the success of the chamber's efforts?
I am optimistic about the future of Iran-South Korea economic relations because these relations have a history of more than several decades, and the two economies have complementary capacities in many areas.
However, I believe we should not merely seek a return to past relations. We must design a new version of Iran-Korea economic relations with a proper and efficient roadmap.
In the future, cooperation can be expanded in the form of capital, technology, and knowledge transfer in areas such as modern technologies and AI, renewable energy, medical and health equipment, environment and water management, joint production, R&D, human resource training, investment, and joint entry into regional markets.
The success of this path should be measured with real indicators: increased trade, increased Iranian exports to Korea, renewed participation by Korean companies, joint investment and production, technology transfer, and most importantly, an increase in operational contracts between companies of the two countries.
I am confident that all our colleagues at the joint chamber are prepared for this phase, because they possess the past experience, the understanding of today's market, and the necessary communication network.
• And your final words?
If I want to say it in one sentence, we should not wait for conditions to change; we should be prepared for the day conditions do change.
In conclusion, I find it necessary to appreciate the efforts of all our Iranian friends in South Korea and especially the esteemed ambassador of this country to Iran, Mr. Kim Junpyo, and his colleagues. In the current very difficult circumstances, he has strived with a constructive and realistic approach to maintain communications between the two countries and especially between economic actors. His travels to Iran's various provinces and his attention to the country's industrial, economic, and tourism capacities also reflect this positive and constructive outlook.
This perspective is very valuable to us in Iran and shows that the relations between the two countries are of long-term importance, transcending temporary political and economic conditions.
Economic actors have always believed that although economic relations are influenced by political relations, they should not be sacrificed to temporary circumstances and political developments.
Iran and South Korea have had valuable experiences of cooperation over the past several decades, and in many areas, the economic capacities of the two countries complement each other.
It is natural that we face problems and limitations today, but these problems should not be seen as the end of relations; rather, they should be regarded as a difficult period in the path of a long and historical relationship.
The joint chamber considers it its duty to preserve this bridge during this difficult period and to prepare the ground for a new leap in trade, investment, technological, and economic cooperation between the two countries for the day when political and economic conditions become more favorable.
We are optimistic about the future of Iran-South Korea relations, despite all the existing problems and hardships, and we see it as bright.
Because these relations do not belong only to today; they are the result of decades of understanding, trust, and cooperation. Capital that has been built over decades does not easily disappear and can serve as the foundation for much broader and deeper relations in the future.
We want to preserve the Iran-Korea bridge in the toughest days so that in better days, we can turn it into a broad economic, technological, investment, and human pathway between the two countries.

Taiwan and US launch patent exchange system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:12:53 UTC
13:12:53 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Intellectual Property Office said Friday it launched an online patent exchange platform with the US.
The patent office said it co-developed a Priority Document Exchange system with the US Patent and Trademark Office. It added that online filing saves firms time and fees.
The office said that Taiwan submits 20,000 patent applications to the US every year. At the same time, the US files 7,000 patents in Taiwan annually, ranking second in volume.
The office said the partnership began on November 22, 2023, when the American Institute in Taiwan and the Taiwan Economic and Cultural Office signed a data security pact. It added that similar exchanges with Japan and South Korea began in 2013.
According to the office, US patents are mostly utility, plant, or design-related. Patents are approved on a first-come, first-served basis and take months to complete. The system streamlines the process, allowing the office to prioritize accordingly.

According to next year’s defense budget, the Armaments Bureau’s Production and Manufacturing Center plans to invest more than NT$14.14 billion (US$446.25 million) between 2026 and 2032 to carry out new projects at its 202, 205, 209, and 401 arsenals, Liberty Times reported. The Armaments Bureau said that as demand for various types of ammunition rises, it will expand production lines for items such as shells, primers, propellants, explosives, gun barrels, optical systems, and gas masks, and introduce semi-automated and automated equipment, according to Liberty Times.

Taipei home prices rise despite broader market slowdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:12:51 UTC
13:12:51 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s housing market is seeing home prices decline as transactions slow, but Taipei remains an exception.
Cabinet data showed that the number of homes sold nationwide fell 25.5% year-on-year to 261,000 in 2025, the lowest level in nine years. The national housing price index fell to 143.85 in the first quarter of this year, its lowest level in nearly six quarters, after reaching a record 150.98 in the fourth quarter of 2024, according to CTEE.
Taipei has also seen fewer sales. A total of 10,662 units were sold in the city in 2025, down 30% from the previous year, according to UDN Money.
Despite the drop in transactions, Taipei home prices have remained resilient. The average home price last year reached NT$839,000 (US$26,500) per ping, equivalent to 3.3 square meters, up 2.6% from a year earlier.
Tighter access to mortgages has been one factor weighing on sales. The Central Bank’s seventh round of mortgage controls in 2024 tightened borrowing rules for people seeking to purchase additional homes.
One Taipei couple's experience illustrates how stricter lending requirements can affect buyers who rely on bank financing. The dual-income couple in their 40s told Nikkei Asia that they had planned to borrow about 80% of a home's purchase price, but their bank approved only 70% after a stricter review. Facing a down payment requirement several million Taiwan dollars higher than expected, the couple decided not to proceed with the purchase.
Sinyi Realty, Taiwan’s largest real estate brokerage, said cash purchases now account for around 20-30% of high-end property transactions in Taipei, compared with roughly 10-20% in 2020.
As they can complete purchases without relying on mortgage approvals, cash buyers have gained an edge in the market. In one case, a buyer secured a 4% discount on a secondhand condominium in Taipei’s Daan District, paying NT$120 million in cash this spring, according to Nikkei Asia.
Looking beyond Taipei, Sinyi Realty analyst Tseng Ching-te (曾敬德) said the housing market has shifted toward lower transaction volumes and more stable prices since mortgage controls were tightened, according to Sun Media and CTEE.
The Central Bank has since eased some of those restrictions. In March, it raised the maximum loan-to-value ratio for second-home purchases to 60% from 50%, signaling a move away from efforts to cool the market and toward stabilization, Sinyi analyst Tung Li-ting (童莉婷) said. Tung added that housing transactions are unlikely to recover in the near term, although activity is gradually picking up from its low point.
Chinatrust Real Estate Research Division Deputy Manager Chuang Szu-min (莊思敏) said the market has shifted from broad-based price increases to greater differences between locations and property types. Areas supported by transportation projects and industrial development may continue to perform relatively well. In contrast, high-priced properties and areas without strong growth drivers could face further downward pressure, according to CTEE.

Increasing pollution from wildfires and heat waves risks undermining global efforts to improve air quality and protect human and ecosystem health, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) warned Monday.
In its annual Air Quality and Climate Bulletin, the UN agency highlighted the close links between climate change and air pollution and called for coordinated policies to address both.
