Europe wrestles with impact of historic regional gains for Germany's AfD
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:07:23 BST
13:07:23 KST

Europe wrestles with impact of historic regional gains for Germany's AfD
- Published
"Seismic", "a socio-political earthquake", "a watershed moment for Germany".
This was how political analysts and many media outlets described the stunning victory of the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in local elections in Germany on Sunday. Is that an exaggeration?
Saxony-Anhalt is one of the smallest of massive Germany's 16 regions. It boasts a mere 1.7m out of 59m eligible voters nationwide. How significant can its political sentiments be, especially since the AfD narrowly failed to win an outright majority?
The answer: very significant.
First and foremost, at home in Germany.
The vote may have been regional but it impacts at national level. The AfD landslide piles even more pressure on the already beleaguered centrist coalition government in Berlin. It may prove to be the nail in the political coffin of Germany's deeply unpopular conservative Chancellor, Friedrich Merz. He had promised to slash the AfD's popularity.
These political woes will further weaken and distract Germany, the EU's most powerful player, at a time of continental crisis - as Europe struggles to contain Russian aggression, Donald Trump's tariff tantrums and the economic threat from China.
The Saxony-Anhalt result also provokes soul-searching throughout Germany, where the Nazi past still looms large. This is the first outstanding electoral landslide for a hard right nationalist party since the fall of the Third Reich in 1945.
The German authorities have labelled the AfD, in part, anti-democratic and a number of regional factions of the party, including Saxony-Anhalt, far right extremist.
The AfD is well known to be particularly popular in east Germany but it's now also polling as the biggest political party nationwide.
Germany's political mainstream has failed voters, it would seem. What does Europe's biggest single economy, its most populous nation not counting Russia, do now?
Tiny Saxony-Anhalt is causing waves outside Germany too.
None other than the President of the United States swiftly posted the Saxony-Anhalt exit poll on his Truth Social platform on Sunday.
The AfD's anti-immigration, anti-woke, "Germany for Germans" message chimes closely with Donald Trump's MAGA missive. Along with a number of other nationalist parties in Europe, the AfD borrows heavily from the Trump playbook - undermining mainstream media, questioning the neutrality of judges and promising to "make Germany great again".
Interesting to note though - the US president is rarely name-checked on the campaign trail in Europe. Politicians are keenly aware just how unpopular he is amongst voters.
Hot on Donald Trump's social media heels on Sunday night was the influential Russian businessman Kirill Dmitriev, CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund. He declared the AfD result "historic", Germany's national government "discredited" and the German Chancellor "humiliated", comparing Friedrich Merz to the UK's not-long-gone prime minister, Keir Starmer, who felt forced to resign this summer.
What interest might Russia have in German regional elections, you might ask, and what was Dmitriev's dig at the UK all about?
The German government is the largest single donor to Ukraine and the UK is known to have provided Kyiv with missiles used to strike inside Russian territory. This has deeply angered Moscow.
The AfD, by comparison, is pretty pro-Russia. It wants to stop sending military aid to Ukraine, halt sanctions against Moscow and start buying much cheaper Russian energy again. Energy-hungry German industry suffered a huge economic blow after the country halted Russian energy imports, following the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The AfD's softly-softly approach to Russia has another appeal in Germany's east, which remains far poorer than the west. This, despite Germany spending between 2.3 and 3 trillion euros (depending on reports and whether inflation is taken into account) to help integrate the former communist part of the country after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall.
Saxony-Anhalt is Germany's poorest region and there, as in much of east Germany, you often encounter what's known as "Ostalgie" amongst voters; essentially "nostalgia in the east" for comparatively more stable times under communism.
Also watching the Saxony-Anhalt election closely was the European Union. The next 12 months is bumper election season across the EU. Ballots are expected in key nations France, Italy, Spain and Poland. Brussels fears more "extreme" parties, left but particularly right of the political spectrum, may benefit across the board.
The leader of Spain's nationalist Vox party, Santiago Abascal, posted on X on Sunday that the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt was " a great hope for Germany and for Europe".
By contrast, France's Europe Minister, Benjamin Haddad, an ally of centrist President Emmanuel Macron, warned "this is a serious moment in Europe, seeing the far right win in a regional election in Germany".
Neither the AfD, nor other European parties labelled "extreme right" or "hard right", accept the label. They also differ from one another in tone and party programme. France's National Rally under Marine Le Pen kicked the AfD out of its grouping in the European Parliament two years ago, for being too "radical". What the parties do tend to share, however, is an anti-immigration platform and strong nationalist messaging. And that really worries the EU.
Whether it's a rallying cry for "Germany First" or "Italy First" or "France for the French!", the concern in Brussels is that the rise of nationalist parties strains European cohesion at a time when outside events demand it more than ever.
Nationalist parties like the AfD or Italy's League Party tend to be deeply Eurosceptic, but Brussels says Europe needs to stand united to counter Donald Trump's bullying, for example, or to effectively protect European business against China's goods dumping.
Europe's defence establishment also warns that fractures in European sanctions against Russia or countries going tepid on Nato membership (as you see in Marine Le Pen's National Rally for example, or Germany's AfD) just emboldens Moscow.
Security chiefs say nations must stick together to stop Russia in Ukraine, otherwise the Kremlin will be tempted to attack inside Nato, such as the Baltic states.
The thing is, Europe's voters are very aware of these outside threats and the impact they have at home. They worry about the impact of wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, about crumbling health services at home and dwindling economic security for themselves and their family. Uncontrolled immigration and safety on the streets are huge concerns too.
And this is where the significance of the Saxony-Anhalt vote shines bright. A flashing red warning to traditional political parties, but also to institutions across Europe like the judiciary and security services. Those the AfD dismisses as the self-interested "Establishment".
Voters on this continent feel lost and let down by parties they've supported over and again for decades. Looking right or left now at election time does not mean they've all suddenly become extremist.
The AfD campaign slogan in Saxony-Anhalt was an upbeat "Anything is Possible!" Plus a promise to make Germans feel proud of their country again. Till now untried and untested in government, people seem increasingly willing to give them a go.

The US, South Korea and Japan began a five-day joint military exercise Monday to enhance their operational and joint response capabilities across multiple domains, local media reported.
The Freedom Edge exercise kicked off in international waters east and south of South Korea's southern island of Jeju, Yonhap News Agency reported, citing a statement from the country's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS).
The drill began as scheduled despite the administration of US President Donald Trump shortening the bilateral Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise with South Korea last month in an effort to encourage North Korea to return to talks.
"The three nations will leverage the drills to enhance operational capabilities and joint response capabilities across multiple domains, including maritime, air and cyber, while maintaining a robust and stable cooperative relationship," the JCS statement said.
The drills will involve major maritime and air assets from the armed forces of the three countries, with a joint exercise control group overseeing the operations for their systematic and safe execution.
The Korean military said the joint drills are aimed at enhancing deterrence and response capabilities against North Korean nuclear and missile threats while safeguarding regional peace and stability.
North Korea has long denounced the allies' drills as war rehearsals.
The three countries will deploy six Aegis-equipped destroyers along with maritime patrol aircraft, fighter jets and refueling tanker aircraft, the report said, citing sources familiar with the matter.
The South Korean Navy is deploying the 7,600-ton ROKS Yulgok Yi I and ROKS Seoae Ryu Seong-ryong destroyers, said the sources.
Japan's Joint Staff of the Self-Defense Forces said last month that it will deploy the 7,700-ton Atago and 5,100-ton Asahi destroyers, P-1 maritime patrol aircraft, SH-60K helicopters and F-15 fighter jets.
The US Navy announced on social media last week the arrival of its 6,900-ton Arleigh Burke-class USS Benfold at a port in South Korea's southern city of Busan in a possible sign that it is joining the trilateral drills.
No US aircraft carrier is expected to participate in Freedom Edge given the ongoing US war against Iran, according to sources.

Europe's busiest ports ranked: Which cities lead in volume of goods transported?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:02:15 UTC
13:02:15 KST

Sea shipping keeps Europe fed, fuelled and supplied — and this year, the Iran war's disruptions to shipping routes have thrust it into the headlines. Euronews looked at the busiest ports in Europe by volume of goods transported.
Maritime transport plays a key role in moving goods.
Globally, around 13 billion tonnes of traded goods were transported by sea in 2024. In the EU, ports handled around 3.4 billion tonnes of goods. This corresponds to 26% of the global total.
Almost 90% of the EU’s external freight trade is also carried by sea according to the EU Blue Economy Observatory.
So, which are the busiest ports in the EU and which countries handle the most goods?
Shipping mainly consists of two types: short sea shipping and deep sea shipping. Short sea shipping refers to transporting goods over relatively short distances by sea whereas deep sea shipping covers longer, intercontinental routes across oceans.
For the EU, short sea shipping does not only cover maritime transport within the bloc. It also includes candidate countries, Iceland, Norway, the Baltic Sea area, the Mediterranean Sea area and the Black Sea area.
Rotterdam and Antwerp-Bruges are the EU’s busiest ports
As of 2024, two EU cities are by far the busiest ports when measured by total sea shipping according to Eurostat. Rotterdam in the Netherlands is the busiest port, with 397.3 million tonnes of goods transported to and from the port.
Antwerp-Bruges in Belgium follows Rotterdam, with 243.7 million tonnes of goods handled.
Hamburg ranks as the third-busiest port, but its volume is considerably lower than the top two. The German port handled 97 million tonnes of goods.
After the top two ports, the total weight of goods transported to and from ports falls gradually, and the differences between cities are relatively small.
Spain’s Algeciras is the fourth-busiest port, with 81.5 million tonnes. Amsterdam, another Dutch port, completes the top five at 78.8 million tonnes of goods transported.
France’s busiest port ranks sixth in the EU. HAROPA (Le Havre and Rouen) handled 76.6 million tonnes of goods in 2024. The Polish port of Gdansk follows closely at 71 million tonnes.
Another French port, Marseille, is also among the top 10 at 66 million tonnes.
Valencia is another busy port at 64.5 million tonnes.
Romania’s Constanta is in the top 10
One port from Romania, Constanta, is also in the top 10. The port handled 57.6 million tonnes of goods.
Among the ports ranked 11th to 20th, the gross weight of goods transported by sea ranges from 36.8 million tonnes in Dunkerque, France, to 55.5 million tonnes in the Spanish port of Barcelona.
The busiest Italian port is Trieste, at 53.5 million tonnes, followed by Genova at 47.4 million tonnes.
Sines in Portugal is also among the top 20 busiest EU ports at 44.1 million tonnes. Greece’s Piraeus follows at 43.7 million tonnes.
Apart from Hamburg, Bremerhaven is another busy port in Germany, handling 42.5 million tonnes.
Sweden’s Göteborg is also in the top 20 at 38.5 million tonnes.
Zeeland Seaports is another Dutch port contributing to the Netherlands’ strong position in the EU.
Dutch ports handle the most goods
Looking at countries by the gross weight of goods handled in all ports, the Netherlands is the champion in the EU. Dutch ports handled 538.1 million tonnes of goods.
Although Italy has three ports in the top 20, the country ranks second in the EU at 488.6 million tonnes, very closely followed by Spain at 486 million tonnes.
These three countries are well ahead of the rest, as fourth-ranked Belgium handled only 274.9 million tonnes of goods.
France, a Mediterranean country, handled 269.8 million tonnes, slightly less than Germany at 273.9 million tonnes.
Greece, Sweden and Poland also handled more than 100 million tonnes of goods.
Turkey ranks second with candidates included
When EU candidate countries and EFTA members are included, Turkey ranks second at 524.7 million tonnes while Norway ranks eighth at 212.1 million tonnes.
The European Commission emphasises that “maritime transport has been a catalyst for economic development and prosperity throughout its history” in Europe.
In March 2026, the Commission adopted two strategies to boost competitiveness, sustainability, security and resilience across the EU’s wider waterborne sector, including ports, shipping and shipbuilding.

Could NVIDIA's purchase of Hugging Face boost the EU's AI sovereignty?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:00:33 UTC
13:00:33 KST

The deal, marking NVIDIA's increased focus on open-AI models, is likely to draw significant regulatory concern from the EU due to its size and implications for the bloc's digital and AI sovereignty.
On Thursday, American chipmaker NVIDIA announced they will buy the artificial intelligence library Hugging Face for $13 billion (€11.2bn).
It's an astonishing amount of money for a platform that started as an age-appropriate chat app for teenagers, but has since pivoted to being one of the premier databases hosting open-source and open-weight AI models.
Though the deal is mostly taking place in the United States, the company's founders are French with have half of their employees in Paris. They are hoping to become a key part of the open-source AI ecosystem in Europe.
This acquisition will raise a lot of eyebrows in both Paris and Brussels, particularly among competition regulators and AI industry watchers who will want the EU AI Act enforced where necessary, and a regulatory review of the terms found in the deal.
Open vs. closed
NVIDIA is now tallied as the largest publicly traded company in the world by market cap, a position they rocketed to after the boom in demand for their GPUs in dedicated AI data centres.
In the last year, the company has doubled down on its embrace of open AI models, providing dozens of models for free on its on platforms and leading policy efforts to ensure competition among both closed-source and open-source LLM providers.
For innovators in the European Union who may not have the resources or capital to train and launch their own models on the same level as Anthropic or Open AI, the use of Hugging Face's platforms could end up being a valuable tool for providing solutions for Europeans.
"For many of the problems that exist in AI, open-source can be a solution," explained Hugging Face co-founder Clément Delangue in a 2024 interview with Le Monde.
_"_Because the proprietary models are black boxes that make it difficult to analyse their bias or sources of truth."
The European approach to AI has been one of stipulating rules and policies to provide a global blueprint, some of which favor domestic industries and broader continental goals.
But innovation is happening at every level of the stack, not just among European LLM makers like Mistral or DeepL that are covered by the EU AI Act.
The Dutch company ASML, for example, is the largest supplier for all global semiconductors companies, making the machines that are integral to chip production used in every processor.
ElevenLabs, founded by Polish researchers, has excelled as a speech and voice processing model now integrated in thousands of AI products.
The push for sovereignty
Beyond founders and innovators, many of the open models can also be used for creating custom versions for governments and agencies, hosted locally and trained on data that may be sensitive or protected.
Vendor lock-ins are a real concern for EU regulators, as reported, but open models could help provide real competition and reduce reliance on larger tech firms that host data outside the EU.
This would call for much more expertise particularly in government agencies, but it would be a welcome sign for those who are wanting to de-risk European systems from reliance on Chinese or American infrastructure.
Of course, building EU data centers is a major goal of European regulators, but the software within those data centers will matter as well.
For people using AI every day, consumers and small companies alike, the most exciting element of open models is just how much is available to everyone to use at little or no cost.
This will be a boon to researchers and practitioners in the arts and sciences who may not have the budgets of large companies.
_"_Open science and open source AI distribute economic gains by enabling hundreds of thousands of small companies and startups to build with AI. It fosters innovation, and fair competition between all," testified Hugging Face co-founder Clément Delangue in 2023 before a U.S. House Committee.
No matter the model used by a consumer or small company, that's a call to fork it, tune it, customise it, and upgrade it.
This story was originally published on EU Tech Loop and has been shared on Euronews as part of a syndication agreement.

UN expert Francesca Albanese calls for ‘true paradigm shift’ as Miliband resets policy on Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:00:25 UTC
13:00:25 KST

The UK’s planned ban on trade with unlawful Israeli settlements is a welcome, if overdue, first step and must be judged according to its practical impact, a UN expert has told the Guardian.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has vowed to act more decisively against Israeli settlements, as well as continued restrictions of aid into Gaza, prompting the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, to claim on Saturday that Downing Street was motivated by “Jew hatred”.
Miliband said what he had been told about restriction on aid into Gaza had reinforced the need for more decisive action. But Huckabee, writing on X in support of the Israeli foreign ministry’s own criticisms, said: “The Brits have lost it. The Jew hate of their government knows no boundaries and knows no facts.”
Huckabee did not mention in his statement that Miliband is himself Jewish. The Israeli foreign ministry had said: “Had the foreign secretary been interested in facts rather than stories, he would have known that there are no restrictions whatsoever on bringing medicines into the Gaza Strip, and that no medicine is being blocked.”
Palestinian groups in the UK are holding judgment until they see the fine detail of Miliband’s policy, due to be announced on Tuesday, but are expecting the most significant shift since a previous foreign secretary, David Lammy, withdrew most arms export licences in September 2024.
Speaking to the Guardian, Francesca Albanese, the UN’s special rapporteur on the occupied territories, said a “ban on settlement goods was a change in UK government stance and absolutely important”. She added she would “not join those dismissing it as theatre before the details had been announced”.
She said a settlement trade ban would have to be part of “a true paradigm shift to Israel-Palestine that ultimately seeks to implement the international court of justice advisory opinion in 2024”, which stated that Israel’s presence in the occupied territories was “unlawful in its entirety”. The opinion, she added, said that “all states carry an obligation – not a preference of an obligation – not to recognise the situation as legal, and not render aid and assistance in maintaining it”.
Albanese also said the trade ban could not be narrowly confined to goods – such as agricultural products and cosmetics – since “they are a fraction of what sustains the occupation, and a fraction that Israel can absorb without difficulty”.
The package should also aim to include trade in services, she said, progressively suspending British intelligence cooperation, all arms licensing and the unexamined flights out of RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Albanese warned that if the steps were not taken or were “completely off the table”, the changes would “over time come to be seen as not amounting to a reckoning, but a press release”.
She said that a state banning “dates from Ma’ale Adumim [a city in the West Bank]” while “continuing to licence the equipment used to enforce the checkpoints around it” had not “changed its relationship with the occupation … It has rearranged its communication strategy.”
Albanese added that, “because the 2024 ICJ advisory opinion declares the entire Israeli presence in the occupied territories as unlawful, third states’ obligations ‘not to render aid or assistance’ extends to everything that sustains that unlawful presence as a whole.”
Albanese said the UK needed to end any ambiguity around the tender for the E1 settlement that will sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank and cut the territory in two, adding: “Since bids close a week before Israel’s elections on 27 October, there is nothing that London can realistically do in September that can change that calendar.”
But she warned the government could not let the tenders simply pass, pointing out that Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, had already said E1 was designed to “bury the idea of a Palestinian state”.
“There is a difference between the tenders closing and the settlement getting built and financed,” she added. “Construction on this scale needs finance, insurance and construction firms, and since E1 amounts to annexation and not just settlement expansion, sanctions or similar have to be threatened against those firms that seek to cooperate with the building of E1.”
Albanese also called on the UK government to join South Africa before the ICJ, and also support Nicaragua on Monday when the ICJ hears preliminary oral objections from Germany over claims filed by the Central American country that Berlin’s continued arms sales to Israel makes it complicit in genocide.
She said: “Britain is not a party to that case. It can still choose which side of the argument it stands on: whether it treats participation in international accountability mechanisms as a threat to an alliance, or recognises that an alliance built on anything other than principle and the rule of law is not an alliance at all. It is an arrangement of convenience, honoured only until convenience changes.”
Finally she urged the UK to issue guidance to UK-based firms not to overcomply with sanctions imposed by the US on the international criminal court prosecutor, the deputy prosecutors, eight judges and an increasing number of others, including herself and Palestinian human rights groups that have cooperated with the court. “This has frozen bank accounts, everywhere, for people doing nothing other than their judicial function or providing evidence lawfully requested by an international court,” she said.

Ukraine’s asset recovery and management agency (Arma) has been tasked with instructing independent management to take over the running of the company whose other minority shareholders include the Georgian government.
The Ukrainian agency’s head, Yaroslava Maksymenko, said they had repeatedly run into legal and bureaucratic obstacles owing, in part, to the shareholders’ resistance to give up control of their assets.
The agency further claims to have been the subject of a cyber-attack during one attempt to find an independent manager for the company although there is no evidence as to who was responsible and the Patarkatsishvili family is not suspected.
However, Maksymenko claimed New World Value Fund Limited, the vehicle for the Patarkatsishvili’s investment in IDS Ukraine, had pursued an unfounded claim of unlawful conduct by Arma’s officials which she said was “misinformation”.
An investigation by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine into the claims of unlawful conduct continues.
Maksymenko said her agency had concerns over potential money laundering and value extraction from IDS Ukraine if it remained under the current management although there have not been any official findings of such criminality.
There are separate proceedings in the Ukrainian anti-corruption high court in which the shareholders are fighting attempts to nationalise part or all of the ownership of IDS Ukraine, which is seen by some in government as a key strategic asset at a time of war.
A spokesperson for the Patarkatsishvili family said they had been committed supporters of Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022, adding that the family were being unfairly targeted and would seek justice in the international courts if necessary.
They said: “The Patarkatsishvili family strongly believes that an asset should not be taken away from non-sanctioned shareholders against whom there are no allegations or concerns, and is defending this position through all relevant proceedings before the Ukrainian courts and authorities.
“If the Patarkatsishvili family is unable to obtain justice through the Ukrainian courts, and the asset is ultimately taken away through the Arma process, it will, of course, have no choice but to seek justice before the international courts, as it has consistently done in the past.”
The family’s shareholding in IDS Ukraine was inherited in 2008 by Liana, her sister, Iya, and mother, Inna, after the death of Badri Patarkatsishvili, a businessman who made his fortune during the breakup of the Soviet Union.
Patarkatsishvili fled to the UK in 2007 but died in 2008 of a heart attack at the age of 52 with an estimated fortune of £6bn. Iya Patarkatsishvili and her husband made headlines last year for being granted a refund after buying a £32m London mansion that was said to be infested with moths.
Last summer, Liana Patarkatsishvili staged a large-scale immersive theatre production called Storehouse about “misinformation” through her production company Sage & Jester, starring the actors Toby Jones and Meera Syal.
A spokesperson for IDS Ukraine said: “Throughout its operations, the IDS Ukraine Group of companies has operated and continues to operate in accordance with the requirements of Ukrainian law, including tax and financial legislation.
“No competent state authority of Ukraine, including the state tax service of Ukraine, has established any facts of money laundering, unlawful withdrawal of funds or any other financial activity of this nature on the part of IDS Ukraine.
“We are not aware of any investigations or other current inquires of Ukrainian authorities into the operations of IDS Ukraine with respect to any such allegations.
“IDS Ukraine has also not ceased operations for a single day since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion. The group continued production and supplied Ukrainian consumers with drinking water even amid continuous missile and drone attacks.”
The spokesperson added: “We are aware of statements by the asset recovery and management agency implying but not saying it directly that [a cyber-attack] is somehow connected with the IDS Ukraine Group of companies. However, this information is simply false and in reality completely irrelevant.”

Designers should not fear being replaced by AI, industry leaders say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:00:25 UTC
13:00:25 KST

Professional designers should not feel “threatened” by the rapid growth of generative AI, according to business leaders, despite fears over job losses in the sector.
With design and film production companies and manufacturers all adopting AI at an accelerating pace, industry bodies said the technology would be used to enhance the work of designers rather than replace them.
Mat Hunter, the chief executive of the Design Council – a charity which champions the industry – said that while AI was increasingly being used by designers, “they are using it to add value”.
He said: “We are aware that technology always displaces people with new ways of working. However, we believe in the imagination and inventiveness of designers to find opportunities. We believe the UK needs more professional designers, so overall employment should continue to grow.”
Deborah Dawton, chief executive of the Design Business Council, said: “What protects great designers from AI is skill, experience, empathy and deep understanding of the sectors they operate in. So, no, [workers] shouldn’t feel threatened if they operate at this level.”
Earlier this year research, conducted by The King’s Institute for Artificial Intelligence and the Policy Institute, showed 57% of the public think AI will lead to widespread unemployment. Last week, freelancers including designers told the Guardian they were picking up “soulless” work correcting AI errors.
The Design Council said on Monday that its analysis showed the sector – which covers everything from the design of household products and fashion to building and transport design – had grown by 40% between 2019 and the end of 2023, beating the economy’s 23% average rate of expansion and leapfrogging the size of the retail industry.
Research funded by the council for its triennial overview – Design Economy 2026 – showed that sectors like construction, services and manufacturing support 2.27m design jobs, and that there has been a 15% increase in employment between 2020 and 2025.
While the figures estimating the size of the industry pre-date the arrival of dominant AI tools including ChatGPT and Claude, the employment figures to the end of last year indicate that their use has done little so far to affect the demand for workers with design skills.
Hunter said design was often considered to be an add-on or nice-to-have, but was essential to industries from advanced manufacturing to digital services.
“People don’t realise design is everywhere and is about trying to make things usable,” he said.
He added that the government’s consolidation of hundreds of public sector websites into one consistent design was an example of improvements in a service that can be supported by designers.
Dawton said AI was being used as a substitute for the work done by human designers, but “rip-offs have been happening for a very long time – AI hasn’t enabled that”.
The industry went through a similar transition when companies began using computer-aided design software, displacing draughtspeople, but Dawton said modern workers could find jobs elsewhere in the industry as it expands.
She added: “The key thing to remember is that these copycats look the same but they aren’t the same. The materials, finishes, methods of manufacture, assembly, colour, etc, mean that they are very different products.”
Over the longer term, she said: “We have to adapt to any technological change that takes place around us. The difference with the design industry is that large chunks of it drive that change.
“For most in business, efficiency/optimisation is the main conversation around AI. Designers have a second conversation with AI, which is about the potential it opens up in the hands of a creator.”
Andrew Duff, head of the Society of Garden and Landscape Designers, said many people working in his industry were nervous about AI. He said design companies were more likely to use AI as “the intern in the office” than as a replacement for skilled staff.
The Design Council report said some regions had grown strongly over the last eight years, though from a low base. There was an 88% increase in income from design across all industries in Wales and a 67% rise in the north-east of England. The south-east remained the hub for design industries, accounting for £43.3bn of gross value added (GVA) – a calculation of income from economic activity – compared with just £3.1bn in the north-east from a UK total of £136.7bn.
Its contribution was larger than the UK’s retail sector, worth £114bn, and nearly twice the size of the accommodation and food service industry, worth £70bn.
Hunter said a lack of skilled workers was a bigger problem than AI after entries for design and technology GCSEs declined by 68% over the decade to 2024.
Dawton said: “We need specialist teachers and equipment in schools if we’re going to inspire the next generation of world shapers at an early age.”

Her Christian Democrats party, a junior partner in Sweden’s three-party centre-right coalition government, called for reindeer numbers to be cut, for reindeer husbandry to no longer be considered a “national interest” and for the state to “reclaim responsibility” for land used by herders.
The government’s goal is to open up the country’s sparsely populated north for mineral resource exploitation – as Sweden and the EU more generally seek to reduce dependence on Chinese imports – and to expand its nuclear power capabilities.
Larsson Blind said that anti-Sami sentiment in the run-up to elections – especially at the local level – was not new, but that the scope of the recent rhetoric was “quite astonishing”.
“If you look at it from afar, it means that the deputy prime minister is highlighting one group of people … as being the enemy of development in Sweden,” the board member of the Sami parliament, which exists to safeguard Sami interests, said in an interview. “She is really clearly not feeling the need to have the support of the Sami.”
Issues of Sami land rights have moved from local to national prominence in the run-up to the 13 September vote. In its manifesto, the Christian Democrats pledged to “resolve the conflicts between reindeer husbandry and industrial development” and to protect “everyone’s right to hunt on state-owned land”. The far-right Sweden Democrats – who could enter government for the first time after the vote – have also singled out reindeer herders in their manifesto, pitting them against industrial development, tourism and the wider Swedish public and questioning their land rights.
The row has centred on the state-owned mining company LKAB’s plan to expand a vast iron ore mine next to the town of Kiruna to encompass the Per Geijer deposit, which holds Europe’s largest known reserve of rare-earth elements. The plan involves relocating subsidence-hit Kiruna itself to a new and more stable site. Last summer, the town drew global attention when its striking red wooden church, designed to resemble a lávvu (a Sami hut), was rolled 5km to its new home.
Many among the Sami population near Kiruna – Sweden’s most northerly town – fear the pitting of mineral resources against land rights heralds a larger threat to their livelihoods and culture.
The traditional herding routes of the Gabna Sami people have already been significantly affected by the Kiruna mine. Anna-Karin Niia, a Gabna herder, said she felt ignored by Stockholm. The Sami people are Indigenous “constitutional protectors”, she said. “It’s not just a simple matter of quietly reducing reindeer herds and making these kinds of statements so that you win the 2026 election.”
“Even if the state or the government or the EU says it is important to have minerals, at the same time, Indigenous rights, Sami rights, the local[s] are just as important. We also need nature.”
For Larsson Blind, the government’s positioning has shattered hopes that Swedish politicians might take their responsibilities seriously when it comes to Sami people. “It is very harsh but I think it has also opened eyes in our own ranks. It has really opened up a divide that is very hard to overcome,” she said. “Even if we have known that previous governments haven’t prioritised Sami rights issues, it hasn’t been politically correct to say it so abruptly and out loud. But now it is possible to do that, so the boundaries have been pushed.”
Lars-Marcus Kuhmunen, the head of the Gabna community, said LKAB’s plans for Per Geijer would “put an end to everything” for the Sami, because it would cut off the connection between the calving grounds and the mountain area and forest region. He also believes it would act as a “starting gun” for increased industrialisation across Sweden. “It will affect all Sami villages,” he said. “We feel like we have a lot resting on our shoulders.”
Over coffee at his home in Kiruna, Nils-Johan Labba, a master craftsman and politician in the Sami parliament, said the relocation of Kiruna had left the town “bleeding”, affecting everything from transport to education. He said he wished the government had focused on resolving the town’s problems instead of “hating on minorities”.
Peter Kullgren, a member of the board of the Christian Democrats, said: “Sweden has a responsibility to protect Sami rights, but the government must also be able to weigh up Sami rights with other very strong public interests. Our mineral resources are strategically important for Sweden and Europe and we already have high standards of consideration, dialogue and influence but the state must also be able to make decisions about when important public interests are working against each other.”
In a statement, LKAB said the process of expanding the Kiruna mine was still at an early stage. “Our intention is to continue evaluating the potential of the mineral deposit,” it said. “The application is currently being reviewed by the mining inspectorate of Sweden, and the consultation process is ongoing.
“We understand that our plans for the new deposit would have an impact … We have submitted a reindeer herding impact assessment that includes proposed measures intended to support the conditions for continued reindeer herding in the area.
“Our starting point is not to dismiss the concerns that have been raised, but to work toward solutions that can reduce impacts and create the conditions for safeguarding both interests over the long term.”

How China’s green tech is undercutting Trump’s ‘drill, baby, drill’ oil strategy in Africa
Record photovoltaic additions and major infrastructure deals allow developing nations to bypass fossil fuel price shocks
Cost appears to be a deciding factor for most African countries when it comes to energy as they observe the factors that influence US and Chinese policy decisions.
With China’s advances in solar generation and battery technologies making acquisitions cheaper, a consensus is coalescing across the continent around renewables.
“Africa’s solar revolution is here,” said Sonia Dunlop, CEO of the Global Solar Council (GSC). “Growth is spreading to new markets across the continent, and rooftop and distributed systems are putting power directly into the hands of households and businesses.”
Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East had delivered “two major fossil fuel supply shocks in four years” that “exposed the brutal cost of energy dependence”, Dunlop noted. But cheap solar and improved battery storage had enabled the rapid replacement of fossil fuels with solar power across Africa, she said.

Israel prepares for prolonged water crisis as algae clogs desalination plants
Israeli authorities are preparing for a prolonged water crisis after an experiment aimed at combating the algae bloom that has disrupted most of the country's desalination plants failed to produce a solution, according to a source familiar with the matter.
For more than a week, unusually high concentrations of microscopic algae along Israel's Mediterranean coast have repeatedly forced desalination plants to shut down or operate at reduced capacity.
Water supplies to homes and farms have so far remained normal, but only because authorities have shifted to emergency operations and increased pumping from the Sea of Galilee and groundwater reserves.
Officials involved in situational assessments say the crisis could be prolonged. With no indication of when the algae will disappear, the Water Authority is now pressing desalination plants to stockpile replacement membranes – the filters used to remove salt from seawater – so they can be replaced as they become clogged by the algae.
The Sorek B and Palmachim plants have already acquired supplies for replacement membranes, and the authority is prepared to pay to fly additional equipment into Israel rather than wait for shipments by sea.
The preparations follow an experiment last week in which the Water Authority sprayed chemicals, including copper sulfate, into the Mediterranean off the coast of Ashkelon in an attempt to reduce the concentration of algae. The substances were dispersed from aircraft along a nine-kilometer stretch of coastline.

Ulrich Siegmund: from CDU member to AfD lead candidate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
04:00:07 UTC
13:00:07 KST

Ulrich Siegmund is the AfD's leading figure in Saxony-Anhalt: 35, media-savvy and aiming to be minister-president. At the next state election he wants to lead his party into government.
Ulrich Siegmund was born on 25 October 1990 in Havelberg, Saxony-Anhalt. The now 35-year-old has been a member of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament since 2016 and, since August 2022, has co-chaired the AfD parliamentary group together with Oliver Kirchner. In 2025, he was chosen as the AfD’s lead candidate for the 2026 state election.
His professional path did not start directly in politics. Siegmund trained as a wholesale and foreign trade clerk. He then studied business psychology and business administration, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree.
Before entering politics, Siegmund made his money in fragrances. In 2014, at the age of 23, he founded a company in the field of scent marketing. The firm sold fragrance oils, scent accessories and scenting technology, and offered consultancy services in marketing and sales. Siegmund’s studies in business psychology and business administration were also directly linked to his business: his bachelor’s thesis examined the psychological impact of scent marketing on purchasing behaviour.
In 2014, Siegmund and a business partner founded the company "Berlin duftet". The idea was to use targeted ambient scents to make, among other places, BVG and S-Bahn stations more pleasant and thereby reduce stress, aggression and vandalism. In a report by WELT at the time, Siegmund said he was thinking, for example, of a relaxing scent such as lavender.
Particularly interesting is that Siegmund, at the time, pointed to experiences in New York, where busy train stations were subtly perfumed with vanilla. He drew on studies suggesting that pleasant smells can improve people’s mood.
Siegmund was initially a member of the CDU before switching to the AfD. He joined the AfD at the age of 24. Two years later, he entered the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament for the first time.
The social media politician
Today, Siegmund is one of the best-known AfD politicians in Germany. He owes a significant part of his success to his social media strategy. More than 400,000 people now follow him on Instagram; on TikTok, he has more than 763,500 followers, making him one of the most-followed politicians in Germany.
Siegmund often comes across as friendly, easy-going and close to ordinary people, posing for photos with supporters and relying heavily on his election campaigns at family festivals, citizen dialogues and personal encounters.
International media often describe him as the AfD’s "sunny face". The Financial Times portrays his campaign as deliberately community-oriented and family-focused.
Siegmund is calling, among other things, for a far more restrictive migration policy, deportations and a fundamental change in state policy.
His family and other private details
Siegmund is married and has a daughter. His wife, Julia, has also already appeared on camera, though not in a political context. She featured in the VOX wedding docu-soap "Zwischen Tüll & Tränen", where she was looking for her wedding dress for her marriage to Ulrich Siegmund.
For his party, he works extensively with concepts such as home, security, family and change.
In 2017, Siegmund left the Catholic Church. Its values, he says, he carries "in his heart", but he rejects the German institution behind them. In his office hangs a portrait of Otto von Bismarck from nearby Schönhausen, beneath the sentence: "An idea that is right cannot be lied away in the long run."
His older brother sits on Tangermünde’s town council as an independent. His mother died in an accident in 2019.
Controversies in the media
In 2026, Siegmund’s father, Andreas, came under scrutiny for "nepotism". The 66-year-old works in the parliamentary office of AfD MP Thomas Korell in the Bundestag. He had previously worked for other AfD MPs. Siegmund defended in principle the hiring of relatives and party friends and pointed out, among other things, that it was difficult for the AfD to find good people because anyone working for the party is stigmatised.
A widely reported media controversy involving Martin Sellner and Ulrich Siegmund also centred on a meeting near Potsdam in November 2023. Siegmund took part in the gathering, at which Austrian right-wing extremist Martin Sellner spoke about "remigration". By this, Sellner meant not only the return of foreigners obliged to leave the country, but also measures against "non-assimilated citizens" with a migration background.
Siegmund subsequently described his participation as private and explained, in essence, that mere attendance at a lecture does not imply agreement with its content.
On Abgeordnetenwatch, Siegmund was asked in January 2024 whether he distanced himself from Sellner’s "master plan for remigration". His reply was: "The accusations must be rejected."
The Saxony-Anhalt Office for the Protection of the Constitution, a department of the CDU-led Interior Ministry, classified the AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch on 7 November 2023 as a "proven right-wing extremist endeavour". The grounds cited included anti-Muslim, racist and antisemitic statements by AfD officials and elected representatives.
However, the classification is legally disputed and under review by the courts. The AfD is challenging it; the proceedings are currently suspended.
Siegmund has also managed to turn to his advantage the fact that SPIEGEL’s mid-August cover dubbed the lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt "Germany’s most dangerous man". In the election campaign, he signed piles of copies of SPIEGEL with his photo on the cover, which are being auctioned on eBay for sky-high sums.
From state MP to potential minister-president
Siegmund’s political rise has occurred in just a few years. In 2016, he entered the state parliament for the first time; in 2022, he and Oliver Kirchner took over the chairmanship of the AfD group. In 2025, the party placed him at the top of its state list for the 2026 election.
Now it is about far more than another parliamentary seat: Siegmund wants to become minister-president of Saxony-Anhalt. However, he has himself said that he will only govern if the AfD alone commands an outright majority.
If the AfD does indeed win a governing majority, Siegmund could become Germany’s first AfD minister-president.

Von der Leyen visits Greenland amid Trump pressure
September 7, 2026
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is in Greenland for a two-day visit as the European Union plans a major boost in investment in the region amid threats of US annexation under President Donald Trump.
Alongside the EU investments, she is expected to announce closer political ties with the autonomous Arctic territory which is part of the Kingdom of Denmark.
The European Commission head arrived in Greenland's capital Nuuk on Sunday in a show of support for Greenland and Denmark, and was received by Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
In a post on X, Von der Leyen said the EU is committed to "contributing to a safe, peaceful Arctic and to the security of Greenland."
What does the EU investment package include?
The EU package is expected to include hundreds of millions of euros in investment in:
- critical minerals,
- satellite communications
- renewable energy
Von der Leyen said the package would be "substantial" but gave no details.
Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen described the visit as an opportunity to deepen the territory's "close friendship and good partnership" with the EU.
The largely autonomous Greenland left the EU in 1985, although its population of about 57,000 are EU citizens through Danish citizenship.
Why is Trump demanding 'total access' over Greenland?
Von der Leyen's visit comes as the Arctic gains strategic importance for the US, Russia, China and Europe, with melting sea ice opening new shipping routes and increasing access to the region's mineral resources.
Trump has repeatedly stated that the US "needs" Greenland for its "national security," pointing to his claims — without providing evidence — that the island is "covered with Chinese and Russian ships all over the place."
Trump has maintained that Denmark cannot adequately defend the island against China and Russia.
His campaign bid to gain "total access" to the Danish territory has strained US-European relations and raised tensions within NATO as both Greenland and the Danish government have rejected Trump's demands.

‘The spark for protests in Iran has not yet come- but it will,’ Israeli officials says
Israeli security officials believe that while the Iranian gov't new measures may preserve stability in the short term, it cannot offer a sustainable solution as economic conditions continue to worsen
Iran’s worsening economic crisis has yet to trigger widespread protests, but senior Israeli officials tells i24NEWS that mounting pressure will eventually drive Iranians back onto the streets.
Sharp inflation, steep price increases and disruptions to oil exports and commodity trade have deepened economic hardship across the country. Despite the deterioration, Israeli assessments indicate that Tehran has so far managed to contain public discontent.
“It is not known when the spark that will ignite a protest in Tehran will come, but it will come,” an Israeli sources told i24NEWS.
Iran’s government has decades of experience managing the effects of international sanctions and has developed mechanisms to limit their immediate impact. Israeli security officials believe those measures may preserve stability in the short term but cannot offer a sustainable solution as economic conditions continue to worsen.
Alongside the possibility of future domestic unrest, Israel and the United States expect Tehran to seek relief from mounting American pressure through regional action.
Israeli assessments suggest Iran may attempt to draw Israel into a broader confrontation in an effort to destabilize the region and persuade Washington to ease its sanctions and wider economic pressure on the Iranian government.

Viet Nam, 81 years of independence: from renovation process to stepping confidently into a new era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
03:52:33 UTC
12:52:33 KST

Viet Nam, 81 years of independence: from renovation process to stepping confidently into a new era
TEHRAN- On 2 September 1945, President Ho Chi Minh, the revered leader of the Vietnamese people, proclaimed to the world the birth of an independent and free VietNam. This historic day has since become the National Day of the Socialist Republic of Viet Nam. From that historic milestone, independence and self-reliance have remained guiding principles throughout the cause of national defense and development. Eighty-one years may not be a long period in the history of a nation, but they represent a proud journey for Viet Nam – from a country that had just regained its independence, through years of extremely difficult war, to an economy with a GDP of more than US$ 500 billion.
With an indomitable spirit and extraordinary determination, we fought to defend our national independence and achieved lasting peace and national reunification in 1975. In just four decades of the Renovation process (1986–2026), rising from the ashes of war, with an exhausted economy and under a policy of encirclement and embargo, Viet Nam, drawing on its national intellect and aspiration for renewal and prosperity, together with the support of international friends, has emerged as a dynamic country deeply integrated into the global economy.
In 2025, Viet Nam’s GDP grew by 8.02%, bringing the size of the economy to US$ 514 billion. GDP per capita exceeded US$ 5,000, while the poverty rate, according to the United Nations standard, fell to just 1.3%. Also last year, total import and export turnover reached US$ 910 billion, while Viet Nam attracted nearly US$ 38.5 billion in foreign investment. VietNam welcomed over 21 million international visitors, the highest number ever recorded. Viet Nam has trade relations with 230 countries and territories, and diplomatic relations with 195 countries, including 30 countries with which it has established strategic or comprehensive strategic partnerships.
Throughout the process of national development, VietNam has remained steadfast in pursuing the goals of national independence and socialism, while consistently pursuing the Renovation policy, continuously renewing its thinking and approaches to development and maintaining political stability. It has always placed the people at the centre, ensuring that economic development goes hand in hand with social equity and that no one is left behind.
As a country that has experienced many wars, VietNam cherishes every moment of peace and makes every effort to preserve it through diplomacy and dialogue. Viet Nam pursues an open foreign policy and seeks to be a friend to all countries, regardless of their political systems, while proactively and actively engaging with the international community. Throughout its development, it has consistently regarded national independence and sovereignty, the right of peoples to self-determination, and the preservation of national identity as principles that cannot be compromised.
Today, the world is undergoing rapid and unpredictable changes, creating new opportunities for development while also presenting considerable uncertainties and challenges for all countries. The achievements of more than four decades of Renovation have given Viet Nam the foundation and confidence to enter a new era of development, with a clearer understanding of the strengths that need to be harnessed and the limitations that need to be overcome, so as to propel the country into a new era of national advancement.
Viet Nam enters a new era of development
The 14th National Congress of the Communist Party of Viet Nam, held in January 2026, set the goal of making Viet Nam a developing country with modern industry and upper-middle income status by 2030, with annual GDP growth of 10% or higher.
To achieve these objectives, Viet Nam is pursuing three strategic breakthroughs. First, it is focusing on accelerating institutional reform, streamlining administrative procedures, strengthening decentralisation and continuing to streamline the state apparatus. Second, it is promoting a new growth model based on science and technology, innovation, digital transformation and a green economy. Third, it is improving the quality of human resources, accelerating investment in strategic infrastructure, while identifying tourism as a key economic sector.
Viet Nam will continue to deepen its external relations, promote international integration and diversify partnerships and engagement across different regions of the world, thereby expanding its development space and enhancing the autonomy of the economy. The Middle East is an important region, with a strategic geopolitical position, abundant energy resources and dynamic development. Recent tensions in the region have affected regional security, energy markets and international transport routes. Viet Nam hopes that the Middle East will achieve peace and long-term stability at an early date through negotiations and dialogue, on the basis of respect for national sovereignty and the principles of international law and the Charter of the United Nations.
53 years of maintaining the bridge of friendship between Viet Nam and Iran
Viet Nam and Iran established diplomatic relations on 4 August 1973, just a few months after the signing of the Paris Peace Accords. From the very beginning, the two sides based their relations on enduring principles: respect for independence and sovereignty, non-interference in each other’s internal affairs, and the assurance of each other’s legitimate interests.
Although geographically distant from one another, VietNam and Iran are both countries with long histories that attach great importance to independence, sovereignty and national identity, while seeking to expand their economic relations with the world. Both countries hold important geopolitical positions. VietNam is an active member of ASEAN, with an extensive network of economic linkages across the Asia-Pacific. Iran lies at the heart of the Middle East, at the crossroads of major global flows of energy and trade.
Over the past 53 years, Vietnam has consistently attached importance to developing friendly, mutually beneficial cooperation with Iran, regarding Iran as one of its important partners in the Middle East.
The two countries have maintained political trust and cooperation in the economic and cultural spheres, while strengthening exchanges of delegations and people-to-people ties. A particularly significant milestone came in 2023, when the two countries marked the 50th anniversary of diplomatic relations through a series of commemorative activities and high-level exchanges. The two countries have also maintained effective cooperation at multilateral forums.
In April 2026, in his congratulatory message to General Secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam To Lam on his election as President of Viet Nam, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian noted that the bilateral relationship held great potential and should continue to be deepened and broadened in line with the interests of both countries. In July 2026, when receiving Iranian Ambassador to Vietnam Akbar Ghasemi Ali Abadi, who presented his credentials, General Secretary and President To Lam proposed four areas for further promoting Viet Nam - Iran relations: strengthening political trust; prioritising economic cooperation; creating breakthroughs in science and technology; and expanding cooperation in culture, education and training, and tourism. These orientations provide an important basis for the relevant agencies of the two countries to implement multifaceted cooperation programmes in the years ahead.
Trade has always been a priority area of cooperation. The economic structures of Viet Nam and Iran are highly complementary. Viet Nam has strong export sectors, including products that rank among the world’s top exporters such as rice, coffee, pepper, cashew nutsand garments, as well as other competitive products including seafood, processed food, consumer goods, electronics and industrial products. Iran has considerable strengths in a number of sectors, including industry, construction, pharmaceuticals, materials, minerals, fruit and meat products.
Despite the above-mentioned difficulties, bilateral trade turnover has continued to grow year on year: US$133 million in 2022, US$ 164 million in 2024 and US$170 million in 2025. This demonstrates that there remains considerable room for cooperation between the two countries, not only in trade, but also in other fields of cooperation.
In the new era of development, Viet Nam - Iran relations should be carried forward not merely through the memories of more than half a century of friendship, but through new connections in the fields of the economy, science and technology, education, culture and people-to-people exchanges. In the period ahead, as the regional situation improves, we believe that relations between the two countries will be further strengthened across a wide range of areas, in a manner commensurate with their considerable potential.
On the occasion of the 81st anniversary of the National Day of the Socialist Republic of Viet Nnam, we would like to express our sincere appreciation to the State, Government and people of Iran for their sincere and effective support for Viet Nam’s national development over the years.
May the friendship between our two countries continue to flourish, for the cooperation and prosperity of our two peoples, and contribute to peace, stability and development in the region and around the world.

Volcano in Indonesia erupts, canceling hundreds of flights and stranding thousands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
03:46:51 UTC
12:46:51 KST

A volcano erupted in Indonesia on Sunday, prompting the cancellation of all flights at Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and disrupting other domestic airports.
Jakarta's main airport and three others have extended their closures until 6 pm on Monday following a volcanic eruption, stranding tens of thousands of passengers.
Mount Anak Krakatau, situated roughly 150 kilometres from Indonesia's capital, erupted on Saturday, spewing lava and towering plumes of ash.
The transport ministry confirmed that eight airports across the region halted operations over the weekend after ash drifted into their airspace, disrupting hundreds of flights and stranding more than 170,000 travellers.
Airport operator Angkasa Pura announced on social media that at least four hubs, including Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, extended their operational suspensions until 6 pm (1100 GMT) on Monday.
"In connection with the increasing eruption activity of Mount Anak Krakatau, flight operations at several airports have been suspended; passengers are advised to regularly monitor their flight status with the respective airlines," the operator stated.
The company confirmed that Halim Perdanakusuma, a smaller facility handling both commercial and military flights, also extended its closure.
According to the national geology agency, the likelihood of further eruptive activity remains high through Monday morning.
The volcano has been sporadically active since emerging from the sea early last century inside the massive caldera formed by the cataclysmic 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatau.
In 2018, a partial collapse of Anak Krakatau triggered a devastating tsunami that killed 429 people and displaced thousands.

What to Know About the Miami Plane Crash That Killed 5 People
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
03:45:19 UTC
12:45:19 KST

At least five people were killed and five others were injured after an Amazon cargo plane overshot the runway upon landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon.
Miami-Dade County officials said in an evening press conference that 21 Air Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 freighter operating on behalf of Amazon, crashed into several vehicles shortly before 2 p.m.
The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration said they are investigating the incident.
"The airplane, which was operated by 21 Air, was attempting to land when this incident occurred,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement. “We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to learn more and will cooperate fully with any investigation.”
Nantel said the company’s “deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
Amazon contracts out its cargo flights.
The incident has impacted operations in “America’s busiest airport for international freight and second busiest for international passengers,” according to the Miami airport’s website.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on social media that travelers should anticipate significant delays and potential flight cancellations. A full ground stop had earlier been issued but was lifted about three hours later. Authorities said ground delays are expected until early Monday.
Here’s what we know so far.
How it unfolded
According to the FAA, Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft, departed from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico.
Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said during the news conference that the crash happened at around 1:58 p.m. Data from tracking site Flightradar24 shows that the plane had a speed of nearly 130 mph when it left the usable portion of the diagonal runway.
It’s unclear what caused the plane to overshoot, and the NTSB and FAA are investigating. The airport’s runways and taxiways were closed, and the aircraft was left disabled at the northwest end of the airport. Some of the runways were later reopened.
According to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, more than 60 units and approximately 200 personnel responded to the scene, arriving at the airport “to find an airplane that had stopped beyond the airport operational boundary with heavy flames and smoke showing.” Photos and videos from the scene showed black smoke billowing from the plane.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue chief Raied Jadallah said in the news conference that several people were trapped in their vehicles.
“What we found was a very complex situation here,” Jadallah said, and added that responders also conducted search and rescue of the pilot and co-pilot who were trapped in the aircraft.
What we know about the victims
Jadallah said there were a total of 10 people involved in the crash: five were killed, three are in critical condition and were transported to the trauma center, and another two were transported to a local hospital. It was not clear on Sunday evening whether those killed and injured were on the plane or on the ground.
What we know about the carrier and the plane
North Carolina-based cargo airline 21 Air began operating Boeing 767-300 freighters on behalf of Amazon in 2024. The company was founded in 2014.
Keith Winters, the airline’s CEO, said in a statement on their website that they were “devastated by the accident” and that the company’s “deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives.”
Flightradar24 data shows the plane involved in the crash was a 32-year-old Boeing 767. The aircraft model is used for both passenger travel and freight delivery. The first Boeing 767 flew on Sept. 26, 1981, and started commercial operations in 1982 with United Airlines.
Amazon’s cargo flight history
Amazon Air’s cargo network oversees more than 100 aircraft and over 250 flights daily. It contracts all of its cargo flying to other operators. In its fleet are Boeing 737 and 767 planes, as well as the Airbus A330.
Citing details from aviation analytics firm Cirium, the New York Times reported that 21 Air runs eight planes for Amazon Air, while Air Transport International operates about 40 planes, and low-cost carrier Sun Country Airlines operates 22.
It’s not the first plane crash involving Amazon Air. In February 2019, Atlas Air Flight 3591, a cargo plane flying from Miami to Houston, crashed into Texas’s Trinity Bay. All three people onboard were killed, and a subsequent federal investigation attributed the crash to pilot error.
Sunday’s incident is the latest high-profile crash involving a cargo aircraft in the U.S. Last November, more than a dozen people were killed after a UPS plane crashed into an industrial area in Louisville, Ky. shortly after departing Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport.

Swans AFLW star says club's men's and women's players closer than ever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
03:31:52 UTC
12:31:52 KST

Swans AFLW star Cynthia Hamilton says the club's men's and women's players are closer than ever before in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal.
Hamilton revealed players are doing breathwork sessions together, with men's star Errol Gulden playing a key role.
She described the club's culture and unity as "actually beautiful".
Believing Sydney's men's and women's teams are closer than before, AFLW star Cynthia Hamilton has described the embattled club's resilience amid turmoil as "actually beautiful".
Hamilton is urging fans to continue their support, vowing the Swans won't disappoint on the field in Sunday's Sydney derby against rivals GWS at Henson Park.
The Swans women play in the Harbour City for the first time since the SCG double-header in round two, having played a home game in Coffs Harbour in round three.
Fans came out in force at the SCG in the immediate aftermath of the men's Pullman Hotel scandal, with a crowd of 16,672 turning up for the victory over Essendon.
The attendance more than doubled Sydney's previous highest crowd for a home AFLW game.
In contrast, the men's team recorded its lowest SCG crowd of the season, just 30,058 fans watched them beat North Melbourne.
Star players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — All-Australian contenders before they were banned from being selected — are among the five serving club-imposed bans.
Important tagger James Jordon and defender Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.
As the men's team aims to rebuild respect for the famed "Bloods" culture, Hamilton says the club have come together even over the smallest of details.
"This has honestly brought us closer. We're doing breathwork in the morning together, we're doing little things," Hamilton said.
"Errol Gulden's been flicking the message [about breathwork] across to join both teams together as an opportunity to come closer.
"The boys have been bloody awesome. They've really brought the two groups together.
"In light of what's happened, it's actually kind of beautiful how the club has reacted. I would say we're closer than what we were before."
As a healthy contingent followed the women's to Whitten Oval last week, the men's team enjoyed renewed support for their 53-point qualifying final upset of reigning premiers Brisbane and played in front of 37,261 fans at the SCG.
"When you look on the weekend, and you see the support the boys are getting, and then vice versa when we were at the SCG as well, it just shows how special the Bloods bond is and that the culture is there," Hamilton said.
"Keep getting around us, keep showing up, and we won't disappoint, hopefully."
GWS forward Tarni Evans also threw her weight behind the Swans, after urging fans to support the AFLW fixture at the SCG last month.
The 14th-placed Giants are looking to retain derby bragging rights and bounce back from a dour 31-point away loss to the Lions, taking a three-game losing streak to Henson Park.
Sydney is also licking its wounds after a 27-point defeat to the Western Bulldogs, leaving the Swans fifth after a first loss of the season.
Both sides have claimed two wins from four previous derbies in the women's league.
"This weekend, this is such a great opportunity in women's sport, to get out and support it," Evans said.
"Getting people to the game is unreal and that's what we want.
"This weekend will be another testament to that, a great game of footy to watch."

Greater Bay Area 'fortes lie in finance, innovation'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
03:28:25 UTC
12:28:25 KST

Global investors and startups should consider establishing a foothold in the Greater Bay Area given its unique combination of strengths in finance and innovation, Financial Secretary Paul Chan said on Monday.
He was speaking at the opening of the inaugural Co-Development and Investment Conference, which brings together around 300 investors and more than 500 startups alongside industry leaders and academics in the Greater Bay Area.
The six-day event starts at Hong Kong Science Park before moving on to Dongguan and Hangzhou for its final four days.
“For global investors in a world overshadowed by geopolitics, the requirement is twofold: stability and security on the one hand, attractive returns on the other,” Chan said.
“For innovators and entrepreneurs, capital alone is not enough. They need an industrial ecosystem, a steady supply of talent and access to the full range of innovation resources.
“Nowhere is the combination of finance and innovation stronger than in the Guangdong, Hong Kong, Macao Greater Bay Area.”
Chan called Hong Kong a “magnet” for global talent and a hub for fast-rising innovation, making it a natural complement to sister Greater Bay Area cities that excel in advanced manufacturing, commercialisation and scaling.
The city, he added, is also building a capital ecosystem tailored to support startups and drive innovation.
These efforts are already bearing fruit, Chan said, pointing out that the technology sector's share of turnover on the Hong Kong bourse has risen from 15 percent to 47 percent over the past decade, with overall turnover growing more than eightfold.

AfD wins big in German regional election, falls short of outright majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
03:25:51 UTC
12:25:51 KST

AfD wins big in German regional election, falls short of bid to become first far-right party to lead a state since WWII
The far-right Alternative for Germany party surged to a resounding victory in a regional election Sunday, but fell a little short of winning a majority in its quest to form the country's first far-right state government since World War II.
The party of Germany's unpopular leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, slumped to a disastrous result in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. The anti-migration and Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany's candidate for governor said that "we have written history" and the party had a clear mandate to govern.
Ulrich Siegmund, 35, told public broadcaster ARD that voters had sent a signal that "things cannot carry on like this." He said that "a very good campaigner for us in this election campaign was Friedrich Merz."
Alternative for Germany, or AfD, was seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature to govern alone and overcome the so-called firewall of mainstream parties' refusal to work with AfD.
Final results showed AfD falling three seats short, with 39 lawmakers in an 83-member parliament. Siegmund said it wouldn't engage in "games" such as a minority government. But it wasn't evident how its divided opponents could assemble any stable government without it.
A first state government would be the biggest prize in the anti-migration party's 13-year history, at a time of widespread discontent with a national government that has yet to persuade voters that it can get the country's sluggish economy moving.
Whether or not AfD ends up governing, the result is a blow to Merz, whose center-right party has led Saxony-Anhalt for 24 years.
Unlike other countries in Europe, modern Germany hasn't yet had a far-right or right-wing populist party leading a national, state or major-city government.
AfD is the biggest opposition party in Germany's national parliament and is strongest in the formerly communist and less prosperous east, where Saxony-Anhalt is located.
Its regional branch in Saxony-Anhalt is one of several classified as a proven right-wing extremist group by the domestic intelligence agency, which points to members' denigration of migrants from Muslim countries, among other things.
The party talks of "remigration," a politically charged term for the deportation of immigrants. Its leader in a neighboring state appealed two convictions for knowingly using a Nazi slogan.
AfD vehemently rejects accusations of extremism and says they're politically motivated.
AfD won 43.8% of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin.
That was far ahead of Merz's Christian Democratic Union, which polled 17.2% — losing about half its support — and won 15 seats. The center-left Social Democrats polled 9.3%, the Greens 8.9% and the Left Party 8.6%, winning eight seats apiece.
The BSW party, which has said it wouldn't elect either Siegmund or incumbent Sven Schulze as governor but criticizes the "firewall" against AfD, took 5.3% and five seats.
Turnout was very high at 77.8%. AfD appeared to have won over many people who didn't vote at all five years ago.
AfD's national co-leader, Alice Weidel, described the result as "sensational." She said the party's "hand is outstretched to all who want to make Saxony-Anhalt better and move Germany forward." It may hope to attract defectors from other parties.
Schulze congratulated AfD on becoming the state's strongest political force and said that "we as the CDU will also have to deal with this result," without specifying how.
Franziska Hoppermann, the national general secretary of Merz's party, rejected backing off its refusal to deal with AfD.
"AfD is a right-wing extremist party. It wants to leave the euro; that would be economic downfall ... it works closely together with Russia, it wants a completely different social model," she said. "We will not work with them."
Once previously AfD won a state election but didn't end up governing. That was two years ago in neighboring Thuringia, where a CDU governor took power with a minority government, but AfD was much further short of a majority there.
Any attempt by Schulze to put together an alliance against AfD would be delicate because it would require at least some tacit support from the Left Party, a hard-left party with which the CDU refuses to form coalitions.
Germany's 16 states have extensive powers, for example in overseeing security matters and running the education system.
Siegmund has listed among his top priorities "a deportation offensive" and dropping incentives for people to come to Germany and "exploit our social system." He wants to initiate a long process to withdraw Saxony-Anhalt from the regional public broadcaster, citing concerns about "disinformation."
AfD in Saxony-Anhalt wants to allow home schooling, which so far isn't permitted in Germany. It pledges to ban schools from officially raising the rainbow flag, which it says "stands for the devaluation of the family," and ensure they fly the national flag.
It opposes taxpayers' money being "given away" to Ukraine and says it would push to lift sanctions against Russia, but that isn't a matter state governments can decide.
The 16 states' governments also sit in Germany's upper house of parliament, which has to approve some government legislation. The influence there of Saxony-Anhalt, one of the smaller states in a nation of 83.5 people, is limited — it controls four of the 69 votes.

10 killed, 64 injured in central Mexico pyrotechnics explosion
