MEXICO CITY, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- At least 10 people were killed and 64 others injured after stored pyrotechnic material exploded Saturday night during patron saint festivities in Temascalcingo, central Mexico's State of Mexico, the state government confirmed Sunday.
The explosion occurred at around 9:30 p.m. local time Saturday (0330 GMT Sunday) at a church, the state government said in a statement.
The blast caused part of the church roof and a nearby wall to collapse, burying several people under the debris.
Eight of the victims died at the scene and the injured were taken to hospitals near the municipality, reports said.
Civil protection personnel, the Armed Forces and state police responded to the emergency and activated security protocols.
The State of Mexico Pyrotechnics Institute inspected the site for active explosive material and issued recommendations for specialists to dismantle and disable it to reduce risks. ■

Feature: Connected by algorithms and shared interests, young Chinese build social lives across screens and streets
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
11:25:26 CST
12:25:26 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 7 (Xinhua) -- "Anyone want to bike this evening? Not for speed. Just enjoy the breeze and stop whenever we get tired."
After finishing work on a recent Friday, Chen Jiahao, 26, a programmer in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, posted this invitation on Xiaohongshu, a popular Chinese app for sharing lifestyle tips and hobbies.
It didn't take long for people to start leaving comments.
That evening, three strangers met and set off along a bike path near a local river. They rode at an easy pace, taking in the view and stopping now and then to chat about work and things they had been watching or reading lately.
More than two hours later, they parted and headed home.
"I wasn't really looking to make a new friend," Chen said. "Sometimes you just feel like doing something on the spur of the moment, and it's nice when you happen to find someone who wants to do the same thing."
This encounter lasted an evening. That was enough.
It points to a broader shift in how young Chinese are building their social lives -- and perhaps to what they now expect from one another.
For generations, friendships grew almost by default out of the places and communities people shared: school, work, neighborhoods and family. But as young people move more often, live more independently and spend more time online, those old settings no longer necessarily determine who enters their social lives.
Liu Shengzhi, a professor of communication at Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, said young people increasingly connect online over shared interests and then take those relationships offline, sometimes in more fleeting forms: someone to eat with, walk with or watch a movie with.
Their social lives are becoming more lightweight, activity-based and modular, according to a 2026 social trends report by an institute under Soul, an AI-powered immersive social platform in China, in collaboration with Fudan University.
Liu described such lighter forms of socializing as a response to modern urban life, where maintaining traditional, close-knit relationships can demand considerable time, money and emotional energy.
This shift is hardly unique to China. Sociologists often describe the broader process as social atomization, which can leave people feeling isolated and lonely, but can also give them greater freedom, autonomy and private space.
What may be changing, experts say, is not young people's desire for connection, but the terms on which they seek it. They want to find "their people," but without giving up their own space.
Sometimes a simple connection remains just that.
Sometimes it becomes something more.
For Maggie Gong, 35, the large online group for bouldering enthusiasts has largely fallen by the wayside. She now mostly makes plans in a group chat with two people she climbs with regularly.
The user-interface designer, who lives in Chengdu in southwest China's Sichuan Province, picked up the sport as a way to get out of the house. Working mostly from home, she had spent a lot of time sitting alone when she came across bouldering videos online.
"Bouldering is a bit like solving a problem with your body," Gong said. The sport makes it easier for her to get a sense of her climbing partners' personalities.
Those who insist on finding the best way up may call out the next move as their partner climbs. Others prefer to work out a route on their own and are more open to different solutions.
"It requires trust. For a few minutes, quite literally, your safety is in someone else's hands," she said.
For Li Xinyu, 25, who works at a bank in Dalian, Liaoning, shared interests have provided something more enduring: a reason to stay.
She decided to settle in the northeastern city after graduation, in part because she had found like-minded friends online through her interest in animation and comics.
Li often hangs out with these friends at comic conventions, dressed in cosplay, taking photos and browsing "guzi" shops. The term "guzi" is a Chinese phonetic rendering of "goods" and refers to merchandise associated with anime, music, gaming and other fandoms.
People may differ in age, education or profession, but a shared passion can give them a sense of belonging that might otherwise be hard to find, Li said.
The rise of these casual ties in China is not simply because young people want them. Young people elsewhere do this, too. What may set China apart is a growing digital and physical infrastructure that is lowering the barriers to turning online interests into offline activities.
Algorithms that sort and connect people by interests, location and online behavior have made social discovery far more efficient and precise, allowing young people to find each other at little cost, said Liu.
The physical environment matters, too. In Shanghai, a former cement plant has been turned into a cultural and commercial complex where young people can bring their pets, grab a drink, stroll along the waterfront or visit an art gallery. In Chengdu, an elevated cycling path runs through a shopping mall and connects with cycling routes around the city.
Meanwhile, real-name verification, reputation systems and the growing overlap between online communities and offline activities can make meeting a stranger feel less like a leap into the unknown.
Behind this trend lies a clear commercial logic.
As user growth plateaus, China's internet platforms are looking for ways to keep people engaged for longer. Interests can serve as a gateway, taking users from content to conversation, commerce and eventually offline experiences.
Douyin and Taobao have increasingly integrated content, commerce and payments, while Soul has introduced a feature that enables users to quickly form groups around shared interests and activities.
In Kunming, the capital city of southwest China's Yunnan Province, where the feature was piloted, the platform completed the full chain -- from posting a request and forming a group to organizing an offline activity and making a payment -- in less than a week.
Soul said the pilot showed that when platforms make it easy for people to find others who want to do the same thing at the same moment, young people are surprisingly willing to take those connections offline.
Even so, lightweight connections cannot replace deeper ties that offer emotional intimacy, unconditional acceptance and long-term commitment, said Liu.
A survey of 1,333 young people by China Youth Daily found that 81.6 percent considered deep relationships necessary, though 71.4 percent said they felt it had become harder to maintain them.
Gong has noticed the limits of online connection.
Connecting with someone online via a shared interest can make a first encounter easier, she said. But it cannot do the work of a relationship.
"Whether two people can build on that initial connection still depends on their personalities, values and the rhythms of everyday life," Gong said.
The ease of finding a companion online also comes with risks. Users have reported being abandoned midway through trips, falling victim to online scams, or even facing verbal or physical abuse.
Li tends to choose busy public places, like shopping malls and exhibition halls, for first meetings with people she has met online. She also lets friends know where she is going and what she plans to do.
"And I'm especially cautious when money is involved, whether it's buying tickets for someone or sharing a hotel room," she said. "Just because you hit it off with someone online doesn't mean you should immediately put your trust in a stranger."
There is another, less obvious risk.
The same algorithms that make it easier to find people like you can also make the world around you look increasingly like you, Chen said.
After he searched a few times on his phone for cycling routes and activities, his feed increasingly showed him the same narrow slice of the world: people roughly his age, interested in similar activities and talking about similar things. Even the destinations they visited began to converge.
Chen said he tries not to let the feed dictate who he meets. He chats with potential companions a little longer, asking about the details to see whether they are actually a good fit. Sometimes he also searches for things far outside his usual interests, or follows activities recommended by other people, simply to throw the algorithm off his trail.
"An algorithm can help me find someone to bike with tonight," he said. "But I don't want it deciding who I spend time with over time." ■

South Korea, US, Japan conducting Freedom Edge military drills

Unknown Publisher

03:25:01 UTC
12:25:01 KST

SEOUL, September 7. /TASS/. South Korea, the US, and Japan have begun the trilateral Freedom Edge naval drills in international waters south and east of Jeju Island, the Yonhap news agency reported, citing the South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff.
The exercises are taking place in several areas and will also involve air forces. "These maneuvers will enhance the countries' operational and joint response capabilities in various environments, including at sea, in the air, and in cyberspace," the defense officials noted. Freedom Edge will last five days.
Seoul insists that the drills are defensive in nature and are being conducted in accordance with international law. It is unclear exactly which South Korean ships will participate. Seoul assures that the scale of the forces involved will be comparable to last year's.
On August 16, US President Donald Trump reiterated his "good relations" with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and announced that he had ordered a reduction in the scale and duration of the Ulchi Freedom Shield military drills with South Korea. It later came to light that the US would not participate in the Ssangyong joint Marine Corps exercises due to the situation in the Middle East.
The first Freedom Edge exercise was held in June 2024, with the second and third iterations taking place in November 2024 and September 2025.

‘Trumpapalooza’ tests Republican bet on unpopular US president

‘Trumpapalooza’ tests Republican bet on unpopular US President
- Republicans hold a "Trumpapalooza" convention in Dallas to rally support for Donald Trump and promote his record despite his low approval ratings.
- Many Republican candidates avoid attending due to campaign duties, costs, or reluctance, raising concerns about party unity.
- The event faces competition from NFL games, but aims to energise activists, raise funds, and boost voter turnout for November midterms.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US Republicans will gather in Dallas, Texas, this week for a two-day convention aimed at convincing voters that Donald Trump is effectively on the ballot in November – even as the deeply unpopular President threatens to become a liability for his own party.
The Sept 9 to Sept 10 gathering – dubbed “Trumpapalooza” by organisers – is an unusual midterm experiment, designed to rally voters around Trump’s record as the party faces increasingly grim forecasts for elections that could cost it control of Congress.
Decision Desk HQ projects Democrats to win the House of Representatives by 229 seats to 206, while putting the Senate at a knife-edge 50-50.
Republican leaders have nevertheless decided that the answer is more Trump, not less.
“The President’s going to look right into the camera and say, ‘I am on the ballot,’” House Speaker Mike Johnson told supporters in Texas ahead of the gathering.
“Because, even though his name isn’t, his administration, his legacy, the America First agenda is.”
Trump will appear both days at Dallas’s American Airlines Center, headlining on Sept 9 and delivering closing remarks at Sept 10’s finale after Vice-President J.D. Vance’s keynote address.
Trump promised a musical celebration of the party’s “tremendous victories” and “incredible candidates” in a social media post billing the event as “the greatest rally of them all”.
Staying home
Organisers hope to showcase the administration’s tax cuts, immigration policies and other achievements while portraying Democrats as increasingly extreme.
But the strategy carries risks.
Trump’s approval rating has fallen into the low-to-mid 30s amid stubborn inflation, high fuel prices, an unpopular war with Iran and a costly trade dispute with Canada.
Perhaps more tellingly, many of the Republican candidates whose races will determine control of Congress appear reluctant to join the celebration.
A Politico survey of more than 70 lawmakers and candidates found most either did not plan to attend or had yet to commit, with dozens more declining to disclose their plans.
Some vulnerable Republicans have cited campaign commitments, debates or family obligations, while others have complained privately about being asked to contribute at least US$25,000 (S$31,670) to attend.
Johnson acknowledged that some members need to remain home but insists most Republicans will make at least an appearance, describing the event as an opportunity to put the party’s record before a national television audience.
“We have a real opportunity to defy history and win the midterms,” Johnson said in a video promoting the gathering.
Football competition
There are also doubts over how much of that television audience will actually be watching.
Both convention nights clash with the opening games of the National Football League (NFL) season, potentially forcing Trump’s prime-time show into competition with one of America’s most popular sporting events.
Republican organisers reject suggestions the event is mistimed, arguing it will energise activists, raise money and give candidates valuable national exposure.
They expect tens of thousands of attendees.
The convention is also being used as a major fundraising opportunity: donors have reportedly been offered a photograph with Trump for US$88,600, while access to a roundtable with the president costs US$250,000.
For Republicans, however, the bigger gamble is political.
Their November strategy depends on persuading millions of voters who turned out for Trump in 2024 to return when he is not actually on the ballot – while avoiding alienating independents who have increasingly soured on his presidency.
Veteran Republican political consultant Matt Klink, who has worked on hundreds of federal, state and local political campaigns over three decades, said Trump could be both a hindrance and a help in November, depending on the state.
“Some candidates will continue to embrace Trump, while other battleground campaigns are weighing how closely to identify with him amid inflation concerns, the Iran war and his weak approval ratings,” he told AFP.
“Bottom line, Republicans can’t break with Trump because Democrats and the media won’t let them. But they can work to focus on local issues and priorities, and paint opponent Democrats as radical extremists.” AFP

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ontario Tower Buzzers, the Los Angeles Dodgers' Single-A affiliate, held their first Taiwan Heritage Day at ONT Field on Sunday.
The event was held during the Tower Buzzers' final regular-season home game of their inaugural season. The team partnered with local Taiwanese community groups for the event, which featured a Taiwan flag displayed prominently behind home plate and painted on the field near the pitcher's mound.
Tower Buzzers General Manager Allan Benavides said the flag represented the team's cultural connection to Taiwan. “We will hold this event every year, and it will grow larger each year,” Benavides said, per CNA.
The event also celebrated 20-year-old Taiwanese outfielder Ko Ching-hsien (柯敬賢), who has emerged as one of the team's leading hitters. Ko finished the season playing in 114 games, with 21 home runs, 85 RBIs and a .260 batting average. Those offensive numbers ranked him second on the team.
Despite rain that delayed Sunday's game by about two hours, the Taiwan Heritage Day festivities drew an enthusiastic response from fans. Taiwanese rapper Dwagie (大支) and singer Chloe Tung (董梓甯) performed before the game. They were joined by Jason Ma (馬博元), director general of the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Los Angeles, in throwing out the ceremonial first pitch.
Benavides said the team paints flags on the field for various culturally themed days. He added that ONT Field grounds superintendent Sean Cheng (鄭項) is from a Taiwanese family and is one of the best groundskeepers in the country. During Sunday's Taiwan-themed event, Cheng wore a Taiwan national team baseball cap while working on the field, per CNA.
The Tower Buzzers are playing their first season in Ontario as part of a California League realignment with the Rancho Cucamonga Quakes now becoming affiliated with the Los Angeles Angels. The Buzzers would go on to lose their final regular-season home game 3-8 to the Rancho Cucamonga Quakes.
ONT Field is located near Ontario International Airport and incorporates an aviation theme throughout the ballpark. MLB reported that the venue is about 64 kilometers from Los Angeles. The airport also provides a direct connection to Taiwan. Ontario International Airport lists Taipei as a nonstop destination served by both China Airlines and Starlux Airlines.

Lai urges lawyers to support Taiwan sovereignty amid Chinese pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
03:22:41 UTC
12:22:41 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) urged the legal community to continue defending Taiwan’s sovereignty at home and abroad.
Speaking at a lawyer banquet on Saturday, Lai said that in addition to political and military pressure, China is contorting UN Resolution 2758 by claiming Taiwan as part of its territory, per the Presidential Office.
He pointed out that the US State Department has publicly stated that World War II-era documents such as the Cairo Declaration, the Potsdam Proclamation, and the San Francisco Peace Treaty do not establish that Taiwan is part of China. UN Resolution 2758 addresses China’s representation at the UN and has nothing to do with Taiwan, Lai said.
The president said his foremost responsibility is to protect the nation, safeguard sovereignty, and defend its democracy and freedom.
As the need for AI law rises, building the necessary legal framework and resolving related issues will require collective efforts from all sectors, Lai said. Issues such as digital human rights and intellectual property rights will require greater involvement from legal professionals to help protect Taiwan’s key position in global supply chains, he said.
Lai added that Taiwan must pursue a smart, net-zero transition. He expressed hope that the legal community will help implement ESG-related regulations and help turn international green standards into a competitive advantage for the country's industries.

"Knowing that it's out of our control, so just getting back to sleep and waking up. No-one was going to feel sorry for us."

Israel must fight harder to keep its doctors in the country - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
03:07:11 UTC
12:07:11 KST

Israel is losing doctors at an alarming rate. It should be doing everything possible to keep them. But it should also recognize an opportunity: Israel can recruit more Jewish doctors from around the world to make aliyah.
The Jerusalem Post recently reported that 1,370 Israeli doctors left the country for more than a year between 2023 and 2025, a 94% increase compared with the equivalent period a decade earlier.
Not every doctor who spends a year abroad is gone for good. Physicians leave for fellowships, research, specialist training, and other reasons before returning. But the trend should concern policymakers. After accounting for returning physicians, Israel recorded a net loss of 509 doctors in 2023 and 2024, roughly five times the annual average of the previous decade.
The government’s first responsibility is obvious: Find out why doctors are leaving and give them reasons to stay.
Israeli physicians work under enormous pressure. The healthcare system must offer competitive conditions, professional advancement, adequate staffing, and a sense that young doctors can build their futures here.
Israel's two-pronged path toward doctor retention
But retention should be only half of Israel’s strategy. The other half should be recruitment.
Israel is the national home of the Jewish people, and Jewish communities worldwide contain doctors, nurses, researchers, therapists, and other healthcare professionals. Some already dream of making aliyah. Others might consider it if Israel made the process easier and they saw a clear opportunity to contribute.
Israel already has an International Medical Aliyah Program, run by Nefesh B’Nefesh with the Aliyah and Integration Ministry, Health Ministry, and Jewish Agency. Its goal is to facilitate the aliyah of 2,000 physicians by 2029 by streamlining licensing and helping doctors find placements.
The government should expand and accelerate that effort.
That means removing unnecessary barriers to recognizing foreign qualifications, expanding professional Hebrew programs, helping immigrants find placements, and assisting families with the practical difficulties of moving countries. Israel should also strengthen incentives for immigrant doctors willing to practice where shortages are most severe, particularly in the North and South.
There is ample precedent.
Former waves of aliyah provide a historical blueprint
Successive waves of aliyah have transformed Israel demographically and professionally. Immigration from the former Soviet Union brought thousands of doctors and nurses, alongside scientists, engineers, musicians, and academics. Their contribution to Israeli medicine, science, and technology is difficult to overstate.
There are encouraging signs. More than 1,100 North Americans made aliyah through Nefesh B’Nefesh in August alone. Approximately 2,700 had arrived since the beginning of 2026, and the organization expects more than 4,000 by year’s end. The current wave includes doctors and nurses.
Imagine a Jewish doctor in New York, Toronto, London, Paris, or Melbourne wondering whether Israel might someday become home. Israel could actively make the case: We need you. We will help you navigate licensing, learn professional Hebrew, and connect with hospitals and communities where your skills can make a difference.
That is not merely immigration policy. It is national planning.
None of this should become an excuse for ignoring why Israeli doctors are leaving.
It would be absurd to recruit a physician from New Jersey while failing to address the conditions driving a physician from Jerusalem abroad. A successful healthcare strategy must make Israel attractive both to the doctor considering aliyah and the Israeli medical student deciding where to build a career.
Nor should aliyah be viewed merely as a mechanism for filling labor shortages. People make aliyah for reasons of identity, family, community, faith, Zionism, and belonging. They are citizens building lives, not numbers on a manpower spreadsheet.
But Zionism has always involved matching individual aspirations with national needs.
Israel needs doctors. There are Jewish doctors around the world who may want to make Israel their home. Connecting the two is a natural proposition for a country that prides itself on creative solutions to difficult problems
The physician crisis is a warning and a call to action
The rise in doctors leaving Israel should serve as a warning and a call to action.
Israel must fight harder to keep the medical professionals it has. At the same time, it should open the door wider to those who want to join them.
A brain drain demands a brain-gain strategy. For Israel, part of that strategy may be waiting in Jewish communities around the world.

AI generated
NEW YORK – A quarter of a century after the era-defining attacks of Sept 11, 2001, the United States is eager to keep alive the memory of a trauma that is fading as the proportion of Americans who did not experience it first-hand grows.
US President Donald Trump will pay his respects at the Pentagon rather than in New York, where the attacks by hijacked passenger planes on the World Trade Center towers claimed the largest number of the 2,977 total victims recorded on that day.
But Vice-President J.D. Vance and Trump’s four living predecessors – Democrats Joe Biden, Barack Obama and Bill Clinton, as well as Republican George W. Bush, who was president at the time of the attacks – are all expected at the Ground Zero site in Lower Manhattan on Sept 11.
The anniversary commemorates a watershed moment for the US and the world.
“Many in my generation remember exactly where we were on that horrific day,” said Beth Hillman, 59, president of the 9/11 Memorial & Museum and a US Air Force veteran.
Yet today, “100 million Americans were not even born or are too young to remember” the tragic events.
‘More inquisitive’ young people
After placing major emphasis on the duty to remember, her institution is now focusing on outreach, education and engaging younger generations.
Trained volunteers, including first responders, connect with audiences who have learnt of the disaster solely through their parents or school.
“Even if you were alive but not here or have a connection, it’s a lot easier to understand the magnitude of what took place,” Logan Miller, a 32-year-old who lost an uncle and a grandfather as a result of the attacks, told AFP.
Making sense of 9/11 is “a little tougher for that next generation”, he added.
Miller is one of many volunteers sharing their experiences at the museum, which gets 2.4 million unique visitors per year, or through video clips.
Young people are “more inquisitive” and ask more questions than their elders, who Miller said sometimes hesitate to challenge him for fear of causing offence.
“I wasn’t born at the time and yet it was important for me to be here, to do this trip,” said 22-year-old Ignacio Gaete, a Chilean visiting the museum and memorial featuring two large recessed pools within the footprints of the Twin Towers.
Gaete said that while young people do not have visceral memories of 9/11 like his father does, “I think it can transcend generations”.
But that transcendence requires preservation and education, according to Holly Kafka, visiting Manhattan from Chicago with her husband.
“Our younger generation... they’re always in this little rat race, keeping up with social media,” the 61-year-old said. “We have to stop them and say, ‘Come here and experience it.’”
9,400 more deaths

A third plane struck the Pentagon, while a fourth – which apparently had targeted the US Capitol or the White House – crashed into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought back.

Europe cannot afford to lose the race for biomedical innovation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

Europe cannot afford to lose the race for biomedical innovation
As clinical trials and investment increasingly turn elsewhere, European patients are missing out on breakthrough treatments. Policy can make a real difference here.
Europe stands at a crossroads. For decades, it led the world in pharmaceutical research, delivering medical advances that have transformed the lives of millions. But that leadership can no longer be taken for granted. U.S. trade policies toward the pharmaceutical industry, including tariffs and Most Favoured Nation pricing, underscore the urgency of Europe’s response, while China is advancing at unprecedented speed.
Fina Lladós
The figures speak for themselves. Europe led the launch of new medicines in the 1990s but lost that lead to the U.S. in the following decade and, by 2024, to China as well. Over the past 20 years, the EU’s share of global pharmaceutical research and development investment has fallen significantly, while the proportion of clinical trials conducted in Europe has also declined sharply.
This is particularly alarming in the fields that will shape the future of medicine. Advanced therapies, personalized treatments, and solutions for genetic diseases and certain cancers are increasingly being developed elsewhere. Every clinical trial that moves away and every patent filed outside Europe mean a real loss of knowledge, skilled jobs and opportunities for Europeans.
This is not a theoretical risk. The pandemic exposed how reliance on external supply chains can threaten access to essential medical products, underscoring why the pharmaceutical industry is now recognized as strategic for Europe’s competitiveness, security and autonomy. A strong biopharmaceutical industry is therefore not only an economic asset; it is essential to health security and to Europe’s ability to respond to future crises.
Every clinical trial that moves away and every patent filed outside Europe mean a real loss of knowledge, skilled jobs and opportunities for Europeans.
Much of Europe’s declining appeal can be explained by developments across the Atlantic. The U.S. represents a much larger share of the global pharmaceutical market and has long offered stronger incentives for innovation, steadily attracting research investment. New measures to reinforce domestic production and draw further investment to the U.S. risk accelerating this trend. For Europe, the message is clear: strengthening our own regulatory and fiscal incentives for innovation is no longer optional — it is urgent, and it is entirely in our hands.
Greater competitiveness also requires faster and fairer access to treatments by removing unnecessary restrictions. Access to innovation is not only an industry issue; it is also a societal one. Scientific investment must reach patients, because better health also strengthens the economy.
Europe still has an exceptional scientific and academic base, but it has not always translated that knowledge into innovation that delivers wellbeing and social progress on the same scale. The priority now is to build a life-sciences ecosystem that translates research into tangible solutions for citizens.
Developing a medicine takes 10 to 15 years, which is why companies need predictable regulation, legal certainty and policies that recognize the value of innovation.
Spain illustrates this paradox clearly. It is Europe’s fourth-largest pharmaceutical market and a leader in clinical trials, yet patients still wait too long for approved treatments. Scientific excellence does not automatically translate into timely access; closing that gap is a challenge for all of Europe, not Spain alone.
Developing a medicine takes 10 to 15 years, which is why companies need predictable regulation, legal certainty and policies that recognize the value of innovation. Intellectual property protection is central to this. Weakening it will not sustainably lower medicine costs; it will only reduce the incentive to research and develop new treatments in Europe.
Europe’s competitiveness also depends on its ability to attract and conduct clinical trials, where scientific ideas become treatments and much of biomedical innovation’s economic value is created. Faster approvals, harmonized procedures across member states and stronger research infrastructure would make Europe a far more attractive destination for global investment.
Europe also needs an ambitious industrial policy to expand and modernize its biopharmaceutical manufacturing capacity. Research and industry reinforce each other, and advanced therapies, personalized medicine and AI-driven drug discovery require industrial capabilities that Europe must build now.
This is why the forthcoming European Biotech Act matters. If it reduces unnecessary administrative burdens, improves access to venture capital and creates real regulatory sandboxes for advanced therapies, it could send the strongest signal yet that Europe is serious about global competitiveness. This opportunity must not be weakened by half-measures.
Policymakers must now act with urgency: protect and reward innovation, remove barriers to faster access, strengthen Europe’s industrial and research base, and make biomedical innovation a strategic priority.
AI can accelerate the discovery of new molecules, optimize clinical trials and enable more precise medicine, provided it is supported by modern regulation that ensures transparency, data protection and human oversight. The European Health Data Area could be decisive if Europe guarantees interoperability, simplifies procedures, and fosters public trust. Together, these tools can accelerate research, improve data-driven decision-making, and ultimately benefit patients and society.
In an aging society, biomedicine and new technologies are delivering increasingly complex treatments that can also reduce broader public costs, such as those linked to sick leave. Yet healthcare systems remain underfunded and rarely account for the wider social value of biopharmaceutical innovation.
Europe’s biopharmaceutical industry and wider life-sciences ecosystem have enormous potential to invest, innovate and grow. But that potential must be consistently recognized and supported at the European level. Policymakers must now act with urgency: protect and reward innovation, remove barriers to faster access, strengthen Europe’s industrial and research base, and make biomedical innovation a strategic priority. This is not only about competitiveness, it is also about ensuring European patients can benefit earlier from the treatments of the future and that Europe can respond autonomously to the health challenges ahead. The choice is clear: Europe must act now.

AI data centres are less thirsty now, tech giants say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:40:00 UTC
11:40:00 KST

AI data centres are less thirsty now, tech giants say
NEW YORK – Data centres are running into a wall of public anger in the United States over their thirst for water and power.
The tech giants spending billions of dollars on them say the water part, at least, is solvable.
Data centres are the warehouses full of computer servers that run the internet and, increasingly, artificial intelligence.
The computers get hot and keeping them cool takes water.
American chip giant Nvidia said in a June report that it can eliminate water consumption almost entirely at some facilities when deploying DSX, its newest system for designing and managing AI data centres.
It is a bold claim and one that the industry is under mounting pressure to make good on.
In 2025, data centres consumed 222 billion litres of water worldwide for cooling, according to consultancy Rystad Energy.
Without adaptive measures, the figure could nearly triple to 644 billion litres by 2030, Rystad estimates. Steps to limit the growth could keep it under double.
Nvidia’s new method uses a closed-loop cooling system in which liquid flows directly through the servers, as close as possible to the chips, whose temperature can rise above 80 deg C.
The problem is that “there’s a pretty direct trade-off between how much water is used and how much energy is used” for temperature control, said Andy Masley, an independent researcher who covers AI and data centres.
Cutting back on water use usually means more power as the liquid in those sealed pipes still has to be cooled down somehow, usually by blowing air over it – and that takes electricity.
Nvidia gets around some of this by letting the liquid enter the servers warmer than usual, at 45 deg C.
Most other closed-loop systems ran at about 32 deg C in 2024, according to the Uptime Institute, which certifies data centres.
By starting with warmer water, Nvidia does not need to pump in cooled air year-round.
Josh Parker, Nvidia’s head of sustainability, said “simple fans circulating the air” are often enough, although sometimes, a mix of methods is needed.
At sites in extreme climates, or during a heatwave, chill airflow or water evaporation is still necessary.
Public relations
Microsoft, Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Meta told AFP that they also use closed-loop systems, which they said involve no net water loss.
The two cloud computing giants, which have been expanding their already huge data centre footprints, used more water overall between 2022 and 2025, but the water-use efficiency improved by 25 per cent at Microsoft and 37 per cent at AWS, according to their most recent sustainability reports.
There is no industrywide consistency, however, in how companies report data on so-called environmental, social and governance (ESG) efforts.
Elon Musk’s SpaceX, now a major player in data centres after it acquired his AI company, xAI, has never published an ESG report.
In June, ratings agency MSCI gave SpaceX its lowest ESG score.
Ren Shaolei, an engineering professor at the University of California, Riverside, said that “because water is generally much cheaper than electricity”, companies have less incentive to cut water use on cost grounds alone.
There are incentives, Ren said, but they have more to do with public relations amid the growing backlash to data centres across the US.
Another obstacle is that upgrading an older data centre to newer, less thirsty technology is expensive.
This may matter less than it sounds.
Older data centres are smaller and less powerful than the enormous new ones being built now, so they need less cooling in the first place, said Minh Khoi Le, who leads data centre and hydrogen research at Rystad.
And the water a data centre uses directly is only part of the story.
Water is used to generate the electricity that powers the data centre and to manufacture its chips and servers.
In the US, that hidden water use can be twice the amount a data centre consumes on its own. AFP

The Kang Gon destroyer is the second ship of the Choe Hyon-class destroyers. It possesses "integrated combat capability" and can carry out operational missions in any waters, the Korean Central News Agency noted.

====================================================================================================

Israel loses 1,370 doctors in three years as brain drain intensifies: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:34:59 UTC
11:34:59 KST

Zein Khalil and Tarek Chouiref
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
At least 1,370 doctors left Israel between 2023 and 2025 according to a new study by Tel Aviv University, highlighting a deepening brain drain from the country’s medical sector.
The findings were published Sunday by the Israeli newspaper Haaretz.
The study classifies doctors as having left if they spent more than 270 days abroad during their first year away and did not subsequently remain in Israel for more than three consecutive months.
Prof. Itay Ater, one of the study’s authors, said economists had warned since 2023 of an accelerating departure of skilled professionals amid Israel’s political and security turmoil.
He said concerns first emerged during the government’s judicial overhaul push and intensified after the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks and the war that followed.
Researchers focused particularly on doctors over 45, who have typically completed specialist training and play a central role in training younger physicians.
One in five doctors who left Israel during the three-year period was over 45, a trend the study described as worrying.
The losses were particularly pronounced in several specialties.
Some 116 ophthalmologists, dermatologists and ear, nose and throat (ENT) specialists left Israel, equivalent to 6.2% of physicians in those fields, while 188 surgeons – around 6% of the total – also departed.
The Tel Aviv area recorded the highest departure rate, with 5.4% of doctors leaving, according to the study.
The findings follow a report by the Israeli Finance Ministry last week showing that around 24% of specialist doctors in public hospitals are expected to reach retirement age in the coming years.
Another 25% have already passed retirement age but continue working amid shortages in medical staff.
Ater warned that the trajectory, rather than the current situation alone, was the greater concern, saying the trend could worsen after Israel’s general election scheduled for Oct. 27.
The study adds to broader signs of rising emigration from Israel.
Another Tel Aviv University study published in August found that 268,509 Israelis left the country between 2023 and 2025 for at least three months, a figure the Israeli public broadcaster KAN described as a record.
Israeli reports have linked the rise in departures to the war, high living costs and the political crisis surrounding the government’s efforts to weaken judicial powers.
A Kantar poll for KAN in August found that around one in five Israelis had considered emigrating over the previous two years, while 12% said the outcome of the upcoming election could affect their decision to remain in the country.

Taiwan finds new uses for agricultural waste
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:33:04 UTC
11:33:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan is turning agricultural waste into new products as part of efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, with the initiative generating NT$150 million (US$4.7 million) in output, according to the Ministry of Agriculture.
The drive toward net-zero agriculture began in 2022, when the ministry unveiled a strategy to cut emissions by 2040. Since then, Agriculture Minister Chen Junne-jih (陳駿季) said the program has helped develop 49 products made from agricultural waste.
A total of 19 companies have joined the initiative, with combined investment reaching NT$320 million as businesses seek ways to put materials that would otherwise be discarded to new uses.
One example is yarn made from discarded oyster shells by a textile company in Tainan. The firm has also combined oyster shell powder with recycled plastic bottles to produce functional fibers, according to CNA.
Agricultural waste can also be reused as an energy source. A dried longan farm in Tainan, for instance, processes pruned branches and other dry wood from its grounds into biomass pellets. The pellets are then burned as fuel to dry longan.
Chen said cutting emissions from agriculture requires more than reducing energy consumption. Changes in farming and livestock practices are also needed, including measures to reduce methane emissions from rice cultivation and livestock manure, as well as nitrous oxide emissions linked to fertilizer use.
Farmers have increased their use of nitrogen fertilizer to boost crop yields. However, excess nitrogen can be released as nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas that traps nearly 300 times more heat than carbon dioxide, according to the Agricultural Technology Research Institute.
Taiwan’s agricultural sector emitted about 6.5 billion kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024, accounting for approximately 2.38% of the country’s total emissions. The figure includes emissions from crop production, livestock, forestry, and fisheries, according to the Climate Change Administration.

For months, Ukraine has conducted a sustained campaign of drone and missile strikes against Russian oil infrastructure. Damage to energy facilities has prompted Moscow to impose export restrictions as domestic supplies have tightened and long queues have formed across the country.
Ukraine's General Staff announced on September 4 that two major Russian oil facilities have suspended operations following Ukrainian drone strikes in August. 
Lukoil's NORSI refinery in Kstovo, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, located about 800 kilometers (nearly 500 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was shut down due to damage suffered in a Ukrainian drone attack on Aug. 26. The General Staff also said the Novatek-Ust-Luga complex in Slobidka, Leningrad Oblast, had suspended operations following Ukrainian drone strikes on Sept. 1. Located about 850 kilometers (nearly 530 miles) from the Ukrainian border, the facility is one of Russia's largest ports on the Baltic Sea and home to an oil terminal that serves as a major hub for exporting crude oil and petroleum products.

This strategic partnership is particularly special because it rests on the solid foundation of our long-standing cultural and political ties,” he said.

Romain Rolland’s writings on Ramakrishna Paramahamsa and Swami Vivekananda brought our societies closer,” he said.

in brief
- More than 210 of Bathla's 350 staff were stood down at a meeting in Sydney on Monday morning.
- Homebuyers who bought off-the-plan have been left in the dark, uncertain when, or if, their properties will be completed.
Property developer Bathla Group has stood down almost two-thirds of its workforce following its entry into voluntary administration earlier this year.
About 213 of Bathla's 350 staff were stood down at a meeting in Sydney on Monday morning, and construction on several projects has halted as the embattled firm clings to life.
Administrators said they had secured short-term funding to keep some of the firm's projects going.
Insolvency adviser Teneo announced it had secured the funding through five lenders linked to the projects, but the amounts and participants were kept confidential.
Administrator Stephen Longley said the funding would enable Bathla Group to maintain limited operations for a further two weeks while longer-term solutions were explored.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Our immediate priority has been to secure sufficient short-term funding to maintain a minimum viable operating structure," he said.
"The arrangements agreed allow us to provide the central support required for construction to continue on projects associated with the lenders participating in the funding package.
"Significant work remains to secure the funding required to progress and ultimately complete all projects currently under construction. We will continue to work closely with lenders and other key stakeholders to pursue those arrangements."
Figures presented to creditors put Bathla's total debt at $3.4 billion, including $3.08 billion to secured lenders, $130 million to unsecured lenders, $145 million to the tax office and $4 million to employees.
Bathla is one of Sydney's largest residential developers, with 45 projects under construction.
The home developer entered voluntary administration in late August after the NSW government declined to bail it out.
According to the company's website, the group has 20,000 apartments and 7,000 dwellings in its delivery pipeline, comprising a significant share of the NSW government's target of 75,400 new homes a year for five years until 2029.
Homebuyers who bought off-the-plan have been left in the dark, uncertain when, or if, their properties will be completed, while contractors have been left scrambling to recoup debts.
Founded in NSW in 1997, Bathla is among a long list of Australian home developers that have recently entered voluntary administration or liquidation.

US must drop ‘hegemon’ mindset for Ukraine peace – Jeffrey Sachs
US backroom diplomacy on Ukraine cannot achieve peace without Washington accepting that it is no longer the world’s sole superpower, economist and public policy scholar Jeffrey Sachs has told RT.
The comments follow separate closed-door talks held by US special envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky in Kiev over the weekend. Details of the proposals exchanged during the meetings have not been made public.
“The US still has a grandiose idea that it is the world’s hegemon and the sole superpower, and it is not. Clearly, we are in a multi-polar world,” Sachs told RT in an exclusive interview on Sunday.
Sachs argued that a peace settlement requires taking Russia’s security interests into account and abandoning the expansionist foreign policy the US has pursued for more than 30 years.
“It seems to be psychologically very difficult” for Washington to openly accept that “basic reality,” he argued, saying this is why it resorts to “backroom negotiations” and secrecy that ultimately produce no tangible results.
Sachs also described the situation in Ukraine as an “endgame situation,” arguing that Kiev is in a desperate position militarily, socially, and politically.

Watch: CCTV captures moment Delhi's Satya Niketan building collapse, leaving 6 dead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:20:26 UTC

The CCTV footage showed the building suddenly giving way, sending debris crashing onto the road
NEW DELHI: CCTV footage has captured the moment a multi-storey building collapsed in Delhi's Satya Niketan area, killing six people and triggering a major rescue operation.The building, which housed a boys' paying guest accommodation near Delhi University's South Campus, collapsed around 1.30 pm on Sunday while repair and construction work was underway. The death toll rose to six after one more person rescued during the night was declared dead.The CCTV footage showed the building suddenly giving way, sending debris crashing onto the road. Rescue and search operations continued through the night as teams searched the rubble for anyone who may still be trapped.
Multiple agencies, including the Delhi Police, Delhi Fire Service, National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and Delhi Disaster Management Authority, have been involved in the operation."One more person was rescued during the night but was brought dead, taking the toll to six," Deputy Commissioner of Police (Southwest) Amit Goel said, PTI reported.Police have registered a case against the building owner and others, while a magisterial inquiry has also been ordered. Officials are continuing efforts to trace people allegedly connected with the incident.To the residents, the collapse felt like a quake. “We felt the ground shake.
When we ran outside, we saw that a house had completely collapsed,” said Roshan Pal, a student from Lucknow.“When I came out, a cloud of dust was spreading in all directions. That’s when we realised that the building had collapsed. We started removing one part of a wall soon after. Seven students were under it,” said Rahul Gaur, a resident, TOI reported.
10 patients taken to Trauma CentreAccording to AIIMS, the JPN Apex Trauma Centre received 10 patients injured in the building collapse. Of the 10 patients, five were brought dead, while another patient who was in critical condition later succumbed to injuries.Three patients have been admitted and are undergoing treatment. One of them underwent limb surgery, while another patient with minor injuries was discharged after observation.Investigators are examining whether construction work carried out in the basement may have contributed to the collapse.Initial inquiries suggested that the basement was prone to waterlogging, which may have weakened the structure. Investigators are now examining whether construction work aggravated the situation and contributed to the collapse.The MCD is also looking into the matter. Similar concerns over basement work, water accumulation and the structural condition of the building have emerged in the preliminary probe.Police are likely to examine whether permission had been obtained for the work and why construction was being carried out during the monsoon, sources said. "The building owner, contractor and labourers will be interrogated," an investigator said, TOI reported.It was not immediately clear whether the building owner had obtained permission for the construction or whether the work was being carried out illegally, allegedly in connivance with local authorities.
MCD orders demolition of dangerous buildingAccording to the MCD, the premises of Building/House No. 13, Satya Niketan, New Delhi, was found to be in a "ruinous, dangerous condition" and posed a threat to people occupying, visiting or passing by the building as well as those in the neighbourhood.Under Section 348 of the DMC Act, 1957, read with Section 491 of the Act, the MCD has ordered the property to be demolished within three days of receipt of the order.The order said that if the owner fails to comply within the specified period, the MCD will demolish the building and recover the demolition charges as arrears of tax.The collapse has raised fresh questions over the safety of buildings being used as paying guest accommodations and the enforcement of construction and fire safety norms in densely populated areas of Delhi.Congress leader and AICC Uttarakhand in-charge Kumari Selja questioned the BJP government over the safety of students living in such accommodations.“What is the BJP government doing? They have forgotten what happened at the coaching centre. A mafia is operating in Delhi. These children are sent away with so many hopes. They are the only support for their parents. Who is responsible for their safety?” Selja said.
Former Delhi chief secretary Omesh Saigal said the incident should not be viewed in isolation and raised concerns over unauthorised construction in parts of the capital."Look at the kind of buildings constructed in Delhi—I would say that in some areas, one in five buildings is unauthorised; either the blueprints weren't approved, extra floors were added, or the construction is substandard," he said.Saigal also called for restrictions on new construction in areas that are already overcrowded. "At the very least, we should ban new construction in these areas. We must halt new construction or stop sanctioning building plans, for areas that are already over-congested and over-built. These are the things that need to be addressed," he added.

Awad Rjoob and Tarek Chouiref
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Israeli authorities have ordered the demolition of five Palestinian homes north of occupied Jerusalem, giving residents as little as 24 hours to evacuate, the Jerusalem Governorate said Sunday.
One of the homes is located near the Jaba military checkpoint, while four others are in the Coptic neighborhood of Al-Ram, according to the governorate.
The owner of the house near the checkpoint was given 24 hours to leave before demolition, while residents of the other four homes were ordered to evacuate within two days.
The governorate said Israeli forces carried out 40 demolition and land-clearing operations targeting Palestinian structures in Jerusalem during August.
In a separate statement Sunday, it said Israeli authorities issued around 15 orders barring Palestinians from Al-Aqsa Mosque during the first six days of September alone.
The new orders brought the total documented since the beginning of 2026 to 800.
That figure is already close to the 23 exclusion orders recorded during July and August combined, including 17 in July and six in August.
By the end of August, the governorate had documented 785 such orders since the start of the year, including 762 during the first half of 2026.
Most targeted Palestinians were barred from Al-Aqsa Mosque particularly in the period leading up to and during Ramadan, the governorate said.
It said the sharp rise in September reflected an intensified use of exclusion orders ahead of the Jewish holiday season, which runs from mid-September into early October.
Around 750,000 Israeli occupiers live in 194 illegal settlements and 400 outposts across the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem. They carry out almost daily attacks aimed at forcibly displacing Palestinians from their land.
Since Israel launched its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip on Oct. 8, 2023, the occupied West Bank has witnessed daily raids by the Israeli army and attacks by Israeli occupiers.

US Navy SEALS conducted covert four-month mission to clear Strait of Hormuz mines - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:15:48 UTC
11:15:48 KST

US special forces spent four months conducting a secret mine-clearing mission in the Strait of Hormuz in an attempt to open up the waterway, the Financial Times reported Sunday.
Iran has said it placed mines in international and Omani waters following the outbreak of the war. The International Maritime Organization estimated in June that roughly 80 mines had been deployed along important shipping routes.
The covert operation was carried out amid ongoing exchanges of strikes between the US and Iran in and around the Strait, according to people familiar with the mission.
Navy SEAL divers worked with unmanned vessels, robots, and specialized underwater equipment to locate and remove suspected Iranian mines, often operating at night.
The objective of the operation was to make the strait safer for commercial vessels that had largely avoided the waterway since the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
US President Donald Trump announced last week that “all mines” in the strait's international waters had been removed or destroyed, a claim subsequently confirmed by the US military.
The announcement came despite reports showing that three US vessels normally assigned to mine-countermeasure operations in the Gulf had been operating in the Indian and Pacific oceans since at least early June.
US uses divers, unmanned systems to clear mines
Mine-clearing can be painstaking, lengthy, and inherently dangerous in peacetime, and an active conflict adds further risks.
For these operations, small teams of Navy divers worked from inflatable-hulled boats, supported by unmanned surface vessels and submersibles equipped with advanced sonar to locate underwater objects. Despite the advanced technology, divers may still have had to approach and destroy the mines directly.
“That is usually followed up by a navy diver who’s got to get in the water and approach the mine, and then put a charge on it and destroy it,” retired US Navy captain Bill Hamblet told the FT.
No US casualties have been reported in connection with the operation.
“It is an extremely time-consuming process,” said Nitya Labh, an associate fellow at Chatham House. “They are doing, essentially, active bomb detonation underwater.”
Questions remain over whether Strait is mine-free
Despite Trump's declaration, uncertainty remains over whether the entire Strait of Hormuz has been cleared.
Shipping companies and maritime security advisers believe areas near Oman, where the US has been directing ships through the strait, have likely been cleared, but remain less certain about the rest of the waterway.
“It doesn’t take much to put a mine back in because there is a lot of small-boat traffic going across Hormuz every night," a tanker industry executive said.
The uncertainty itself gives Tehran leverage. Even the possibility of mines can discourage commercial shipping and increase insurance costs, while concerns remain that Iran could deploy new mines in areas already cleared by US forces.
Oil prices dropped five percent following Trump's announcement but have since returned to their previous levels as strikes have resumed.
“It’s hard to know what to believe,” said Ethan Connell, assistant director of Taiwan Security Monitor and a mine warfare expert. “Iran is certainly trying to re-mine.”
Hamblet said Iran benefits strategically from the perception that it can disrupt the critical waterway.
“The Iranians have realized that their strongest card is the perception that they control the Strait of Hormuz. If they can convince the world that they can threaten the strait, that’s their strongest source of strategic leverage,” he said.

Ben-Gvir tells police commissioner he will not approve officer appointments until after election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:15:47 UTC
11:15:47 KST

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir informed Police Commissioner Insp.-Gen. Danny Levi that he would not approve appointments of senior police officers until after the election, and in a letter sent to him on Sunday argued that advancing appointments at the current time could harm public trust.
In the letter, titled “Your desire to hold a round of police officer appointments about a month and a half before elections,” Ben-Gvir noted that the election is expected to take place on October 27 and that the Knesset has already entered recess. He said that during an election period, restrictions apply to government activity, including appointments in the public service.
He also claimed that about four months ago he suggested to the commissioner that a round of appointments be advanced, but Levi did not provide him with a list of candidates at the time. Ben-Gvir wrote that his position is that “there is an obligation to act with restraint and moderation, due to concerns of harming public trust,” adding that he opposes holding a round of senior police appointments at this time.
According to Ben-Gvir, “this is not, God forbid, any kind of statement against the wonderful male and female officers of the Israel Police,” but rather a public and legal issue concerning conduct during an election period.
The minister also recalled that when the current government took office, the attorney-general sent a letter to the previous minister ordering a sweeping ban on senior police appointments ahead of the incoming government. Ben-Gvir argued that a similar standard should now be applied, concluding: “I hereby inform you that as the minister responsible for the police, there will be no further appointments of senior officers in the Israel Police until after the elections.”
Later Sunday night, Ben-Gvir’s office said: “Following reports regarding recommendations for police appointments, and as the minister announced earlier today, there will be no appointments before the elections, except in exceptional cases. Approval of exceptional cases will be discussed individually by the minister, after the commissioner presents reasons. All other appointments will be discussed gladly after the elections.”
Ben-Gvir blocks Attorney-General's candidate for police legal adviser deputy
The letter also comes amid another dispute between Ben-Gvir and the police commissioner. Sources close to the minister said that Levi, who had complained to Ben-Gvir about the number of Israel Prison Service appointments made by Commissioner Kobi Yaakobi, had initially received approval to move forward with preparing recommendations for police appointments.
However, according to the minister’s associates, Levi later met on Thursday with Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara, and discussions included the issue of appointing a deputy to the police legal adviser.
According to those sources, Baharav-Miara was willing to allow the appointments to proceed, but requested the appointment of a deputy to the police legal adviser and even named a candidate for the position.
At a later meeting between Ben-Gvir and Levi, when the commissioner raised the name of that candidate, the minister presented his letter and the attorney-general’s previous position regarding appointments during an election period, effectively blocking the move.
Sources close to Ben-Gvir told Maariv, “The commissioner can hold a ceremony for the commissioner’s recommended appointments, but the minister will not approve the appointments.”
Police officers threaten to petition High Court over appointments
Senior officials close to the commissioner, police officers with the rank of deputy commissioner, said Sunday evening that if Ben-Gvir does not sign off on appointments approved during a meeting held on that day at the commissioner’s office, they will not hesitate to petition the High Court of Justice.
The meeting was held with the participation of senior command staff and a representative of the National Security Ministry, Moshe Bachar from the ministry’s budget department. “This will be a disgraceful mark against the minister,” the officials said.
The officials also claimed that about NIS 500 million, transferred in March to the National Security Ministry and allocated for the Israel Police, remains “stuck” at the ministry.
“Under the commissioner’s instructions, renovations began at several police stations, but the work stopped because the budget is not being transferred to the police, even though it belongs to it. Patrol vehicles have not been purchased despite the critical need to deal with crime in general and crime in the Arab sector in particular. In the north, criminals drive Rubicons, while we are stuck with five-year-old vehicles. We did not ask for a personal vehicle, but rather patrol cars and vehicles for special units,” they said.
The officials said the commissioner does not intend to back down on the appointments issue.
“The commissioner will not give up and will not compromise regarding the appointment of officers, because this is an opportunity and this is what the police need. If the commander of the Ayalon District has announced his retirement, then it is clear that a deputy commissioner must be appointed in his place, and this is a large district. How can the police operate without a head of the Planning and Organization Division? The commissioner will also request special approval for that.”
The officials added, “One thing needs to be understood: The commissioner and the senior command staff have the authority to appoint officers up to the rank of deputy commissioner without anyone else’s approval, and the minister has the final authority to approve the appointments with his signature. These are purely professional appointments, not matters of connections or politics.”
They also said, “Only recently, more than 40 senior officers were appointed in the Israel Prison Service and the minister approved them, so how can he prevent approval of appointments in the ministry’s largest organization?”
Meanwhile, senior officials close to the commissioner pledged to the police leadership that they would not retreat from their professional positions.
“I am made of a different material. I will not fold and I will not give up on things I believe in professionally. It is possible that I made mistakes in one appointment or another, but I did not act based on any consideration that was not professional,” Levi said.
“I respect the person who appointed me, but I am not easily pressured, rather I am rough and tough. I am giving this days, not more than that, because the police belong to the public and everyone, including the minister, wants a strong police force. Despite what people are trying to portray, we have built a police force here and the data can prove it. If they want me to continue for another year, as a fourth year, an event I am not thinking about at the moment, as someone who loves and breathes policing I would be happy to continue on my path and implement the goals,” was his claim.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07

Security officials are expected in the coming days to decide how to carry out the destruction phase in what they consider the most effective way.
The operations by commando forces and the elite Yahalom combat engineering unit were conducted under the command of the IDF’s 36th Division.
Hezbollah’s leadership is deeply concerned by Israel’s determination to eliminate its remaining assets on the ridge and is seeking ways to stop the operation, according to Israeli security assessments.
Israeli officials believe Hezbollah is trying to draw Iran more directly into the confrontation in an effort to create a new deterrence equation that would prevent Israel from destroying the infrastructure.
At the same time, Israel’s security establishment is closely watching Washington and President Donald Trump, hoping the United States will not pressure Israel to halt the operation before it is completed.
Once a decision is made to finish the operation, IDF forces are expected to withdraw to defensive positions farther back. Preparations for that move are already underway.
The military’s goal is to establish a significant and fortified defensive line ahead of the Jewish holiday period, while continuing to maintain the existing framework with Lebanon in designated pilot areas.
Israeli military officials acknowledge, however, that developments on the ground have not yet produced progress they consider satisfactory.
Escalation spreads across southern Lebanon
Tensions around the ridge are rising as the cycle of escalation in southern Lebanon widens.
On Saturday, Hezbollah launched two explosive drones toward Israeli troops controlling the security area in southern Lebanon. One of the drones was intercepted by troops, and no Israeli casualties were reported.
The IDF described the launches as a blatant violation of the ceasefire agreement and responded with a broad wave of airstrikes in the Nabatieh area and elsewhere in southern Lebanon.
Israeli fighter jets struck what the military described as Hezbollah weapons storage facilities and military buildings.
The IDF also said it struck an active Hezbollah command center established inside a building that had previously served as a hospital.
According to the military, Hezbollah operatives had recently used the site to advance attack plans, conduct surveillance and direct artillery fire.
Before the strikes, the IDF said it took steps intended to reduce harm to civilians, including issuing an urgent evacuation warning to residents of the village of Arab Salim and instructing them to remain about 300 meters from the targeted site.
The military said it would continue operating forcefully around the Ali Taher Ridge and across southern Lebanon to remove threats and would not allow Hezbollah to attack Israeli troops or civilians, while maintaining Israel’s commitment to the ceasefire agreement.
The tension surrounding the ridge is expected to continue in the coming days as Israeli officials determine how best to destroy the remaining infrastructure.
For now, the IDF’s objective is to complete the operation without triggering repercussions that could spread into other arenas.

Ukrainian forces had previously struck the Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez oil refinery on July 29 as part of Ukraine's broader missile and drone campaign against Russian energy and oil infrastructure far from Ukraine. 
The Atesh partisan group regularly sabotages Russian military infrastructure in Ukraine's occupied territories and in Russia.
The group claimed credit for the sabotage of an electric substation powering a military plant in southern Russia on June 20. Members of Atesh allegedly sabotaged an electric locomotive used by the Russian military in Russia's Lipetsk Oblast on May 10.
The group is also active in Russian-occupied Crimea, where it has reported an increase both in people wishing to join and in those willing to pass on important information about Russia's military facilities and weapons.

Poland’s anti-Ukrainian turn spills into violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:01:00 UTC
11:01:00 KST

WARSAW — Poland’s nationalist right is turning hostility toward the country’s roughly 1.5 million Ukrainians into a potent political issue, tapping into local resentment over social benefits and wartime history just over a year before a pivotal parliamentary election.
During Poland’s 2025 presidential campaign, politicians began portraying Ukrainians in Poland as freeloaders straining the country’s public finances.
This summer, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, of Poland’s highest honor, the Order of the White Eagle, in reaction to Zelenskyy’s decision to name a military unit after the World War II-era Ukrainian Insurgent Army, or UPA. The group murdered tens of thousands of Poles during an ethnic-cleansing campaign in 1943-1945, although it also fought against the Soviet Union.
Advertisement
Warsaw has been one of Kyiv’s strongest supporters against Russia since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. But the nationalist camp, which Nawrocki seeks to lead, has sought to capitalize on tensions over the Ukrainian presence in Poland and the wartime massacres.
Anti-Ukrainian rhetoric is already intensifying ahead of the fall 2027 parliamentary election, when Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s broadly pro-Ukraine coalition will face the nationalist Law and Justice party and two other far-right parties. Polls show Tusk is far from certain of victory.
The libertarian Confederation party denounced Ukrainians getting social welfare, while Gregorz Braun, the European Parliament member who leads the far-right Confederation of the Polish Crown party, said: “The Kyiv regime is neither our ally nor our friend, it is our enemy,” during a summer gathering commemorating the wartime killing of Polish civilians by Ukrainians.
Przemysław Czarnek, the candidate for prime minister from the Law and Justice party, said July: “Military aid to Ukraine must be suspended until that country changes its historical policy.”
Rafał Pankowski, a sociology professor at Warsaw’s Civitas University and co-founder of the Polish anti-racism group Never Again, believes that while the Polish population is broadly supportive of Ukraine, fissures are beginning to show.
“Solidarity with Ukrainians remains strong among many Poles, but populist anti-Ukrainian rhetoric has created fertile ground for attacks, turning a large and visible minority into a target and helping verbal hostility spill into violence. Russian propaganda seized on the opportunity, too,” he said.
Advertisement
Ukrainian Ambassador to Poland Vasyl Bodnar is worried about politicians using Ukraine as a wedge issue.
“Part of Poland’s political class is trying to exploit the Ukrainian issue for political gain. Some focus on developments in Ukraine, others on the behavior of Ukrainians living here. One way or another, Ukraine features in the narrative of every political group — it is simply packaged differently,” he told POLITICO.
In the line of fire
The latest Polish-Ukrainian row might have faded from the headlines, but the fear it helped instill has not.
Vasyl Bodnar is worried about politicians using Ukraine as a wedge issue. | Adem Altan/AFP via Getty Images
“I’ve lived in Poland for about 10 years. I came here to study and stayed,” said Olena, a guide at a Warsaw cultural institution whose name POLITICO changed at her request because she feared for her safety.
“It took me quite a while to integrate, but I have never felt as alienated as I have over the past year. I have become afraid to speak Ukrainian in public, and I have started worrying about my friends and loved ones who live here or come to Poland to visit,” she said.
Opinion polls show a decided shift against Ukrainians.
Advertisement
In an annual survey by the state-run pollster CBOS, sympathy among Poles toward Ukrainians fell from 51 percent in 2023 to 29 percent in January 2026, while antipathy rose from 38 percent to 43 percent over the last year.
Another CBOS poll found that 45.4 percent of those polled attributed the deterioration to disputes over the wartime massacres and historical policy, with social benefits for Ukrainians in second place at 36.4 percent.
Ivan, a Ukrainian national who works at the University of Warsaw and asked to only be identified by his first name, said a neighbor confronted him over Zelenskyy’s decision to name a military unit after the UPA.
“We were in the elevator. My neighbor started yelling at me, telling me to go back to Ukraine and explain to Zelenskyy that he shouldn’t have done that. It was absurd,” Ivan said.
Olena recalled a Polish woman following the group she was guiding and complaining that hearing her speak Polish was “an embarrassment” to her as a Pole.
“I said loudly that Polish was not my native language, that I came from Ukraine,” Olena said.
Advertisement
For Ivan and Olena, the hostility remained verbal. For other Ukrainians, it has turned violent.
In July, two men were arrested after two Ukrainians, Anastazja, 20, and her 21-year-old partner Maksym, were beaten outside a Wrocław grocery store. The attack was denounced by Poland’s Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha thanked the police for the arrests.
Earlier that month, an off-duty employee of Bielsko-Biała’s municipal bus company hurled nationality-based abuse at three Ukrainians, including two 11-year-old schoolgirls, on a bus.
Donald Tusk attends a ceremony in London on May 27, 2026. | Pool photo by Jack Taylor via WPA/Getty Images
In August, a Ukrainian man was attacked on a tram in Poznań.
The Polish police recorded 180 reports of ethnically motivated crimes against Ukrainians in the first half of this year, a 30 percent increase over the same period last year, reported the Rzeczpospolita newspaper.
The Polish government — which has tightened Ukrainians’ access to welfare, even though their collective contribution to Poland’s economy far exceeds public spending on them — set up 50 specialist prosecution teams in early 2026 to investigate hate crimes.
Advertisement
Between February and June, Polish prosecutors sent 283 cases to court. Ukrainians were the victims in more than 80 percent of such cases, up from 4 percent in 2014 and 74 percent in 2023.
Tusk said in July that attackers had become bolder because they believed they enjoyed political protection and called on Nawrocki to speak out on the matter.
“I am appealing directly to the president to stop remaining silent on this matter,” Tusk said. “We must wage a decisive fight against this violence, because the bandits, the hooligans, this violent pathology has gained courage and audacity because it has also received political patronage.”
The Roman Catholic Church has also weighed in, issuing an appeal “not to fuel nationalistic sentiments.”
Ambassador Bodnar hopes politicians will stop inflaming relations between the two countries.
“The best response will be effective communication — from politicians, the media, and, of course, government officials — who would communicate in a positive manner and resolve those issues that are painful or important to both sides,” Bodnar said.
Advertisement
For Ivan, the change in tone is making him more wary of drawing attention to himself in Poland.
“I still speak Ukrainian, and I wear a pin with the Polish and Ukrainian flags. What has changed is the way I feel about potential conflicts. I used to not be afraid to speak up and stand up for myself if someone attacked me because I’m Ukrainian,” he said. “Now I’m afraid no one would help me and that I would be accused of violating some law and simply deported, even though I’ve already built my life in Poland.”
The government’s policy is to deport Ukrainians even for minor offenses — one Ukrainian 18-year-old was kicked out of Poland for jumping a barrier at a concert.
