Russia has entered Sweden’s election campaign, center-left front-runner warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

STOCKHOLM — Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson must urgently take action to address claims that his potential far-right coalition partner may have been infiltrated by Russia ahead of this month’s general election, the front-runner in the race told POLITICO.
The call by Magdalena Andersson, leader of the center-left Social Democratic Party, which polls have on course to win the Sept. 13 election, comes after the campaign was rocked by claims that an official inside the far-right Sweden Democrats party had longstanding ties to Russia.
If Andersson wins, she’ll join embattled Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez as one of the few center-left politicians around the European leaders’ table. However, the gap between her coalition and a right-wing faction led by Kristersson has been narrowing as the election draws near. If Kristersson wins, the Sweden Democrats stand to enter government for the first time after the prime minister said he would govern with the far-right party.
Advertisement
“Ulf Kristersson must come clean about the security crisis,” Andersson told POLITICO in an interview. “These are extremely serious allegations … Russia is the greatest threat to Sweden.”
The claims, laid out in a Sept. 3 article by non-governmental group Expo, allege that a female Sweden Democrats official promoted pro-Kremlin narratives for a decade, cultivated ties with a Russian state-backed group in Sweden, and brought Russian family members onto the grounds of the Swedish parliament. The official, Polina Malaberg, who remains employed by the Sweden Democrats, previously held roles linked to parliamentary committees focusing on EU affairs.
Malaberg’s partner, Gustav Gellerbrant, is a senior civil servant and Sweden Democrats member who heads the party’s Coordination Office inside the government, acting as a liaison between the party and Kristersson’s current governing coalition. While Gellerbrant himself is not accused of Russia ties, his relationship with Malaberg raises questions about his security clearance, Andersson argues.
“Is there information relating to national security that may have been exposed?” Andersson asked. “What measures has the prime minister taken and what measures does he intend to take?”
Both Kristersson and Jimmie Åkesson, leader of the Sweden Democrats, have publicly addressed Expo’s claims. Kristersson said Malaberg should be fired if the allegations turn out to be true. “We are in a European war … You can’t have people who sit around promoting pro-Russian narratives and work in the Swedish parliament,” he told newspaper Aftonbladet.
Advertisement
Åkesson said his party had been unaware of the pro-Kremlin posts by Malaberg but conceded “we have to look at this and sort this out,” adding that the party was investigating the claims and that Malaberg could not continue to work for them if she maintained her pro-Russian views.
But these answers aren’t enough, said Andersson, a former finance minister and prime minister of Sweden. “When did the prime minister’s office become aware of this, and what information has been given to the prime minister?” she asked, adding: “This is about Sweden and the security of the Swedish people.”
Speaking to POLITICO from her parliamentary office in Stockholm, Andersson argued that the risks of having the Sweden Democrats in government go beyond security. “We’ve seen journalists threatened” since Kristersson started ruling with backing from the Sweden Democrats, she said. “NGOs are threatened if they criticize what the government is doing. They’ve been threatened to have their state support withdrawn.”
Ulf Kristersson has been in power since 2022. | Pool photo by Jaimi Joy via EFA/EPA
“There could be a Swedish government where half of the ministers, including the foreign minister and the EU minister, come from a party that thinks we should have an inquiry on exit” from the European Union, she added.
The question is whether Swedish voters will agree with Andersson that it’s time for a change (Kristersson has been in power since 2022).
Security and migration remain top campaign issues. Kristersson’s camp vows to crack down harder on gang violence while ramping up deportations, including plans to deport some migrants who have been schooled in Sweden when they turn 18.
Advertisement
Quizzed about her migration stance, Andersson said Sweden’s previously open border policy was “unsustainable.” The country now requires a “very strict” migration policy, she said, adding that her party is open to supporting third-country “return hubs” — external deportation centers for migrants whose asylum applications have failed — if she wins.
But she said a Sweden Democrats proposal to strip permanent residency from some migrants crosses a line. “Once you have permanent residency, it’s permanent, right? You can’t say yes and then ‘no, we changed our minds’… That’s not how Sweden works. Many of these people work. They are bus drivers. They are entrepreneurs creating work… It’s insane.”
Asked whether she was closer to Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen or Spain’s Sánchez on migration, Andersson sidestepped, citing both as close contacts in Europe’s center-left camp.
Andersson touted strong support for Ukraine, a continued “frugal” stance on EU budget negotiations, and tough-on-crime policies as areas where she would maintain continuity with Kristersson’s government. She also favored using Russia’s frozen assets to help fund Ukraine and opposed “decoupling” with the United States.
“Many people say it’s enough now” with Sweden’s current government, Andersson concluded. “We’re the Social Democratic Party. Jobs and household economy, together with welfare, schools, hospitals and elderly care. These are the main issues.”

Author's YA book partly inspired by experience as sex educator in schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:55:22 UTC
10:55:22 KST

Bad Queer by Gayathiri Kamalakanthan and Chi Nwosu tells affirming coming-of-age story
Surya feels like a bad queer. When an ice cream man misgenders them, they stay silent.
"I pray for a sharper tongue," they think when a classmate harasses them for not looking like either a boy or a girl.
Surya is the protagonist of Bad Queer, a young adult novel-in-verse written by London-based Gayathiri Kamalakanthan and illustrated by Chicago artist Chi Nwosu.
Coming into their final year at school, Surya has come out to their parents, who are queer and non-binary, and their close friend Maha, but not to everyone.
They're also yet to have their first romantic relationship.
"I would really like to like someone.
But I know I can't force it," they reflect.
'Poetry and illustration are a beautiful match'
Throughout Bad Queer, Nwosu's line drawings help develop Surya's journey of self-acceptance.
Sometimes the illustrations capture a detail from the text, like Surya's hands writing in their journal or the tiles in a family game of Scrabble.
Elsewhere, they take us into Surya's internal emotions, like a flurry of stars and swirls that surround the text as Surya practices deep breathing in a bathroom stall.
"I think poetry and illustration are a beautiful match because they're both asking the reader to interpret and really be part of co-creating the story," Kamalakanthan says of the book's unusual format.
Nwosu, a Black, non-binary, queer Nigerian American artist and designer, relates to how Surya feels connected to their ancestors and how they're searching for representation of their queer and non-binary self in Tamil culture.
"I find myself looking towards Igbo history in a similar way," Nwosu says.
"I want to know where are the others? Where are the outliers? How did folks treat people who were different or had a different orientation towards the world?
"[Surya's story] reflected my own experience as someone who didn't fit neatly into a binary."
One aspect of the project Nwosu particularly enjoyed was learning about Tamil symbolism and incorporating it respectfully into their work.
"A lot of my own art incorporates cultural and spiritual symbols as a way to learn, remember and honour my Igbo culture and the histories of global solidarity and queer solidarity," they say.
Finding themselves on stage
Surya's life changes when, on a whim, they audition for their school's youth theatre.
"It's as if this one audition is a mini protest
against all the times I've said nothing" they think.
The group, led by the enthusiastic Mr Ali, proves a safe space for Surya to explore and embrace their identity.
In this new environment, Surya soon befriends Akhil, who proudly wears a "GAY AF" badge and Sade, who gives Surya a worry stone to soothe their pre-audition anxiety.
Then there's Blessing, a newcomer with a "perfectly crooked" smile. Surya is soon smitten.
Kamalakanthan says their own experiences working in the theatre, including writing a play, Period Parrrty, were "foundational" for them.
"I gained confidence to really step into the intersection of my Tamilness and genderqueerness," they say.
"There's something about theatre being a communal act. You're not just writing in a room by yourself. You're in rehearsal rooms, trading mood boards, figuring out a shared vision with a director and cast, and that collective imagining really opened up my confidence."
'I wanted him to get things wrong and keep trying'
As Surya's relationship with Blessing develops, they gain the confidence to live as their true self.
While Blessing is kind and empathetic, it's also a journey for him to embrace being in a queer relationship.
"Because of the binary world we live in, [Blessing] has a difficult time understanding Surya's transness," Kamalakanthan says.
"I wanted him to get things wrong and keep trying and not shy away from doing his own thinking and research about what he doesn't understand yet."
Kamalakanthan says the arc of the relationship was inspired by their previous work as a sex and relationships educator.
"I noticed students were often more fluent in naming sexual harm than articulating consent and the type of touch they might be comfortable with," they say.
"I wanted characters in Bad Queer to model those exact conversations: fumbling, hesitant and laughing nervously through the words … and importantly working out their boundaries before any touch happens.
"There's so much in books and TV about sexual violence, which is of course an important topic to understand.
"But I also wanted to write consensual, caring relationships. We need templates for those conversations too."
'Stories that I really longed for as a young person'
Kamalakanthan and Nwosu hope Bad Queer strikes a chord with young people coming to terms with their gender identity and sexual orientation.
"As a young person, I felt like I didn't quite have the words to describe the feeling of queerness that I had inside," Nwosu says.
"To understand what it means to find dignity for yourself as a queer and genderqueer person and to learn to accept the parts of yourself that maybe make other people uncomfortable was one of the profound takeaways from the book for me.
"It was incredible to work on a book intended for young people and to know they will have these stories that I really longed for as a young person."
Kamalakanthan says they want to present a different kind of narrative around queer and trans youth, who often don't get support or understanding from their parents.
"I wanted to write a family where being trans is incidental alongside the usual messiness and tenderness of any family," they say,.
"Surya's parents won't always have all the answers, but they're people who Surya knows are safe enough to express worries and anxieties to, including if anything unsafe or harmful is going on.
"For a lot of queer people I know, our teenage years were spent hiding, feeling unsafe and managing how we were perceived, rather than discovering the fullness of who we could be.
"I want the characters in my stories to have the teenage adolescence a lot of us didn't get to have, that I hope young people get to have now."
Bad Queer is published by Allen & Unwin.

AfD wins Saxony-Anhalt election with 43.8% of vote — election commission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:47:01 UTC
10:47:01 KST

BERLIN, September 7. /TASS/. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party secured a decisive victory in the the Saxony-Anhalt election, receiving 43.8% of the vote, the regional election commission said in releasing preliminary official results.
This is the best result the AfD has ever achieved in a German state election, doubling its share of the vote compared to five years ago. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) came in second, losing about half of its votes compared to 2021. The party received only 17.2% of the vote, marking the CDU’s worst performance in Saxony-Anhalt to date. Conservative candidates failed to win a single constituency seat.
The Social Democratic Party of Germany received 9.3% of the vote, Alliance 90/The Greens 8.9%, and the Left Party 8.6%. The BSW (formerly the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance - Reason and Justice party) also entered the state parliament with 5.3% of the vote.
Approximately 1.7 million people were eligible to vote in Saxony-Anhalt. Voter turnout was the highest in the region since German reunification, with about 77.8% of eligible voters casting ballots.
Following the election, the formation of a state government became extremely complex, as all parties except the BSW refuse to cooperate with the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. Moreover, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party rules out cooperation with the Left Party as well. Meanwhile, the Alternative for Germany party narrowly missed securing an absolute majority. However, it could form a regional cabinet for the first time if it receives support from the BSW.
Experts view the CDU’s defeat as a personal defeat for Chancellor Friedrich Merz and as evidence of the public's rejection of his government's policies, including those regarding Russia.

Israel plans to destroy 2 tunnels in Lebanon, block return of displaced residents: Report

2026-09-07

Said Amori and Tarek Chouiref
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Israel is preparing to destroy two underground routes in southern Lebanon and intends to prevent displaced residents from returning to areas its forces may leave, the Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported Sunday.
The routes, located beneath the Ali al-Taher Heights, are expected to be blown up in the coming days, KAN said, citing unnamed military officials who claimed that no “living armed operatives” remained at the site.
The army is then expected to begin a phased withdrawal from what Israel calls its “security belt” in southern Lebanon.
The plan is due to be presented this week to the head of the Israeli army’s Northern Command before being sent to the political leadership for approval.
Under the proposal, Israeli troops would pull back from the so-called “yellow line” to a “gray line” roughly 2 to 4 kilometers (1.2 to 2.5 miles) from the Israeli border, where the army plans to establish around 20 permanent military positions.
On Thursday, the Israeli army claimed it had established “operational control” above and below ground in the Ali al-Taher Heights area. The Hezbollah group did not comment on the claim.
KAN also said Israel had relayed a message to the Lebanese government through the US that displaced residents would not, for now, be allowed to return to areas vacated by Israeli forces.
The issue is expected to be raised in direct Israeli-Lebanese talks due to resume this month in Rome.
The report comes amid heightened tensions in southern Lebanon where Israeli attacks have intensified in recent days after the Israeli army claimed it intercepted a drone that was allegedly launched by Hezbollah toward its forces operating in what Tel Aviv calls a “security zone” in southern Lebanon.
The strikes come despite a US-sponsored framework agreement signed between Israel and Lebanon on June 26 which provides for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army.
Israel has carried out attacks on Lebanon since March 2, killing 4,362 people and injuring 12,378 others while displacing more than 1 million people, according to Lebanese authorities.
Israel continues to occupy areas of southern Lebanon, including territory it has held for decades and other areas occupied during the 2023-2024 conflict, while its forces have advanced more than 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) into Lebanese territory during the current conflict.

Saxony-Anhalt: Preliminary official results show AfD tops vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:35:00 UTC
10:35:00 KST

Saxony-Anhalt: Preliminary results show AfD tops vote
Published September 6, 2026last updated September 7, 2026
What you need to know
- Far-right AfD hails 'sensational' results in the Saxony-Anhalt vote
- AfD expected to struggle with coalition building as many parties reject cooperation
- Left-wing populist BSW open to working with AfD on some issues
- Merz's CDU suffers worst Saxony-Anhalt result since German reunification
Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state held an election on Sunday, September 6. Follow all the developments on Monday, September 7, here.
Elon Musk congratulates AfD on election victory in Saxony-Anhalt
Tech entrepreneur and the world's richest man, Elon Musk, who has backed Germany’s far-right AfD, congratulated the party on its Saxony-Anhalt election victory.
"Gut gemacht!" (Well Done!) Musk wrote on his social media platform X in response to a post by AfD co-leader Alice Weidel congratulating the party's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund on the result in Saxony-Anhalt.
Siegmund promptly replied to Musk, thanking him for his "support."
"If we take responsibility here, I would very much welcome the opportunity for strong and constructive cooperation. Germany would once again be a place worth investing in," Siegmund wrote.
Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, the AfD has strengthened its ties with Washington, with Alice Weidel calling the US president a role model and AfD representatives attending his inauguration.
Elon Musk, then a close Trump adviser, openly campaigned for the AfD and continues to back far-right political figures.
Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance sees a 'political reset'
Sahra Wagenknecht, founder of the populist BSW, called for a "political reset" in Saxony-Anhalt after the party narrowly cleared the 5% threshold to enter the state parliament.
"There are hopefully now majorities in the Magdeburg state parliament for a change in energy policy, an end to the Russia sanctions, better education and a fundamental reform of public broadcasting," Wagenknecht told dpa.
Since its founding in January 2024, Wagenknecht’s BSW has positioned itself as economically left-wing but culturally conservative. She supports higher minimum wages and rent caps but also backs tougher immigration policies.
She has repeatedly blamed the West for Russia’s war in Ukraine and opposed sanctions against Moscow. BSW politicians, like some AfD figures, have also been accused of maintaining ties with supporters of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"The BSW’s comeback has begun," she said, adding "the result would boost her party’s campaign ahead of state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin."
The far-right AfD fell short of an outright majority, leaving the shape of a government in Saxony-Anhalt unclear. Wagenknecht has ruled out a coalition with the AfD but not cooperation, potentially giving her party the balance of power.
"The policy of keeping the AfD out of government has failed. Simply trying to form another coalition to exclude the AfD would be an affront to voters." she said.
AfD faces uncertain coalition options after Saxony-Anhalt win
According to preliminary official results, the AfD emerged as the largest party but fell short of a governing majority in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. The far-right party therefore faces challenges in forming a government.
AfD lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt Ulrich Siegmund said his party’s result represented "a clear mandate to govern."
At the same time, the 35-year-old said he currently saw no potential coalition partners. However, he added that he did not know what might happen in the coming days.
"I don’t know whether there are individual lawmakers who might say: 'That’s it, I’m not playing along with this anymore,'" he said, adding, "A lot can still happen." Following the historic win, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said: "Ulrich Siegmund will definitely run as a candidate for state premier in the state parliament. That much is certain."
If efforts to form a government fail, Siegmund said a new election could also be an option. "In the worst-case scenario, there would simply be new elections, and then we would get 50% or 55%," he said.
Is coalition without AfD possible?
The only coalition that would have a numerical majority without the AfD would be an alliance of all the other parties. However, under a resolution adopted previously, the center-right CDU rules out not only a coalition with the AfD but also with the Left Party. This policy is known as the " political firewall."
That would also be a stumbling block for a CDU-led minority government. In addition, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) could potentialy hold the balance of power with five seats. Its leadership has ruled out supporting CDU.
Following the election, the previously governing coalition of the CDU, SPD and FDP will end. However, state premier Sven Schulze and his Cabinet will remain in office in a caretaker capacity until a new state premier is elected.
Is Germany’s "political firewall" against the AfD collapsing?
Germany’s mainstream parties have long maintained a "political firewall" against cooperation with the far-right Alternative for Germany. But that firewall is under growing pressure following the AfD’s historic win in the Saxony-Anhalt state election and prospects in other forthcoming state elections.
The term refers to efforts by established parties to prevent extremist parties from gaining political influence through cooperation or shared votes. The center-right CDU formally rejected cooperation with the AfD in 2018.
But in January 2025, a CDU motion in the Bundestag passed with AfD support, prompting accusations that Chancellor Friedrich Merz had breached the firewall.
The AfD’s growing electoral strength is now raising fresh questions about how long the firewall can hold and what its future means for Germany’s political center.
Read here for more context: What is the 'political firewall' against Germany's far-right AfD?
AfD wins most votes in Saxony-Anhalt, preliminary official results show
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 43.8% of the vote in Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state election, according to preliminary official results, making it the largest party, but falling short of a governing majority in the regional parliament.
Six parties will be represented in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt, which has 83 seats:
- Alternative for Germany (AfD) — 43.8%, 39 seats
- Christian Democratic Union (CDU) — 17.2%, 15 seats
- Social Democratic Party (SPD) — 9.3%, 8 seats
- Green Party — 8.9%, 8 seats
- Left Party — 8.6%, 8 seats
- Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) — 5.3%, 5 seats
Meanwhile, the business-focused Free Democrats (FDP) secured only 2.6% of the vote, failing to reach the 5% threshold.
According to the preliminary results, turnout was almost 78%, the highest in Saxony-Anhalt since German reunification in 1990.
WATCH: "Migration alone no longer explains the party’s rise"
Historian Katja Hoyer says the AfD's breakthrough was fueled by a more upbeat campaign around Ulrich Siegmund, while mainstream parties struggled to offer a positive vision of change.
CDU fails to win a single direct mandate in Saxony-Anhalt state election
As a major setback for Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right CDU, the party came away empty-handed in the individual constituencies.
The CDU failed to win a single direct mandate in the Saxony-Anhalt state election.
According to preliminary figures from the state election authority, CDU candidates were defeated in all 41 constituencies.
Alternative for Germany (AfD) candidates prevailed in 38 constituencies, including lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund in Genthin. Candidates from the Left Party won the remaining three constituencies: one in Magdeburg and two in Halle.
In the 2021 state election, the CDU won direct mandates in 40 of the 41 constituencies, while the AfD won one.
In Germany, voters have two votes. The "first vote" determines the winner of a constituency and the direct mandate. The "second vote" determines the distribution of seats among parties in the state parliament.
WATCH: DW's Max Hofmann analyzes what AfD's win in Saxony-Anhalt means for Germany
The immediate political fallout from the Saxony-Anhalt election results could put pressure on the governing coalition in Berlin over the AfD's growing popularity.
Germany’s next federal election is scheduled for 2029, and political parties are likely to closely watch how the AfD’s rise shapes the country’s political landscape, says DW Berlin bureau chief Max Hoffmann.
Is Saxony-Anhalt's economy really struggling?
Saxony-Anhalt's economy has grown more slowly than Germany’s overall economy in recent years, with lower wages, higher unemployment and economic output per capita at only about three-quarters of the national average.
These challenges have helped fuel support for the far-right AfD, which argues the eastern state has been left behind socially and economically.
Key sectors of the state economy include chemicals, engineering, manufacturing and tourism.
But has the eastern state been left behind as some suggest.

Czech parliament speaker congratulates AfD on Saxony-Anhalt result
Tomio Okamura, the far-right president of the Czech parliament's lower chamber, congratulated the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party on its success in the Saxony-Anhalt state election.
According to Okamura, this is the result of the "bad politics" by the "liberal, EU-friendly" parties in Germany.
Okamura's far-right SPD party is part of the Czech governing coalition.
 
READ: What an AfD government could mean for Saxony-Anhalt
An AfD-led government could bring major changes to migration, education and social policy in Saxony-Anhalt.
The party wants more deportations, mandatory work for asylum-seekers and cuts to integration programs. It also plans to change school curricula, ban rainbow flags in schools and reduce funding for pro-democracy projects.
Some proposals could face legal limits or fall outside state powers. The AfD also wants closer ties with Russia, although foreign policy is mainly decided at the federal level.
For a closer look at what an AfD-led government could mean for Saxony-Anhalt, read our full analysis here.
WATCH: CDU's Schulze concedes defeat as AfD tops vote
"We're going to have to live with this result," the CDU's lead candidate Sven Schulze said after congratulating the AfD on becoming the Saxony-Anhalt's strongest party.
AfD success 'serious moment', French minister says
The election results of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the Saxony-Anhalt state election is a "serious" moment, France's Europe Minister Benjamin Haddad said.
"This is a serious moment in Europe, seeing the far right win in a regional election in Germany," Haddad posted on his X account.
"We must listen with humility to the anger, the concerns, the fears, and respond to them," he added.
WATCH: AfD's Siegmund vows to 'take our country back'
"We have made history," said Ulrich Siegmund, the lead candidate for the far-right AfD, after the party won around 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt.
Projected results put BSW in Saxony-Anhalt state parliament
The latest projected results show the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) will get seats in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament.
The left-wing populist party will have five seats and has said it would work with the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which picked up 39 seats according to the projected results. The AfD had earlier seemingly ruled out working with the BSW.
The Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which headed previous coalition-led state governments, only managed to get 15 seats, while the socialist Left Party ,the center-left Social Democrats and Greens look set to get 8 seats each.

Jamaica to file slavery reparations petition during UK visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Jamaica to file slavery reparations petition during UK visit
Petition to King Charles questions the legality of slavery under English law and UK’s responsibility for reparations.
A Jamaican delegation to the United Kingdom has said it will file a petition addressed to King Charles III to seek legal guidance on the question of slavery reparations.
This is the first time a British Commonwealth state will use this legal route “for the cause of reparatory justice”, the Jamaican delegation said, as the visit to London kicks off Monday.
Jamaica’s Ministry of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport said its minister, Olivia Grange, will lead the delegation “to advance Jamaica’s push for reparations for the African ancestors who suffered under hundreds of years of enslavement”.
The ministry added that it will meet with the British Museum to discuss “the repatriation of cultural artefacts taken from Jamaica”.
The petition will ask the king, Jamaica’s head of state, to answer three questions on the transatlantic slave trade to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the Caribbean island’s highest court of appeal based in London.
Under the Judicial Committee Act of 1833, the UK monarch has the authority to refer legal matters to the court for an advisory opinion.
The questions include: whether the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was legal under English common law, whether it violated international law, and whether the UK has a legal obligation to provide a remedy for the harm caused by slavery.
Grange said she would not speculate on whether Jamaica was asking the UK to pay reparations for the slave trade.
“We want the answers. Once we get the answers, or once we get a response to those questions, then the next steps will be determined,” she said.
“We understand the Jamaican government is seeking a petition to be heard before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council,” a Buckingham Palace spokesperson said in response to Jamaica’s inquiry.
The palace acknowledged the king’s constitutional role in the petition as Jamaica’s head of state but said he had no role in deciding the substance of the claim.
British merchants enslaved and forcibly transported 600,000 to 1 million Africans to Jamaica between the 17th century and the early 19th century.
Shortly after abolishing slavery in 1833, the UK paid slave owners $27m in compensation, amounting to 40 percent of the Treasury’s annual income. To raise the cash, the government took out considerable loans, finally paying off its debts in 2015.
The Jamaican government estimates that the country is owed about $10bn, but the UK has repeatedly refused to pay for historical slavery.

Hong Kong’s local schools should not have to brace for the worst
Unknown

The vast majority of Hong Kong’s students are 
back in school now
. With traffic expected to be horrendous last week, it was good that the government sounded the warning early, urging residents to allow more time for their morning commute.
The government did more than that, actually. The Emergency Transport Co-ordination Centre was working at its highest operational tier at 6.30am on September 1 to monitor and coordinate public transport and traffic flow. Deployment of staff on the ground ensured that conditions were reported in real-time. Preparedness wins the day and the government deserves good marks for its efforts. It wasn’t raining when Noah built the ark, but it was on our first day of school.
For those averse to change, the start of the school year can be comforting because it can be counted on to bring the same disruptions.
Traffic is one thing, but parents of school-going children know that the first week means suffering from information overload, wading through an avalanche of notices and filling out paperwork into the wee hours.
The certainty extends to the news cycle. Bad behaviour at 
university orientation camps
 almost always makes headlines every year. For those of us who have had our share of wild days in our youth, 
the video
 of a shirtless young man carrying a young woman wearing a bra and shorts at an orientation camp this year may not seem too troubling. But a former university student is on trial facing multiple charges of rape and indecent assault. Predators have no place in our educational institutions. Youth can never be an excuse.
With couples in Hong Kong increasingly reluctant to have children, the dismal birth rate is no longer news. And so just as the sun rises in the east, we can count on the shutting of Primary One classes in recent years. This academic year, 
126 Primary One classes
 have been wiped out, an 8 per cent decrease year on year. The worst, according to a primary school principal, is yet to come.
Whether our government has given up on boosting the birth rate will be revealed in time, with the chief executive delivering his policy address on September 16. We’ll know then whether baby bonuses will be continued and whether the 
HK$2,500 (US$318) annual student grant
 will be resuscitated. If there are no efforts beyond handing out money, we will know our government is out of ideas.

Robert Pattinson Is Disturbing and Alluring in Primetime, a Sordid Movie About a Sordid TV Show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:17:33 UTC
10:17:33 KST

In the early 2000s, if your idea of a cheap thrill was to see presumed sicko pedophiles caught on camera as they advance upon their ostensibly underage prey, NBC’s To Catch a Predator was your show. The host, Chris Hansen, had once been considered a serious journalist, spearheading investigative reports on events like the Columbine shootings and the World Trade Center attacks. But on the sleazy, sensationalistic To Catch a Predator, he was more of a vigilante showman. The show worked like this: A crusading organization called Perverted Justice would initiate conversations in online chatrooms designed to attract potential sex offenders. Then they’d be lured to sting houses outfitted with hidden cameras, where Hansen and his crew would await their arrival, ready to enact a pruriently dramatic Gotcha! moment, generally followed by an arrest. Nobody likes a pedophile, and without leaving the Barcalounger, viewers could revel in the self-congratulatory certainty that they too were helping to keep the world safe for the kiddos.
Documentary filmmaker Lance Oppenheim’s first fiction feature Primetime—premiering here at the Venice Film Festival—fills in some background pixels on the show’s rise and fall, focusing particularly on an ambitious, egotistical, and at least somewhat delusional Hansen, played by Robert Pattinson. It’s 2006, and Hansen and his beleaguered producer Andie (Merritt Wever, bringing an edgy nervousness to the role of a woman struggling to stay afloat in the ruthless world of TV news) get a chance to move their show into a primetime slot. The stakes are high, but the potential rewards are great. Hansen’s hubris balloons, and he infects others with his own inflated sense of the public service he claims to be providing. To complete its mission of reeling in the bad guys, the show employs youthful-looking decoys posing as underage kids. One of these is an elflike performer named Del (singer-songwriter Phoebe Bridgers) who can impersonate either a boy or a girl; she passes some tips along to a nervous newcomer who will come to be known as Decoy Dan (Skyler Gisondo, in a performance laced with touching eagerness). Though he hopes to become a real actor and thinks this is his way in, he wants to quit when he sees how demeaning the gig actually is. But Hansen, with his crocodile smile and purring, almost sultry intonation, persuades him to stick with it, assuring him that he’ll be helping to cleanse the world of evil.
Hansen has gotten high on what he perceives as his own power, and his ambitions grow even greater as he and his team try to draw in a “whale,” ideally a major government figure, rather than the pathetically sad—though still dangerous and repellent—lowlifes who tend to creep into their trap. These thankless roles are heroically played by an assortment of actors including Tony Revolori; despite his character’s unsavory and illegal intentions, his tremulous shock at being caught underscores the show’s legally questionable entrapment methods.
Hansen’s unfolding mania is one of the chief features of Primetime, and Pattinson’s performance is one of the only reasons to see it. As he practices dialogue that he’ll use in the show, drawn from the chatroom fodder that has lured the show’s marks into its trap, he relishes the prurient material a little too much: “I will undress you, you will undress me.” His theatrically precise diction is both disturbing and weirdly alluring.
Still, it’s not exactly clear what Primetime is aiming for: it seems to be making the point that while sexual predators are unequivocally bad, the people who make trash TV—particularly a sordid show that’s masquerading as a means of protecting kids and meting out justice—are also immoral, scheming, and just all-around unpleasant. That’s a shaky equivalence. Oppenheim, director of docs like Spermworld and Some Kind of Heaven, structures the film as if he were shaping a mosaic from disorienting shards; sometimes the scenes feel jaggedly disconnected. He and cinematographer David Bolen have given the picture a grubby, grainy look, including sections that mimic early-2000s-style video recording. If you feel dirty watching it, that’s by design—and if you enjoy feeling dirty, that’s your choice.

WASHINGTON, September 7. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump expressed support for a proposal to rename New Mexico "New America" on his Truth Social page.
"Many people suggested changing the name of New Mexico, one of the great vote cheating states of all time, to New America. An AI-generated video accompanying the post shows the president changing the state’s name on a roadside sign in New Mexico while dancing to the Village People’s hit "YMCA."
According to the US Constitution, the federal government cannot change state names; this is the prerogative of state authorities and residents. After the new name is approved by the state legislature and then by the population in a referendum, the relevant amendments must be made to state law. If the proposal is approved, state authorities will inform Congress and the US government of the changes. New Mexico media outlets have reported that residents do not support renaming the state.
Previously, the president signed executive orders renaming the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario the Gulf of America and Lake America, respectively. These orders change how the federal government and federal maps refer to these places. However, future presidents could sign executive orders reversing these changes.

Ukraine lost $1.2 bn to defense fraud and waste in one year – NYT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:12:05 UTC

Ukraine lost $1.2 bn to defense fraud and waste in one year – NYT
Ukraine lost around $1.2 billion to fraud, waste and mismanagement in military procurement in 2024 alone, the New York Times has reported, citing confidential government audits and court records.
Seven of the country’s ten largest military contractors continued to receive new orders despite fraud investigations, previous failures to deliver, or the arrests of executives on corruption charges, the paper wrote on Sunday, describing the pattern as a “persistent phenomenon.”
Auditors also identified 18 companies awarded contracts despite earlier defaults, six of which had failed to fulfill a single deal.
Defense industry fraud is “a longstanding tradition” in Ukraine, American anticorruption expert James Wasserstrom has told the NYT. “Anything that isn’t nailed down in Ukraine will be stolen,” he said.
Among the cases highlighted by the Times was the state-owned Pavlohrad Chemical Plant, which supplied the military with 233,000 unusable mortar rounds. Nevertheless, the company later received more business, including a contract to supply nearly all of Ukraine’s 122mm artillery rounds in 2025.
The audits also found that cheaper offers were sometimes bypassed. In one tender, Kiev reportedly bought Turkish-made munitions for multiple-launch rocket systems through a Czech intermediary for around $5,100 each despite the manufacturer offering them directly for roughly $4,200.
The losses accumulated as Vladimir Zelensky repeatedly appealed to Western governments for more weapons, warning of critical shortages on the battlefield. In April 2024, he said Kiev was in “dire need” of increased support and pressed its backers to deliver promised arms and ammunition.
The report comes amid a series of high-profile graft investigations involving top Ukrainian officials and figures close to Zelensky. In August, the Ukrainian leader sacked deputy head of his office Irina Mudraya, while other recent corruption probes have implicated former ministers, diplomats and senior officials.
Former Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov, meanwhile, accused the government of “systemic corruption” following his dismissal in July. Fedorov, who had sought to overhaul military procurement, has claimed that entrenched defense-industry interests resisted his reforms and has since called for wartime elections.
Zelensky’s five-year presidential term expired in May 2024, but he has refused to hold a new election, citing martial law imposed after the conflict with Russia escalated in February 2022.
Moscow has long argued that the scandals are evidence of systemic corruption in Ukraine. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said earlier this year that corruption “permeates the entire Ukrainian power structure, including Zelensky’s inner circle and Zelensky himself.”

Volcano eruption in Indonesia leaves 170,000 travellers stranded as eight airports closed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:11:34 UTC
10:11:34 KST

Eight Indonesian airports, including two serving Jakarta, remained closed early on Monday morning because of volcanic ash from eruptions at Mount Anak Krakatau, the transport minister said.
Ash from Anak Krakatau, which sits halfway between Java and Sumatra islands, has blanketed Jakarta and several surrounding areas since it erupted late on Friday, leading to the closure of the airports for safety reasons.
The transport ministry said 170,000 people have been affected by flight cancellations.
The suspension at Jakarta’s main airport has been extended until 6pm Monday local time, the airport authority said in an Instagram post.
“We cannot ascertain when this will end due to the dynamic weather,” transport minister Dudy Purwagandhi said. At the time of that statement, the seven other airports, which included the ones serving Jakarta’s nearby provinces of Lampung and West Java, were to remain closed until at least 8.59am.
“To date, 1,558 flights have been delayed at the eight affected airports, with 170,000 passengers stranded,” the ministry said in a statement on Sunday.
More than 900 affected flights were to and from the Soekarno-Hatta, it added.
Schools across Jakarta were also affected with classes moving online on Monday, the city said in a statement, without specifying how long the measure would be in place.
Some shipping has also been disrupted.
Eruptions of Anak Krakatau on Saturday produced a fountain of lava and booming sounds that could be heard up to a few hundred kilometres away, the geology agency said in a statement.
There were more eruptions on Sunday, with the volcano monitoring agency’s website showing the most recent occurring on Sunday at 8.23pm.
The agency warned on Monday that “the probability of further eruptions in the coming periods remains high”.
Ash from the volcano was detected in the airspace surrounding Soekarno-Hatta international airport, prompting authorities to suspend operations, the ministry said.
The disruption left some passengers scrambling to find alternative flights.
Henny Yensan, 44, who had hoped to go back to her home town with her mother, said “everybody was disappointed”.
“No one flew into a rage because, after all, this is due to natural disaster,” the businesswoman who had to reschedule her flight to Tuesday told AFP.
Volcanic ash also reached the city of Bandar Lampung in the southern tip of Sumatra, blanketing parked cars and roadsides.
Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatau, sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra.
Ships passing through the strait were asked to increase vigilance for possible disruption to navigation safety due to volcanic activities.
Vessels are prohibited from approaching an exclusion zone of a 3km radius from the volcano, local port authorities said in a statement.
The volcano has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera that formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatau.
That disaster was one of the deadliest and most destructive in history with an estimated 35,000 people killed.
Geology agency head Lana Saria warned against approaching Anak Krakatau, saying materials ejected from the volcano could endanger those within the exclusion zone.
She said the most recent series of eruptions do not have the potential to trigger a tsunami.
A 2018 tsunami triggered by a collapse of parts of Anak Krakatau killed 429 people and left thousands displaced.
Indonesia, a South-east Asian archipelago nation, sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where the meeting of continental plates causes high volcanic and seismic activity.

Why is Kenya cracking down on foreign traders and small retailers?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:08:55 UTC
10:08:55 KST

Why is Kenya cracking down on foreign traders and small retailers?
President Ruto says small businesses should be reserved for Kenyans as his government moves against foreign traders.
Kenya is beginning a crackdown on foreign nationals operating small retail shops and engaging in hawking, after President William Ruto directed authorities to shut down such businesses from September 7.
Ruto made the announcement on September 2 while addressing micro, small and medium-sized enterprise (MSME) traders at State House in Nairobi.
He said foreigners should not compete with Kenyans in businesses such as hawking and small retail, while foreign investment was welcome in activities requiring greater capital and investment.
What is Kenya doing?
Ruto directed authorities to begin shutting down small businesses operated by foreign nationals from September 7, saying hawking and small-scale retail should be reserved for Kenyans.
He said the government would take administrative action while the Parliament of Kenya considers the proposed Local Content Bill, 2025.
He also directed National Assembly Majority Leader Kimani Ichung’wah and Trade Cabinet Secretary Lee Kinyanjui to accelerate the bill’s passage through Parliament.
Why is Kenya moving against foreign traders and small retailers?
Hesbon Hansen Owilla, a professor at Aga Khan University in Nairobi, said the policy would help protect Kenyan traders.
“Yes, this is the best way to protect Kenyan small businesses and traders,” he told Al Jazeera. “Kenya is trying to bring in only investors who are bringing capital that can spur economic development by creating jobs rather than allow small-time foreign traders who only stifle Kenyan small traders while enjoying the robust infrastructure that Kenya has built and social securities.”
“It’s like expatriates. A country cannot allow expatriates in for jobs locals have expertise in,” he said.
The proposed Local Content Bill, 2025, would require foreign companies to increase local sourcing and employment, among other measures.
The bill is still being considered by Parliament and has not yet been enacted into law.
What businesses and traders are affected?
The directive is aimed at foreign nationals operating small retail shops and engaging in hawking. Ruto specifically referred to hawking and small shops when announcing the crackdown.
Kenya’s broader micro, small and medium-sized enterprise (MSME) sector covers a wider range of businesses. The government has not publicly provided a comprehensive list of all businesses covered by the September 7 directive or an estimate of how many foreign nationals will be affected.
Ruto also directed Ichung’wah to engage the State Department for Immigration’s principal secretary and establish the requirements governing permits issued to foreign investors and traders. It is therefore not yet clear how the directive will apply to foreign nationals who already hold permits to conduct business in Kenya.
Foreign Affairs Principal Secretary Korir Sing’Oei said on September 6 that foreign nationals who meet Kenya’s legal requirements, including holding the necessary work permits and licences, remain legally protected to operate businesses in the country. He said Ruto’s remarks had been taken out of context and were made in the context of the Local Content Bill, 2025.
How significant is foreign investment in Kenya?
Kenya’s 2024 Foreign Investment Survey, the latest such survey published by the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS), put the country’s stock of foreign direct investment at 1.458 trillion Kenyan shillings ($11.27bn) at the end of 2023, up 8.5 percent from 1.343 trillion Kenyan shillings ($10.4bn) at the end of 2022.
These figures cover foreign investment across the Kenyan economy and are not limited to the small-scale trading activities targeted by Ruto’s directive.
Surveyed foreign-invested enterprises employed 224,769 people in June 2024, including 221,267 Kenyan employees. Foreign employees accounted for 1.6 percent of the workforce in those enterprises.
What is the Tata Chemicals case?
The Tata Chemicals dispute is separate from the small-business crackdown.
Tata Chemicals Magadi operates a soda ash business at Lake Magadi in Kajiado County. On July 28, the Kenyan government suspended the company’s mining operations, citing alleged compliance issues under the country’s mining laws. The suspension also affected its soda ash exports.
On September 3, Ruto said he had ordered Tata Chemicals to leave Kenya, saying the company had not provided sufficient benefits to the local community in Kajiado County. He said the government would bring in two new companies to establish glass and chemical manufacturing facilities in the area.
Tata Chemicals said it had submitted the information requested by Kenyan authorities and was awaiting further communication. The company has said it complied with regulatory requirements and remained committed to resolving the matter through legal and regulatory channels.
The Tata dispute concerns the company’s soda ash operations at Lake Magadi. This is separate from the directive targeting foreign nationals operating small retail businesses and hawking.
What does this mean for foreign investment?
International business consultant and Sols Inclinations Ltd Managing Director Solomon Kinyanjui said the distinction was not between welcoming foreign investment and rejecting it, but between foreign capital that complements Kenyan enterprise and activity that displaces it.
“The issue is not whether foreign capital is welcome, but what role it should play in Kenya’s economy,” he told Al Jazeera. “Foreign investment should complement Kenyan enterprise, not substitute for economic activities Kenyans can competitively undertake themselves.”
He said the stronger case for foreign investment was where it brought capital, technology, skills, industrial capacity and access to export markets, but warned that the government needed to draw the boundary clearly and apply its rules predictably.
Hafsa Abdiwahab Sheikh, a journalist, said the policy could have both benefits and costs depending on how it is implemented.
“The policy could create more jobs for Kenyans and encourage skills transfer, while helping protect local employment,” she told Al Jazeera.
“However, if implemented unpredictably, it may discourage foreign investment and increase business costs, leading to higher prices. It could also affect relations with foreign communities if foreigners are blamed for unemployment.”

According to the Ministry of Defence, the military facility was used to store confiscated fireworks, grenades, and TNT-based explosives.
Three of the dead were confirmed as soldiers, whilst the identities of the three bodies recovered in recent hours remain unverified.
"The death toll from Friday's explosions at the military facility in Viacha has risen to six," the ministry stated, placing the number of missing personnel and conscripts at 11.
Casualties and investigation
Rescue teams continued searching through the debris on Sunday.
The violent shockwaves tore roofs off structures, launched rocks across the vicinity, uprooted trees, and damaged dozens of civilian homes in adjacent neighbourhoods.
Whilst the precise cause of the detonations remains under active investigation, the public prosecutor's office in Viacha has initiated a formal inquiry into manslaughter and associated criminal offences.
The disaster has triggered sharp political recriminations.
Evo Morales, Bolivia's first Indigenous president who led the nation from 2006 to 2019, strongly criticised centre-right President Rodrigo Paz over the administration's handling of the crisis.
"The irresponsibility with which the government has handled this tragic event is nothing less than a war crime that warrants a complaint before the International Criminal Court," Morales wrote on the X platform.

Kyiv introduces tiered air threat alert system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
00:36:00 UTC
09:36:00 KST

Kyiv introduces tiered air threat alert system
According to Ukrinform, the Kyiv City State Administration announced this on Telegram.
From now on, city residents may receive the following alerts:
Yellow level: “Drone danger”;
Red level: “Massive drone threat”; “Missile threat”; “Missile and drone threat.”
Green: “All clear” – no threats or dangers.
Each new alert indicates the current type and level of threat.
If the type of threat changes, a new alert automatically replaces the previous one.
A separate “All Clear” is not issued between different types of threats.
For example, if a “Missile Threat” alert follows a “Drone Danger” alert, this means that a missile threat is now active.
An “All Clear” alert means that none of the listed air threats have been detected in the city at this time.
The Kyiv City State Administration noted that the differentiated alert system is currently in place in all districts of Kyiv except Pecherskyi.
In the Holosiivskyi and Sviatoshynskyi districts, it is partially operational. This is because, in certain areas, differentiating between types of threats is not yet technically feasible.
Therefore, the procedure for audible alerts remains unchanged there: in the event of any air danger or threat, a standard siren signal is sounded without separate differentiation by threat type and without an “All Clear” signal.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Ukraine will update its air threat warning system, specifically introducing a “yellow” threat level for drone attacks and a “red” level for missiles. There are also plans to differentiate the audio signals and the geographic scope of the alerts.

Washington's envoys have brought new, "more effective" proposals on ending the war with Russia to Kyiv, a senior Ukrainian presidential official told AFP Sunday.
Earlier Sunday, Zelensky had said the war with Russia looked likely to continue into the winter.
While both he and the US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had given upbeat assessments of the talks, neither announced any breakthroughs on ending the conflict.
But the senior Ukrainian official told AFP: "It's not the same as it was before. This one now is more effective. They're still talking. This is actually the most important part."
Witkoff, who is President Donald Trump's business ally, and Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, travelled to Kyiv a day after meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow -- the latest of several visits to the city.
Ukraine's rail operator announced their departure from Kyiv in a post on Telegram early Monday, accompanied by a photo of the two envoys' standing under a station sign announcing the "Peace Express".
Sunday's visit to Kyiv was their first to the Ukrainian capital, which has been enduring deadly Russian strikes for more than four years.
Zelensky said: "We very much hope that we will be able to reach agreements with our American partners, and we are counting on the support of our European partners if the war continues in winter -- and this is how it appears at the moment."
Zelensky also said Ukraine would hold talks with the US, France and Germany, but did not elaborate. And he repeated his call that only a meeting between the two leaders could solve territorial issues.
Thanking the US envoys for their visit, Zelensky said on X: "The main thing is to achieve peace for Ukraine -- a dignified, reliable, and lasting peace. We are directing all our efforts toward this."
Read moreUkraine-Russia talks: What are the US objectives?
'On same side'
Moscow occupies large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine and the Kremlin told the Americans on Saturday it was feeling "confident" it would advance more.
Moscow has said it wants not just the territories it occupies but the land it claims as Russian to be recognised as its own -- terms unacceptable to Kyiv.
Witkoff said both sides would need to compromise, adding: "We think we have the ingredients to get to that place.
"We've had a very meaningful discussion, substantive, important, and we are very encouraged and we look forward to continuing this as long as it takes."
Kushner added: "Hopefully this trip has come out with some new ways to advance forward. I think we've learned a lot from the trip."
Witkoff and Kushner travelled to the region hoping to revive the Trump administration's push for peace in Europe's worst conflict since World War II, after a summer of escalation.
British, French and German representatives attended a separate round of the talks.
Zelensky said he was grateful the Europeans were there, adding: "Here we are all on the same side."
Like all visiting officials, the US delegation had arrived by train, with "Peace Express" written on the platform at Kyiv Central Station.

EU to boost Greenland investment amid Trump annexation claims

EU to boost Greenland investment amid Trump annexation claims
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is expected to announce increased EU investment in Greenland on Monday, including in critical minerals, satellite communications and renewable energy. Her two-day visit signals support for Greenland and Denmark amid US President Donald Trump’s push for American control of the Arctic territory.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is expected to unveil on Monday a boost in EU investments in Greenland and closer political ties with the Danish Arctic territory, which Donald Trump has insisted should belong to the United States.
Von der Leyen arrived in Greenland on Sunday for a two-day visit serving as a show of support for the governments of Greenland and Denmark, which have strongly rebuffed Trump’s campaign to annex the world’s largest island.
The head of the 27-nation European Union's executive body, von der Leyen is expected to unveil plans to invest in sectors including critical minerals, satellite communications and renewable energy in Greenland, a semi-autonomous part of the Danish realm.
Read moreNATO's Arctic activity poses 'direct threat' to Russia, Lavrov warns
On Sunday in Nuuk, the capital, von der Leyen said the package would be "substantial" but gave no details. Greenland Premier Jens-Frederik Nielsen said his country wanted to build on its "close friendship and good partnership" with the EU.
Von der Leyen's visit reflects the increasing geopolitical importance of the Arctic to major powers, such as the United States, Russia, China and Europe, as melting ice opens new shipping routes to make the region’s mineral wealth more accessible.
"Greenland's stunning landscapes and natural beauty will stay with me for a long time. But so will the visible scars of climate change on the ice sheet," von der Leyen posted on X after a boat trip under clear blue skies in a fjord scattered with chunks of ice.
"As the ice melts, a new reality is taking shape."
Trump, the US president, sparked a crisis in US-European ties and turmoil within the transatlantic NATO military alliance this year when he stepped up his demands for the US to control Greenland, arguing that fellow NATO member Denmark could not defend it.
Read moreTensions in the Arctic: Greenland issues sharp rebuke to Trump-linked oil company
European officials stressed Greenland is part of NATO territory, meaning it is covered by the alliance’s mutual defence pact, and that the US already has the right to increase its military presence there under a longstanding treaty.
Tensions lowered after Trump and NATO boss Mark Rutte agreed in Davos in January that the United States, Denmark and Greenland would begin talks to resolve their differences and NATO would step up its role in Arctic security.
However, the trilateral talks have yet to yield an agreement and, at a NATO summit in Turkey in July, Trump restated his insistence that the US should control Greenland.
While Denmark is a member of the EU, Greenland left the bloc in 1985. But its people, as Danish citizens, are also citizens of the EU.
The EU has long provided funding to Greenland, mainly to pay for fishing rights and support its education system. The package to be announced by von der Leyen will represent not only a big increase in funding but a broadening of the sectors that will receive EU cash, according to EU officials.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

Breaking: Labuschagne retained for South Africa Test series despite pressure

Marnus Labuschagne will travel to South Africa for next month's Test tour of South Africa after being named in a 16-man squad.
There have been calls for the number three to be dropped after more than three years without a Test century, but the 32-year-old has kept his spot for the tour despite being left out of the side for six ODIs leading up to the Test series.
Australia's men's team will play three ODIs against Zimbabwe in Harare followed by three more 50-over games against South Africa in Durban, Johannesburg and Potchefstroom before the Tests in Durban (October 9-13), Gqeberha (October 18-22) and Cape Town (October 27-31).
Chairman of selectors George Bailey said a pure focus on red-ball cricket "may be a benefit" for Labuschagne.
"Not shying away from the fact we'd like some more runs from Marn, that's clear," he said.
"But we're also confident he can still make a positive contribution to that squad."
Labuschagne has never played a Test in South Africa, where he was born and spent the first 10 years of his life.
Big-hitting Cooper Connolly, spinner Matthew Kuhnemann and seamer Michael Neser, another South Africa-born Australian, have been added to the group that contested the second Test against Bangladesh in Mackay last month.
Bailey said Connolly, who bowls part-time spin, had been selected primarily for his batting, with Josh Inglis the only other batter in the squad outside the XI from the Bangladesh series.
Both players have traditionally batted in the middle order in first-class cricket.
It leaves the team without a huge number of options for change if the batting line-up continues to struggle.
"Our batting group in its entirety, not just Marn, probably hasn't been functioning as successfully as we would like," he admitted.
"But we've continued to win a lot of Test matches over that period and that ultimately is the key, scoring more runs than the opposition."
Connolly, 23, is one of three players in the squad under 30, along with 29-year-old Kuhnemann and 27-year-old all-rounder Cameron Green, with the latter the only incumbent in the team.
It raises concerns about an impending transition as the majority of the team ages out with little Test experience in younger players behind them.
"Age is a big focus for some, performance I think is important," Bailey said.
"We're confident around where that group's at and also over the ensuing months years as the transitions occur, be that through performance or players dropping out of formats, there'll be good people that are well placed to come in and perform in whichever team that is."

“The time has come for us to exercise our sovereignty at sea and under water,” Kim said, according to KCNA.
He said that “dangerous shadows must be erased” and that North Korea was under constant threat in the “sea east of the Korean Peninsula and nearby waters”, KCNA reported.
KCNA did not specify what weapons systems might be deployed on the Kang Kon, but said it has the same weapons systems as the 5,000-tonne warship Choe Hyon launched in June.
A previous KCNA report said Choe Hyon-class destroyers can carry a range of weapons, including missiles that analysts say are capable of carrying a nuclear payload.
The ship was commissioned a day before the US, South Korea and Japan were set to begin a five-day military exercise in waters east and south of South Korea’s Jeju Island.
South Korea’s military said in a statement that the Freedom Edge exercise is defensive in nature and meant to respond to North Korean nuclear and missile threats as well as promote regional peace and stability.
North Korea has previously slammed the trilateral drill as a “reckless show of strength”.
Sunday marks the third launch of the Kang Kon; the destroyer partially capsized during the first commissioning in May 2025 before it was repaired and relaunched the following month. It underwent further repairs and sea trials before completing weapons testing in July this year.
Kim said he would demonstrate another stage of North Korea’s naval buildup in eight months, KCNA said, without giving details.
North Korea has accelerated efforts to modernise its navy as Kim pursues a broader expansion of the country’s nuclear-capable forces.
He also said the construction of naval bases on North Korea’s east coast was under way and that the country would create new naval units and build different classes of warships.
Pyongyang, which calls itself an “irreversible” nuclear state, frames the build-up as deterrence against Washington and Seoul. The Korean Peninsula remains technically at war, and Kim has accused the allies of driving the region “to the brink of a nuclear war”.

NUUK, Greenland – European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is expected to unveil on Sept 7 a boost in European Union investments in Greenland and closer political ties with the Danish Arctic territory, which US President Donald Trump has insisted should belong to the United States.
Von der Leyen arrived in Greenland on Sept 6 for a two-day visit serving as a show of support for the governments of Greenland and Denmark, which have strongly rebuffed Trump’s campaign to annex the world’s largest island.
The head of the 27-nation EU’s executive body, von der Leyen is expected to unveil plans to invest in sectors including critical minerals, satellite communications and renewable energy in Greenland, a semi-autonomous part of the Danish realm.
On Sept 6 in the Greenlandic capital Nuuk, von der Leyen said the package would be “substantial” but gave no details.
Greenland Premier Jens-Frederik Nielsen said his country wanted to build on its “close friendship and good partnership” with the EU.
Von der Leyen’s visit reflects the increasing geopolitical importance of the Arctic to major powers, such as the US, Russia, China and Europe, as melting ice opens new shipping routes to make the region’s mineral wealth more accessible.
“Greenland’s stunning landscapes and natural beauty will stay with me for a long time. But so will the visible scars of climate change on the ice sheet,” von der Leyen posted on X after a boat trip under clear blue skies in a fjord scattered with chunks of ice.
“As the ice melts, a new reality is taking shape.”
Trump’s push to acquire Greenland sparked crisis
Trump sparked a crisis in US-European ties and turmoil within the transatlantic NATO military alliance in 2026 when he stepped up his demands for the US to control Greenland, arguing that fellow North Atlantic Treaty Organization member Denmark could not defend it.
European officials stressed Greenland is part of NATO territory, meaning it is covered by the alliance’s mutual defence pact, and that the US already has the right to increase its military presence there under a longstanding treaty.
Tensions lowered after Trump and NATO boss Mark Rutte agreed in Davos in January that the US, Denmark and Greenland would begin talks to resolve their differences and NATO would step up its role in Arctic security.
However, the trilateral talks have yet to yield an agreement and, at a NATO summit in Turkey in July, Trump restated his insistence that the US should control Greenland.
While Denmark is a member of the EU, Greenland left the bloc in 1985.
But its people, as Danish citizens, are also citizens of the EU.
The EU has long provided funding to Greenland, mainly to pay for fishing rights and support its education system.
The package to be announced by von der Leyen will represent not only a big increase in funding but a broadening of the sectors that will receive EU cash, according to EU officials. REUTERS

Austria's Islamic headscarf ban in force as under-14s go back to school
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
01:01:32 BST
09:01:32 KST

Austria's Islamic headscarf ban in force as under-14s go back to school
- Published
As the new school year begins in Austria, a law banning headscarves in schools for girls under 14 has gone into force.
The law forbids "traditional Muslim" head coverings, such as hijabs or burkas, in public and private schools across the country.
Integration Minister Claudia Bauer, from the conservative People's Party (ÖVP), says the headscarf is "a sign of oppression and a means of controlling girls from the earliest childhood".
But critics say the new law is fuelling anti-Muslim feeling in the country and could be unconstitutional.
The law was brought in by the conservative-led coalition of three centrist parties, the ÖVP, the Social Democrats (SPÖ) and the liberal Neos. They say the law is a "clear commitment to gender equality" and is intended to protect the rights of young girls.
Carla Amina Baghajati, from the official Islamic Community in Austria (IGGÖ), told the BBC that the organisation "firmly opposes the ban".
"We believe it unjustifiably restricts the fundamental right to freedom of religion and disproportionately affects Muslim girls," she said.
"Rather than protecting children, it singles out a specific religious practice and risks excluding the very children it claims to support."
The IGGÖ said it would support legal challenges by girls and their families "who believe that their fundamental rights are being infringed" and who wished to bring their cases before the Constitutional Court.
The court struck down a previous ban on headscarves in primary schools in 2020 on the basis that it contravened the principle of Austria's religious neutrality.
Teachers are expected to enforce the new ban if they see a child wearing a headscarf by holding a series of talks with the student and their legal guardians.
If there are repeated violations, child services must be notified and as a last resort, guardians could face fines of up to €800 (£685).
Some teachers have expressed concerns about having to enforce the ban.
The Green Party's Sigi Maurer accused Education Minister Christoph Wiederkehr, from the liberal NEOS, of "creating new conflicts and offloading them onto the teachers".
She said teachers were "already under enormous strain" and that Wiederkehr wanted to "foist the role of police officers onto them" on top of their other duties.
The opposition far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) says the current ban doesn't go far enough. It is calling for a general prohibition on headscarves and face coverings in schools for students and teachers alike.
The FPÖ's Ricarda Berger said there was "no place for political Islam in Austria, and certainly not in our schools".
Austria's Chancellor Christian Stocker, leader of the ÖVP, recently called for a constitutional ban on political Islam, telling Austrian public broadcaster ORF he did not "want to live in an Islamic state".
In France there has been a ban on wearing any conspicuous religious symbols, including headscarves, turbans and kippas, in schools for more than 20 years.
The Austrian law differs from French legislation in that it specifically targets head coverings worn by Muslim women.
Austria, like several other European countries including France, Belgium and Denmark, bans the full face veil (niqabs or burkas) in public.
Baghajati said the IGGÖ was concerned about "a troubling trend" across Europe "in which complex social challenges are reduced to symbolic measures aimed at minority groups."
"Such approaches may generate political attention, but they rarely solve the underlying problems," she said.
