How cognitive shortcuts fuel American political divisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
00:00:07 UTC
09:00:07 KST

When politically engaged individuals clash over public policy, their mutual dislike is often driven by how recognizable and organized their beliefs are. People who consistently hold strong liberal or conservative views express much more animosity toward opposing thinkers than those with moderate or mixed political opinions do. These findings, published in Political Behavior, suggest that the structure of a person’s worldview plays a central role in driving modern political divisions.
Political scientists often trace interpersonal hostility back to disagreements over specific public policies. In recent years, researchers have identified a divide in American politics based on political engagement. This divide separates individuals deeply involved in political conflict from bystanders who lack strong attachments to political parties. Not everyone approaches politics with the same level of intensity or organization.
Some voters possess highly structured belief systems. For these individuals, a stance on one issue reliably predicts their stance on another. Other citizens hold a mix of liberal and conservative views, or they remain ambivalent on major national issues. Tadeas Cely, a political science researcher at Masaryk University and Dartmouth College, wanted to find out how these different belief structures influence political hostility.
Past research often combined all policy disagreements into a single category. Cely sought to test whether clashing with a staunch ideologue generates different emotional reactions than clashing with a moderate. The research focused on two main traits: opinionatedness and belief alignment. Opinionatedness describes the tendency to hold strong views rather than neutral ones.
Belief alignment refers to how consistently a person’s views match a single political ideology, such as modern liberalism or conservatism. Together, these traits define what political scientists consider an ideologue. Cely hypothesized that disagreements among ideologues result in higher expected disagreement and greater mutual animosity.
When confronted with broad policy agendas, individuals often rely on cognitive shortcuts to inform their political decisions. In the context of public policy, belief patterns that follow recognizable structures provide mental cues for emotional reactions. Foundational literature on this topic describes a specific type of political thinker who knows which political ideas typically group together. For these individuals, a single political stance serves as a reliable indicator of a much larger worldview.
These politically sophisticated individuals can infer an entire belief system from a few distinct opinions. When ideologues encounter someone who expresses unambiguous, organized views, they instantly recognize the structural pattern. If the pattern aligns with their own, it signals a likable, belief-congruent peer. If the pattern opposes their own, it triggers an immediate emotional response of dislike, long before every individual policy is debated.
To investigate these dynamics, Cely conducted a large survey experiment involving 2,000 adults in the United States in early 2024. Participants reviewed hypothetical profiles of fellow citizens, each displaying stances on eight different public policies. The hypothetical citizens represented varying degrees of opinionatedness and ideological consistency. Participants then rated their feelings toward each profile on a standard thermometer scale measuring interpersonal warmth, ranging from completely cold to completely warm.
The results revealed that the nature of the opposing belief system heavily influences interpersonal affection. Disagreeing with an opinionated counterpart resulted in a substantial drop in positive feelings. For every single issue where opinions strongly clashed, warmth ratings plummeted. When participants disagreed with a centrist profile, meaning someone holding neutral positions on the issues, the resulting animosity was nearly four times lower.
The specific topic also mattered. Disagreements on highly debated issues like abortion, firearms regulation, and immigration produced the largest drops in warmth. The organization of a participant’s own beliefs also altered their emotional response. Participants with aligned beliefs, meaning they were consistently liberal or conservative, reported steep declines in affection when faced with an opposing profile.
Among these ideologically aligned individuals, the warmth gap between a similar-minded profile and a different-minded profile was massive. At the exact same level of policy disagreement, these structured ideologues experienced a much colder emotional reaction than non-ideologues. Participants with mixed or unstructured beliefs showed much less hostility toward profiles they disagreed with. They did not feel particularly warm toward similar-minded counterparts, but they also did not react with extreme animosity toward differing views.
A second large experiment, also involving 2,000 United States adults, explored why these structured belief systems produce such strong reactions. This survey tested whether ideologues expect to disagree more than others, even when the observed level of disagreement is identical. Participants read text-based descriptions of hypothetical citizens featuring four specific political opinions. These profiles represented either consistently liberal, consistently conservative, centrist, or mixed viewpoints.
Participants were then told the hypothetical citizen held opinions on two additional, unrevealed issues. These hidden issues were student debt relief and a ceasefire in Gaza. The participants had to predict the citizen’s stance on these hidden issues and estimate how often they would disagree with the person overall.
Cely found that ideologues use recognizable belief patterns as a mental shortcut. When a consistent liberal or conservative recognized an opposing ideological pattern in a profile, they anticipated high levels of disagreement on the unrevealed issues. Participants without a structured ideology did not make these same sweeping assumptions. This lack of assumptions among non-ideologues led to lower expectations of future conflict.
The anticipation of conflict was most pronounced among politically sophisticated participants. These individuals successfully recognized which political views typically group together. Because they could easily fill in the blanks of an opposing worldview, these politically savvy individuals expected the highest levels of overall disagreement. This assumed friction appears to fuel greater animosity before a specific policy is even discussed.
The research relies on a simplified measure of moderate beliefs. The survey design does not distinguish between participants who hold genuine, centrist policy preferences and those who are simply ambivalent. Separating these two groups could provide a more precise understanding of how moderation affects interpersonal hostility. Additionally, the study design measures the outcomes of differing belief systems but does not isolate the exact psychological mechanisms at play.
The heightened animosity among ideologues might stem from a general tendency toward closed-mindedness or intolerance of differing worldviews. Future research could involve directly manipulating the presentation of belief structures to isolate these cognitive processes. Expanding this framework to democracies outside the United States, where two to five distinct belief systems often coexist, would help determine how broadly these patterns apply.
The study, “Hatred Takes An Ideologue: Recognizable Belief Patterns Lead to More Animosity and Disagreement,” was authored by Tadeas Cely.

6 killed in Satya Niketan building collapse; FIR against owner

Hours after the building collapse in a student-dominated area near Delhi University’s South Campus, the MCD has ordered action against illegal buildings with four or more storeys.One more body was recovered during late-night operations, taking the total number of fatalities to six.
Teams from the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), Delhi Fire Service, Delhi Police and other agencies continued rescue operations at the site as they worked to remove the debris.The collapse that took place on Sunday afternoon, has raised fresh questions over the safety of buildings being used as paying guest (PG) accommodations and the enforcement of construction and fire safety norms in densely populated parts of the national capital.The Rekha Gupta-led Delhi government has ordered a magisterial inquiry into the incident and directed that an FIR be registered against the building owner, the chief minister’s office (CMO) said.
The decision was taken following an on-site review and a preliminary assessment of the incident, the CMO said.“Following an on-site review and based on the preliminary assessment, the chief minister has ordered a Magisterial Inquiry of the incident and an FIR against the building owner,” the CMO said.It added that those found responsible for the incident would be held fully accountable and face the strictest provisions of the law.Meanwhile, Congress leader and AICC Uttarakhand in-charge Kumari Selja questioned the BJP government over the safety of students living in such accommodations. She said students are sent to Delhi with hopes of building their future and questioned who would be held responsible for their safety.“What is the BJP government doing? They have forgotten what happened at the coaching centre. A mafia is operating in Delhi. These children are sent away with so many hopes. They are the only support for their parents. Who is responsible for their safety?” Selja said.Former Delhi chief secretary Omesh Saigal said the incident should not be viewed as an isolated case, claiming that similar incidents occur every few months. He also raised concerns over unauthorised construction in parts of Delhi.Saigal alleged that some buildings either have unapproved blueprints, additional floors added later or substandard construction, and questioned whether authorities responsible for approving building plans had adequately checked their safety."Look at the kind of buildings constructed in Delhi - I would say that in some areas, one in five buildings is unauthorised; either the blueprints weren't approved, extra floors were added, or the construction is substandard," he said.He also called for restrictions on new construction in areas that are already overcrowded and over-built, saying authorities should consider stopping the sanctioning of new building plans in such areas and examine the safety of existing structures."At the very least, we should ban new construction in these areas. We must halt new construction—or stop sanctioning building plans—for areas that are already over-congested and over-built. These are the things that need to be addressed," he added.NSUI President Vinod Jakhar described the situation as extremely grave and said rescue operations were continuing under difficult conditions."Rescue operations are ongoing, and conditions are dire. Almost all the students being pulled out are dead. We tried our best to get those students out; we actually succeeded in rescuing about three of them. Had the medical facilities, medical teams, police, and fire brigade arrived on time—had all necessary resources and responsible officials been present promptly—perhaps more students could have been saved. But the BJP has no disaster management plan. Just look at how the country's Home Minister inaugurates a grand BJP office in Goa today, while here, a building collapses. BJP offices never collapse because they are built using money extorted from PG and coaching centre operators. Our only demand is justice for the students. Several of our colleagues have also sustained serious injuries. There is absolutely no accountability," Jakhar told news agency ANI.Meanwhile, Delhi Bharatiya Janata Yuva Morcha president Rajat Choudhary said the situation remained serious and appealed for speedy rescue efforts. The opposition should not do this; they should stand in solidarity," he said.In a separate response, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) ordered the immediate sealing of all illegal constructions with more than four floors and warned of strict action against officials found responsible.“All illegal constructions with more than four floors will be immediately sealed, and strict action will be taken against the guilty officials, leading to their immediate dismissal. These orders will be implemented with immediate effect,” the MCD said.

Hormuz traffic dips to lowest since May after US, Iranian strikes on ships
- Ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dropped to an average of 10 per day, the lowest since May, following strikes by US and Iranian forces on oil tankers.
- US attacked three Iranian oil tankers on Sept 5, and Iran's IRGC retaliated by targeting three tankers using unauthorised routes and US vessels.
- The conflict has escalated maritime risks, with 27 projectile strike incidents since July, greatly raising danger for commercial shipping in the region.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – An average of 10 commodity ships transited the Strait of Hormuz per day over the past 10 days, the lowest since May, according to shipping data on Sept 7, after US and Iranian strikes on tankers.
The 10-day moving average was 10 on Sept 6, down from more than 15 on Sept 4 and nearly 13 on Sept 5, data from analytics firm Kpler found.
Only two vessels passed through the strait on Sept 5 while six went through on Sept 6, mostly using the Iranian route.
US forces struck three Iranian oil tankers on Sept 5, US Central Command said, including one off Kharg Island, Iran’s key oil export hub, following attacks by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on US warships in the region.
In retaliation, the IRGC navy said on Sept 5 it targeted three oil tankers travelling unauthorised routes in the strait as well as three additional US vessels in other areas.
The three Iranian tankers were Downy, Stark I and Kylo, also known as Noxen, maritime intelligence firm Marisks said in a note.
The Saturday attacks represented a “major escalation in the maritime conflict”, Marisks said.
“Commercial tankers are now being deliberately used as instruments of reciprocal economic pressure, substantially weakening the previous distinction between military confrontation and commercial shipping,” it added.
“Risk is therefore assessed as extreme for Iranian/Iran-linked tonnage and materially elevated for US-linked or US-escorted shipping throughout the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman.”
There have been 27 projectile strike incidents since July 6, resulting in damage to vessels operating in and around the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said in its weekly report.
On Sept 6, one very large crude carrier and three bulk carriers laden with metals, grains or oilseeds entered the strait, Kpler data showed.
A tanker carrying refined products loaded from a Saudi port attempted to exit but was turned back, data from LSEG showed.
No very large crude carrier exited the strait since Sept 2, according to Kpler data. REUTERS

Kushner added: "Hopefully this trip has come out with some new ways to advance forward".
A White House official confirmed the envoys discussed substantive plans in Moscow that will be announced in the coming weeks.

‘Mayday’ film review: Kenneth Branagh plays ‘a good Russian’ for a change as a former KGB officer who loves Top Gun and fights like Liam Neeson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
23:46:01 UTC
08:46:01 KST

‘Mayday’ film review: Kenneth Branagh plays ‘a good Russian’ for a change as a former KGB officer who loves Top Gun and fights like Liam Neeson
A film about a downed U.S. Navy pilot and a former KGB officer who become friends while trying to escape the Soviet Union in 1987 is now streaming on Apple TV. Shakespearean actor Kenneth Branagh once again plays a Soviet citizen — hardly new territory in his career — while Ryan Reynolds sticks to his familiar persona. The film was commissioned by Skydance Media, a studio that reportedly has close ties to the Trump administration. Critic Eduard Zhuravlev examines what a campy, cliché-ridden Hollywood portrayal of the Soviet Union can look like in 2026.
It’s 1987. Dashing U.S. Navy pilot Troy Kelly (Canadian actor Ryan Reynolds) accepts a secret CIA mission: fly a reconnaissance plane into the Arkhangelsk region to find out whether the Soviet leadership is building missile silos there. The mission goes wrong. Kelly’s plane is hit, and he is forced to eject over the snow-covered taiga. In the forest, the wounded American is rescued by bearded carpenter Nikolai Ustinov (Irish actor Kenneth Branagh), a former KGB officer who is anti-Soviet and a huge fan of the action movie Top Gun. Ustinov agrees to help Kelly escape; a ruthless “Red Army” led by “head of internal security” Alexander Volkov (Polish actor Marcin Dorocinski) is already hunting him.
Mayday may seem like just another streaming action movie destined to fade from memory before the credits finish rolling. These movies usually star some Chris — Evans (The Gray Man, Ghosted), Pratt (Mercy, The Tomorrow War), or Hemsworth (Extraction, Extraction 2). This time, though, viewers got lucky — and not because the lead happens to be a Ryan. Reynolds has plenty of streaming junk on his own résumé.
Mayday is a funny, propulsive buddy road comedy that holds its own even against 1980s genre classics. It also reimagines the caricatured Soviet clichés Hollywood produced in abundance during the Reagan era, from Red Dawn and Rocky IV to Red Heat and Rambo III. That makes it a politically charged film.
John Francis Daley and Jonathan Goldstein wrote and directed the film. Their credits include the reboot of the 1980s comedy series Vacation, the hilarious and hard-edged comedy Game Night, the brisk fantasy Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves, and the screenplays for Horrible Bosses and Spider-Man: Homecoming. The pair could easily rank among Hollywood’s most skilled comedy filmmakers working today.
Skydance Media is another important “author” here — the same studio that merged with Paramount, plans to buy Warner Bros. Discovery, and reportedly has close ties to the Trump administration. Its résumé includes not only the Terminator and Mission: Impossible sequels and a good half of the mass-market schlock starring the Chrises mentioned above, but also films about the complicated relationship between East and West, including The Gorge and Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit.
Branagh, incidentally, directed Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit and played its main villain, Russian oligarch Viktor Cherevin, who plots a terrorist attack on Wall Street. Branagh, an award-winning filmmaker known for adaptations of Shakespeare and Agatha Christie — plus one Marvel outing — has played a Russian character roughly once every six years. After Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit came Tenet, in which the Irish actor played another Russian oligarch, Andrei Sator. International relations are almost beside the point for Sator: dying and bent on revenge, he is prepared to destroy the world. Now Branagh has unexpectedly played “a good Russian.” True, Ustinov is a former KGB officer who tortured people on the job, but the filmmakers show little interest in that detail.
This is one of the first roles in Branagh’s career that has asked him to throw punches. The 65-year-old Irishman does a remarkably convincing Liam Neeson impression in action scenes, at times staged with the choreographic swagger of Atomic Blonde and the John Wick films. In one scene, filmed almost entirely without cuts, the unflappable comrade takes out a group of volunteer patrolmen with a pool rack to the tune of Belaya cheremukha; in another, he dispatches an entire train car full of Red Army soldiers — literally.
Branagh’s unexpected performance — his character recalls Robin Williams’s Soviet saxophonist in Moscow on the Hudson — easily overshadows Reynolds’s efforts. Troy Kelly is yet another exhausting, chatty wisecracker in Reynolds’s career; the actor has not dropped the persona even off camera in roughly 15 years. Still, the two actors have chemistry to rival Deadpool and Wolverine.
The filmmakers bring plenty of wit of their own. For starters, Mayday is both the international distress signal Kelly transmits and simply “a day in May” — the final showdown unfolds on Red Square in the middle of the Victory Day parade.
Moscow was filmed in Budapest, as usual, but with respect and humor. Ustinov drinks moonshine and eats bear meat, but the clichés are played for laughs rather than treated seriously. The actors playing Russian characters either speak Russian without a foreign accent or clearly make an effort. A Party apparatchik keeps The Atheist’s Dictionary and The Luzhin Defense at his dacha; a village grandmother keeps a jar of chicory on a shelf. There is even a Wes Anderson-style montage of a ride in a Zhiguli past Stalinist skyscrapers, Khrushchev-era apartment blocks, and a combined heat and power plant — all set to Bruce Springsteen.
Volkov, a revanchist played with impish gusto by Polish actor Marcin Dorocinski — who also played chess player Vasily Borgov in The Queen’s Gambit and the unnamed captain of the sunken submarine Sevastopol in the latest Mission: Impossible films — keeps a portrait of Chernenko in his office. Before you have time to think the filmmakers are off by two years, Chernenko is replaced by Gorbachev. “I didn’t want to hang a portrait of the man who’s destroying my country,” Volkov says. He dreams of restoring the empire and putting an end to glasnost.
At the same time, the filmmakers urge people to get along, discard propaganda slogans, and stop equating “Party policy” with individual citizens. At first, Kelly says, “Silence is complicity,” and calls everyone living in the Soviet Union part of the problem. He gradually changes his mind both about supposedly faceless Soviet people and about American democracy, after learning that his father developed cancer from asbestos exposure. Ustinov also revises his view of America, which had been shaped by the militaristic propaganda in Top Gun.
The filmmakers’ love for the biggest hit of 1986 is, of course, another meta-joke. It is hard to imagine a KGB officer born in the 1920s — even a former one — watching a bootleg VHS tape of an action movie about young, muscular pilots facing unidentified MiGs 100 times a year. The joke seems intended to remind us that ideological manifestos can be found in pop culture, not just in scientific communism classes.
Skydance Media also made Top Gun: Maverick, the sequel released 36 years after the original — and the highest-grossing film of Tom Cruise’s career. In 1986, Ustinov had to watch the movie on a bootleg VHS tape (“You could go to prison for that!”); by 2022, Maverick was playing in theaters near Arkhangelsk through gray-market distribution. The franchise makes a fitting symbol: a book about the brief period without a Cold War could well be titled “From Top Gun to Top Gun.”

What is celebrated on September 7 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
02:42:10 EEST
08:42:10 KST

What is celebrated on September 7 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On September 7, Ukraine observes Military Intelligence Day, while under the auspices of the UN, it is Clean Air Day. Brazil celebrates Independence Day.
On September 7, Ukraine celebrates Military Intelligence Day, the International Day of Clean Air for blue skies is held under the auspices of the UN, and Brazil celebrates Independence Day. According to the church calendar, under the new style it is the Forefeast of the Nativity of the Theotokos and the day commemorating the Martyr Sozon, while under the old style it is the Translation of the Relics of the Apostle Bartholomew and the day of the Apostle Titus, UNN reports.
Military Intelligence Day of Ukraine
An official holiday established by a Decree of the President of Ukraine in 2022 to honor the special importance of military intelligence in protecting the national interests, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of the state. The date commemorates the issuance, on September 7, 1992, of the decree establishing the Directorate of Military Strategic Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
Unique special operations, the acquisition of critically important strategic information, and the analytical work of intelligence officers play a decisive role in countering military aggression and planning the defensive actions of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
International Day of Clean Air for blue skies
An official environmental observance under the auspices of the UN, established in 2019 to draw attention to the problem of air pollution, which is considered one of the greatest environmental risks to human health.
The observance calls on governments, businesses, and society to strengthen international cooperation, reduce harmful emissions, introduce renewable energy, and ensure every person's right to a clean environment.
World Duchenne Awareness Day
A global medical and social initiative aimed at spreading information about a rare genetic disease that leads to progressive muscle wasting in children.
The event encourages the mobilization of resources for research in gene therapy, expanded access to early diagnosis, and support for patients and their families around the world.
Independence Day of Brazil
The country's main national holiday commemorating the proclamation of independence from Portugal on September 7, 1822, by Regent Prince Pedro, known as the "Cry of Ipiranga."
The day is marked by large-scale military parades in the capital, Brasília, mass cultural festivals, and ceremonial events throughout the country.
Victory Day in Mozambique
A public holiday commemorating the signing of the Lusaka Accord in 1974 between the Mozambican liberation movement FRELIMO and the government of Portugal, which ended the colonial war and paved the way for the proclamation of a sovereign state.
Forefeast of the Nativity of the Theotokos
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers observe the Forefeast of the Nativity of the Theotokos—a day of prayerful preparation for one of the twelve greatest Christian feasts.
The day also commemorates Saint Sozon the Martyr, who suffered for the Christian faith at the beginning of the fourth century in Cilicia, and Saint John, Archbishop of Novgorod.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate the Translation of the Relics of the Holy Apostle Bartholomew and also remember the Holy Apostle Titus of the Seventy, a disciple of the Apostle Paul and the first bishop of Crete.
In the folk calendar, this day was called "Titus the Leaf-Faller" or "Titus the Mushroom Gatherer," as the date was considered the deadline for the mass gathering of wild mushrooms and marked the beginning of the active autumn leaf fall.

At least 25, mostly children, killed after bus plummets from cliff in Cabo Verde
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

23:40:29 UTC
08:40:29 KST

Bus plummets from cliff in Cabo Verde killing at least 25, mostly children
At least 25 people, mostly schoolchildren and teenagers, have died after a bus fell into a ravine on Cabo Verde’s island of Fogo. The deadly crash prompted the authorities of the archipelago nation to declare a two-day mourning period.
The accident occurred on Saturday, when the bus, carrying children on a field trip, plumetted off a cliff while en route to the village of Cha das Caldeiras. The village, known for its unique wines, is located within the large crater of the active Pico do Fogo volcano.
The annual trip was set up by a private individual. The organizer, who is believed to have been behind the wheel, was killed in the crash. Most of the 32 people aboard the bus were killed in the accident, while others received injuries of varying severity.
“I am heartbroken. This is an irreparable loss, a part of the future that is being said goodbye to: the overwhelming majority of the victims are young people and teenagers,” The country’s president, Jose Maria Pereira Neves, said in a Facebook post.
The president, alongside other top officials, attended the funeral of some 18 victims of the crash on Sunday, while other deceased were buried in a separate ceremony earlier in the day. The country’s authorities are investigating the accident.

Yemeni Coast Guard intercepts oil tanker after ‘unauthorized’ delivery to Houthi-held port
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
23:32:38 UTC
08:32:38 KST

Aziz Ahmadi and Rania Abushamala
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Yemeni Coast Guard forces intercepted an oil tanker Sunday after it unloaded an “unauthorized” cargo at the Houthi-held Ras Isa port in Al-Hudaydah governorate, government media reported.
The Comoros-flagged tanker Nerida unloaded the cargo without prior approval from the Yemeni government or undergoing established procedures through the UN Verification and Inspection Mechanism for Yemen (UNVIM), Yemen’s state-run television channel quoted an unnamed Coast Guard Authority source as saying.
Based in Djibouti, UNVIM inspects goods and cargo bound for Houthi-controlled ports to ensure compliance with an international arms embargo.
The source said the tanker disabled its Automatic Identification System (AIS) during parts of its voyage before its signal briefly reappeared south of Al-Hudaydah after it departed Ras Isa port and headed toward the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
“After the vessel left areas under the militia’s control, a government Coast Guard patrol intercepted it in the Gulf of Aden,” the channel reported.
“The vessel initially failed to comply with orders to stop, and armed men aboard opened fire on the patrol boat before it later responded to the call and was escorted to the port of Aden,” it added.
No casualties were reported, and there was no immediate comment from the Houthi group.
UNVIM was established in December 2015 at the Yemeni government’s request to ensure that vessels sailing to ports outside its control comply with UN Security Council Resolution 2216.
It is managed by the UN Office for Project Services.
The incident comes amid escalating clashes between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis in recent weeks.
Government forces said Saturday that they had made battlefield advances on fronts in Taiz and Al-Hudaydah governorates while the army captured dozens of Houthi fighters.

One Nation pushes for early super access for renters and mortgage holders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
23:27:49 UTC
08:27:49 KST

One Nation pushes for early super access for Australians paying rent or mortgage
In short:
One Nation is proposing a radical change to the superannuation system that would allow Australians who rent or pay a mortgage to divert a portion of their super payments as salary for up to three years.
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson says the change will give Australians who opt in "breathing room" to deal with the cost-of-living crisis.
What's next?
The peak body super funds body says the plan is "economically disastrous" and will drive up inflation while making retirees poorer.
Pauline Hanson has insisted One Nation's proposed superannuation early access policy would have a "neutral" impact on inflation, despite warnings it would create a sugar hit for Australians while making the cost-of-living crisis worse in the long term.
Under the proposal, Australians who pay rent or a mortgage would be given a choice to divert a portion of their superannuation to their take-home pay for up to three years.
The full 12 per cent compulsory super contribution would still be paid by employers, but 3 per cent would be paid directly to the person by the super fund if they opted in.
The payments would also remain subject to the concessional tax rate of 15 per cent, rather than the higher personal income tax rate.
Senator Hanson said the average full-time worker earning about $90,500 would get an extra $2,300 in their pocket each year.
That works out to about $44 a week, which she said would provide "breathing room".
"For a working couple earning $168,000 between them, it is about $4,300 a year after tax, or $82 a week, back in the family budget," she said.
Judo Bank chief economic advisor Warren Hogan said the proposal would provide short-term relief for Australians, but raise the cost of living over the long term.
"There is no example in recorded history of us effectively getting our cost-of-living issues under control with more spending,"
"It ultimately makes the problem worse. We need to bring demand in the economy down to take pressure off the supply side in our economy to allow price pressures to ease."
The Reserve Bank has increased interest rates three consecutive times this year in an attempt to curb inflation.
One Nation insists policy will not be inflationary
Mr Joyce insisted the inflationary impact would be "incredibly small".
"If someone was paying, for instance, $600 a week for rent and they get assistance, guess what? They are still paying $600 a week in rent," he said.
Asked what people would do with the additional cash in that scenario, he indicated they would invest it, similar to how it is treated within a super fund.
Loading...
He also pushed back on suggestions people would immediately spend the extra cash as it came into their accounts.
"It's like saying, well, if you've got all this money in the bank, you just go out and spend it that evening. People don't do that," he said.
But Mr Hogan said under the guardrails set out by One Nation, the policy would stimulate spending.
"An initiative like this will put money in people's pockets at an average of $50 or $60 a week, and that money multiplied over half the population, probably, will be a significant stimulus and make the inflation problem worse," he said.
Mr Joyce argued although the scheme would be open to anyone paying a mortgage or rent, which is about 7 million people, it was likely only those experiencing hardship would access it.
"We're not going to have 7 million people in rental stress or housing stress," he said.
Plan would erode retirement nest egg
Health Minister Mark Butler labelled the proposal an "absolutely terrible plan" and pointed to the Morrison government's experiment allowing people to access more of their super during the COVID-19 pandemic, which left some with a depleted nest egg.
"It's going to make a huge difference, a bad difference to their retirement decades down the track," he said.
Analysis from the Super Members Council showed a typical 30-year-old full-time worker who withdraws superannuation under the early access policy would be about $25,000 worse off at retirement.
Over the full three years, that person would get about $6,900 in their pocket, but miss out on more than $18,000 in compounding interest.
Senator Hanson said she would prefer Australians to access their super early if they were "on the cusp of losing their home" or "out on the street".
"I would rather see them get that help and assistance they need now, not later in life," she said.
Australians are already allowed to access their superannuation before retirement for several reasons, including financial or medical hardship.
Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume dismissed the proposal as nothing more than a "headline" and said One Nation had questions to answer about how the policy would interact with a person's super balance or their concessional caps.
"This so far is nothing more than a headline. It hasn't really been explained," she said.
"Are we turning our superannuation funds into banks?"
Asked whether One Nation should spell out to people that taking money out of their super now would affect their balance in the future, Mr Joyce said, "people are competent enough to work that out for themselves".
"People aren't stupid," he said.
"There's no point telling a family they'll be better off in retirement if they can't afford the mortgage or their rent payment today.
"A good retirement starts with keeping a roof over your head."
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said One Nation was attempting to "raid" Australians' super instead of facilitating a real pay increase.
She said people who opted in to the plan would be "thousands of dollars worse off in retirement".

Hendel and Zelekha cross threshold as Eisenkot bloc loses ground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
23:23:55 UTC
08:23:55 KST

A poll published Sunday evening by Israel's Kan public broadcaster projects that the Reservists' Party, led by Yoaz Hendel, will cross the electoral threshold following the addition of former accountant general Yaron Zelekha. The party is projected to win four mandates, the same number as Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael party.
The Netanyahu bloc maintains its strength from last week at 52 mandates, excluding Hendel and Zelekha. Meanwhile, the bloc of parties opposed to Netanyahu, led by Gadi Eisenkot, loses four mandates and is projected to win 51.
Yashar and Likud each lose one mandate compared with last week's poll, with 23 and 20 mandates, respectively. The Together party, led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, also loses one mandate and is projected to win 13.
The Arab parties maintain their combined strength at 13 mandates. The Joint List falls to seven, while Ra'am rises to six.
The Democrats lose one mandate and are projected to win eight, the same number as United Torah Judaism. Yisrael Beiteinu, Otzma Yehudit and Shas each win seven mandates.
The Religious Zionism Party, led by Bezalel Smotrich, gains one mandate following its merger with Moshe Feiglin and is projected to win six.
As in the previous poll, Blue and White and the Haredi Public party, led by Moti Leitner, fail to cross the electoral threshold. The Unity party, led by Gilad Erdan, which had been included in polls in recent weeks, has withdrawn from the race.
The poll was conducted by the Kantar Institute, headed by Dudu Hassid, among 551 respondents. The margin of error is 4.2 percent.

Halis Sunnetci
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Federico Gatti scored a stoppage-time equalizer as Juventus secured a 1-1 draw against AC Milan on the third matchday of Serie A on Sunday.
Juventus created the better opportunities in the first half, with Francisco Conceicao at the heart of their attacking play.
Conceicao slipped while attempting to shoot from inside the penalty area in the 25th minute, allowing AC Milan’s Mike Maignan to intervene, but Juventus’ Nicolas Gonzalez sent the rebound wide from close range.
Maignan denied Conceicao again in the 37th minute, pushing away the Portugal international’s outside-of-the-foot effort at the near post.
Milan reached halftime without registering a shot on target, while Juventus were unable to capitalize on their chances.
Conceicao came close to breaking the deadlock in the 55th minute after Manuel Locatelli dispossessed Yunus Musah and released him, but his low shot struck the base of the far post.
Milan took the lead against the run of play in the 68th minute through substitute Alphadjo Cisse.
Samuel Chukwueze, who had also recently entered the match, raced down the right before switching play to Cisse, who controlled the ball and fired a low shot through Pierre Kalulu’s legs into the bottom corner.
It was the 19-year-old attacking midfielder’s second goal of the season.
Juventus pushed for an equalizer, but Nick Woltemade fired wide after Manuel Locatelli lifted the ball into the penalty area in the 85th minute.
Juventus head coach Luciano Spalletti made his final change in the 88th minute, sending center-back Gatti on for Zeki Celik as the hosts chased an equalizer.
The substitution paid off four minutes later when Teun Koopmeiners delivered an accurate cross to the edge of the six-yard box. Gatti rose highest and headed the ball off the underside of the crossbar and into the net.
The draw moved both Juventus and AC Milan to seven points after three matches.

Several killed in Amazon cargo plane crash in Miami
September 7, 2026
An Amazon cargo plane barreled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people as it struck vehicles and burst into flames, authorities said.
The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. local time, or 18:00 GMT, after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalized with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials said at a press conference.
"Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being and care of everyone involved. We’re doing everything we can to support those affected," officials said, adding that it was too soon to determine whether those killed were on the plane or in vehicles struck by the aircraft.
According to the authorities, the crash sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky and trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit, as well as some people in cars.
Investigation launched into cause of crash
The Prime Air aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.
The NTSB said in an X post on Sunday the B-767-300 cargo airplane was flying into Miami from San Juan, Puerto Rico and they have "launched a go team to investigate Sunday's runway excursion accident."
The flight was operated by 21 Air, a North Carolina-based cargo carrier. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to Flightradar24.
Amazon said it would cooperate with the investigation.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said in a statement. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones and all those affected by this devastating loss."
About 250 flights were delayed at the airport by late Sunday afternoon, according to FlightAware. Fire crews were still dealing with a fuel leak several hours later, according to reports.
Eyewitness say they saw 'thick black smoke billowing into the sky'
Jackson Lee, who runs an electronics shop near the crash site, told news agencies that he went outside with four colleagues after the crash and saw smoke rising near the airport’s fences.
"We hear planes taking off and landing every five minutes. I thought I’d got used to it," Lee said. "I never thought it could come this close to us."

Gilad Erdan, Ayelet Shaked announce they will not run in upcoming election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
23:14:36 UTC
08:14:36 KST

Former Israeli ambassador to the UN Gilad Erdan and former justice minister Ayelet Shaked announced Sunday that they will not run in the upcoming election, citing the political reality and the difficulty of advancing their vision for a broad unity government.
Erdan, chairman of the Unity Party, said he decided to withdraw the party from the race after concluding that it was unlikely to cross the electoral threshold and that efforts to merge with other parties had not succeeded.
“Throughout my life, I have served the people of Israel and the State of Israel,” Erdan said. “Out of this sense of mission, I established the Unity Party several weeks ago, because I believe Israel needs a broad Zionist government that can pass a genuine conscription law and resolve disputes.”
“I believed that the terrible massacre of October 7 and the horrific price paid by Israeli citizens required us to change direction,” he added.
Erdan said that after a month of campaigning, it had become clear that most Israelis were primarily focused on determining who should serve as prime minister, rather than forming a broad unity government.
“Unfortunately, after about a month of campaigning, reality shows that in the upcoming election, a large majority of the public is primarily seeking a clear decision regarding the identity of the prime minister. The need for a broad unity government is not high on the public’s list of priorities,” he said.
Erdan: Withdrawing from election is responsible decision
“Despite the many efforts we made, the support for the Unity Party I established does not currently provide a high likelihood that we will cross the electoral threshold,” Erdan said. “In addition, the options for joining with other parties in the unity bloc have not materialized.”
“Therefore, I have decided that the Unity Party will not run in the upcoming election,” he said.
Erdan said withdrawing from the race was a responsible decision intended to ensure that his supporters’ votes would not be wasted.
“Leadership also means recognizing reality as it is and acting responsibly, and I believe we must ensure that the votes of our supporters influence the election results and do not go to waste,” he said.
Ayelet Shaked announces she will not run in upcoming election
Shaked also announced her decision not to run in the upcoming election, expressing disappointment that Israel’s political system had not shifted toward greater cooperation following the October 7 massacre.
“I admit that I hoped that after October 7, Israel’s political reality would change,” Shaked said. “Unfortunately, it appears that even in the upcoming election, the political system is returning to the same patterns of camps and boycotts, with two blocs that, in my view, are tearing the country apart.”
Shaked said she believed a broad government spanning political blocs was necessary to address Israel’s security, diplomatic, and economic challenges, but concluded that such a government was not possible in the current election cycle.
“I think and believe that a broad government spanning the political blocs is necessary to address the security, diplomatic, and economic challenges before us. But it appears that such a government is not possible in the current election cycle,” she said.
Shaked thanked supporters who encouraged her to return to politics and said she would continue contributing to Israel outside the political system.
“I promise that, as always, I will continue contributing to the State of Israel in every way I can,” she said. “Better days will come.”

Yoaz Hendel of the Unity Party and Prof. Yaron Zelekha would cross the electoral threshold with four seats in the upcoming election, according to a new KAN News poll published Sunday evening.
The survey follows the split between Chili Tropper and Hendel, who announced Sunday that they were pursuing “separate political paths.” Their party, Zionist Home-The Reservists, has consistently polled below the electoral threshold.
Following his split from Tropper, Hendel announced that he would run jointly with Zelekha, an Israeli economist and political figure who heads the New Economic Party, which has also consistently failed to cross the electoral threshold.
Tuesday, September 8 is the final deadline for political parties to submit their official candidate lists for the upcoming national elections.
With Hendel and Zelekha’s party projected to enter the Knesset, neither the Netanyahu bloc nor the Eisenkot bloc would have enough seats to form a government on its own, potentially forcing both sides to seek additional coalition partners after the election.
According to the poll, the Netanyahu bloc would hold 52 seats, while the opposition bloc would hold 51 seats.
Both blocs fall short of 61-seat majority
With Hendel and Zelekha’s party included, the poll projects the Netanyahu bloc at 56 seats and the Eisenkot bloc at 55 seats, leaving both sides short of the 61 seats needed to form a government.
The poll showed that Likud (20), Yashar led by Gadi Eisenkot (23), and B’Yachad led by Naftali Bennett (13) each lost seats compared with previous polls. The Democrats, Otzma Yehudit, United Torah Judaism, and the Joint Arab List also each lost one seat.
Ra’am and the Religious Zionist Party both gained strength, rising to six seats each.
Eisenkot still leads in suitability for prime minister
Eisenkot continues to lead Netanyahu and Bennett on questions of suitability for prime minister. Among respondents, 38% said Eisenkot was more suitable for the role compared with 35% who chose Netanyahu. Netanyahu led Bennett by 37% to 32%.
Respondents were also asked about Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct on the morning of October 7, against the backdrop of a KAN News report stating that he spoke with the IDF chief of staff only three hours after Hamas’s attack began. Sixty-two percent gave Netanyahu a “not good” rating for his conduct that morning, while 26% said his conduct was “good.”
The poll was conducted on September 6, 2026, by the Kantar Institute. A total of 2,450 people were invited to participate, of whom 551 men and women aged 18 and older responded. The poll was conducted through an online sample and also included Arab sector respondents. The margin of error is plus or minus 4.2%.

Muetaz Wannes and Rania Abushamala
07 September 2026•Update: 07 September 2026
Libya’s Government of National Unity announced Sunday that it had dismantled an organized “sabotage cell” involved in attacks using explosive-laden drones on oil and electricity facilities in the capital Tripoli and the western city of Zawiya.
An intelligence and security operation conducted by the Defense Ministry led to the arrest of five Libyan and foreign suspects, the government said in a statement, without disclosing the foreigners’ nationalities.
During the first half of August, facilities at the Zawiya oil complex, located about 50 kilometers (31 miles) west of Tripoli, were targeted in unidentified attacks involving remotely detonated explosive drones, damaging oil infrastructure.
Power generation and water facilities in the city were targeted in similar attacks during the same period.
Other attacks targeted an oil storage tank and a power station in Tripoli but caused no damage.
The government said the Defense Ministry also thwarted “other plots that were close to being carried out,” including plans to attack a power station south of Tripoli, other vital facilities, and political, security and military figures.
Available information confirmed that the incidents were “not isolated or random acts, but rather part of a broad and interconnected sabotage plot involving multiple parties, tools and objectives,” the statement said.
The plot “systematically targeted infrastructure, energy resources and oil and electricity facilities,” it added.
“Dismantling this cell is not the end of the operation but the beginning of uncovering all the threads and extensions of this plot,” the government said.
It vowed to continue pursuing the remaining suspects and identify those who planned, financed, supported, facilitated and incited the attacks or provided cover for them.

Five killed after Amazon cargo plane overruns runway at Miami airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
23:02:58 UTC
08:02:58 KST

At least five people were killed and five others injured after an Amazon cargo plane overran a runway while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday, striking several vehicles before catching fire and sending thick black smoke into the air.
Three of the injured were in critical condition and taken to a trauma center, while two others were transported to a local hospital, Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Raied “Ray” Jadallah said at a news conference Sunday evening.
Several people were trapped inside vehicles struck by the aircraft and had to be rescued, he said.
Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said there was no apparent threat to the public, though emergency crews remained at the scene because of an ongoing fuel leak.
More than 60 emergency units responded to the crash, according to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, arriving to find the aircraft engulfed in heavy flames and smoke.
The cause of the runway overrun was not immediately clear. CNN reported that a review of air traffic control audio showed the pilots did not declare an emergency before landing.
The aircraft, a 32-year-old Boeing 767 operated by cargo airline 21 Air, was flying for Amazon from San Juan, Puerto Rico. It landed on Miami International Airport's Runway 30 shortly before overrunning the pavement at around 2 p.m. local time, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
The runway is more than 9,000 feet long.
“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement to CNN. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”
“The airplane, which was operated by 21 Air, was attempting to land when this incident occurred,” the statement added. “We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to learn more and will cooperate fully with any investigation.”
The National Transportation Safety Board said it was gathering information about the crash, while the FAA said it would investigate.
Inspection crews found no aircraft parts or debris on the runway itself, though the plane damaged navigational equipment after leaving the paved surface.
A ground stop at Miami International Airport was lifted at around 5 p.m. Eastern Time, but delays were expected to continue into Monday because of the disabled aircraft, according to the FAA.
21 Air is a cargo carrier with an operations center in Miami that operates Boeing 767 aircraft for companies including Amazon and DHL. CNN said it had contacted the airline for comment.
Runway excursions, the aviation term for aircraft veering or overrunning the end of a runway, are the most common type of aircraft accident worldwide, according to the International Air Transport Association.
Miami International Airport's runways, like those at many major airports, are surrounded by designated safety areas intended to provide additional space when an aircraft leaves the runway.

John Healey will argue the government’s plans to boost growth across the whole country will enable the British economy to “turn a corner” despite anxiety over volatile bond markets derailing Labour’s crucial first budget.
The chancellor is expected to argue that fiscal discipline is “indivisible” from good growth, especially at a time of difficult global headwinds, amid concerns that his cautious approach jars with Andy Burnham’s more radical policy plans.
In a speech in the West Midlands on Monday, Healey will set out how the government plans to boost regional economies by easing Treasury bureaucracy and giving more powers to local leaders to drive business investment, innovation and skills.
But public finances are under pressure from soaring global bond yields, which hit an 18-year high last week, driving up government borrowing costs, resulting in Healey putting Britain on notice for a tough 28 October budget.
Economists have predicted that the chancellor – who has said he wants a “buffer against uncertainty” – will have to put up taxes or cut spending to protect the £24bn fiscal headroom his predecessor Rachel Reeves had last year.
“Fiscal credibility is indivisible from good growth,” the chancellor is expected to say. A Treasury source said this was “true at any time, but especially at a time of global uncertainty” amid warnings that Donald Trump’s war in the Middle East would push up inflation and hit public finances.
Healey will say that, despite the bleak global backdrop, pursuing growth across every region will help unlock “huge latent potential” and show Britain is “turning a corner”, with people, businesses and communities ready to seize the opportunities of new technologies.
The prime minister argued at the weekend that it would be impossible to build a dynamic economy on crumbling infrastructure, with businesses needing affordable energy and reliable transport, and so more investment would be needed.
But in a move that will undermine Labour’s efforts to reindustrialise, the UK’s biggest carmaker, Jaguar Land Rover, which is based in the West Midlands, was expected to announce thousands of job cuts.
During a speech at a manufacturing site on Monday, Healey is expected to reiterate that Britain’s growth must extend beyond its biggest cities.
“The prime minister laid out a clear diagnosis of what has gone wrong in the past,” he is expected to say. “The solution is a fundamental shift that starts with putting power in the right places. The next chapter of Britain’s growth story will be written in more places.”
National government must work with the new No 10 North on a “dual mission” to remove obstacles for local leaders and businesses, he is expected to say. “Instead of getting in the way with complexity and red tape, we need a strong, strategic centre wired to enable local leaders and their ambitions.
“I want to see wealth creation in this country. I want to see businesses make a profit. And to create the conditions for that we need an active, accountable state at all levels to remove blockages and create the conditions for more investment.”
Healey will announce that the British Business Bank will allocate £150m to scale up businesses across the north of England. The pot will offer investments from £5m to £15m to help university spinouts and the expansion of other innovative companies.
He will underline the government’s commitment to “place-based” growth, building on Reeves’s attempts to move the focus of the Treasury away from the south-east. “Ask an economist what growth is and you’ll get a number,” he will say. “But ask the country and you’ll get a different answer.
“A young person getting a new job in a company that’s on the up. A sole trader winning a new contract that pays for a holiday with their kids. A business winning a new export order, giving the community around it a new lease of life.”
However, businesses are braced for what they fear will be higher taxes to fill a fiscal hole caused by rising borrowing costs and Burnham’s new spending plans. In an interview with the Financial Times on Saturday, Healey refused to rule out increasing levies on bank profits.
Healey has also been under pressure over the timeline to hit defence spending targets, after quitting Keir Starmer’s cabinet over the issue. On Sunday, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, indicated the government would spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence by 2030.
“We’ve made some clear movements early on to show that direction of travel … [Healey] has not moved away from the target you’ve said. He said the fundamental target is the 2035 3.5% of GDP on defence spending that is our Nato commitment. The trajectory to that covers the 3% but that is the principal target,” said Reynolds.
Robert Jenrick, Reform UK’s economic spokesperson, said: “Even Rachel Reeves had more vision than this guff. Days after a market meltdown, when grip and direction are required, John Healey has revealed himself to be an empty vessel with no idea about how to rescue our economy.”
Andrew Griffith, the new shadow chancellor, described Healey’s speech as a “policy-light word salad”, saying it would do little to comfort families and businesses who were worried about more tax rises or the rates of government borrowing.
On the BBC on Sunday, Griffith, who was a Treasury minister at the time of Liz Truss’s disastrous mini-budget, said there had been “lots of good things” in that fiscal statement – including tax cuts and cutting regulation – attracting criticism from Labour.

‘Gigantic spaceship’: University of Bristol’s flagship £500m campus opens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
23:01:18 UTC
08:01:18 KST

Not so long ago, the first impression for visitors arriving by train to Bristol’s main railway station was a derelict building described by David Cameron as looking like the entrance to a war zone.
On Monday, a shiny new University of Bristol campus on the site of that crumbling Royal Mail sorting office next door to Temple Meads is opening its doors to students, teachers and members of the public.
The proximity of the Temple Quarter Enterprise Campus (TQEC) to the station should make it easier for students and staff who cannot afford Bristol’s expensive property and rental market to commute, and for business and research partners from all across the country to attend meetings.
The campus is also designed to be “porous”, with many areas completely open to the public, turning it into a front door to the university for Bristolians in a way that its grand buildings high on the hill in the leafy Clifton area never have been.
The £500m campus is a major part of one of the UK’s biggest regeneration schemes, Bristol Temple Quarter, which is to bring thousands of new homes, work spaces and health and education centres to one of the city’s – and England’s – most deprived neighbourhoods. The scheme is so important to Labour locally and nationally that it got a mention in Andy Burnham’s first prime minister’s questions.
Speaking in a garden space in TQEC almost directly above Temple Meads’ platform 15, Judith Squires, deputy vice chancellor and university lead for the TQEC, said the new site put the university “front and centre” in the city.
“We think it opens up lots of opportunities that we haven’t yet explored,” she said. “One of them will be for students who commute to Bristol, which I think may become an increasingly important trend given that rent is such an expensive cost. Living at home is becoming an increasing option for students.
“It also means that it’s very accessible for a lot of our staff who can commute in, but also for our industrial partners who will be coming to do research and collaboration in the building.”
The site will be a hub for teaching and research across areas including business, innovation, digital engineering, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, advanced telecommunications and quantum technologies.
It features a rare example of a circular lecture theatre. When the Guardian visited, an actor and voice coach from Bristol Old Vic theatre was showing lecturers how to best use the space.
But the university is keen to emphasise that it is is not just for academic types to use, but for all of Bristol’s citizens.
A new entrance from the station to the campus has been created, and new footpaths and cycleways added.
Spaces aimed at citizens include the Bristol Rooms and the Story Exchange on the ground floor, which are designed to bring academics and students together with business, public sector and community organisations.
Sessions on topics important to Bristolians, such as health inequalities, reparative justice and the climate crisis, have already been organised.
Members of the public are to be allowed more casual access to the campus. They will be able to have a coffee on the campus, plug in a laptop and work or use it as a meeting spot.
Squires said: “We wanted to make it a porous place so that people can feel it is a space for them, designed with them in mind. It’s really great to have such an accessible front door to the university where everybody can find it, so we don’t feel so cut off from the city. I think it positions us physically and symbolically in a different way with the city.”
The main building has cost £241m and is named the Sloane Robinson building, after a foundation set up by the former Bristol University student and hedge fund manager Hugh Sloane, which donated £20m.
The West of England Combined Authority (WECA) has invested £35m into the campus and £25m into the station entrance and new paths.
The university has snapped up other parcels of land nearby so it can expand the campus in the coming years, taking the cost of the campus up to £500m.
Behind the Sloane Robinson building, work on the wider Bristol Temple Quarter project is under way in the St Philip’s Marsh area of the city, currently a place of factories, waste disposal sites and Bristol’s fruit market.
Though the new quarter will be 30 years in the making, workers in hi-vis are preparing the way for new homes, shops, community spaces. A bridge is to be built from TQEC to link to it.
Helen Godwin, the mayor of the West of England, said the opening of the campus was a major milestone for Bristol. “Our investment in Bristol Temple Quarter will unlock a giant leap forward for the West of England,” she said.
Martin Booth, editor of the independent magazine and website Bristol 24/7 and author of 111 Places That You Shouldn’t Miss in Bristol, said the new site looked as if a “gigantic spaceship” had crash-landed next to the station. “But it is a manifestation of the university’s efforts to be a more visible part of our city – not just in their privileged position on top of a hill in Clifton,” he said.

Almost 75% of A&E staff in UK face violence or aggression daily or weekly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
23:01:17 UTC
08:01:17 KST

Nearly three-quarters of A&E staff experience violence or aggression daily or weekly, according to a survey highlighting the “appalling” abuse of NHS workers.
The Royal College of Emergency Medicine (RCEM) said understaffed and overcrowded emergency departments were contributing to increased targeting of medics.
In a survey of more than 2,000 workers in the UK, 63% said they had suffered discrimination including racism, sexism and homophobia, while 73% said violence or aggression of all kinds was a daily or weekly occurrence. Almost all (96%) said they had experienced abuse from patients or members of the public.
Dr Ian Higginson, the president of the RCEM, said: “No one should go to work fearing or, worse, expecting to be attacked, intimidated or abused. Nor should they lack confidence that their employers have their backs, or that the judicial system will kick in.
“Yet that’s the reality faced by the majority of my colleagues in EDs [emergency departments] across the country. They often do not feel safe to care for patients. It is an appalling state of affairs which is contributing towards many people seriously considering whether emergency medicine – or even healthcare in general – is for them.”
Senior nurses said in January that abuse of NHS staff had become a national crisis.
In the survey, emergency department workers said long waiting times and overcrowding had made violence and aggression a “routine” part of working on the hospital frontline. Staff shortages and corridor care – patients being treated in non-clinical spaces because of overcrowding – were also cited as main reasons behind the abuse.
One anonymous resident doctor said: “Working in the ED, you brace yourself for a lot, but nothing truly prepares you for direct, hateful verbal abuse, especially when it’s racially charged.”
A senior emergency doctor told the survey they had been kicked in the face by an aggressive patient lying on a trolley.
Ministers have pledged to get key waiting times across the NHS back on track before the end of this parliament in 2029. However, the leaders of professional bodies have called for faster action after a series of targets were missed at the end of the financial year in March.
The NHS was told to ensure 78% of A&E patients were treated within four hours by March. While it came close to that target – 77.6% of patients were treated within four hours that month – the proportion has since slipped.
Higginson called on the government to accelerate its drive to reduce waiting times and overcrowding. “Much has been said by us and other organisations over the years about violence and aggression towards healthcare staff. But the problem seems to be getting worse, not better,” he said.
“It’s time for action, time for governments, employers and organisations stand up for NHS staff, and time to ensure that those who intimidate, abuse or assault those who are trying to care for them face meaningful consequences for their actions.”
The worsening conditions in A&E would have “devastating” consequences for the workforce if they continued, the RCEM added.
Only 4% of those surveyed said they always felt safe working in A&E, while 75% reported short-term stress and anxiety, 40% said they had experienced burnout and 28% long-term stress or anxiety.
In January, data obtained by the Guardian revealed that more than 295,000 incidents of physical violence and aggression by patients against staff had been recorded by 212 NHS trusts in England between 2022 and 2025.
Hospitals records showed the number of violent incidents, which ranged from violent threats to attempted and actual assaults, had risen from 91,175 in 2022-23 to 104,079 in 2024-25. This was equivalent to about 285 cases being reported every day in the most recent year.
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “Any acts of violence, abuse or harassment towards NHS staff are completely unacceptable and will not be tolerated. Everyone working in our national health service has a fundamental right to be safe at work, and it is deeply concerning that so many emergency department staff continue to experience this behaviour.
“That is why this government recently introduced new NHS staff standards, which set out the steps that every NHS employer across the country must take to prevent and reduce violence and abuse against their staff and help ensure they can do their jobs safely.”

New evidence links slain Belgian development worker to Hamas as Israel demands apology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
22:56:43 UTC
07:56:43 KST

Abdullah Jamal Sobhi Nabhan, a Palestinian employee of the Belgian development agency Enabel, was killed in an Israeli airstrike in Rafah on April 24, 2024. His 7-year-old son Jamal, his father, his brother and his niece were also killed in the strike.
At the time, Enabel said Nabhan had joined the agency in April 2020 and worked as a business development officer on a European project supporting small businesses in the Gaza Strip.
Then-Belgian Development Minister Caroline Gennez and Enabel condemned the strike. Belgium’s then-foreign minister, Hadja Lahbib, summoned Israel’s ambassador at the time, Idit Rosenzweig-Abu, and demanded explanations.
Nabhan had also appeared in Enabel material from the COP27 climate conference in Egypt in 2022. According to the agency, he and members of his family were included on a list of Enabel employees submitted to Israeli authorities in an effort to secure their evacuation from Gaza.
His death was reported by international media, including Reuters and Al Jazeera, and Enabel Director General Jean Van Wetter later spoke publicly about the circumstances of his death.
Following the Belgian Foreign Ministry reprimand in 2024, the Israeli ambassador said she had expressed sorrow over the deaths of civilians. She said the house where the family was staying belonged to a senior Hamas member from the extended family who had been the target of the strike.
She added at the time that Israel was still examining the incident and would provide Belgium with further information once the review was completed.
Israel later provided Belgian authorities with names of Hamas operatives it said were employed by the Belgian aid agency, according to Israeli officials. The Israeli account says Enabel took no action over the information.
The case resurfaced on September 4, 2026, when open-source researcher Gabriel Epstein published material that he said showed Nabhan had been a member of Hamas’ Khan Younis Battalion.
Epstein presented a mourning poster published by a channel associated with the battalion. The poster described Nabhan as a “mujahid,” or jihad fighter, and included an image showing him in military-style uniform.
The channel has previously published material about Hamas operatives, at times before the organization itself issued official announcements, according to the information cited by Israel.
Epstein also highlighted a 2025 post by a relative in which Abdullah Nabhan and his brother Ahmad were both described as “mujahideen.”
‘Before rushing to condemn Israel, facts matter’
Following the publication of the material, Israel’s Embassy in Belgium said on its X account that the new evidence indicated Nabhan had belonged to Hamas’ Khan Younis Battalion.
The embassy recalled the summoning of Israel’s ambassador and the international criticism that followed the 2024 strike.
“Before rushing to condemn Israel, facts matter,” the embassy wrote. “Those who accused Israel then should now acknowledge the evidence.”
Israel’s ambassador to Belgium, David Saranga, went further, calling directly for an apology.
“A public apology would be the proper thing to do, but a private apology would also be accepted,” he wrote on X.
The post drew tens of thousands of views and hundreds of shares, according to the report, and prompted renewed discussion within Belgium’s political system over the case.
Belgium has since undergone a change of government, with a center-right coalition replacing the previous center-left, liberal-progressive government.

India, 163 others vote at UNGA for map with bigger Africa, shrunk North America

India, 163 others vote at UNGA for map with bigger Africa, shrunk North America
Agencies / Sep 07, 2026, 04:06 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
United Nations General Assembly voted Friday to adopt a new world map that makes the African continent bigger while shrinking North America and Europe, drawing ire from Washington.Aimed at "a more accurate representation" of continental landmasses, the resolution was supported by 164 countries, including India. US voted against it and six nations abstained.The new map, known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection, improves "the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world", the resolution said. It urges member states to use the new map in place of the traditional Mercator projection.Foreign minister Robert Dussey of Togo, which sponsored the resolution, said maps "guide education, nourish imagination, and influence collective perceptions"."They are therefore never neutral; when they present a distorted image of our planet, they risk perpetuating inaccurate representation that is passed down through generations," he said.African Union Commission chair Mahmoud Ali Youssouf said, "Beyond cartography, this initiative underscores the importance of representing Africa on the basis of objective and scientifically established realities...
Africa must be represented as it truly is: in its true dimensions and in its rightful place in the world."US, however, slammed the resolution, saying such moves are "the reason this institution is losing its credibility". Representative Yaryna Ferencevych said, "Instead of focusing on genuine problems... this body is debating map projects from the 16th century and their role in promoting reparations and cognitive justice."The Mercator projection was designed for maritime navigation by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569. It focused on depictions of the shapes and angles of land masses but their relative sizes were often inaccurate, largely due to the challenge of rendering a three-dimensional globe onto a two-dimensional map.
It inflated northern regions and compressed equatorial ones, making Europe and North America appear much larger, while shrinking Africa and South America. Africa appears to be roughly as big as Greenland, though at 30.3 million sq km, it's about 14 times as large.France, which co-sponsored the resolution, announced Friday it would abandon the Mercator projection, in which "US, Russia and China take on a disproportionate visual prominence". Foreign minister Jean-Noel Barrot said, "Changing maps obviously doesn't change the world," "But correcting a distorted representation is already an act of truth."

“And it is precisely because we both speak the language of patriotism and of defending our respective countries that we are capable of having constructive discussions.”
“We are moving towards a world that, in reality, respects only strength. We have to recognise that and take it into account,” Bardella said, adding that leaders who display weakness or naivete will be crushed by great powers. BLOOMBERG

UN-backed map must depict India's territory accurately: Govt
TNN / Sep 07, 2026, 04:04 IST
Comments

UN-backed map must depict India's territory accurately: Govt
NEW DELHI: After endorsing a UN General Assembly resolution on equal-area world map, the govt warned Sunday that the proposed new map must depict India's sovereign territory, including the Union territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, in accordance with India's official map and any inaccurate or misleading depiction would be unacceptable."Our position on India's sovereignty and territorial integrity is clear, consistent and non-negotiable," said MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, replying to media queries.
MEA: Resolution doesn't endorse any specific map
India was among the 164 countries that voted in favour of UN General Assembly's Sept 4 resolution, "Correct the Map: Rebalancing Global Cartographic Representation and Promoting Equitable Representation of the World's Regions, Particularly Africa".MEA said the resolution's purpose is to encourage the use of equal-area map projections that preserve the relative sizes of continental landmasses, and it neither adopts nor authenticates any particular world map, nor does it address political cartography, including international boundaries, disputed territories or place names."India voted in favour of the resolution and also made an explanation, stressing the underlying principle of promoting equal-area cartographic representation.
We also highlighted that the resolution does not constitute endorsement of any specific map, projection or depiction of national boundaries," said Randhir Jaiswal.The resolution received abstentions from Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine, and a lone vote against it from US.
The resolution noted that the Mercator projection remains widely used in educational, media, digital and official materials, despite the considerable distortion of landmasses to the North and South, far from the equator.It expressed concern that this distortion contributed to minimising the perceived sizes of Africa, Latin America and South Asia, and perpetuating an unbalanced view of the world. India welcomed the intention behind the resolution to promote more accurate and representative cartographic practices.

Since 2018, more than 205,000 undocumented migrants have crossed the English Channel to the UK in inflatable boats. The problem of illegal immigration has worsened in the UK since its exit from the EU, despite the fact that illegal immigration was one of the main reasons for Brexit.
