Netanyahu trial resumes as defense phase moves beyond prime minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:49:37 UTC
02:49:37 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s criminal trial resumed at the Jerusalem District Court on Sunday after the summer recess, beginning a new stretch of the defense case in which the remaining witnesses for Netanyahu and his three co-defendants will take the stand.
Netanyahu completed his own testimony in June after 98 hearing days spanning a year and a half. Sunday’s hearing focused primarily on organizing the witness schedule and determining which defense witnesses will be called, rather than hearing new evidence.
Four hearing days are planned this week. According to a notice submitted by Netanyahu’s defense, MK Ze’ev Elkin’s cross-examination is scheduled to continue on Monday.
Ronit Mandelbaum is expected to testify later that day if necessary, while Police Chief Superintendent Shmuel Sharvit is scheduled to take the stand on Tuesday and Wednesday. The defense asked the court to issue summonses for Mandelbaum and Sharvit.
Their testimony will form part of the defense effort to challenge the prosecution’s account of how the investigations in the case were conducted, and whether evidence was lawfully and properly obtained.
The trial is also returning to its original venue in Jerusalem. Netanyahu’s testimony was heard at the Tel Aviv District Court building under special security arrangements.
The most consequential unresolved question as proceedings resume is the bribery charge in Case 4000, the Bezeq-Walla affair.
Judges continued to see evidentiary difficulties in proving bribery
After Netanyahu completed his testimony, the judges told the parties that their assessment from June 2023 had not changed: They continued to see evidentiary difficulties in proving bribery and believed the prosecution should consider withdrawing that charge.
This was not an instruction, nor was it very detailed. The prosecution has not withdrawn the charge, and the indictment remains unchanged.
Case 4000 alleges that Netanyahu, while serving as prime minister and communications minister, advanced regulatory decisions benefiting Bezeq and its then-controlling shareholder, Shaul Elovitch. In exchange, prosecutors allege, Netanyahu and his family received unusually favorable and responsive treatment from the Walla news site, which Elovitch also controlled.
Netanyahu and the Elovitches deny that there was any such exchange. Netanyahu has argued that Walla remained hostile to him and that the regulatory decisions were professionally justified.
Even if prosecutors withdraw the bribery charge, Case 4000 would not disappear. Netanyahu would continue to face allegations of fraud and breach of trust over the same affair, alongside fraud and breach of trust charges in Cases 1000 and 2000.
Case 1000 concerns gifts, including cigars and champagne, that Netanyahu and his wife, Sara, allegedly received from wealthy businessmen, principally Arnon Milchan. Prosecutors allege that Netanyahu provided official assistance in matters affecting Milchan while receiving those gifts. Netanyahu says they were presents exchanged within a genuine friendship.
Case 2000 concerns recorded conversations between Netanyahu and Yediot Aharonot publisher Arnon “Noni” Mozes. Prosecutors allege that the two discussed improving Netanyahu’s coverage in exchange for steps that could have weakened the newspaper’s principal competitor, Israel Hayom. Both men deny wrongdoing.
Mozes and Shaul and Iris Elovitch are standing trial alongside Netanyahu and will also be able to call witnesses in their defense.
The dispute over the Case 4000 bribery charge is closely connected to the battle over how quickly the trial should now proceed. Netanyahu’s attorney, Amit Hadad, has said that if the charge remains, the defense may seek to call hundreds of witnesses to challenge the prosecution’s account.
The judges have instead been pressing the parties to narrow the witness lists and accelerate a trial that began in May 2020. Beginning October 4, hearings are scheduled to take place five days a week, from Sunday through Thursday.
Both the defense and prosecution opposed the five-day schedule when it was discussed in June. Hadad argued that it would leave Netanyahu’s lawyers without sufficient time to prepare witnesses and warned that members of the defense team could withdraw if they could not provide adequate representation.
Court instructed the defense teams to prepare witnesses and alternatives
The court has nevertheless instructed the defense teams to prepare witnesses and alternatives for each hearing day to avoid further cancellations.
The timetable is particularly pressing because the head of the three-judge panel, Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman, is expected to retire in March 2028. The panel also includes Judges Moshe Bar-Am and Oded Shaham.
For now, the trial remains in the evidence stage. Once Netanyahu and the other defendants finish presenting their witnesses, the prosecution and defense will submit their final arguments. Only then will the judges deliver a verdict on the charges that remain.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered unauthorized settler outposts in the West Bank to be dismantled, two people familiar with the matter said on Sunday, amid pressure from the US to crack down on settler attacks on Palestinians.
The order applies to outposts established by settlers without official authorization from the Israeli state, the sources said. Outposts typically consist of prefabricated caravans and house a small number of settlers. The state has from time to time demolished such structures and also formally recognized others, allowing them to access government funding.
It was not immediately clear when the operation would begin.
US urges Israel to act against settler violence
Netanyahu had ordered the eviction of the unauthorized outposts in response to pressure from the United States, the country's closest ally, the sources said.
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee on Saturday denounced violent settlers as terrorists and called for them to face severe consequences following a meeting with several Palestinian Americans in a West Bank Palestinian town.
Ynet earlier reported that the orders targeted around 100 outposts across the West Bank.
The Israeli prime minister's office and the military, who would normally take part in clearing any outposts in the West Bank, did not immediately respond to a request to comment.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, asked at a conference in Jerusalem about the Ynet report, said Netanyahu has given "an instruction to evict places built in Areas A and B."
Under the Oslo Accords, interim peace agreements reached in the 1990s between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), the West Bank was split into three zones: A, B and C.
Smotrich, a settler himself who has overseen settlement housing projects and formally recognized homes built illegally, said that while he disagreed with Netanyahu's decision, the government had made huge strides in advancing settlements in Area C.
Settler violence on the rise
Last month, Israeli settlers besieged the homes of Palestinians in a nearby village, including one owned by a Palestinian American, before the military forced them from the area. The village's Palestinian residents have said they have continued to face harassment and intimidation by Israeli settlers.
The Israeli government has condemned the attacks and said that it would act to stop settler violence.
On Saturday, Huckabee said it was in Israel's own interest to take action against settlers carrying out what he described as "criminal behavior and terrorism."

Greece wants deeper ties with both Israel and Arab countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:48:23 UTC
02:48:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Greece wants deeper ties with both Israel and Arab countries
Greece will press ahead with its strategic defence cooperation with Israel but also wants to deepen relations with other states in the Middle East, Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said Sunday.
Greece-Israeli ties and defence, security and energy cooperation have grown closer over the past decade, and Mitsotakis enjoys a friendly rapport with his counterpart, Benjamin Netanyahu.
Shared concerns about Turkey have helped boost ties. The two countries signed a 3-billion-euro ($3.5 billion) deal on 31 August for Israel to build an air defence shield in Greece.
Mitsotakis told reporters in Thessaloniki that Greece is one of only five NATO countries spending at least 3.5 percent of its GDP on core defence.
Greece’s traditionally high spending has been fueled by almost constant tensions with Turkey, and its questioning of Greek sovereignty over parts of the Aegean Sea and the Eastern Mediterranean.
Greece recognises only the demarcation of the two countries’ respective maritime zones as an issue to be negotiated or sent to international arbitration.
Asked about US President Donald Trump’s expressed desire to sell the advanced F-35 multirole combat aircraft to Turkey, Mitsotakis replied that he will not tell the US what to do, but noted that legal obstacles remain as Turkey was sanctioned for buying the S-400 air defence system from Russia.
Greece will take delivery of its first 20 F-35s in late 2028, with an option to buy 20 more.
Mitsotakis also said he planned to visit Saudi Arabia soon, and that the recently concluded Mecca Joint Defence Agreement among Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey changes nothing in Greece’s relations with Riyadh.
Greece has maintained an air defence battery in Saudi Arabia since 2021, and has used its Patriot missiles four times since July to down drones and ballistic missiles, allegedly from Yemen, aimed at the kingdom’s oil refineries.

US energy secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday morning that the US may not be able to reach a nuclear agreement with Iran that would prevent the country from having nuclear weapons.
Asked on ABC on Sunday morning about any sign of such a deal, as negotiations appear stalled and the US-Israel war on Iran continues, Wright said: “There may not be a nuclear agreement.”

“We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime,” he said.
In an earlier interview with CNN on Sunday, Wright declined to declare the strait of Hormuz safe for oil tankers – unless they are being escorted by the US navy – and stopped short of saying whether the navy would need to remain in the Gulf region “indefinitely” in order to keep the vital energy passageway operating, as the conflict drags on.
This came despite Donald Trump’s repeated claims that ships can safely navigate the narrow marine waterway, and the US president’s insistence last week that the US controls the strait, while floating the idea that it be named after him – statements that were followed by further strikes from both sides in the area.
Wright, appearing for an interview on CNN’s State of the Union show on Sunday as well as ABC and CBS, was asked whether he could “unequivocally” assure safety to merchant ships transiting the strait. The question came after a New York Times report found that August was the deadliest month for merchant vessels in the area since March.
“We’re working cooperatively with fleets that do want to transit. Some ships aren’t transiting, and, of course, that’s their choice. But the United States is working with teams from all the nations in the Gulf to get transits and to continue to ramp them up,” Wright said.
“But you’re not saying that it’s currently safe?” host CNN Dana Bash asked, to which Wright replied: “We’re getting a lot of ships through, but, of course, it requires the US military to do that. We are not [at] pre-conflict levels, if that’s what you’re asking.”
Bash then asked: “If a country or a company wants to send its tanker through the strait of Hormuz, can they do so safely?”
“Well, if they want to work with the United States navy, I think they can,” Wright said.
Bash then asked whether the US navy would remain in the region “indefinitely” and whether its presence in the strait was becoming “the new normal”.
Wright responded: “Well, it is today, but I think, as you look forward, other nations will come and work with us in this endeavor. Certainly, trade for the world is important. It shouldn’t be just the United States’s responsibility.”
“But until Iran changes their position or changes their government, we’ll have to deal with them. But, slowly, their capabilities are being degraded and ours are being enhanced,” he added.
Nuclear and diplomatic talks between the United States and Iran appear to have stalled after a June interim agreement to end military operations collapsed without producing a lasting settlement on peace or the future of what remains of Iran’s nuclear program after US strikes last summer caused huge damage.
Wright was also asked by CNN if he would say the US is still at war. “We’re still in a conflict, for sure,” he said. On Thursday, the US vice-president JD Vance said at a White House press briefing: “I wouldn’t call it a war,” instead referring to a military conflict. Trump then defended Vance, saying: “A lot of people do not call it a war, I would call it a military conflict, because it’s small potatoes for us … it’s not a big thing.”
The Republican US senator John Kennedy of Louisiana was asked on Sunday by NBC if the war would be over by November.
“Probably not,” he said.
The conflict passed the six-month mark in late August. The former defense secretary Leon Panetta warned in an interview with the Guardian this weekend that it could last a lot longer.

Antonelli storms from P19 to win Italian GP, extends championship lead
Unknown

2026-09-06

Halis Sunnetci
06 September 2026•Update: 06 September 2026
Kimi Antonelli produced a remarkable comeback to win the Italian Grand Prix on Sunday, charging from 19th on the grid to victory at his home race and becoming the first Italian driver to triumph at Monza since 1966.
The 20-year-old Mercedes driver passed teammate George Russell on Lap 50, with three laps remaining, and held on to secure a memorable victory.
Russell finished second to complete a Mercedes one-two, while Red Bull’s Max Verstappen took third.
McLaren’s Lando Norris was fourth ahead of teammate Oscar Piastri, with Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton finishing sixth.
The race was interrupted on Lap 2 after Ferrari driver Charles Leclerc crashed heavily at the Parabolica, prompting a red flag. Leclerc walked away from the accident and was cleared following medical checks.
Antonelli, who had qualified seventh, started from 19th after receiving a grid penalty for exceeding his permitted allocation of power-unit components.
His victory equaled the second-furthest-back starting position from which a Formula 1 World Championship race has been won, behind John Watson’s victory from 22nd in 1983.
The Italian quickly made his way through the field following the restart and took the lead from Russell at the beginning of Lap 18.
Antonelli and Verstappen later pitted for fresh tires during a virtual safety-car period, while Russell remained on track and attempted to preserve his hard tires.
Antonelli returned to second place by Lap 38 and gradually reduced the gap to his teammate as Russell struggled with tire wear.
The Italian briefly ran through the gravel while battling Russell on Lap 49 but recovered and completed the decisive pass one lap later.
Russell tried to respond over the closing laps but could not regain the lead, allowing Antonelli to cross the finish line to a huge reception from the home crowd.
The victory strengthened Antonelli’s position at the top of the drivers’ standings.
He arrived at Monza leading Russell by 59 points and increased his advantage to 66, moving to 267 points.
Russell’s second-place finish lifted him to 201 points, while Hamilton dropped to third with 191 after collecting eight points for sixth place.
Mercedes’ one-two contrasted sharply with Ferrari’s fortunes at its home race. Hamilton could manage only sixth, while Leclerc’s early retirement left the Italian team without a podium.
Antonelli became the first Italian driver to win the Italian Grand Prix at Monza since Ludovico Scarfiotti triumphed at the circuit in 1966.
Pole-sitter Pierre Gasly was unable to maintain his qualifying advantage and finished seventh for Alpine.
Racing Bulls rookie Arvid Lindblad took eighth, ahead of Alpine’s Franco Colapinto and Racing Bulls driver Yuki Tsunoda.
Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto finished 11th, followed by teammate Nico Hulkenberg, Williams’ Carlos Sainz, Red Bull’s Liam Lawson, Haas pair Oliver Bearman and Esteban Ocon, Williams’ Alex Albon and Cadillac’s Sergio Perez.
Valtteri Bottas, Lance Stroll, Fernando Alonso and Leclerc failed to finish.

AfD claims landslide victory in Germany’s regional election – preliminary results
The opposition right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has won Sunday’s regional election in Germany’s eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt with 43.8% of the vote, according to official preliminary results. The AfD is set to claim 39 out of 97 seats in the local legislature, falling short of a governing majority.
The vote was marked by a record turnout of 78%, the highest since the reunification of Germany in 1990.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party finished in a poor second, securing just over 17.2% of the vote and 15 seats, the results indicated.
AfD lead candidate in the state, Ulrich Siegmund, said the party has “written history” and that the outcome of the vote would “shake all of Germany.”
“We are going to get our country back, and we are starting with Saxony-Anhalt,” he said.
The Germans have given the AfD their trust and it “will not disappoint them. We will not become like these other parties,” Siegmund added.
AfD co-chair Alice Weidel earlier did not rule out forming a coalition government in the region, including with Merz’s Christian Democrats, should the right-wing party fail to secure an absolute majority.
After the exit polls gave victory to the AfD, Sven Schulze, the CDU lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt and the outgoing regional head, conceded defeat, congratulating the opponents on their electoral success.
“That’s democracy,” Schulze said, adding that voters have sent a clear message which must be heeded, both at the regional and federal levels, as quoted by German media.
Schulze attributed his party’s poor showing to the unpopular policies pursued by the federal coalition government, which is comprised of the CDU and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).
SPD co-leader and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil similarly spoke of a “signal to Berlin,” insisting, however, on the continuation of the so-called ‘firewall’ policy, under which all major parties refuse to cooperate with the AfD.
AfD co-chair Tino Chrupalla said that the outcome of the Saxony-Anhalt regional elections have demonstrated that voters reject the controversial ‘firewall’ policy by ‘voting out’ the mainstream parties.
According to preliminary results, the SPD has finished third with 9.3% of the vote, followed by the Greens and the Left Party with 8.9% and 8.6%, respectively. The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) has also narrowly secured the spot in the legislature with 5.3%.
Over the past several months, opinion polls have consistently shown that the AfD is the most popular party nationwide, enjoying the support of 28% of respondents.
Having the largest opposition faction in the Bundestag, the party campaigns on an anti-immigration platform and is also highly critical of the German government’s support for Ukraine, as well as sanctions against Russia.
An INSA poll published by Bild in late August indicated that support for Germany’s governing Christian Democratic CDU/CSU bloc had fallen to 20%, with some 78% of respondents dissatisfied with Merz’s coalition government.

Dennis Ross: Iran’s resilience during US war continues to ‘surprise’
TEHRAN — The clearest path to a deal to end the US war on Iran may lie in the dispute over shipping fees through the Strait of Hormuz, according to former US negotiator Dennis Ross, as Washington confronts the reality that months of military and economic pressure have failed to force Tehran into submission.
The United States and Israel launched their war against Iran on February 28, apparently expecting that sustained military pressure would weaken the Islamic Republic and compel its leadership to make far-reaching concessions. Instead, Iran has maintained its political and military footing while continuing to challenge US pressure, particularly around the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has repeatedly demonstrated that it can absorb severe pressure while retaining significant leverage over the course of the confrontation. Despite the heavy economic costs imposed by US sanctions and the naval blockade, Tehran has rejected demands that it sees as compromising its sovereignty and has continued to insist that any settlement must address the consequences of Washington’s military campaign.
Ross said Iran could abandon any demand for a formal toll on shipping while retaining the right to charge for legitimate navigational, security or environmental services. Such an arrangement, he argued, could give both sides a way to claim a political victory, allowing Tehran to step back from its demand without appearing to capitulate.
“The Iranians have consistently surprised us in terms of their resilience,” Ross said, adding that he doubted economic and military pressure alone would force an Iranian retreat.
The Strait of Hormuz has become the central pressure point in the confrontation. Washington has sought to use its naval power and economic blockade to restrict Iran’s oil exports, while Tehran has maintained that the strait cannot simply be treated as an instrument of US power. Recent military exchanges around the waterway have further demonstrated the risks of trying to resolve the dispute through force.
“If you could announce that the strait were reopened, I think Trump would do a deal,” Ross told The Associated Press.
For Washington, such a deal could provide a face-saving way to end a costly confrontation. For Tehran, reopening the waterway while preserving its sovereign rights and securing an end to the pressure campaign could equally be presented as a victory.
After months of war, the emerging lesson is that Iran’s resilience has become one of the central factors pushing the US to search for an exit from the conflict.

Iranian writer, poet and artist Javad Mojabi passes away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:27:49 UTC
02:27:49 KST

Iranian writer, poet and artist Javad Mojabi passes away
TEHRAN- Javad Mojabi, the prominent Iranian writer, poet, satirist, painter and literary and art critic, passed away on Saturday following a period of illness. he was 87.
Mojabi was one of the prominent figures of contemporary Iranian literature and art, whose career spanned more than six decades and encompassed literature, visual arts, journalism and art criticism.
Born in 1939, in Qazvin, Mojabi began his literary and artistic activities in the 1960s. He produced more than 50 works in various forms, including poetry, short stories, novels, satire, plays, screenplays and research.
His first book, the poetry collection “A Season for You,” was published in 1965 when he was 25. Mojabi later recalled that the publication of the book served as his formal entry into the literary world of his generation.
Alongside literature, painting remained an important part of his artistic life. He began painting as a child with his brother, Hossein, and later became recognized as one of the pioneering figures in the field of painting criticism and research on visual arts in Iran.
Mojabi pursued his professional career in journalism as well, while continuing to write extensively on literature and contemporary art. His critical and research works on painting and Iranian artists appeared in various publications and books, further establishing his position as a figure active across several branches of the country’s cultural life.
He was also widely known for his contribution to contemporary Iranian satire, which he explored through different literary and artistic forms. His fiction output included works such as “The Lost Garden,” “Naked Narrative,” “In This Weather” and “Speaking While Saying Nothing.”
Mojabi remained artistically active during the final years of his life. In 2026, while he was hospitalized at Iranmehr Hospital, a collection of his paintings titled “White Nights of the Hospital and Me” was put on display, reflecting his continued engagement with painting despite his illness.
Through a career extending over more than six decades, Mojabi became part of a generation of Iranian intellectuals and artists who moved between literature, visual arts, journalism and cultural criticism. His multifaceted body of work left a lasting presence in Iran’s contemporary cultural landscape.

Russia’s 20,000-Ton Icebreaker Admiral Makarov Goes Up in Flames at Kronstadt Shipyard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:27:21 UTC
02:27:21 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s 20,000-Ton Icebreaker Admiral Makarov Goes Up in Flames at Kronstadt Shipyard
A fire broke out aboard Russia’s 20,000-ton diesel-electric icebreaker Admiral Makarov while the vessel was undergoing repairs at the Kronstadt Marine Plant near St. Petersburg.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The fire erupted aboard the vessel on September 5, with Russian emergency services deploying 52 firefighters and 10 pieces of equipment to the shipyard. The blaze covered an area of roughly 80 square meters before being brought under control, according to Russian Telegram channel 112.
Firefighters extinguished within approximately two hours. No casualties were reported. The cause of the fire and the extent of damage to the icebreaker have not been disclosed.
Admiral Makarov is a Project R-1039 diesel-electric icebreaker built by Wärtsilä in Helsinki, Finland, in 1975 as part of the Yermak class constructed for the Soviet Union.
The vessel has a displacement of approximately 20,247 tonnes and is nearly 135 meters long. Its propulsion system produces about 30.5 megawatts of power, allowing the icebreaker to navigate through continuous ice up to 1.5 meters thick at around two knots.
Admiral Makarov previously operated in Russia’s Far East and Arctic regions before being transferred to Rosmorport’s Northwestern Basin Branch in late 2025. After completing repairs, the vessel was expected to escort ships to Russian ports in the eastern Gulf of Finland during winter navigation.
The icebreaker has been undergoing repairs since spring 2025, including work on its hull, propellers, three propeller shafts, and main engines. Repairs to the engines were scheduled to continue through the end of 2026.
Kronstadt, located on Kotlin Island in the Gulf of Finland, is also home to a major Russian naval base. In June 2026, Ukrainian drones struck the Russian Project 20380 missile corvette Boykiy at the Kronstadt naval base, causing a fire aboard the vessel.
In October 2025, another major accident hit a Russian shipyard when the unfinished PK-700 heavy floating crane capsized at the Sevastopol Marine Plant in temporarily occupied Crimea, killing two people and injuring at least 20 others.

Sydney art exhibition highlights Minab tragedy, voices of war, resilience
TEHRAN – The “When the Earth Embraces the Sky” art exhibition, featuring works addressing war, loss, displacement and resilience, has opened in Sydney, Australia, with the Iranian section focusing on the Minab school tragedy and commemorating the children who lost their lives in the attack.
The exhibition opened on Sunday at the Frank Oliveri Community Centre in Heckenberg, New South Wales, and will remain open to the public through September 13. The event brings together more than 50 artworks from artists and community members from diverse backgrounds, including Iranian, Afghan, Iraqi, Lebanese and Palestinian communities.
Organized by the Conference of Birds – Shia Hub for Art & Culture, the exhibition explores the human consequences of war and displacement while emphasizing memory, resistance, resilience, connection and hope for renewal.
The event brings together representatives and artists from communities whose countries have experienced war and military conflict in recent decades. Through painting, drawing, photography, mixed media, sculpture, calligraphy and other forms of visual art, the exhibition seeks to transform experiences of loss and destruction into a broader reflection on human dignity and resilience.
The Iranian section has been dedicated to the tragedy at Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Hormozgan province, and serves as a memorial to the children killed in the attack.
The Minab tragedy occurred on February 28, when the school was struck during the opening phase of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Iranian authorities reported that 168 people were killed and at least 95 others wounded in the attack, which struck the school while children and teachers were attending classes.
As part of the program, the documentary “Minab,” directed by Iranian filmmaker Maryam Yousefi-Sadr, was screened on Sunday following the opening ceremony. The screening was proposed by the Benevolent Iranian Women Association, which is also participating in the exhibition’s Iranian section.
The exhibition’s broader theme draws on the enduring concepts of memory, loss and rebuilding, while seeking to present the experiences of communities affected by conflict beyond images of destruction alone. According to the organizers, the event aims to highlight the capacity of individuals and communities to remain rooted, rebuild and envision a more hopeful future.
Inspired in part by the spirit of Karbala and Imam Hussein (AS), the exhibition also seeks to create a space for dialogue among Sydney’s multicultural communities and demonstrate the ability of art to bring together people with different cultural backgrounds around shared experiences of grief, displacement and hope.
The exhibition is free to the public and continues at the Frank Oliveri Community Centre in Heckenberg until September 13.

Strikes across Khuzestan: US missile strikes struck three distinct locations near Ahvaz and Aghajari in Khuzestan Province on Tuesday, martyring seven people and wounding eight others, according to provincial officials.
Kuhestak Wedding Ceremony Bombing: US forces struck a residential building in Kuhestak, Hormozgan Province on Tuesday, while a local wedding reception was taking place. The strike resulted in the martyrdom of at least five people and wounded 68 others, including women and children.
In direct response to these violations, Iran’s armed forces executed coordinated salvos of retaliatory missile and drone strikes targeting hostile US military positions and bases spread across Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, and Bahrain. Furthermore, Iranian defensive actions led to the striking of three additional US-linked vessels that attempted to breach Iranian security zones or facilitate hostilities.
The current combat operations mark an intensification of the conflict that erupted on February 28, when the United States and Israel initiated unprovoked, large-scale military attacks against Iran in clear violation of the United Nations Charter.
Since February 28, Washington has repeatedly violated international law, targeting sovereign territory, critical national infrastructure, and civilian neighborhoods. However, Tehran's defense strategy has transformed the confrontation into an operational strain on the US military.
Independent security analysts and strategic defense reports confirm that the continuous deployment of interceptors against complex Iranian missile and drone salvos has severely depleted US military stockpiles.
Interceptor exhaustion: US stocks of key interceptors, including Patriot PAC-3 and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missile systems, have been depleted by well over half.
Strategic vulnerability: Defense intelligence estimates indicate that the rapid consumption of these high-cost interceptor inventories has pushed American air defenses in multiple theaters to critical levels, creating global operational gaps that will take defense manufacturers years to rebuild.
While Washington faces a rapidly shrinking stockpile of high-grade munitions and logistical strain, Iran’s defense doctrine—built upon domestic production, underground missile facilities, and vast stockpiles of asymmetric assets—has demonstrated enduring strength.
Despite sustained military pressure and illegal blockades from Washington, the national resilience of the Islamic Republic remains unbroken. The defensive actions executed by the IRGC have consolidated popular support across Iran, proving that threats and military coercion cannot alter Tehran's posture.
By striking high-value naval assets, enforcing strict control over the Strait of Hormuz, dismantling American intelligence platforms, and enduring external attacks, Iran's armed forces continue to demonstrate that foreign aggression will consistently carry unacceptable costs. As the IRGC leadership affirmed, the Iranian nation stands stronger than ever, fully prepared to maintain its sovereignty and deliver decisive responses to any future hostile miscalculations.

Thales to Localize Production of 70 mm Rockets in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:13:37 UTC
02:13:37 KST

India will establish assembly and partial local production of guided and unguided 70 mm rockets.
Thales announced this in a press release.
Thales and Kalyani Strategic Systems Limited (KSSL) have signed a strategic alliance agreement under India’s Make in India program to establish advanced manufacturing capabilities for 70 mm rocket systems in the country.
Thales’ 70 mm rockets are already used by Indian HAL Rudra and HAL Prachand attack helicopters equipped with compatible launchers from the FZ family. In addition to engaging ground targets, the guided version of Thales’ 70 mm rockets can be used to engage drones.
As part of the cooperation, Thales will provide technological expertise in 70 mm rockets and launchers developed in Belgium.
KSSL, for its part, will use local manufacturing and testing facilities to produce and integrate components from Thales’ certified supply chain. The first fully assembled rocket made in India is planned for early 2027.
“Thales has partnered with India for decades and this collaboration with KSSL is a testament to our deep and long-standing engagement with the local defence ecosystem. By combining our combat-proven 70 mm rocket expertise from Belgium with KSSL’s engineering and manufacturing strengths, we are co-creating capabilities that will enhance India’s operational readiness and advance its vision of self-reliance in critical defence technologies,” said Ankur Kanaglekar, Thales’ vice president in India.
Kalyani Strategic Systems Limited (KSSL) is a wholly owned subsidiary of Bharat Forge Limited and is responsible for the defense business of Kalyani Group, one of India’s leading engineering and technology industrial groups.
The company’s portfolio includes artillery systems, armored and protected vehicles, small arms, ammunition, naval systems and unmanned platforms.
This is not Thales’ first attempt to localize 70 mm rocket production in India.
In 2023, the company signed an agreement with state-owned Bharat Dynamics Limited to establish manufacturing capabilities for the FZ275 rocket and integrate Indian components into Thales’ global supply chain.
In 2024, Thales signed another memorandum, this time with Adani Defence & Aerospace. The agreement covered the localization of production of both the guided FZ275 LGR and unguided FZ90 FFAR.

Palestinian farmers battle settler sabotage to save Hebron crops, livestock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:03:20 UTC
02:03:20 KST

Palestinian farmers battle settler sabotage to save Hebron crops, livestock
West Bank farmers defy daily settler attacks, sheep theft, and military restrictions to protect their land from agricultural sabotage.
Amid the grapevines that once provided a steady income for her family, 56-year-old Palestinian farmer Theeba al-Sabaa spends much of her day guarding her home and farmland in the occupied West Bank from settlers.
From dusk till dawn, she works on her land in the town of Beit Ummar, north of Hebron, known by locals as “Jabal Sabaa”.
Theeba is engaged in a daily battle against the encroaching settler outposts that have emerged among the rolling hills that surround her, and which block access to sections of her land.
“By God, the land has taught me patience, and to cling to my right, for as long as I have a right, I must take it and never let it go,” she told Al Jazeera.
“I will never leave it because I worked hard on it, I toil and sweat on it, so I will not leave my toil and sweat, or the toil of my children and my husband, to go to someone else.”
Weaponising livestock
Since mid-2024, when settlers established new outposts on the nearby hills, every one of Theeba’s moves has been monitored.
Settlers frequently approach the perimeter of her home and deliberately release livestock into the cultivated fields.
“They enter with their sheep into our land after we plow and fix it, grazing in it, trampling the crops, and stomping on them with their sheep, leaving nothing,” Theeba said.
“As soon as they feel any movement or anyone entering the land, you find them attacking us immediately.”
This intimidation extends to the adjacent fields, where 59-year-old Anwar Sabarneh lives with his extended family of seven brothers.
Due to the repeated settler violations, two of his brothers have been forced to abandon their land.
Sabarneh, who supports a family of 14, owns several dunams of vineyards located just 300 metres (980 feet) from his home. With aggressive settlers around, reaching them has become a dangerous ordeal.
Military complicity
Sabarneh said that the Israeli army even demands permits from Palestinians to work on their own land.
“The army came with the settlers to ask me for a permit so I can work in my home, in front of my house’s door, and on my land where I am the rightful owner,” Sabarneh said.
Farmers are also barred from building anything on their land. Sabarneh’s sheep have also been locked in a barn for over eight months due to the dangers posed by settlers.
“If they see me taking the sheep out, the settlers chase me, kidnap them, and steal them,” he said.
When Sabarneh’s children have tried to retrieve their stolen sheep, Israeli soldiers have arrested and beaten them.
A forced exodus
Repeated pogroms by settlers against Palestinian farmers reflect a broader strategy targeting agriculture across the southern West Bank.
Settlers and the Israeli troops carried out 11,074 attacks in the West Bank during the first half of 2026, according to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission. This includes 3,488 carried out by settlers.
Hasan Breijieh, a settlement affairs expert and director at the commission, told Al Jazeera that continuous settlement expansionism, alongside restrictions on Palestinian movement, are the primary reasons that so many Palestinians have been forced to flee their farms.
“Military gates erected at the entrances of Palestinian communities have tightened control over… access to their orchards and vineyards,” he said.
Bypass roads, built by Israel, have also hindered “connectivity between Palestinian communities”, Breijieh said.
Under such restrictions, Palestinian farmers have faced a fourth consecutive season without being able to harvest olives, grapes, or guava. Their lands have been “neither plowed nor pruned”, and have been forcibly abandoned.
In the face of such oppression, Palestinian women like Theeba al-Sabaa have continued to play a pivotal role in protecting their land, particularly when men have been killed or detained by Israeli forces.
“They continue to maintain their leadership role in preserving the family’s agricultural legacy today,” Breijieh said. “This land was historically the primary source of livelihood for families, and a Palestinian cannot leave it voluntarily, no matter the sacrifices.”
He recalled his own grandfather, who went to his fields to bid farewell before dying. “Goodbye, vineyard,” he said to his land.

EU faces 300,000 factory job cuts as China ‘colonises’ supply chains, industry warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:00:10 UTC
02:00:10 KST

Job losses in EU manufacturing will rapidly increase unless Brussels stops the “colonisation” of industry by Chinese component manufacturers, a leading industry trade body has warned.
Eurometal predicts 300,000 job losses in manufacturing in the rest of 2026 because of expanding competition from China, which is now enjoying a record €1bn-a-day trade surplus with the bloc.
On Monday, Eurometal will bring its concerns to decision-makers in Brussels, staging a protest using 10 symbolic coffins in a procession around the European Commission headquarters.
The coffins will be marked with phrases such as “EU competitiveness”, “industrial jobs” and “European factories”.
European manufacturers fear that the commission is not fully alive to the cannibalisation of their industries as China becomes embedded in supply chains through the sale of components.
Alexander Julius, the president of Eurometal, told the Guardian: “China has made no secret of what it is doing. It is in their five-year plan.
“China doesn’t want to be a raw material supplier, it wants to be a finished product supply. They want to be in key product supply chains because they know that once they control the supply chain, they own the complete value chain.” He wants the commission to understand fully the impact of Chinese exports at component level, including metals and chemicals used in 90% of manufacturing.
The EU has already taken action on electric vehicles by imposing tariffs on Chinese imports in 2024, and in June introduced higher tariffs on imports of foreign steel. The bloc’s trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, has also said the EU’s €360bn (£310bn) annual import/export imbalance with China is “not sustainable”, with both sides agreeing to hold three months of talks, ending in October, to try to avert a trade war.
“You look at the job losses stacking up in industries in places like Germany. The media, the politicians can see the consequences, but they don’t go after the virus that is causing it,” Julius said. “They don’t see why it is happening or ask why companies are either relocating to China or India or going bust.”
Among the conditions allowing the “virus” to spread is the increasing costs borne by European metal manufacturers with tariffs on steel imports and carbon emissions taxes for those high-energy sectors.
Components manufactured in China face none of those levies, said Julius, and that, combined with the undervaluation of the Chinese currency, the yuan, makes it challenging to compete with Chinese rivals, he added.
Companies have to satisfy shareholders and will continue to buy from China, whatever the political rhetoric coming out of Brussels, he said.
“When manufacturing leaves Europe, Europe not only loses production but investment, knowhow and long-term economic resilience,” Eurometal said ahead of the protest.
Analysis by the European Commission in June projected potential job losses of more than 1m on the back of high energy costs and global competition, which will include the 100,000 job cuts at Volkswagen confirmed by the German carmaker last week.
China has repeatedly accused Europe of protectionism. It threatened “resolute countermeasures should the EU further target Chinese companies or products”, according to the state-owned Xinhua agency earlier this year. Since then, the EU and China have agreed a three-month truce.

An invasion is underway in Canada, but not in the way you think – opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

For much of its modern history, Canada has enjoyed a strategic privilege few countries possess.
Geography provided distance from the world’s most volatile regions, while powerful alliances and North American stability allowed Ottawa to view many international crises principally as matters of foreign policy.
That distinction is becoming obsolete.
Emerging threats do not necessarily cross Canadian borders in recognizable military form; they travel through cyberspace, financial networks, intelligence relationships, criminal intermediaries, political influence, and transnational repression.
The central national-security question is therefore no longer simply how Canada responds to instability abroad, but how it defends its sovereignty when authoritarian states project power into Canadian society itself.
The Islamic Republic of Iran provides a revealing case study of this transformation. Tehran has traditionally been viewed in Ottawa through the lenses of nuclear proliferation, terrorism, sanctions, and Middle Eastern instability.
Those concerns remain substantial, but they are no longer sufficient.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) has identified Iran as a relatively sophisticated actor in foreign interference, employing intelligence services, proxies, and intermediaries to pursue opponents abroad.
It also warns that such activities and transnational repression may intensify as the regime perceives growing threats to its survival.
The implication extends beyond Iran: the boundary between foreign affairs and domestic security is disappearing.
Transnational repression should therefore be understood not merely as a human-rights problem but as an intrusion upon sovereignty.
When an authoritarian government attempts to determine what a dissident may say in Toronto, whom an activist may meet in Vancouver, or what a journalist may publish in Montreal, it is extending its authority into Canadian territory.
The victim may be Iranian, Chinese, or Russian, but the principle violated is Canadian. A state that tolerates such coercion permits a foreign government to establish an invisible sphere of authority within its borders.
Iran is particularly important because asymmetric power has shaped the Islamic Republic’s strategic culture for decades.
Aware of its conventional weakness against the Western alliance, Tehran has converted vulnerability into leverage through proxies, covert operations, cyber capabilities, intelligence networks, and non-state actors.
Its sophistication lies not in any single instrument but in combining them under layers of deniability.
Ottawa needs to pay attention: Networks that appear unconnected may very well be
Western governments, by contrast, often separate these threats into bureaucratic categories: cyberattacks, criminal investigations, sanctions violations, intimidation, and foreign interference.
What appears institutionally fragmented in Ottawa may be strategically integrated in Tehran.
Therefore, Canada needs what might be called network-based national security: the ability to recognize connections among apparently separate events.
When credible foreign interference is detected, investigations should extend beyond the immediate actor to the surrounding architecture – financing, facilitators, digital infrastructure, intelligence contacts, criminal intermediaries, and organizations providing legitimate cover.
Modern counterintelligence succeeds not merely by identifying who operates, but by illuminating the network that makes it possible.
Canada should become an increasingly difficult environment in which hostile states cannot build such networks undetected.
Ottawa has already taken important steps.
Canada designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a terrorist entity in 2024, while CSIS has described credible Iranian threats and Tehran’s willingness to use proxies and individuals connected with transnational organized crime against perceived enemies abroad.
Canada’s Foreign Influence Transparency Registry provides another instrument for exposing arrangements through which foreign principals seek to influence Canadian political and governmental processes.
Together, these measures recognize that foreign power can operate through structures far removed from traditional espionage.
Yet effective counterintelligence requires precision as much as vigilance. 
Canada must never confuse Iranian identity with allegiance to the Islamic Republic. Iranian Canadians are often among the regime’s most determined opponents, many having left Iran precisely because they rejected its political system. 
Indiscriminate suspicion would therefore be both unjust and strategically counterproductive, alienating the very communities authoritarian governments seek to intimidate.
The essential distinction is not between Canadians and foreigners, but between legitimate civic activity and covert activity conducted at the direction or for the benefit of a hostile state.
This distinction points toward a broader principle of democratic security. An authoritarian state can protect itself by closing society; a democracy must protect itself while remaining open.
Universities, political organizations, and diaspora communities must remain free and accessible. The task of security institutions is not to construct walls around Canadian society, but to identify where openness is being deliberately exploited.
A sophisticated democracy does not cast a wider security net; it develops a more discriminating one.
Ground invasions don’t threaten Canada pe se – cyber ones do
Cyber operations make this challenge particularly urgent. Physical distance once insulated Canada from conflicts thousands of kilometers away; digital infrastructure has radically reduced that advantage.
Iranian-linked cyber actors have targeted Western governmental, technological, and critical infrastructure, while Canadian security reporting has addressed cyber-enabled activity directed toward dissidents.
As such, geography can no longer define the boundaries of national security.
A hostile actor may be geographically distant while remaining operationally present inside the networks upon which Canadian government, commerce, and society depend.
Nor should Canada understand Iran in isolation. CSIS has identified China, Russia, India, Iran, and Pakistan in connection with significant foreign-interference or espionage concerns.
Iran is therefore part of a broader transformation: authoritarian and revisionist states recognize that open democracies possess vulnerabilities precisely because they are open – their institutions are accessible, political participation decentralized, and economic relationships international.
Canada’s response to Iran should contribute to a broader doctrine of democratic resilience capable of confronting different adversaries without sacrificing the constitutional freedoms that distinguish Canada from them.
Such a doctrine requires deeper integration of intelligence, law enforcement, financial intelligence, border security, and cyber defense.
Democracies naturally prefer to respond after wrongdoing becomes visible and evidence meets the standards of prosecution; intelligence operates earlier, recognizing patterns before they mature into operations.
The challenge is to act upon sophisticated warning while maintaining rigorous legal oversight. Security and liberty are not opposing objectives when the threat itself is designed to undermine the conditions under which liberty can safely exist.
Iran offers Canada one final strategic lesson: regimes under pressure do not necessarily become less dangerous abroad.
As conventional options narrow and domestic insecurity grows, asymmetric instruments become more attractive because they are inexpensive, deniable, and disproportionately effective.
A weakened authoritarian state may therefore rely increasingly on intelligence operations, cyber activity, proxies, and coercion abroad.
CSIS’s warning that Iranian foreign interference and transnational repression could increase as threats to the regime intensify should be understood in precisely this strategic context.
Canada is thus confronting a question larger than its policy toward Tehran.
Traditional sovereignty was primarily territorial: governments defended borders, institutions, and populations from external attack.
Sovereignty in the 21st century must protect something more: the independence of political decision-making, the integrity of digital infrastructure, the freedom of diaspora communities, the autonomy of public institutions, and the right of every person on Canadian soil to speak without being subjected to the coercive authority of a foreign state.
Canada’s great challenge is not to choose between openness and security. It is to understand that a democratic society can preserve openness only if it develops the intelligence, institutional confidence, and strategic imagination necessary to defend it.
The threats of the coming decade may rarely resemble invasion in the traditional sense. They may instead appear as networks, influence, intimidation, cyber penetration, and deniable coercion.
Recognizing that transformation is the beginning of an effective national-security doctrine.
Canada does not need to become a fortress. It needs to ensure that its openness remains a democratic strength rather than an authoritarian opportunity.
The writer is a Middle East political analyst. His latest book, Tehran’s Dictator, examines the theocratic era of Ali Khamenei (1989-2026). @EQFard

What a Saxony-Anhalt AfD victory means for Germany's minorities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:59:26 UTC
01:59:26 KST

Breadcrumb
What an AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt means for Germany’s minorities
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has scored a historic victory in Saxony-Anhalt, exit polls showed on Sunday, winning 44.5 percent of the vote and more than doubling its 2021 result of 20.8 percent.
For Muslim, Syrian, Palestinian and other migrant communities, the result is more than a regional political upset. It brings some of Germany’s most openly exclusionary rhetoric on Islam, refugees and national identity closer to executive power in a German state.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) was projected to fall to 18.5 percent, down from 37.1 percent in 2021 — a major setback in a state it has governed since 2002.
It remained unclear whether the AfD’s result would be enough to allow it to form a government. The other major parties have ruled out joining an AfD-led coalition under Germany’s longstanding political "firewall". As a result, the party would probably need to secure a majority of seats in the state parliament to govern alone.
An AfD-led government would be the first far-right state administration in Germany since the Nazi era — a prospect that has drawn concern from mainstream parties, civil-society groups and many people from minority backgrounds. The AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch is officially classified as right-wing extremist by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency.
Even if it falls short of an outright parliamentary majority, the scale of the party’s first-place result will strengthen its capacity to set the terms of German political debate — particularly on immigration, asylum, Islam, crime and national identity.
The AfD has long insisted that “Islam does not belong to Germany”. Its Saxony-Anhalt programme repeats the message more specifically, declaring that “Islam belongs neither to Germany nor to Saxony-Anhalt.”
The party distinguishes in its own language between Muslims it says accept Germany’s constitutional order and what it calls political Islam or "Islamism".
But its programme also sets out proposals that would limit visible Islamic religious life, including opposition to the call to prayer, restrictions related to mosque construction, an end to Islamic religious instruction in schools and a move away from university chairs in Islamic theology towards non-confessional Islamic studies.
Germany’s constitution guarantees religious freedom, and so some proposals would face serious legal and constitutional hurdles. But a state government influences the tone and priorities of public institutions, as well as decisions around education, local integration, policing, funding and public administration.
Syrian refugees and Germany's Gaza debate
For Syrian refugees and other people who arrived in Germany during or after the 2015 refugee influx, the AfD’s language around "remigration" has drawn particular concern.
The term has become central to the party’s political project. AfD figures have used it to advocate the departure or removal of people without a right to remain, while critics warn that it can blur the line between deporting people with no legal status and a broader politics of expulsion directed at migrants and citizens with migrant backgrounds.
In Saxony-Anhalt, the party has campaigned for stronger deportation enforcement and proposes a specialised deportation task force.
Germany is home to about 1.28 million people with a Syrian refugee or migrant background, including roughly 936,000 Syrian nationals at the end of 2025, making it the largest Syrian-origin population in Europe.
Much of asylum and immigration law is set federally or by European rules, meaning a state government cannot simply abolish asylum rights or remove people who are legally protected from deportation.
But the state plays an important role in administering asylum systems, running or overseeing accommodation, implementing deportation orders, supporting or cutting integration programmes, and shaping schooling and access to local services.
With regards to education, the party’s state programme also proposes separate classes for refugee children, drawing criticism from opposition groups who argue that separating children risks entrenching exclusion and limiting the social contact needed for integration.
The election is also being watched by Palestinian and Arab communities well beyond Saxony-Anhalt, at a time when Germany’s political debate over Gaza, antisemitism and pro-Palestine activism remains highly charged.
Although the AfD does not offer a detailed programme for Palestinian statehood, Gaza or the genocidal war's humanitarian consequences, its policy is rooted in an open-ended support for Israel, combined with the notion that antisemitism in Germany is principally an imported phenomenon associated with migration from Muslim-majority countries.

At least 120 Roman-era inscriptions, worship to unknown goddess identified inside Spanish cave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:57:17 UTC
01:57:17 KST

At least 120 Latin inscriptions, dating to the first and second centuries CE, were successfully identified at Valencia’s Cova Dones in eastern Spain, marking a significant jump from the roughly 15 inscriptions known at the site before 2026.
The findings, announced in late July by the University of Alicante, were made in May and June by a team led by Virginia Barciela of the University of Alicante and Aitor Ruiz-Redondo of the University of Zaragoza.
The inscriptions were found on the walls and ceilings of a cave previously discovered in 2024 at the site, located over 200 meters underground. The cave’s floor is dotted with small natural pools, known as gours, formed by water seeping through the rock.
“Preliminary results indicate that Cova Dones was a cave-sanctuary frequented by women, since several female names appear among the inscriptions documented so far,” explained the team.
Epigrapher Silvia Alfayé of the University of Zaragoza said that five votive inscriptions confirm that Roman-era visitors had worshipped a deity they called "Domina," meaning “the Lady” in Latin, and that women played an active role in her cult.
“Three of these inscriptions bear the name 'MALACI',” a previously unknown epithet for a goddess,” Alfayé added. “This goddess had a specific aspect, perhaps related to water, the definitive interpretation of which we are currently working on.”
Sergio García-Dils, an epigraphy specialist who worked on the readings, said that the presence of at least five inscriptions dedicated to the same deity rules out casual or one-off visits for a generic purpose, but rather points to specific cultic activity dedicated to a single deity.
“Likewise,” he said. “The fact that the texts are concentrated in a specific and delimited area of the cave, away from the entrance, confirms that it is an organized cult.”
Barciela noted that the research team at the site had found several spindle whorls, used to increase the rotation of a spindle, in addition to the inscriptions.
This indicates that worshippers at the site may have used spindles as offerings, which, in antiquity, “was associated with the female sphere,” Barciela explained. “This fact would fit with the epigraphic evidence pointing to the active participation of women at the sanctuary.”
“In this regard, it is worth considering the first written name that refers to the site: Cova de les Dones (Cave of the Women). It is possible that this is the fossilization of a toponym alluding to the presence of women or female entities there.”
Known to archaeologists since 2023
Cova Dones first drew archaeologists’ eye in 2023, after over 100 Paleolithic paintings were discovered inside it, making it the largest Paleolithic “art collections” found in the eastern Iberian Peninsula.
The site’s Roman layer was only found a year later, in 2024, when excavations uncovered the cave where the newly identified inscriptions were found.
Also found in 2024 were around 15 Latin inscriptions and a coin from the reign of Roman Emperor Claudius (41 CE to 54 CE).
In 2025, researchers succeeded in identifying over 100 pieces of stalagmite that had been altered by human hands.

Jerusalem Rabbi Moshe Yazdi sentenced to 18 years for rape by deception
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:57:10 UTC
01:57:10 KST

The Jerusalem District Court sentenced Rabbi Moshe Yazdi to 18 years in prison on Sunday for repeated sex offenses against two women who sought his religious guidance, after finding that he deceived them into believing the acts were divinely sanctioned “spiritual corrections.”
Yazdi was convicted in March of multiple offenses of rape and indecent acts by deception, as well as financial crimes. The court found that one series of sexual offenses continued for approximately 12 years and another for three to four years, amounting to dozens and possibly hundreds of offenses against each woman.
The sentence also includes a one-year suspended prison term and NIS 150,000 in compensation for each of the two women. Time Yazdi has already spent in custody will be deducted from his sentence.
Sexual acts falsely presented as religious requirements
The finding of rape by deception centered on how Yazdi obtained the women’s apparent agreement. The court found that they submitted to the sexual acts because he falsely presented them as religiously required measures that would achieve a spiritual correction or benefit the world.
Yazdi had led the Amudei Hashalom community and a similarly named nonprofit organization since 1997. He ran a soup kitchen, assisted people in need, and taught Torah classes, building a following that included people who had become newly religious.
Yazdi taught his followers to subordinate their views and feelings to “da’at Torah,” or Torah authority. He portrayed himself as one of the 36 hidden righteous people in Jewish tradition and claimed to possess divine inspiration and to consult deceased rabbis before advising followers on their private lives.
He also taught that wrongdoing created “sparks of impurity” and that he could correct them by descending into impure places and sanctifying them. The court found that he used those claims to persuade the two women that sexual acts with him were spiritual interventions rather than ordinary sexual encounters.
The judges said Yazdi exploited the women’s trust, personal distress, youth and susceptibility to his influence. His conduct harmed their bodies and mental well-being, as well as their autonomy and ability to make informed decisions, the court said.
Yazdi did not accept responsibility for the offenses. He acknowledged in his final statement that he had “sinned,” but did not accept that he had wronged the victims, instead continuing to place responsibility on them. The judges also described his conduct during the trial as manipulative and an abuse of the judicial process.
Yazdi faced allegations involving eight women but was convicted concerning two
The prosecution’s original case was broader. Yazdi faced allegations involving eight women but was convicted of sexual offenses concerning two. The sexual allegations involving the other six women did not result in convictions, and he was acquitted on five of the indictment’s nine counts, including additional sexual and financial allegations.
His financial convictions included money laundering, acts intended to prevent legally required financial reporting, dealing in prohibited property and defrauding creditors. Prosecutors argued during sentencing that Yazdi used bank accounts belonging to followers to conceal money from creditors while he was in bankruptcy proceedings.
The court considered evidence of Yazdi’s charitable work, including his operation of a soup kitchen and assistance to people in financial difficulty. It found, however, that this carried little weight when weighed against the severity and duration of the harm inflicted on the two women.
Yazdi may appeal his conviction and sentence to the Supreme Court.

Downside of Burnham’s devolution drive | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:48:09 UTC
01:48:09 KST

John Harris correctly recognises that “England’s 14 regional and metro mayors are right to see a growing opportunity for a civic political renaissance”, but justifiably points out how areas remain excluded from the new arrangements, or are at best a poor fit (Cities are the big winners in Burnham’s devolution drive. But what happens to the rest of England?, 30 August).
Allowing for a further batch of city region-based authorities over half of England’s population does not suit this model. Where are the city regions and “strategic authorities” in most of rural Devon, Surrey, Hertfordshire and much of Kent and Essex?
If Andy Burnham goes ahead with the local government reorganisation (LGR) he inherited from Steve Reed, we will be faced with vast tracts of non-place authorities with names such as Devon Coast and Countryside and North West Essex, which do not make sense as strategic authorities. They are what remain when the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government has completed its long-term aspiration of reducing the number of English councils and councillors.
We estimate that when this LGR is completed, 90% of councillors and 75% of councils across England could have disappeared, eliminating almost all authorities based on real places and communities. Germany, with its Basic Law, much admired by Mr Burnham, operates with about 11,000 municipalities in a tiered county-municipality structure, and retains municipalities based on real places. The equalisation elements of the Basic Law, which sparks the PM’s interest, have been achieved without the introduction of huge anonymous unitary councils across Germany. England already has the largest units of local government across Europe; nothing is to be gained from making them larger and more anonymous.
Steve Leach Emeritus professor of local government, De Montfort University; Colin Copus Emeritus professor of local politics, De Montfort University

Rejecting the new town in Enfield isn’t nimbyism | Letter

Polly Toynbee’s article about the proposed new town in Enfield mischaracterises local opposition and overlooks more practical options (Nimbys can’t stand in the way of Labour’s legacy: a 21st-century new town boom, 1 September). Objecting to the town is a rejection of poor planning, not nimbyism.
There is no evidence the new town would alleviate Enfield’s mainly affordability-based housing crisis. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates that the proposed planning reforms will reduce house prices by just 0.8% by 2029-30. And the risks of building on the green belt include increased flooding, loss of access to nature and high car-dependency. All three contradict the government and the mayor’s objectives. Far from being built mainly on golfing greens and “a cluster of glasshouses and garden centres, an unplanned sprawl”, the town threatens 884 hectares of Enfield’s green belt, including wooded land and farmland.
Describing Enfield as “the perfect borough for a new town, with excellent rail connections” ignores reality: the added traffic would cause major problems in the north of the borough. Crews Hill runs just two to four trains per hour, with few to no alternative connections available. The infrastructure will not cope with 40,000-plus additional residents.
Enfield should focus on its capacity to build up to 37,000 brownfield homes, far more than the new town proposal of 21,000 homes. Alternative sites include the 10,000-home Meridian Water development, which has been 10 years in the making but so far delivered just 300 homes. Such developments must take priority over covering the green belt in concrete.
Kathrin Spinnler
London

Turkey pushes KAAN stealth jet as tensions with Israel deepen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:46:19 UTC
01:46:19 KST

Breadcrumb
Turkey pushes KAAN stealth jet as tensions with Israel deepen
Turkey is accelerating development of its fifth-generation KAAN fighter jet as Ankara seeks greater military independence amid increasingly open tensions with Israel and Israeli strikes targeting potential Turkish military expansion in Syria.
The Turkish-built fighter is intended eventually to provide Ankara with a sovereign alternative to the US-made F-35, a programme Turkey was expelled from after acquiring Russia's S-400 air defence system.
Turkey had been a partner in the F-35 programme and planned to operate the stealth fighter before Washington removed Ankara and later imposed sanctions over the S-400 purchase.
The setback left Turkey without an operational fifth-generation fighter, while Israel operates the F-35I Adir, giving it a significant advantage in stealth air power.
KAAN, developed by Turkish Aerospace Industries (TUSAS), is intended to narrow that gap while reducing Ankara's dependence on foreign suppliers for advanced military capabilities.
The aircraft's first prototype flew in February 2024, while a newer prototype began taxi tests in July as Turkey moves towards a more advanced phase of testing.
Turkish officials say the aircraft was designed domestically from the ground up as part of a decades-long effort to establish an independent combat aircraft industry.
KAAN is being developed with stealth, internal weapons carriage, advanced radar, electronic warfare and sensor fusion.
These technologies intend to make the aircraft harder to detect and allow pilots to combine information from multiple sensors into a single battlefield picture.
However, one of the programme's biggest remaining challenges is the engine.
KAAN's prototypes and initial production aircraft rely on US-made General Electric F110 engines.
Turkey is developing the TF35000, a domestic 35,000-pound-thrust-class engine intended eventually to power KAAN, but Turkish Aerospace has indicated that integration is targeted for around 2032.
Developing an advanced fighter engine is particularly difficult because it requires technologies including heat-resistant alloys, turbine cooling, precision manufacturing and sophisticated digital controls.
Until Turkey succeeds, KAAN will reduce some forms of foreign dependence while retaining another through its reliance on US propulsion.
Israeli aggression raises the stakes
That vulnerability has become more significant as relations between Turkey and Israel have deteriorated.
Syria has emerged as a major arena of tension since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024 and the emergence of a new government closely aligned with Ankara.
In April 2025, Israel struck the T4, Palmyra and Hama airbases after Turkish military teams had inspected the facilities as Ankara considered expanding its military presence in Syria.
Sources told Reuters at the time that the attack rendered T4 effectively unusable, with one regional intelligence official describing the strikes as a message that Israel would not accept an expanded Turkish presence.
Tensions escalated further in August, when Israel bombed the Abu al-Duhur airbase in northwestern Syria after claiming Turkish troops were preparing to deploy there.
Turkey and Syria denied that any permanent Turkish deployment was planned.
US envoy Tom Barrack later said US intelligence had examined the Israeli claim and concluded that Turkey was not moving military assets into the base.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has nevertheless warned that Israel would not tolerate an expanding Turkish military presence in Syria.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has also warned President Recep Tayyip Erdogan against what he described as "dangerous" military moves in Syria and against testing Israel's willingness to act.
Israel has also opposed Turkey regaining access to the F-35.
Netanyahu said in July that he opposed a possible US sale of the aircraft to Ankara, arguing that it could alter the regional balance of power.
President Donald Trump has signalled a willingness to reconsider Turkey's access to the F-35, although political and legal obstacles remain.
For Ankara, Israel's fifth-generation air advantage, its strikes on Syrian military infrastructure linked to possible Turkish deployments and its opposition to Turkey acquiring F-35s add further strategic importance to KAAN.
A mature KAAN equipped with a Turkish engine, radar, electronic warfare systems and weapons would give Ankara a degree of independent high-end air power it currently lacks.
Israel, however, already operates a mature and combat-tested F-35 fleet, while KAAN remains in development.
Turkey is also seeking foreign partners for the programme, with Saudi Arabia in advanced discussions over possible involvement.
If Ankara succeeds in combining KAAN with a domestically produced engine and indigenous combat systems, the fighter could significantly reduce Turkey's reliance on Washington while beginning to narrow one of Israel's most important technological advantages over it.

Taiwan eyes silicon photonics as next big tech leap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:42:25 UTC
01:42:25 KST

Taiwan, which accounts for more than half of the global outsourced semiconductor assembly and testing market, is well-positioned to develop copackaged optics (CPO) and manufacture precision silicon photonics chips, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said yesterday.
Silicon photonics are emerging as a mainstream optical communications technology and is seen as key to overcoming bottlenecks in AI computing power.
The technology is a key project under the government’s New 10 Major AI Infrastructure Projects, with industry, government, academia and research institutions working to overcome critical technological hurdles and build a self-reliant silicon photonics supply chain, the ministry said.
Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA
Nvidia Corp in March invested US$4 billion in silicon photonics technology, the ministry added.
The technology was a major topic at Semicon Taiwan, which concluded on Friday last week.
Silicon photonics replaces traditional copper wire transmission of electronic signals between chips with optical signals.
As light generates almost no heat during transmission, the technology can reduce power consumption by 30 to 50 percent, allowing devices to stream high-definition content and generate artificial intelligence content more quickly, the ministry said.
Taiwan has key advantages in the transition, including a comprehensive semiconductor ecosystem and more than 90 percent of global advanced semiconductor manufacturing capacity for 7 nanometer chips or below, the ministry said.
Taiwan accounts for more than half of the global semiconductor assembly and testing market, which gives it a key role in developing CPO, a technology aimed at overcoming the 1.6-terabit-per-second bandwidth limit of traditional electronic transmission.
The government launched a silicon photonics research and development (R&D) initiative under its A+ Enterprise Innovation R&D Program earlier this year to support the development of key technologies.
The ministry and the SEMI have helped more than 30 leading companies, including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), ASE Technology Holding Co (日月光投控), MediaTek Inc (聯發科) and Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海精密), establish the Silicon Photonics Industry Alliance in 2024, it said.
The alliance aims to overcome key technological hurdles, particularly in CPO, and ensure that Taiwan retains control of the silicon photonics supply chain, it said.
