Drone operators fined NT$16 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:36 UTC
01:41:36 KST

Authorities fined drone operators a total of NT$16 million (US$505,849) in 72 cases last year and the first half of this year, with more than 80 percent of the contraventions occurring at airports, reservoirs and science parks, the Civil Aviation Administration (CAA) said.
YouTuber Chung Ming-hsuan (鍾明軒) was fined NT$330,000 for illegally operating a drone near the Ma-anshan Nuclear Power Plant in June and for failure to display a registration number on the aircraft.
Last month, the triggering of a drone-detection sensor in the controlled area surrounding Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport forced the north and south runways to suspend takeoffs and landings for 10 minutes, affecting nine flights.
Photo courtesy of Taoyuan City Councilor Hsu Yu-shu
The CAA fined drone operators in 47 cases last year and 25 in the first half of this year, the agency said.
Twenty-four of the fined infractions took place in airport restricted airspace, 19 at reservoirs and 15 in science parks, it said.
The remaining 14 cases occurred in other restricted areas, such as Taipei Main Station and power plants, it added.
Commercial aircraft travel at high speeds and low altitudes during takeoff and landing, and a drone being sucked into an engine or colliding with an aircraft could cause a major disaster, Chaoyang University of Technology Department of Aviation Technology director Lu Yen-liang (盧衍良) said yesterday.
Reservoirs and power plants are subject to air restrictions to prevent drones from crashing into and damaging equipment, contaminating water sources or causing secondary disasters, he said.
As centers of high-tech industry, science parks must guard against aerial photography to prevent trade secrets from being leaked, Lu said.
A drone crash at a science park could also damage sensitive equipment and injure workers, he added.
While enforcing no-fly zones at airports is a top priority because drone incursions can threaten flight safety, local government no-fly zones have fewer resources and depend more on public reports, meaning some contraventions might go undetected, former National Cheng Kung University Department of Transportation and Communication Management Science associate professor Melody Dai (戴佐敏) said.
Drones are prohibited in reservoirs and science parks, and flying them without approval can result in fines of NT$30,000 to NT$1.5 million under the Civil Aviation Act (民用航空法), and the drone would be confiscated in serious cases, CAA drone office executive secretary Keng Hua (耿驊) said.
People can download the Ministry of Transportation and Communications’ Drone Map app or go to the CAA’s drone management system to see maps of restricted airspace, Keng said.
As of the end of June, there were 36,066 valid drone licenses and 42,016 registered drones, CAA data showed.
One drone operator surnamed Chen (陳) said he checks the CAA’s official Web site before every flight to see whether drones are permitted in the area, but some operators might be unaware of the rules or take their chances and enter restricted airspace.
Notifications from government apps about restricted airspace might not be enough for beginners, who might accidently contravene regulations, drone operator Wu Ming-yang (吳明陽) said.
Retailers should put warning labels on drones and promote the regulations, he said.
Wu called for the legalization of drone flights during the 30 minutes before sunrise and after sunset so photographers can capture better footage.

Doctor warns against lancing boils at home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:36 UTC
01:41:36 KST

A doctor last week warned against treating boils at home, after an octogenarian woman attempted to lance a boil on her buttocks with a sewing needle, but ended up developing a bacterial infection, causing the boil to grow to the size of a baseball.
Tseng Yu-kang (曾禹康), an attending colorectal surgeon from Taichung Veterans General Hospital who sees patients at the Dajia Branch of Lee General Hospital, said that the woman, who lived alone, believed the boil was not particularly serious.
In a scene that could have been depicted in a historical drama, the woman attempted to lance it using a sewing needle that she had heated over a flame to disinfect it, Tseng said.
Photo: Chang Hsuan-tse, Taipei Times
By the time she sought treatment, the affected area had swollen to the size of a baseball, and it took nearly an hour to thoroughly clean out the pus-filled wound, he said.
Jabbing the needle at what might have been inflammation of the hair follicle likely forced the pus into the deeper fascial layer, triggering a more severe infection that eventually swelled into a large and painful boil, he said.
Puncturing a puss-filled boil on the buttocks with the needle is like using a syringe to inject poison into the body, Tseng said.
Fascia is like a highway for bacteria, he said.
If bacteria spread through the loose tissue beneath the skin, they can cause blockages in small blood vessels and tissue death, and without prompt medical attention, the infection could lead to fatal sepsis, he said.
Tseng urged people not to treat boils themselves, as it could worsen the condition.
About 90 percent of infections around the anus originate from infected glands inside the anus, while some start in the skin, Tseng said.
Prolonged pressure on the buttocks, combined with poorly ventilated clothing and dampness from sweat, can help bacteria thrive, he said.
Bacteria can enter through hair follicles or tiny breaks in the skin, causing deeper infections and boils, he added.
Squeezing a boil with the hands or tools before it has come to a head can inadvertently spread bacteria and even cause cellulitis, Tseng said.

CPC Corp, Taiwan (CPC, 台灣中油) on Saturday announced that it would keep its domestic gasoline and diesel prices steady this week, and Formosa Petrochemical Corp (台塑石化) followed suit yesterday, despite a spike in international crude oil prices.
This week would be the sixth consecutive week that CPC and Formosa have maintained domestic crude oil prices, despite crude oil prices moving higher in the wake of renewed hostilities between the US and Iran.
Front-month Brent crude oil futures — the international oil benchmark — last week gained 9.28 percent to settle at US$96.28 per barrel on the Intercontinental Exchange in London, while West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures — the US oil benchmark — increased 9.69 percent to US$91.48 per barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
CPC said its floating price mechanism, based on a weighted average of 70 percent Dubai and 30 percent Brent crude, showed that the average international crude oil price rose to US$99.82 last week from US$91.56 per barrel the previous week.
A stronger New Taiwan dollar, which averaged NT$31.682 last week against the US dollar, compared with NT$31.775 a week earlier, helped CPC slightly ease crude oil purchasing cost pressure, it said.
Retail gasoline prices this week would remain at NT$30.5, NT$32 and NT$34 per liter for 92, 95 and 98-octane unleaded gasoline respectively at CPC and Formosa stations, while prices of premium diesel would remain at NT$29.3 per liter at CPC stations and NT$29.1 per liter at Formosa pumps, the companies said.

At the Met, snakes have to audition for the opera
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:34 UTC
01:41:34 KST

Pretty much everyone on stage at the Metropolitan Opera in New York must audition — even the snake who would briefly take center stage in an upcoming adaptation of a Mozart classic.
In charge of deciding who gets the s-s-s-s-starring reptilian role is Zoe Ziegfeld, a carnival performer-turned-opera actor cast as the snake handler in the Met’s version of Cosi fan tutte, inspired by Coney Island in the 1950s.
Ziegfeld takes each snake, lets it slither and wrap around, then hoists the animal over their head, rehearsing what they would do under the bright lights at center stage for each performance. Ziegfeld looks each one in the eye, almost face-to-face as they evaluate the snake’s demeanor.
Photo: AP
“I need to know that the animal is comfortable with people and with what we are doing,” Ziegfeld said.
In the cold-blooded competition, a boa constrictor named Princess won. She is a larger snake with a better visual presence on stage.
“We will be moving forward with Princess [the big sun-glow boa constrictor who is yellow-peach] in rehearsals on a trial basis! She is a wonderful snake, and the trial is not about her, but rather about me and my strength,” Ziegfeld wrote in an e-mail after the auditions were over.
This is the third time Ziegfeld has played the role of the snake charmer in the Met’s adaptation of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s 1790 opera.
In Mozart’s original, two Italian soldiers decide to test their lovers’ fidelity by pretending to head off to war. They then disguise themselves and try to seduce each other’s girlfriends. In this version, the plot remains mostly the same, but the setting is a 1950s Coney Island carnival complete with vibrant scenery and sideshow performers.
When Ziegfeld tried out several years ago, live snakes were not allowed in the audition space. Instead, Ziegfeld brought a video of their snake-charming act, then hammered home their carnival sideshow bona fides by knocking a nail into their own nasal cavity in what was called the Human Blockhead act.
The snakes came to their audition thanks to Nancy Novograd and her company All Tame Animals.
The first two snakes to audition were a bit small. One might have clashed with Ziegfeld’s top.
The key is personality, Novograd said.
“Animals have to perform as do human talent. Sometimes they have a set type of behaviors that they have to demonstrate. And sometimes they just have to get along with the talent,” Novograd said. “So in this case, they have to be the right color, size, and Zoe has to like them.”

Exchange reserves climb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:34 UTC
01:41:34 KST

Taiwan’s foreign exchange reserves rose to again exceed US$600 billion last month, ending two months of declines, the central bank said on Friday.
Foreign exchange reserves are overseas assets held by a central bank that can be readily deployed, including foreign currency deposits and government securities.
Last month, reserves rose US$7.633 billion from a month earlier to US$601.904 billion, the biggest monthly increase in more than a year, Department of Foreign Exchange Director-General Eugene Tsai (蔡炯民) said during a news conference at the central bank in Taipei.
Photo: Reuters
The increase was driven mainly by investment returns on the central bank’s foreign currency assets, appreciation of major non-US currencies against the US dollar and the bank’s intervention in the foreign-exchange market to maintain orderly trading, Tsai said.
Last month, the US Dollar Index fell 0.49 percent, while most major currencies strengthened against the greenback. The euro and British pound each gained 0.68 percent, the Canadian dollar rose 0.91 percent, the yen advanced 0.49 percent and the yuan appreciated 0.35 percent, central bank data showed.
The New Taiwan dollar was the strongest performer, rising 2.51 percent against the greenback during the month, as foreign investors posted net inflows of about US$1.2 billion to hunt for bargains in the local equity market, Tsai said.
To help maintain the local foreign exchange market stable, the central bank intervened by buying US dollars and selling NT dollars to moderate the greenback’s losses, he said.
Tsai did not disclose how much the central bank spent in last month’s market intervention. The bank announced in a joint statement with the US Department of the Treasury last year that it would release the figure on a quarterly basis.
Tsai said it remained unclear whether the yen’s appreciation was driven by official intervention or short-covering. The yen has unique characteristics as a major international currency, including its role as a safe-haven asset and its use in carry trades, he said.
Movements in the yen could influence other Asian currencies, but the direction of individual currencies would ultimately depend on their own supply-and-demand dynamics, Tsai said.
Meanwhile, the central bank data showed that as of the end of last month, foreign investors held US$1.861 trillion in Taiwan-listed stocks, bonds and NT dollar-denominated deposits, up from US$1.663 trillion at the end of July.
These holdings were worth 309 percent of Taiwan’s total foreign exchange reserves last month, compared with 280 percent a month earlier, the central bank said. A strong rebound in the TAIEX, which rose 6.98 percent in the month, reflected the increase in these foreign holdings, it said.

Building Canada’s post-US economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:33 UTC
01:41:33 KST

US President Donald Trump first hit Canada with substantial tariffs in 2018, targeting aluminum and steel. He did so again after returning to office last year, targeting dozens of goods, although he later exempted those compliant with the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement.
Last week, after trade talks broke down, he repeated his favorite trick, imposing 50 percent tariffs on a vast array of Canadian imports, including wine and mittens. Canada responded with “dollar-for-dollar” retaliatory tariffs.
Trump’s tariffs have come nowhere close to delivering a US manufacturing revival. Instead, they have inflicted losses on businesses and slowed growth in both countries. His actions have also shown that any protectionist US president could exploit trade integration with an ally for practical or ideological ends.
Canada is deeply vulnerable. Its merchandise exports to the US account for one-fifth of its GDP, and nowhere is this dependence more acute than in the auto industry. Given that automobile manufacturing depends on tightly integrated regional supply chains across North America, Europe and Asia, it is difficult to imagine a viable Canadian auto industry without ready access to the Great Lakes-centered manufacturing ecosystem.
To reduce its strategic vulnerability to Trump’s extortion, Canada must develop industries that can operate freely across continents. We analyze these opportunities — and explain how Canada can seize them — in our forthcoming book Canada After America: A Strategy for Prosperity in a Changed World.
Canada’s natural resources are obviously an enormous asset. The planned West Coast oil pipeline is essential to bringing Alberta’s petroleum to Asian markets. Investments in new and expanded mines, and in the infrastructure needed to export their output, are also laudable. Global demand for Canada’s resources is robust, and, crucially, the country does not need access to American supply chains to extract them.
The same goes for several other value-added industries. Pharmaceuticals, manufactured from widely available basic chemicals, derive most of their value from the knowledge embedded in each medicine. Medical devices are expensive, high-value goods often purchased by hospitals rather than individual consumers, and can incorporate specialized inputs from around the world.
Consider aerospace. Like automobiles, it involves intensive manufacturing, but planes are produced at relatively low volumes and according to extremely stringent quality standards. The necessarily slow pace of building an airplane enables genuinely global supply chains, with components sourced from numerous advanced economies.
Canada already has an established aerospace industry, led by Bombardier. It also has a number of notable biotech companies. Yet several of its European peers, including much smaller countries, generate tens of billions of dollars more in exports from these sectors.
All these distance-resilient industries depend heavily on new knowledge and invest in research and development (R&D) accordingly. Although Canada is home to world-leading research universities and a highly educated population, it is a notorious laggard in private-sector innovation. Canadian business R&D spending has hovered at about 1 percent of GDP for decades.
According to the latest Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development data, the US, Germany, Japan, South Korea, Sweden and Israel all spend between two and six times as much relative to GDP.
Canadian private-sector R&D is also unusually concentrated among small companies. In the world’s leading tech economies, by contrast, large firms account for the lion’s share of business R&D expenditures.
Contrary to popular belief, research is chiefly conducted not by start-ups, but by the likes of Space Exploration Technologies Corp and AstraZeneca: firms that have scaled and have the financial wherewithal to invest heavily in developing new technologies.
Canada has relatively few champions of that scale, which helps explain why small and medium-size enterprises (SMEs) account for such a large share of its R&D.
Information and communications technology is a striking exception. Canada’s per-capita R&D spending in the sector is among the world’s highest, and the country has produced several large, business-facing firms like Shopify and OpenText. The core constraint is therefore not a systemic inadequacy. Rather, Canada struggles to build large firms in industries that are more capital and regulation-intensive than software.
The problem is compounded by the structure of government support for private R&D. Canada provides substantial R&D funding through tax credits, but the program, though recently reformed, remains biased toward small firms. Tax credits also leave companies reliant on uncertain refunds after investments have been made. Other countries, like Israel and Germany, have traditionally funded private R&D through upfront grants.
Canada’s growth is further impeded by sluggish regulatory approvals and government procurement practices. The country’s healthcare system relies on multistage reviews of new medicines involving sequential federal and provincial approvals. Other countries expedite approvals by conducting these reviews concurrently. For a Canadian pharmaceutical company developing a new drug, such delays can make the difference between profitability and bankruptcy.
A more ambitious approach to procurement could foster innovation. Government R&D budgets are often below 1 percent of GDP, while purchases of equipment and supplies typically exceed 10 percent.
For example, in Israel, companies compete to solve public problems like emergency-room overcrowding. South Korea requires government agencies at every level to devote 20 percent of their procurement budgets to promising new technologies and companies approved by an independent agency. Governments act as anchor customers, helping innovative firms grow.
Sweden, Switzerland, Denmark, Israel and others show that small countries can cultivate thriving tech industries. Canada can do the same, but first it must confront difficult political questions about healthcare regulation and SME funding. Whatever tensions these debates provoke would pale in comparison to the consequences of remaining subject to the whims and malignant whimsy of its unreliable southern neighbor.
Ricardo Hausmann, a former minister of planning of Venezuela and former chief economist at the Inter-American Development Bank, is a professor at Harvard Kennedy School and director of the Harvard Growth Lab. Eric Protzer is a senior research fellow at the Harvard Growth Lab. Hausmann and Protzer are coauthors of the forthcoming Canada After America: A Strategy for Prosperity in a Changed World.

EU chief due in Greenland to boost ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:32 UTC
01:41:32 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen headed to Greenland yesterday for a two-day visit aimed at reaffirming the bloc’s support for the Danish autonomous territory coveted by US President Donald Trump.
Today, she is due to sign a joint declaration between the EU and Greenland.
“Greenland is becoming increasingly important to the EU as a gateway to the Arctic and because of its geopolitical location, critical raw materials and role in Arctic security,” Royal Danish Defence College researcher Marc Jacobsen said.
Photo:AFP
Trump was adamant earlier this year about Washington’s need to control the vast Arctic island for reasons of national security, although he ultimately ruled out annexing it by force.
A Danish-Greenlandic-US working group has since met regularly to find an agreement on cooperation going forward.
Following Trump’s threats, European countries broadly backed Denmark and Greenland, and in January, Von der Leyen vowed “massive” EU investment in Greenland to step up security in the Arctic.
Greenland is not a member of the bloc although Denmark is.
Brussels has also proposed doubling direct EU aid to Greenland to 530 million euros (US$615.49 million) under the bloc’s next budget for the 2028-to-2034 period.
The Financial Times said Von der Leyen is expected to propose an additional 200 million euros in support during her visit.
Her visit coincides with the start of NATO’s Arctic Shield military exercise, bringing together soldiers from 10 countries.
University of Quebec geopolitics researcher Mikaa Blugeon-Mered said the timing is “not insignificant coincidence.”
The Trump administration has repeatedly accused Denmark of neglecting Greenland and Arctic security. Copenhagen has since reinvested in the region, as has NATO, which launched its Arctic Sentry mission at the start of the year.
“The EU cannot provide Greenland with a military security guarantee in the way NATO can, but it can provide something politically important: a clear signal that Greenland is not standing alone,” Jacobsen said.
The message is all the more important as the US has kept up pressure on Greenland.
“We’ve been getting ‘postcards’ from Trump or those close to him about Greenland every month, showing that they haven’t forgotten,” Blugeon-Mered said.
One such image Trump posted on Truth Social in May showed him peering over the island, with the headline “Hello, Greenland!”
Greenland is also struggling to develop its mining industry, which could help it fund its independence from Denmark.
In this area, Greenlandic and European interests are “highly complementary,” Jacobsen said.
“Greenland needs investment, infrastructure and markets if it is to realize its mining ambitions, while the EU is looking for more secure and diversified access to critical raw materials,” he said.
However, turning Greenland’s geological potential into reality is proving more difficult than expected.
About 135 mining permits are held by more than 60 companies, but only two mines are in operation.
“The question is whether the current geopolitical momentum will ultimately be a game-changer,” Jacobsen said.
Blugeon-Mered said von der Leyen’s visit to Greenland — her second in two years — was a strong signal that European investment is long-term.

John J. Tkacik, Jr. On Taiwan: Happy 75th Birthday, Taiwan!
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:31 UTC
01:41:31 KST

Well, sort of.
Tomorrow is the seventy-fifth anniversary of the San Francisco Peace Treaty, signed by forty-nine nations on September 8, 1951. The Republic of China wasn’t one of them. Article 2(b) of the Treaty reads: “Japan renounces all right, title and claim to Formosa and the Pescadores.” So, tomorrow would be the Diamond Jubilee of Formosa’s freedom from Japanese sovereignty. As my good friend and former Examination Yuan President Yao Chia-wen (姚嘉文) voiced in these pages last year (“San Francisco treaty should be taught: adviser”, Sept. 7, 2025), the Japan peace treaty should be taught in all Taiwan schools to correct the record on the legal status of Taiwan following Japan’s surrender in the Pacific War.
After all, Taiwan was a Japanese colony, and the United Nations principles of decolonization center on the right of all peoples to self-determination and the immediate, unconditional end to colonialism. Mr. Yao, a scholar of comparative legal systems, argues that sovereignty resides in the will of the people. If an international treaty imperfectly addresses a point of sovereignty, then the default sovereignty must reside with the people of the territory in question. This, of course, was the central tenet of former president Lee Teng-hui’s (李登輝) philosophy: “Sovereignty resides in the People” (主權在民).
So, September 8th is “The Future of Taiwan Remains to be Determined” Day. Oh, happy day! At least Taiwan is not under China’s sovereignty. As Shakespeare would say, “there art thou happy!” And Taiwan is a global economic power — there art thou happy. Taiwan is Asia’s most dynamic democracy — there art thou happy.
Not that happy. Under orders from General Douglas MacArthur, a Chinese Nationalist army occupied Taiwan in October 1945 to accept Japan’s surrender. But the Nationalists’ rapacious occupation of Taiwan delegitimized Chiang Kai-shek’s (蔣介石) authority, tarnished his reputation and jeopardized democracy in the entire post-War Pacific.
After the February 28th 1947 uprisings in Taiwan, the State Department advised the US Congress that “although the transfer of sovereignty has not yet been formalized, China’s de facto control over the island is generally recognized…” In other words: “The United States does not yet recognize China’s sovereignty over Formosa.”
President Chiang understood. Years ago, Taiwan’s Academia Historica discovered a dispatch sent by the Generalissimo in Nanking to Taiwan governor Chen Cheng (陳誠) dated January 12, 1949. Chiang cautioned that “the nature of Taiwan’s legal status and sovereignty is that it is held by the ROC as a trust territory until a peace conference with Japan” (台灣法律地位與主權，在對日和會未成以前，不過為我國一托管地之性質). Moreover, Chiang was still fighting a civil war; neither Peking nor Nanking had yet fallen to the Communists. Morale must not waver, so the governor should take care in his characterization of Taiwan’s status.
These same worries perplexed Washington throughout 1949. On April 15, the State Department stated that “the determination of the final status of Formosa must await the conclusion of a peace settlement for Japan.”
On May 1, the American consul general in Taipei also told Governor Chen “that the legal status of Taiwan would not be determined until the Japanese treaty was signed.” Acting President of China Li Tsung-ren (李宗仁) told US Ambassador Leighton Stuart that President Chiang, hearing this, “decided he could not retire to a place where the sovereignty of China might be questioned.”
In 1949, all US policy papers about Formosa carried the disclaimer: “the present legal status of Taiwan is that it is a portion of the Japanese Empire awaiting final disposition by a peace settlement with Japan.”
On January 5, 1950, Secretary of State Dean Acheson argued with two top Republican senators in his office, during which he “pointed out that if one wanted to be legalistic, it could be argued that, in sheer legality, Formosa would not be a part and parcel of China until a stipulation to that effect had been made in the Japanese Peace Treaty.”
But there was a catch. Acheson had no peace treaty with Japan even close to ready, and any treaty with Acheson’s name on it was sure to fail in the Senate. In January 1950, Secretary Acheson was finally persuaded to pursue a formal peace treaty with Japan and he wisely recruited Republican elder statesman John Foster Dulles to get it through the Senate.
Mr. Dulles had a personal interest in the Island of Formosa. As Dulles once explained in a secret Senate hearing: “The sovereignty of Taiwan was vested in Japan I think in the year 1895. It happened that my grandfather went to Taipei and was one of those who turned over the title deeds to Japan in 1895.”
It was true. Mr. Dulles’s grandfather, John Watson Foster, personally crafted the 1895 deed of transfer of Formosa from the Manchu Empire to the sovereignty of Japan. Grandfather Foster then accompanied Viceroy Li Hung-chang’s (李鴻章) godson, by steamship, into Formosan waters off Keelung to the Japanese commander’s flagship to formalize the turnover. There, on June 2, 1895, General Foster reviewed “the instrument of transfer,” the documents were “signed and exchanged, the farewell visits of courtesy were paid, and at midnight the Chinese steamer weighed anchor and we sailed away for Shanghai.”
So it happened that sovereignty over Taiwan was conveyed to Japan in a treaty midwifed by Dulles’s own grandfather as counsel to the imperial court in Peking. Fifty-six years later, his grandson John Foster Dulles would preside over Japan’s renunciation of that same sovereignty. But this time sovereignty would not return to China.
Dulles, a devout layman of the Presbyterian Church and America’s top international lawyer, whose life’s work was in the furtherance of the rule of law among nations, maintained a profound concern for the welfare and freedom of Taiwan’s people. Dulles advised the Secretary of State on October 21, 1950, that:
“The US interest in the Formosan problem is a deep and legitimate one and the US feels it has a special responsibility in view of the close connection between the ultimate disposition of Formosa and the conclusion of a Japanese peace treaty which will formally remove Formosa from Japanese sovereignty. The US, being the chief occupying power in Japan and the one most deeply concerned in a Japanese peace settlement, naturally has great responsibility to see that any solution of the Formosan issue is a sound one which contributes to peace and stability in the Pacific area and the welfare of the people … However, the present Chinese Government on the mainland of China is not the one which was in power at the time of Cairo and Potsdam and it certainly is not clear that the people of Formosa desire to be placed in subjection to that government.”
One year later, the day the San Francisco Treaty was signed, a British delegate clarified the compromise on Taiwan’s fate:
1) the Treaty divests Japan of sovereignty over “Formosa and the Pescadores,” but
2) The treaty itself does not determine the future of these islands;
3) People’s China, an international outlaw warring against the United Nations in Korea, was not a suitable steward of former Japanese territories;
4) In due course a solution to the Formosa problem must be found, but it must be in accord with the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations; and
5) The Treaty conferees “came to the conclusion that the proper treatment of Formosa was for the Treaty to provide only for the renunciation of Japanese sovereignty.”
The question of sovereignty over Taiwan on the day after September 8, 1951, was never answered.
Within a few months, Japan signed a peace treaty with the “Republic of China” limited to “territories which are now, or which may hereafter be, under the control” of the Taipei government. Japan’s prime minister Shigeru Yoshida pointed out to Senator Alexander Smith that Japan was in no position to recognize the “Republic of China’s” sovereignty over Formosa because, under the San Francisco Treaty, “she had renounced all right, title and claim to Formosa and the Pescadores, so Japan had no say about turning Formosa back to anyone.” In 1952, Taipei’s foreign minister George C.K. Yeh (葉公超) told the legislature: “Under present circumstances, Japan has no right to transfer Formosa and the Pescadores to us; nor can we accept such a transfer from Japan even if she so wishes...”
And so, the San Francisco Treaty of September 8, 1951, confirmed that Japan had abandoned Formosa and could have no more to say about the matter. All signatories agreed.
In 1951, no signatory could have foreseen seventy-five years into the future: Taiwan is the Asia-Pacific’s most dynamic democracy, the world’s 20th-largest economy, 10th-most prosperous country per capita, one of the world’s most advanced industrial nations, the world’s 12th-largest exporter, third-largest exporter to America, and third-largest holder of US dollar deposits. In short — if the communists were to take over Taiwan now, it’s curtains for the Free World.
Happy “Undetermined Day”!
John J. Tkacik, Jr. is a retired US foreign service officer who has served in Taipei and Beijing and is now director of the Future Asia Project at the International Assessment and Strategy Center. He is also on the Advisory Board of the Global Taiwan Institute.

It all comes back to Taiwan’s giant geopolitical issue: the multitude of countries cutting diplomatic ties with Taiwan

EDITORIAL: Chiang’s reputation is eroding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:29 UTC
01:41:29 KST

Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) was under constant fire last month over the city government’s questionable public works projects and child protection issues, and last week he sparked another controversy involving his son.
Chiang on Monday last week confirmed that his eldest son, who was recently admitted to Taipei Municipal Chien Kuo Senior High School, would take a leave of absence to participate in a year-long exchange program in the US. The exchange program Chiang’s son was selected for is funded by the Taipei City Government, and is limited to 25 spots for eligible junior-high and high-school students. Chiang was accused of giving his son an unfair advantage in the selection process due to his position, fueling public criticism that the mayor, who should act in the public interest, is instead competing for limited public resources.
While city councilors and residents questioned why Chiang did not recuse himself to avoid a conflict of interest, they also questioned why Chiang’s son needed to apply for the program, as he was born in the US and has dual citizenship, meaning he does not lack of educational opportunities in the US.
More speculation about Chiang’s possible “privileges” arose as reports that his son had graduated from one of the most competitive and selective junior-high schools in Taipei in terms of admission. Both parents and the child need a household registration in the school district several years prior to qualify for enrollment, but Chiang’s family was reportedly registered in another district until a few years ago. This led to his son’s educational background and Mayor’s Award qualification also being called into question.
Chiang on Wednesday said that his family decided to turn down the subsidy without withdrawing from the exchange program and insisted that his son was selected without preferential treatment.
Meanwhile, news media reported that Chiang allegedly kept the more than NT$17.2 million (US$543,788) election campaign subsidy he received for the 2022 mayoral election in his personal bank account for personal use, a claim he confirmed on Monday last week.
Although this does not violate any law, it has a considerable impact on his political reputation, as it differs from an unwritten tradition. Former mayors across party lines, including Chen Shui-bian (陳水扁), Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九), Hau Lung-bin (郝龍斌) and Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) have all donated the subsidy to public welfare foundations and charitable groups. The only exception is when Ko used his 2018 subsidy to pay down a loan secured by his wife’s home.
Chiang has frequently responded to governance questions and controversies, such as failed public works and the delayed handling of a child protection case, by saying that decisions did not contravene any laws and by deflecting blame to the central government or other local governments. He continues to use the same tactic when addressing the latest controversies.
Moreover, he has used frontline workers as a “human shield,” such as saying that “food safety inspectors worked hard” when asked why the city failed to test cooking oil for a carcinagenic substance, stressing “social workers worked very hard” when asked about the months-long delay in placing a victimized girl under protection, and now calling for people to “not target his son and respect his privacy,” although he has repeatedly put his children in the public eye.
The real problem was never frontline workers or his son, but Chiang’s questionable governance, his political ethics and the city government’s systemic flaws that failed to protect or support those in need. However, Chiang continues to dodge accountability and fails to take any action in resolving the issues.
Even if Chiang did not intervene directly during the exchange program review, many believe education department officials would naturally feel pressured to approve Chiang’s son’s application, and that the mayor should have recused himself to avoid a conflict of interest.
Further linked to Chiang’s decision to pocket the election subsidy, many people are questioning whether Chiang always puts personal interests above public ones.
These doubts are eroding public trust in his ability to serve Taipei’s residents, let alone all Taiwanese nationals, as an opinion poll had shown that he is considered the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) best presidential candidate for 2028.
Chiang’s evasive attitude toward public scrutiny is quickly eating away at his reputation and political capital, and is showing through on social media monitoring platforms, where he was the most discussed politician of the past week.

From Shiraz to Zanzibar: A look into centuries-old Persian connection

Unknown Publisher

01:40:18 KST

From Shiraz to Zanzibar: A look into centuries-old Persian connection
TEHRAN - For centuries, the Indian Ocean served not as a barrier separating Iran from East Africa, but as a maritime corridor linking the two regions.
Seasonal monsoon winds carried sailors, merchants, religious scholars and migrants between the Persian Gulf, the Arabian Peninsula, the Swahili coast and the Indian subcontinent, creating networks through which goods, ideas, languages, religions and cultural practices circulated.
Among the most enduring traditions associated with these connections is the story of the “Shirazis”, people said to have migrated from the southern Iranian city, to the East African coast. The story has long occupied an important place in the historical memory of communities in Zanzibar, Kilwa, Mombasa and other parts of the Swahili coast. But historians have increasingly cautioned against interpreting the tradition as evidence of a single, large-scale migration from the Iranian city of Shiraz.
Instead, the history appears to have been shaped by successive movements of people across the western Indian Ocean, including merchants and settlers from the Persian Gulf, as well as by intermarriage and the gradual formation of cosmopolitan coastal communities.
Tanzanian historian Professor Abdul Sheriff has been one of the most prominent scholars to examine this complex history. Born in Zanzibar in 1939, Sheriff studied geography and history at the University of California, Los Angeles, before earning a doctorate in African history from the School of Oriental and African Studies at the University of London. He later became a professor of history at the University of Dar es Salaam and played a major role in the study and preservation of Zanzibar’s heritage. His work has focused particularly on the history of Zanzibar, the Swahili coast and the dhow culture of the Indian Ocean.
His 2010 book Dhow Cultures of the Indian Ocean: Cosmopolitanism, Commerce and Islam places the movement of people between Iran and Africa within the wider history of the Indian Ocean. Sheriff argues that the dhow was not simply a vessel for transporting commodities. Because sailors and merchants often had to remain in foreign ports until seasonal winds allowed their return journeys, maritime trade created opportunities for long-term residence, intermarriage and cultural exchange. Over time, commercial networks developed into social and cultural communities.
The monsoon system was central to this process. Sailors could travel between the East African coast and the Persian Gulf at particular times of the year, then return when the winds changed. Ports such as Siraf and Hormuz were part of a much wider maritime network extending toward the African coast. Zanzibar, meanwhile, occupied a strategically important position at the center of the Swahili coast, where maritime routes connected Africa with Arabia, Persia and India.
One of the best-known accounts of Persian migration to East Africa concerns Ali ibn al-Hasan, traditionally described as a member of a Shirazi ruling family who established himself at Kilwa. The story is preserved in versions of the Kilwa Chronicle, a collection of traditions concerning the history of the city-state.
The traditional account should, however, be treated with caution. Earlier historians interpreted it literally, while later scholars questioned whether the “Shirazi” migration represented a direct movement of people from Shiraz to Kilwa.
Historian Neville Chittick, for example, argued that the available archaeological and documentary evidence did not support a simple account of a direct migration from the Persian Gulf to Kilwa. He suggested instead that the movement associated with the Shirazi tradition may have involved settlers from the Banadir coast of present-day Somalia. His study also connected the emergence of a Shirazi dynasty at Kilwa with archaeological evidence and locally minted coins.
Other research has nevertheless strengthened the case for a genuine Persian component in the history of the Swahili coast. Archaeologist Stéphane Pradines, examining the site of Sanje ya Kati near Kilwa, argued that archaeological evidence points to Persian influence on the East African coast between roughly the 10th and 12th centuries. At the same time, he stressed that “Shirazi” should not automatically be understood as meaning people exclusively from the city of Shiraz.
More recent genetic research has added another layer to the debate. A 2023 study of medieval populations from the Swahili coast found evidence of admixture between African and Persian-associated populations beginning around AD 1000. The researchers said the findings were consistent with accounts of Persian arrivals preserved in the Kilwa Chronicle, while emphasizing the complex African and Asian ancestry of Swahili populations.
The evidence therefore points to interaction rather than replacement. African coastal communities were not passive recipients of an imported Persian civilization. They were active participants in the development of the societies that became known as Swahili.
 
 Trade was one of the principal mechanisms behind this process. Merchants did not merely exchange ivory, spices, timber, textiles and other commodities. They also exchanged technologies, religious ideas, architectural traditions, languages and social practices. The resulting urban culture was distinctly Swahili, even though it contained elements derived from several parts of the Indian Ocean world. 
Architecture provides some of the clearest evidence of these interactions. Historic mosques and houses along the Swahili coast reflect centuries of contact between African communities and societies across the Indian Ocean. The 12th-century Kufic inscription at Kizimkazi in Zanzibar is among the important archaeological remains associated with the early Islamic history of the islands. Sheriff has also examined the architectural connections between Zanzibar, the Swahili coast and the Persian Gulf.
Cultural connections were not confined to architecture and material remains. Elements associated with the Persian calendar have also survived in parts of Zanzibar and the wider Swahili world. The celebration known as Nairuzi, a local form of the name Nowruz, has been associated with communities in Zanzibar and other coastal areas. In Makunduchi, in southern Unguja, the Mwaka Kogwa festival continues to combine ritual combat, singing, dancing, fire and communal celebration.
The story of the Shirazis is consequently not simply a story of migration from one Iranian city to Africa. It is a story of movement, settlement, marriage, commerce and cultural exchange across an ocean that connected rather than divided societies.

Insecurity displaces nearly 1,700 people in Sudan’s Blue Nile: UN migration agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:37:21 UTC
01:37:21 KST

Adel Abdelrheem and Rania Abushamala
06 September 2026•Update: 06 September 2026
Nearly 1,700 more people have been displaced from villages in southeastern Sudan’s Blue Nile state amid worsening insecurity, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Saturday.
In a statement, the UN agency said its field teams estimated that 1,690 people were displaced from the villages of Abigo, Balang and Gambarda in Al-Kurmuk locality on Sept. 5.
The affected families fled to Baw locality, also in Blue Nile state, the agency said.
“The situation remains tense and volatile,” the IOM said.
On Thursday, the IOM announced that around 3,000 people, comprising 500 families, had been displaced from three villages in Al-Kurmuk locality because of escalating insecurity on Aug. 31.
Blue Nile state has witnessed a military escalation in recent days following attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), on several areas.
On Friday, authorities in Al-Kurmuk said the Sudanese army had repelled an attack by the RSF and the SPLM-N on the Al-Baraka area.
In addition to Blue Nile and Darfur, clashes between the Sudanese army and the RSF have continued since Oct. 25 across the three states of the Kordofan region -- North, West and South Kordofan.
Sudan has been engulfed in a war between the army and the RSF since April 2023. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

US envoy Barrack condemns violence, torture in Syria's Suweida

2026-09-06

Breadcrumb
US envoy Barrack condemns violence in Syria's Suweida after militias torture, expel Hijri critic
US special envoy to Syria Tom Barrack has condemned renewed violence in Syria's Suweida province after armed groups detained, allegedly tortured and forcibly expelled a prominent local figure who had criticised Druze spiritual leader Hikmat al-Hijri.
Atef Huneidi, a notable from the village of al-Majdal in western Suweida, arrived in Damascus on Friday after being forced to leave the province following his detention by groups affiliated with Hijri's "National Guard" militia.
Huneidi had issued a statement criticising recent remarks by al-Hijri saying that Suweida was "an integral part of Israel".
The National Guard militia was established last year and brings together armed factions aligned with al-Hijri. After deadly sectarian violence broke out in Suweida last year, they have controlled most of the province and have called for it to be separated from Syria, while expressing sympathy for Israel.
National Guard-affiliated fighters raided Huneidi's home in al-Majdal and detained him, while several relatives and neighbours who attempted to prevent his arrest were beaten, according to sources who spoke to The New Arab.
Suweida's media directorate, which is affiliated to the Syrian government, said Huneidi was asked while in detention to issue a statement retracting his criticism of al-Hijri.
It said Huneidi refused despite being subjected to torture and was subsequently forced to leave the province for Damascus, where he was taken to a secure location.
Huneidi's family condemned the raid and his expulsion, describing it as "a dangerous and reprehensible precedent" that it could not accept "whether against Atef Huneidi or anyone else".
Suweida's Governor Mustafa al-Bakour, who was appointed by Syria's authorities, also condemned the incident on Saturday, saying the storming of Huneidi's home, his detention and his expulsion by what he called "groups outside the law" could not be treated as a normal occurrence.
The controversy prompted an intervention from Barrack on Saturday, who said Washington was "dismayed by the renewed escalation in Suweida".
Barrack said that "gangs" were filling a vacuum created by the absence of state governance in the province and called for Suweida to be reintegrated into Syria under a roadmap agreed by the United States, Jordan and Syria last year.
"Our team is in contact with Mr Huneidi and with others who have fallen victim to this campaign of violence within the community," Barrack said.
He called on all sides to exercise restraint and said the only route to restoring security and creating conditions for displaced people to return was through accountability for those responsible for crimes.
The US, Jordan and Syria agreed a roadmap for resolving the Suweida crisis in September 2025 following talks in Amman.
The plan affirmed Syria's territorial unity while providing for local administration and security arrangements in Suweida, humanitarian access, the release of abductees and return of displaced people, an investigation into violence in the province and an end to foreign interference alongside regional security arrangements.
The latest tensions have exposed deepening divisions within Suweida over al-Hijri's political direction and the province's future relationship with Damascus.
Huneidi had publicly rejected al-Hijri's recent statements concerning Israel and criticised what he viewed as attempts to speak on behalf of the entire Druze community and determine its political future.
Journalist Samer al-Miqdad told The New Arab that armed groups affiliated with al-Hijri had recently adopted an increasingly confrontational approach amid growing Israeli incursions in southern Syria.
"Al-Hijri constantly talks about the scenario of separation, which drives the groups affiliated with him to suppress his opponents inside the province and escalate against Syrian security checkpoints, in parallel with Israeli incursions," al-Miqdad said.
He said the treatment of Huneidi suggested an increasingly hardline approach towards voices opposed to al-Hijri.
"There are high levels of fear among civilians over the militia's dominance, and this is exacerbating the situation," al-Miqdad added.
The episode comes amid continued uncertainty over Suweida's political and security status following deadly violence in the province last year and continuing conflict between local armed factions and the Syrian government.
Barrack urged communities in Suweida to pursue dialogue and warned against another outbreak of violence, saying that alternatives to the agreed roadmap would lead "nowhere except back to sorrow".

"Today's morphology is yesterday's syntax"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:36:40 UTC
01:36:40 KST

"Today's morphology is yesterday's syntax"
« previous post |
Wikipedia's entry on Univerbation tells us that "The univerbating process is epitomized in Talmy Givón's aphorism that 'today's morphology is yesterday's syntax'." Google hands the quote off to Gemini, at least in "AI mode", and explains:
The maxim "today's morphology is yesterday's syntax," coined by linguist Thomas Givon, means that grammatical word endings and affixes (morphology) evolve over time from separate, independent words once used together in phrases and sentences (syntax).
I use this familiar quotation in discussing the traditional "levels of language" in an introductory course. and so I wondered about the context of its source. Eventually I tracked it down to Givón's paper in the 1971 Proceedings of the Chicago Linguistic Society, "Historical syntax and synchronic morphology: An archaeologist’s field trip." That volume is not available on line, but I managed to get a copy via inter-library loan, and scanned it to produce the link above.
The paper starts.like this, with two footnotes on the title:
And it ends with section 5.4, which consists entirely of the quotation I was looking for:
5.4. Moral.- To paraphrase an old master: "Today's morphology is yesterday's syntax".
Footnote 1 offers us an attribution that's probably a joke —
1This trip was inspired in part by an an analect variously ascribed to Confucius but most likely emanating from the greatest of all time trippers, Lao Tse, who is reported to have remarked, on the occasion of being nformed that Chinese was an isolating language: "Weep not, my children, for today's syntax is tomorrow's morphology".
Talmy re-issued that paper, with some modifications, as a chapter in his 2015 book The Diachrony of Grammar, with the following endnote:
This paper was originally published in the proceedings of the CLS #7 meeting (Givón 1971a). My aim at the time was rather modest–explaining Greenberg's (1966) typological correlations between clausal word-order (VO vs. OV) and bound morphology (prefixal vs. suffixal, respectively). At the time, I had read neither F. Bopp (1833) nor H. Paul (1880) nor A. Meillet (1921) nor Jespersen (1917), and thus set out rather innocently to re-invent grammaticalization from scratch. The paper argued the grand theme that synchrony is largely explained by diachrony. The other major explanatory parameters of grammar–communicative function, the neuro-cognitive processor and language evolution–were grafted onto my evolving perspective a few years later (Givón 1979; see chs 2,3,4, below). While the main thrust of the original paper seems sound, I have removed several examples that seem, in retrospect, either dead wrong or irrelevant. I also dispensed with some of the more embarrassing formal discussion of ordered transformational rules and overly abstract syntactic structures.
Footnote 1 is then introduced with the disclaimer "The original footnote, perhaps forgiven in view of the Zeitgeist, went as follows:".
Leaving ancient philosophers out of it, we should add that today's phonetics is tomorrow's phonology, and today's pragmatics is tomorrow's semantics.
And so on…

Restoration work continues at Sheikh Safi al-Din Ardabili shrine complex
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:36:16 UTC
01:36:16 KST

Restoration work continues at Sheikh Safi al-Din Ardabili shrine complex
TEHRAN – Conservation, restoration and infrastructure projects are underway at the UNESCO-registered Sheikh Safi al-Din Ardabili Khanegah and Shrine Ensemble in northwestern Iran, the head of the World Heritage site said.
Fardin Eyni said the projects are being carried out under the site's management and conservation plan, with the aim of preserving its authenticity, integrity and Outstanding Universal Value, while improving the structural stability of the complex, protecting historic elements and upgrading its technical and environmental infrastructure.
Among the major projects currently underway are the completion of decorative elements and tilework on the entrance of the Ali Qapu building, construction of arcades in the complex's commercial section, establishment of a secure and standard storage facility, and acquisition of two properties within the site's boundaries, Eyni said.
Other projects include the organization and restoration of the anthropology museum, structural reinforcement and stabilization of the complex's interior decorations, upgrading electronic equipment, and several research and study projects.
The official added that some projects have already been completed, including the installation of railings and protective barriers around the historic site, improvement of the facades along a passageway from the direction of Sheikh Safi Bathhouse, and completion of the tilework on the entrances of the complex's commercial shops.
According to Eyni, the projects will help safeguard the complex's historical, architectural and artistic values, increase the durability and stability of its physical elements, improve the quality of its cultural landscape and strengthen its conservation and visitor-service infrastructure. They are also intended to improve site management and create better conditions for tourists, researchers and heritage enthusiasts.
 
 The Sheikh Safi al-Din Ardabili complex dates back about seven centuries. According to the Ardabil provincial Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts Department, the site was originally part of a large garden, where Sheikh Safi al-Din Ardabili taught and guided his followers and pupils. During his lifetime, the site functioned as a khanegah, or Sufi lodge.
Following Sheikh Safi's death in 735 AH (1334-35), his son, Sadr al-Din Musa, built the tomb tower known as Allah Allah at the site of his burial. During the Safavid period, additional buildings were added to the original complex, which subsequently became a dynastic burial complex for members of the Safavid family, including women, children and grandchildren, as well as Shah Ismail I and several prominent figures.
The ensemble contains architectural and artistic elements dating from the 14th to the 17th century, including tilework, mosaic tilework, wall paintings, carved and pierced wooden tomb chests, silver doors and the renowned Chini Khaneh, or Porcelain House.
The complex was inscribed on Iran's national heritage list in 1931 and was added to UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2010.
UNESCO describes the Sheikh Safi al-Din Khanegah and Shrine Ensemble as an architectural and artistic masterpiece and an outstanding representation of the principles of Sufism. The complex developed as a microcosmic city containing bazaars, public baths, squares, religious buildings, houses and offices, and became one of the most prominent Sufi shrines and pilgrimage centers in Iran.
The ensemble also reflects architectural traditions from the Ilkhanid and Timurid periods, combined with influences from Sufi philosophy, and served as a prototype for innovative architectural expressions and later khanegah designs.
The site remains an important tourist attraction in Ardabil, drawing visitors during the country's peak travel seasons. Its architectural decoration includes mosaic tilework, muqarnas, stucco, calligraphic inscriptions, wood carving, silverwork, painting, illumination and gilding.
Ardabil, the capital of Ardabil province, is located in northwestern Iran and is a major destination for domestic and international tourists.

Lessons for the aid sector | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:35:47 UTC
01:35:47 KST

Jeremiah A Carew argues that USAID fell because of poor storytelling rather than poor work (How misconceptions and woeful PR allowed Musk to shred USAID so easily, 1 September). Having spent decades in a recipient nation working at the final point of delivery, I see a different lesson. The primary problem was not the story USAID told, but the architecture behind it.
Aid money passes through a heavy supply chain: from prime contractors down through international and local NGOs, with administrative costs absorbed at every layer. Meanwhile, project success is too often measured by easy outputs, such as workshop attendance, rather than long-term systemic impact. There is also a quiet truth: aid workers, including local consultants like myself, often benefit when projects extend, creating incentives to prolong processes rather than complete them.
Comparing USAID to Nasa is equally unhelpful. Nasa delivers visible, binary moments of engineering triumph. Aid involves slow, complex and contested social change shaped by local politics. No amount of polished marketing can package that like a rocket launch.
USAID’s closure was abrupt, but no PR campaign will bring it back. The real lesson for the broader aid sector is to focus less on telling a better story and more on structural reform: shortening the supply chain and funding local actors directly, as some Nordic donors already do, measuring genuine outcomes, and rewarding work that truly finishes.
Monica Kappiantari
Development specialist, Jakarta, Indonesia

Therapists should never play God in people’s lives | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:34:34 UTC
01:34:34 KST

Nicholas Purcell’s article concerns me greatly, not because he recognises that some relationships are abusive and dangerous, but because he appears to place the decision about whether a relationship should “die” in the hands of the therapist (As a therapist, here’s why I sometimes advise couples to end their marriage, 31 August).
As a psychosexual and relationship therapist, I would never presume to know whether a client should leave their relationship. Our role is not to make that decision for them but to help clients understand what is happening within their relationship, explore patterns of behaviour and coping strategies, recognise coercion or abuse where it exists, consider the options available to them, and understand the possible consequences of those choices.
Where abuse is present, couples therapy may be entirely inappropriate. We may need to talk explicitly about risk, a safety plan, involve specialist services and support a client through separation if that is what they decide. But the decision remains theirs, not the therapist’s.
That distinction matters because of the considerable power the client invests in therapists, who often come to us at their most vulnerable. If we begin to regard ourselves as knowing which marriages should live and which should die, we risk replacing our clients’ judgment with our own.
Indeed, in relationships where someone’s sense of self has been diminished through coercion or control, one of therapy’s important functions can be to help restore agency. It would be a troubling tragedy if, in attempting to free a client from someone else’s certainty about what is best for them, the therapist substituted their own.
Karin Blak
Psychosexual and relationship therapist; author of The Essential Companion to Talking Therapy

Ukraine Receives First RCH 155 Self-Propelled Howitzer — German Aid to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:34:07 UTC
01:34:07 KST

Ukraine’s Defense Forces have received the first RCH 155 wheeled self-propelled artillery system.
The German Aid to Ukraine reported this.
Under a contract signed with the German manufacturer, Ukraine is to receive 54 of these artillery systems.
Information about the delivery emerged after Nicholas Drummond, an adviser to the German division of KNDS, reported on his X account in July 2026 that the new artillery system had already undergone combat testing.
Despite the signing of the first contract for 18 systems in 2022, the company was unable to manufacture them on time. In addition, Ukraine and Germany signed two more contracts in 2024 for the delivery of 18+18 RCH 155 artillery systems.
In January 2025, KNDS and then-German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius handed over the first of the 54 RCH 155 wheeled self-propelled howitzers to Ukraine’s ambassador in Kassel. At the time, it was reported that the system would be used to train Ukrainian crews.
In June 2025, it became known that deliveries of the first RCH 155 artillery systems had originally been planned for April but were again postponed indefinitely due to delays in preparations.
Later, in August 2025, the RCH 155 self-propelled artillery systems intended for Ukraine were being modified based on recommendations from Ukrainian servicemen.
Technical issues are still arising as the system’s initial shortcomings are addressed, with specialists resolving them in close cooperation with the Ukrainian side.
In March 2026, a German Federal Ministry of Defence report following Boris Pistorius’ visit to the artillery school in Idar-Oberstein revealed that Germany had completed training for more than 600 Ukrainian service members, who had learned to operate the modern RCH 155 wheeled self-propelled artillery systems.
Apart from Ukraine, firm contracts for the delivery of these systems have so far been signed with the United Kingdom and Qatar. Switzerland has also ordered the artillery module for installation on its own Piranha 10×10 platform.
The United Kingdom has ordered 72 artillery systems, with deliveries scheduled to begin only in 2028 with a test vehicle to be used for crew training.
Switzerland, meanwhile, has ordered 32 artillery systems.
The RCH 155 was developed on the chassis of the GTK Boxer 8×8 wheeled armored personnel carrier. The system features an automated AGM artillery turret module with the gun system of the German PzH 2000 self-propelled howitzer.
The AGM module is unmanned, so the RCH 155 crew consists of only two people. The AGM module carries 30 rounds.
The vehicle has a combat weight of 39 tons, while the AGM module weighs 12.5 tons.
The vehicle is powered by an 815-hp MTU diesel engine. The manufacturer states that its firing range is 40 kilometers, extending to 52 kilometers with V-LAP projectiles. The self-propelled howitzer can also use long-range VULCANO and EXCALIBUR projectiles.
More information in the article “RCH 155 — The Self-Propelled Howitzer That Fires While Moving.”

Transcript: Energy Secretary Chris Wright on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Sept. 6, 2026
The following is the transcript of the interview with Energy Secretary Chris Wright that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sept. 6, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We begin today with the U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright, who joins us from Denver. Mr. Secretary, it is Labor Day, and Secretary Bessent had predicted we'd see three-dollar gas by September 20th, depending on the Iran talks. Do you think we're going to be back at three bucks in the next two weeks?
SECRETARY OF ENERGY CHRIS WRIGHT: Well, we've passed peak demand time with Labor Day tomorrow, the end of the summer driving season, and the Trump administration a couple weeks ago rolled out a change in regulations that'll allow American refiners to produce more gasoline and diesel with their existing equipment. So, seeing demand likely go down in the next few weeks and supply going up, I think prices headed downward is- is not an unreasonable expectation.
MARGARET BRENNAN: What about the diesel fuel that trucks and trains rely so heavily on? We saw that record high price of $5.89 a gallon this week. Is for example, an export ban off the table?
SEC. WRIGHT: You want to keep as much energy flowing as possible. The diesel situation has been challenging because Russian refineries have suffered significant damage. Russia used to be a meaningful exporter of diesel. Today, today they don't export any diesel, and in fact, they've become a meaningful importer of gasoline. So its global refining capacity is why gasoline and diesel prices are high, even more than oil prices. And this is- for 17 years, Democrat policies have been attack hydrocarbons, get as many refineries and coal plants closed. You could summarize their energy and climate policies in two words, expensive energy.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, you could also say Russia shouldn't have invaded Ukraine, and then they'd still be able to export. But to the point of what you're going to do about it, are you looking at an export ban?
SEC. WRIGHT: We consider all options of how you can move prices that are favorable for American consumers, but right now we're leaning in on maximum production, energy addition. Again, in gasoline, in diesel, in the electricity sector, the way to solve a supply shortage is to grow supply.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, I want to ask you about Iran. You were on another network this morning, and you said the U.S. may not reach a nuclear deal with this current Iranian government and may have to wait for a new regime. If that is the current assessment, should the American people prepare themselves that the new normal will be these, for example, strikes like we saw just two days ago on Iranian oil tankers. Are you shutting down diplomatic outreach?
SEC. WRIGHT: No, we are always open for a deal. That's President Trump's goal is always to have a negotiated settlement and not use a military solution unless absolutely necessary, but the biggest role of our military in the region right now is to stop the export of any Iranian crude or crude-related products, natural gas, whatever. We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime, their current strategy is- is slowly failing for them. Our exports of oil through the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest they've been since the conflict started, but they're still causing trouble. But what we can do is add supply in Alaska, in the Gulf, in Venezuela, everywhere we can, and continue to grow the rate of exports from the Middle East as well.
MARGARET BRENNAN: but I mean to that point, Secretary Bessent said something like the Strait of Hormuz will be irrelevant in two years. It takes time to build pipelines to avoid the strait. How do you go from $90 a barrel now back to where we were pre-war, like 50 buck range? How quickly?
SEC. WRIGHT: You know that's that's as as soon as we can get barriers out of the way to grow production. Venezuelan production is well ahead of schedule. 50% growth in oil exports in the eight months we've been involved-that's pretty tremendous. Alaska has been sanctioned more than Iran by Democratic politicians. We've got to unleash Alaska, and that's happening. The Gulf of America has enormous oil and gas reserves there; those are growing as well. And of course, we're in constant dialogue with the Canadians, our neighbors to the north. They've got huge room to expand oil production capacity. So we're trying to center the world on bettering people's lives and economic growth in the long run. Every month, production is growing. Every month, production is growing.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You you mentioned--
SEC. WRIGHT: Refineries is a bigger challenge.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah, you mentioned Venezuela a few times there, sorry, go ahead.
SEC. WRIGHT: Go ahead, Margaret. Go ahead.
MARGARET BRENNAN: This is the problem with remote. We'd love having you in studio, so we don't step on each other. I apologize there. You mentioned Venezuela a few times. How is U.S. investment in Venezuelan oil production consistent with American energy dominance and independence?
SEC. WRIGHT: Well, first of all, it's the Western Hemisphere, it's Americas, and the great thing about this deal, the United States did no cost, zero cost to American taxpayers, but we're going- to we're going to get massive amounts of discounted oil price and ownership interest in some production there. But it's a win for Venezuela as well because it helps the investment climate to draw more and more foreign capital in, mostly American capital, but from elsewhere around the world, to grow their production, lift the incomes and job opportunities for Venezuelans, and lower energy prices for the United States-a classic win-win business deal.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But is it really sustainable if the deal is with an unelected and arguably illegitimate government that has not committed to holding elections, which the U.S. says are a priority. How can you instill confidence when it's a deal with Delcy Rodríguez?SEC. WRIGHT: There will be elections, of course. Those are coming, but this is a win-win deal.
MARGARET BRENNAN--When?--
SEC. WRIGHT: Any government that took power in Venezuela would say, "wow, we're going to draw more capital, grow our production, increase jobs and tax revenues in Venezuela, and tighten our relationship with the United States." That's a pretty big win. I don't think it's that dependent upon which government is in power on whether that deal is a win. So there's also a lot of refining capacity in Venezuela that we will see investment to drive that back up. Under President Biden, we had over a dozen refineries closed in the United States, and Gavin Newsom doubled down and strangled two more refineries in California in the last 12 months. Okay, that's the way to expensive energy in the long term, not just during a conflict.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But just to button that up, you said there will be elections. Do you have a timeline for that? Does this deal with the current government make it impossible, for example, for María Corina Machado, person who won- party won the last election, to actually return for democracy to return?
SEC. WRIGHT: Oh, there are dialogues going on right now between the former leaders of the parliament, the election that was the last sort of fair election in 2015. The opposition leaders that fled the country are back in the country meeting with the existing powers. You need to get secure voter rolls. You need to have rule of law, we need to release the political prisoners and get the conditions for free and fair elections. But those are coming.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, but no time frame on that. Okay, I'm told by the producer that we are going to have to leave it there. Secretary Wright, thank you, and we do hope to have you in person again so that we're not stepping on each other. Face the Nation will be back in a minute. Stay with us.

Sayyari: Iran’s deterrence capabilities have significantly increased after recent wars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:30:42 UTC
01:30:42 KST

Sayyari: Iran’s deterrence capabilities have significantly increased after recent wars
TEHRAN — Iran’s deterrence capabilities have significantly strengthened following the country’s recent military confrontations with the United States and Israel, Rear Admiral Habibollah Sayyari, deputy chief of Iran’s Army for Coordination Affairs, said.
Reacting to recent remarks by US President Donald Trump about maintaining pressure on Iran, Sayyari said Washington’s statements reflected its inability to achieve its objectives on the battlefield.
He said strengthening Iran’s deterrence remained a central responsibility of the Armed Forces and that the military had drawn on its experience in recent conflicts to identify weaknesses and reinforce its capabilities.
“Based on the valuable experiences gained from the 12-day war jointly imposed by the United States and Israel against Iran, as well as the subsequent 40-day conflict, including what we refer to as the Ramadan War and the Hormuz War, we have made extensive efforts to address potential weaknesses and strengthen our capabilities,” Sayyari said.
“These efforts have significantly increased the country’s deterrence power,” he added.
Sayyari was also dismissive of Trump’s remarks about a possible naval and economic blockade of Iran, describing them as unfounded and repetitive.
He said Trump had repeatedly made similar claims about Iran, including that the country did not possess nuclear weapons, that its navy and air force had been destroyed, and that its economy was in severe difficulty.
“We have become accustomed to these unfounded and baseless statements,” Sayyari said.
The senior commander said US officials were well aware of Iran’s military capabilities and argued that Washington would not be able to overcome 'the combat power, resistance and national resolve of the Iranian people.'
“As long as the people remain united and stand alongside the government officials, no one can defeat Iran,” he said.
Sayyari pointed to Iran’s eight-year war with Iraq, from 1980 to 1988, known in Iran as the Sacred Defense, as a historical example of 'the Iranian people’s resilience under sustained military pressure.'
He also praised 'the continued support of the Iranian people for the Islamic Republic,' describing national unity and public resilience as important elements of Iran’s deterrence.

Qalibaf warns of faster, heavier Iranian response to any new aggression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:28:23 UTC
01:28:23 KST

Qalibaf warns of faster, heavier Iranian response to any new aggression
TEHRAN — Iran will respond to any new aggression against its national interests and security with a faster, heavier, and more painful response, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said on Sunday, warning that the era of “proportionate responses” had come to an end.
Addressing an open session of parliament, Qalibaf said the United States should understand that “the rules of the game have changed” and that Iran’s recent strikes against hostile US positions were only the beginning.
“Any aggression against Iran’s national interests will be met with a faster, heavier and more painful response,” he said.
Qalibaf also stated that recent Iranian military strikes against US installations had confused American leaders, accusing Washington of resorting to 'deceptive tactics,' including the use of artificial intelligence to generate fabricated battlefield footage.
The speaker thanked the Iranian public for enduring two “imposed wars” involving the United States and Israel, referring to the 12-day and 40-day conflicts. He said maintaining domestic cohesion and strengthening external deterrence were essential to confronting external threats.
“Any speech or action that weakens these two fundamental pillars is contrary to rational prudence,” Qalibaf said, urging officials to avoid moves that could undermine national unity.
Turning to the economic front, Qalibaf said Iran must respond to intensified sanctions by strengthening domestic production, improving management of imports and supply chains, protecting energy infrastructure and making greater use of the country’s technical and professional expertise.
He also called on the government to improve the quality of public services and move more quickly to address economic difficulties, saying that while Iranians were prepared to endure hardship in confronting the “terrorist US government,” they would not accept mismanagement or inaction.
“The people expect us to manage the current situation properly and swiftly,” he said, describing this as their “indisputable and inalienable right.”

If the war continues through the winter, Ukraine is counting on U.S. support — Zelenskyy
Kyiv • UNN
If the war continues through the winter, Ukraine is counting on additional U.S. support. Zelenskyy also spoke about reliable assistance from Europe.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that if the war continues through the winter, Kyiv is counting on an additional support package from the United States. He said this during a press conference with U.S. President’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, UNN reports.
Details
Zelenskyy noted that Ukraine hopes to agree on reliable support both with the United States and with European partners. According to him, the Ukrainian team positively assesses the further opportunities for cooperation.
"If the war continues through the winter, we are counting on a winter support package from the United States," Zelenskyy said.
To remind you
In Kyiv, Zelenskyy met with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner afterward. Representatives of France, Britain, and Germany also arrived for the talks.
