Ukraine, Europe and US to hold meeting in near future – Zelenskyy
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Ukraine, the US and Europe have agreed to hold another meeting involving their representatives.
Source: Zelenskyy after the conclusion of negotiations in Kyiv, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy noted that national security advisers to the leaders of France, the UK and Germany joined the Ukraine-US negotiations in Kyiv during the third round.
Quote: "We have agreed that Ukraine, Europe and America will meet in the near future.
I do not know where the meeting will be – in Europe, in the United States of America, or perhaps again – as I understood it, Steve liked our railways – so perhaps again in Ukraine. Well, we are open in any case."
Background:
- US presidential special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv by train on 6 September and met with the Ukrainian president at Sofiiska Square. After a tour inside St Sophia Cathedral, they proceeded to negotiations.
- Zelenskyy said that three rounds of negotiations took place on 6 September in total, and all of them were "very substantive" and discussions covered possible parameters for ending the war and short-term support for Ukraine.
- In remarks to the press after the first round of negotiations, Kushner stated that Trump is firmly determined to bring an end to the war.
- On 5 September, the special envoys held negotiations in Moscow. Yuri Ushakov, an aide to the Russian ruler, said Vladimir Putin told the US envoys during Saturday's talks that he is confident his war aims will be achieved. The White House described the talks as "substantive" and announced that the next steps will be unveiled in the coming weeks.

Transcript: Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Sept. 6, 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:25:48 UTC
01:25:48 KST

Transcript: Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Sept. 6, 2026
The following is the transcript of the interview with Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, Democratic nominee for governor, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sept. 6, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We turn now to Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who is the Democratic nominee for governor in Michigan. Good morning to you.
SECRETARY OF STATE JOCELYN BENSON: Good morning. Thanks for having me.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Sure. I want to get to that issue of affordability. A new University of Michigan analysis revealed 40% of the state's population struggles to pay for basic necessities. Is that affordability issue something you can improve on as governor?
SEC. BENSON: Yes. Well, first, thanks for having me. And affordability is the centerpiece of our campaign. Our campaign is ultimately about driving down costs, growing our economy so that we can increase well-paying jobs in our state, protecting democracy and ending corruption. And everywhere I go in Michigan, I hear heartbreaking stories about choices that residents are having to make. Moms having to choose between whether to pay for food or childcare. Seniors on a fixed income trying to decide how they're going to still pay for medicine with these rising costs. The next governor of Michigan must address these, and I've done that as Secretary of State. I know how to fix broken systems. I've run our state agencies well. I've improved our democracy. I improved our Department of Motor Vehicles in a way that has saved people time, saved people money and made their lives easier. I've done that as Secretary of State. I'm ready to do that as Governor.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, one of the challenges in Michigan, of course, is the fact that a large portion of your state's exports, 36%, go north to Canada. On Tuesday, Canada's tariffs on steel and aluminum products, U.S.-made dairy and appliances will go into effect as part of this trade dispute. It's going to be between 15 to 50% on $20 billion worth of American-made goods. How much is that going to hit Michigan?
SEC. BENSON: It already has. I mean, since Trump took office, we've seen our- our expenses go up, and these tariffs, particularly with Canada, have increased prices in Michigan more than any other state. The average Michigan family is paying $5,600 more. That's a tax on our groceries. That's a tax on our small businesses, on gas. And- and what's frustrating to me in this race is that my opponent has been fully supportive of these tariffs. He's voted multiple times in support of them instead of in support of the people of Michigan. That is cowardice, and that is not leadership. And Michiganders need a governor--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
SEC. BENSON: --who will lower their costs and stand up to the president, as I've done as Secretary of State.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
SEC. BENSON: So I announced this week my intention as governor to ensure we're negotiating subnational agreements, partnering with other governors if necessary, to ensure we're developing ways to, in spite of the federal government's best efforts to drive up costs--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
SEC. BENSON: --with these taxes and tariffs, negotiate subnational agreements that will drive down costs and protect the people of Michigan. That's what we need the next governor to be able to do, and that's what I've done and will do as governor.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, your Republican competitor was on this program last weekend. He said he doesn't want more trade dispute and will talk to the White House about it. You just said subnational agreements, but practically speaking, how at the state level can you do anything to cancel out the costs coming from the federal government's dispute?
SEC. BENSON: Well, first, it's important to note my- my opponent could talk a good game, but the bottom line is he's either been silent or he's voted for these tariffs. And that means we call these tariffs in Michigan the John James tax. Because of his actions, because of his inability to stand up to the president as a congressman, we are hit with these taxes, we are hit with these increased prices, and he has to take responsibility for that instead of running away from it. But in addition to that, subnational agreements are things that governors in other states have already talked about and negotiated to drive down costs when the federal government won't do that. So, as governor, I can meet with officials in Canada and identify specific ways we can ensure trade between--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
SEC. BENSON: --Michigan and Canada gets around these tariffs, reduces costs. And in particular, when it comes to our auto industry, we need a governor who's going to stand up for our auto workers, who's going to stand up for this critical industry in our state, and ensure that our partners to the north are working with us collectively--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well--
SEC. BENSON: --to create jobs and drive down costs. That's what a subnational agreement can help guarantee.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Just quickly, what vote are you talking about? Because most of the tariffs have come from executive action.
SEC. BENSON: There was a vote in February in Congress in which our- my opponent voted in support of these tariffs. And also notably, he's been consistently asked on the trail if he would stand up and do anything--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
SEC. BENSON: --about these, and he's been silent on them, both as a congressman as a- and as a candidate for governor.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah. Let me ask you about your current job. Two million Michiganders vote by mail. Ballots go out on the 19th, and a federal judge again this past Friday blocked the postal service from enforcing President Trump's new mail ballot rules. He tried to put those in through executive order. Do you see any impact on voting in your state?
SEC. BENSON: Well, first we have to see this as the latest attempt by this Trump administration to try to create chaos and confusion about our democracy. We've been battling this for the better part of six years now since 2020. And what we will do here in Michigan is continue to ensure that states run elections. And that means in Michigan, where citizens have a right to vote by mail, we'll use every tool in our toolbox to ensure they know the truth about our elections. We'll follow the law. We'll protect the right to vote. And that's why, frankly, state officials who know how to do that and stand up to the president are so important right now. Because this isn't just about 2026, this is about 2028, when we will need a governor in Michigan who will know how to protect democracy and protect our voters' voices and votes. I've done that--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
SEC. BENSON: --as Secretary of State. And notably, when my opponent lost his last statewide race in 2020, he did not stand by the will of the voters. He joined the president in trying to overturn and undermine that election. That is- that makes him unfit to be governor in this moment, and it's why it's all the more important that in this race, Michigan is led by a governor who knows how to protect democracy--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
SEC. BENSON: --and protect citizens' right to vote from home.
MARGARET BRENNAN: President Trump has already sort of laid the groundwork, saying that Detroit is corrupt. He already said, "Don't discount fake mail-in ballots that will show up at the last minute in Michigan." I know that in the last election, Michigan ended up finding non-citizens who did vote. There were 22 cases under review. Your attorney general has charged six people with those election law violations. Given that this is something the president's already focused on, how are you verifying the names on your voter rolls?
SEC. BENSON: You know, we've done more in Michigan than any other state to ensure that our rolls, our voter rolls, are accurate, and that's why we see non-citizen voting so rare in this state. With 5.5 million people voting in 2024, the highest turnout election in our state's history, I'm really proud that our elections have been ranked among the most secure and accessible in the nation. And we, you know, the- the fact that we have identified a handful of individuals who are ineligible to vote, we were able to hold them accountable. That shows the system is working. And I'm proud of the work that our 1,500 local officials do every day to continue to ensure that every eligible vote and only eligible votes are counted in every election.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, Secretary Benson, we wish you well with that upcoming vote, but we also will watch your candidacy and some of these platform issues. Thank you for your time today. We'll be back in a moment.

The Guardian view on Burnham’s devolution plans: power must be accompanied by scrutiny | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:25:09 UTC
01:25:09 KST

Andy Burnham has criticised Britain’s “unaccountable state” that is at once too powerful and too distant from everyday life. He has made English devolution the central idea of his premiership, but his plan to give England’s mayors unprecedented power and money will have to confront a number of tricky realities, not least a landscape in which scrutiny of local government is vastly diminished.
As England’s devolution map has evolved, vital accountability mechanisms have withered. The abolition of the Audit Commission in 2015 deprived Whitehall of information about local government spending. The decision, taken by the then Tory prime minister David Cameron during his “bonfire of the quangos”, coincided with a period when cash-strapped councils were selling off assets and making risky investments. A succession of bankruptcies and scandals have since exemplified the dangers of governing in darkness, including the questions raised at Teesworks, the development led by Ben Houchen, a Tory mayor, where a “culture of excessive confidentiality” has prevailed, according to a damning 2024 government report.
There is wide recognition that greater accountability is needed. But Westminster has tended to create top-down mechanisms where accountability flows upwards and local scrutiny is infantilised. The “trailblazer” deals in 2023, for example, gave the mayors of Greater Manchester and the West Midlands greater flexibility over spending, but made them answerable to quarterly select committees of MPs. Under the current public accounting regime, the Treasury appoints an “accounting officer” to each government department, who answers to parliament for their department’s use of money, including that spent by local authorities. Located in Whitehall, these officers lack knowledge of the places such spending impacts.
Mr Burnham is right to try to wrest power back from the Treasury and recognise that those closest to a community best understand its needs. His government’s recent pledge to appoint the chief executives of mayoral strategic authorities as “local accounting officers” is welcome. But its plans to give England’s mayors a share of income tax generated in their area (a power that Lord Houchen has said he will use to fund rebates) will demand deeper forms of accountability. The English devolution bill in 2026 created a new Local Audit Office and introduced new powers for scrutiny committees. Both are improvements.
A fine place to end up would be the creation of “local public accounts committees”, an idea suggested in the Starmer government’s white paper in 2024. These could be modelled on Westminster’s public accounts committee, whose reports have exposed flagrant misuses of public money. The prime minister wants to take a “place-based” approach to public service delivery. Such local committees, if properly resourced and empowered, could be integral to scrutinising these initiatives.
Yet scrutiny isn’t solely the job of officials. The decline of local media poses another problem. Although new local reporting outlets have flourished in cities like Manchester and Birmingham, an estimated 4.4 million people in Britain live in areas without a dedicated news outlet. A robust solution, once mooted by the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, would be a tax on social media giants to fund local journalism. When mayor, Mr Burnham had a media capable of holding power to account. The same cannot be said for too many places in Britain.

SHENZHEN, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- New popular literature and art, featuring broad public participation in the era of the internet and AI, are helping China better express itself and contribute to a fairer global cultural order, according to a think tank report released on Sunday.
Titled "The Flourishing Development and Global Influence of New Popular Literature and Art," the report was issued by the National High-Level Think Tank of Xinhua News Agency at an international symposium held in Shenzhen, a tech hub in south China's Guangdong Province.
The report said new popular literature and art refer to "a brand-new, composite literary and artistic ecosystem that has emerged in the realm of literature and art, driven by the scientific and technological revolution encompassing the internet, big data and AI."
This ecosystem features broad public participation in creation, dissemination and sharing, and reflects the voice of the people and the themes of the times, according to the report.
"Rooted in everyday life, it responds to the aesthetic needs of the people...and is increasingly showcasing Chinese characteristics, style and manner in global cultural exchanges," the report noted.
At a time when the tides of globalization and digitalization are converging, the report emphasized that new popular literature and art are employing a multiplicity of narratives to shift China's image from one "defined by others" to one "expressed by itself."
They draw on Eastern wisdom to offer a value reference for the shared dilemmas that confront the human race, the report stated. Through openness and collaboration, they help break up the concentrated structure of the global cultural industry. By harnessing technology, they contribute to building a fairer global cultural order. ■

BRUSSELS — The European Union’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas on Sunday was forced to cancel the launch of a new high-level group made up of former political and military leaders following pressure from EU member countries, in what could prove another blow to the former Estonian prime minister.
Kallas is leading a fierce behind-the-scenes push against Franco-German plans to overhaul the European External Action Service, the bloc’s diplomatic corps. Those plans on paper aim to reinforce Kallas’ formal role, but her allies fear they could allow the European Commission to take greater control of foreign policy.
The high-level group — which Kallas described as bringing together “the brightest minds” to come up with ideas to fulfill EU defense gaps “in the shortest timeframe possible in the most effective way” — was seen by some diplomats as part of this resistance. “It’s her way to remain relevant,” said a senior EU diplomat, who like others quoted in this story was granted anonymity to speak freely.
Advertisement
Kallas has been in intense competition with the Commission over these plans, but an EU official said the reason for the cancellation was pressure from some capitals.
“Some member states felt this was not the right path to pursue at this moment,” said the official. “After some discussion with ministers, we have decided not to proceed with the initiative, we are looking at new ways of engaging with member states.”
The presentation had been meant to take place in Brussels at the Bibliothèque Solvay on Monday morning, with some 150 people from EU institutions, think tanks, academia and NATO expected to attend.
The names of group members were kept under wraps by Kallas’ office, but three diplomats said the group was expected to be chaired by former NATO Secretary General Anders Fogh Rasmussen and to include former defense ministers, like Estonia’s Jüri Luik, who also served as NATO ambassador, and France’s Florence Parly, a former minister of the armed forces.
Germany was expected to have a representative, as were other countries from outside the EU such as the U.K. and Ukraine, other diplomats said. Rasmussen was then expected to be tasked with writing a report on the outcome of the group’s work.
The EEAS did not confirm any of the names.
Advertisement
The initiative was meant to be part of efforts to relaunch the EEAS, which has a new leadership team including a new secretary general, former Dutch Defense Minister Kajsa Ollongren, and a new deputy secretary-general in charge of defense, the former French NATO Ambassador David Cvach.
From the outset, some diplomats have warned there is a high risk the new group could overlap with the work of the Commission and in particular with the activity of Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius, who already organizes regular meeting with think tanks and former leaders.
According to some of the diplomats, one of the key reasons behind the decision to cancel the initiative was the lack of proper groundwork and coordination in some capitals.
But a second EU official disputed this account, saying what triggered the cancellation was a problem in Italian local politics and in particular a dispute over potential members of the group.

Germany’s far right AfD heads for its biggest win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:23:22 UTC
01:23:22 KST

BERLIN — Germany’s far right claimed its biggest electoral success since World War II in Sunday’s regional vote in Saxony-Anhalt, with the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party advancing to the cusp of genuine power for the first time.
The state election is seen as a key test of whether the anti-immigrant, Russia-friendly AfD — now comfortably the most popular party in the EU’s biggest economy — can turn its electoral strength into a position in government.
The party itself is candid that it sees the eastern region of Saxony-Anhalt as a blueprint for its national ambitions, using the slogan: “It begins here.”
Advertisement
“We’ve made history. We’re taking back our country. It starts here in Saxony-Anhalt,” Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s candidate for regional premier, said at a victory event in the city of Magdeburg where a crowd chanted his name — “Uli, Uli” — in unison.
With almost all of the ballots counted, the AfD was set to win some 44 percent, a landslide on high turnout which would give it 39 seats in the regional parliament — just shy of the 42 seats needed to rule outright.
The political haggling over whether the AfD can wield power is now likely to center on whether it can come to an arrangement with the BSW, a populist-left party founded by a former member of East Germany’s communist party. The alternative is to persuade lawmakers from other parties to defect.
Sunday’s election is a catastrophe for the Christian Democratic Union of Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Its support crashed to less than 18 percent — a devastating implosion from the 37. 1 percent it scored in 2021.
The success of the AfD in this small state of just 2.1 million inhabitants has even sparked speculation about a potential Kanzlertausch, or chancellor swap.
Siegmund argued the result was a direct signal to Merz.
Advertisement
“Of course, it’s also a message directed at Berlin … Each day of having this man in the chancellery is one too many. That’s how people in Saxony-Anhalt see it, too.”
By 10 p.m., Merz was conspicuous by his absence, not having appeared to address the result, which is widely seen in Berlin as a turning point in the country’s post-war history.
Electoral math
The electoral arithmetic of whether the AfD can govern is still coming down to the wire.
The AfD’s national co-leader Alice Weidel immediately hailed a “historic result” and said the party had “a very clear mandate for governing.”
But Siegmund will now need to determine whether he can drum up support from members of other parties — even on an individual basis — to take him to the 42-seat majority.
Weidel said her party “always has an outstretched hand” for coalition partners. Siegmund also said he was willing to cooperate with other members of the legislature either as “a caucus or an individual representative.”
Advertisement
The most likely partner is the populist BSW party of Sahra Wagenknecht, which has denounced the “firewall” of mainstream parties against the far right as antidemocratic, and looks set to have four lawmakers. But the AfD has also made overtures to CDU members to peel off and join forces.
The BSW has proposed installing a “nonpartisan” premier to lead the state government with “shifting alliances” in parliament. But the AfD is unlikely to agree to such an arrangement; it appears more probable that the BSW could ultimately help the AfD’s lead candidate take power on a more informal basis.
Tino Chrupalla, the AfD’s other national co-leader, predicted the AfD would only get stronger if the other parties united against it to keep it out of power.
“Our position is clear. If the others think they know better and that this election result isn’t a sign of things to come, then they should go ahead [without the AfD], but the next election result will then be 50 plus,” he said.
Body blow to Merz
The outcome is a bruising blow for the CDU, which has governed the region over the past 24 years. CDU General Secretary Franziska Hoppermann called it a “very difficult result” and an “overall defeat” for the Christian Democrats.
Sven Schulze, the current prime minister of Saxony-Anhalt, also conceded the severity of the defeat, particularly since turnout appeared to be very high.
Advertisement
“The winner of the election, the AfD, is now the strongest force in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt, and we in the CDU will have to deal with this result,” he said.
That four in 10 voters in Saxony-Anhalt supported the AfD — even though the state’s intelligence agency has designated its local branch a right-wing extremist organization, and members of lead candidate Siegmund’s inner circle have reportedly belonged to an organization modeled on the Hitler Youth — underscores the widespread distrust in mainstream parties, the media and public institutions in eastern Germany, a region under communist rule during the Cold War.
The party achieved its best result since its founding in 2013 by vowing to deport migrants with a “remigration offensive,” to push for closer relations with Moscow — including by bringing back school exchange programs with Russia — to remove rainbow flags from schools, and to introduce a “baby welcome grant” of €2,000 for the first two children and €4,000 for each additional child. The party also pledged to reform school curricula to reduce material on Germany’s Nazi past in an effort to end what some of its politicians call a “guilt cult.”
However, the party’s success was apparently due less to its own pledges than to voters’ rejection of mainstream parties, particularly Merz and his conservative bloc. Only 9 percent of voters in Saxony-Anhalt approve of Merz’s performance, according to an ARD exit poll.
Saxony-Anhalt is the German state with the lowest average net income, and economic anxiety — over declining industry and rising energy costs — was a major factor motivating voters. Some 70 percent said they were “greatly worried” that rising prices would prevent them from paying their bills, according to an ARD survey, while 58 percent feared they would be unable to maintain their standard of living.
Surveys show that the AfD also leads in the eastern state of Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania, where voters go to the polls on Sept. 20. In Berlin, a traditionally left-wing capital where voters cast ballots the same day, the AfD is also performing strongly with around 18 percent support.
The Saxony-Anhalt result surpasses the AfD’s previous breakthrough in the eastern region of Thuringia, where it won 32.8 percent of the vote in 2024. After that election, the CDU was reduced to forming a minority coalition with left-wing parties.

Breadcrumb
Netanyahu orders removal of illegal West Bank settler outposts
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered unauthorised settler outposts in the occupied West Bank to be dismantled, two people familiar with the matter said on Sunday, amid pressure from the US to crack down on settler attacks on Palestinians.
The order applies to outposts established by settlers without official authorisation from the Israeli state, the sources told Reuters. Outposts typically consist of prefabricated caravans and house a small number of settlers. The state has from time to time demolished such structures and also formally recognised others, allowing them to access government funding.
It was not immediately clear when the operation would begin.
UN bodies and most governments deem all Israeli settlements illegal under international law and consider the West Bank to be occupied territory under military control.
US urges Israel to act against settler violence
Netanyahu had ordered the eviction of the unauthorised outposts in response to pressure from the United States, the country's closest ally, the sources said.
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee on Saturday denounced violent settlers as terrorists and called for them to face severe consequences following a meeting with several Palestinian Americans in a West Bank Palestinian town.
Israeli website Ynet earlier reported that the orders targeted around 100 outposts across the occupied territory.
The Israeli prime minister's office and the military, who would normally take part in clearing any outposts in the West Bank, did not immediately respond to a request to comment.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, asked at a conference in Jerusalem about the Ynet report, said Netanyahu has given "an instruction to evict places built in Areas A and B", referring to parts of the West Bank in which most Palestinians live.
Under the Oslo Accords, interim peace agreements reached in the 1990s between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), the West Bank was split into three zones: A, B and C.
Smotrich, a settler himself who has overseen settlement housing projects and formally recognised homes built illegally, said that while he disagreed with Netanyahu's decision, the government had made huge strides in advancing settlements in Area C.
Hundreds of outposts across the West Bank
There are 340 outposts in the West Bank along with 146 settlements formally recognised by the Israeli government, according to Peace Now, an Israeli organisation that is critical of settlement expansion and advocates for a two-state solution.
Last month, Israeli settlers besieged the homes of Palestinians in Qusra, including one owned by a Palestinian American, before the military was ordered to force them from the area.
The village's Palestinian residents have said they have continued to face harassment and intimidation by Israeli settlers, as well as restrictions by Israeli forces.
The Israeli government has condemned settler violence, though perpetrators are rarely arrested and even less frequently prosecuted, with rights groups detailing that settler attacks are state-sanctioned.
On Saturday, US Ambassador Huckabee said it was in Israel's own interest to take action against settlers carrying out what he described as "criminal behaviour and terrorism".
Huckabee is a well-known advocate for Israel's illegal settlement project in the occupied West Bank, as well as for Israel's annexation of the territory.
Settler attacks and settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank has garnered greater condemnation by Western states in recent years, with the UK preparing sanctions, including against trade with Israeli settlements.

This woman was the link between the Soviets, the CIA, and feminism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:20:06 UTC
01:20:06 KST

This woman was the link between the Soviets, the CIA, and feminism
It’s impossible to fully understand the legacy of American feminist icon Gloria Steinem without mentioning Russia.
Steinem – who fought her entire life to promote the radical concept that women should be able to choose whatever kind of life they want – passed away peacefully at her New York home last week at the age of 92. Judging by all the hair-pulling going on over her involvement with the CIA, you’d think that she had been tasked with planting exploding cigars on Fidel Castro.
But here’s what actually happened. Fresh out of Smith College in her early 20s, she took off to India to report for two years for a murky “fellowship,” capturing a newly independent country experimenting with Gandhian social reform, where women were actively collaborating to find their place.
When she returned home, she wanted to keep the party going and spread the same kind of enlightened ideals. She asked around about funding. Shockingly, corporations weren’t interested. But THE Corporation was.
The CIA was willing to fork over some cash, but it would involve setting up a think-tank: the Independent Research Service. She could load up a flight with liberal-minded young American students and professionals who were psyched about leftist ideals – but not too psyched – and take them over to the Soviet-organized World Youth Festivals in Helsinki and Vienna as an option to Communism. In exchange, she just had to produce some deliverables with her observations.
Basically, she was at the scrimmage line on the global playing field for Western-style liberalism during the Cold War against Communist ideology.
But what does any of this have to do with her lifelong fight for women’s rights and equality? Lots, actually.
Right around the same time as Steinem was being paid by the CIA to take Americans to the festivals, the agency published a report expressing its concern over the use of peace, brotherhood, and social progress to attract non-Communists from around the world to these festivals.
It cited a 1956 Moscow Radio broadcast: “The World Festival which is to be convened in Moscow” will “greet the festival of youth and peace with new labor achievements… Let us show our foreign contemporaries the results of the inspired creative labor of the Soviet people, the wealth of our socialist motherland, and everything of which the Soviet people are proud.”
One of those things of which Soviet society was very proud was the leading role of women in the workforce. In the wake of WWII’s losses, it was an inevitability that women were going to be stepping up as a matter of pragmatic reality.
The Committee of Soviet Women (KSZh) leveraged the 1957 Moscow festival to establish relationships with women from the developing world. The committee’s later reports indicate that women from Africa and South Asia were interested in the Soviet model, including such things as childcare provisions and female workforce participation, according to diplomatic historians.
Soviet archives say that visitors encountered Soviet institutions and it prompted them to think about “new possibilities for their societies.” The status of women was specifically one of the areas around which Soviet hosts and foreign visitors developed solidarity.
At the 1957 Moscow World Youth Festival, the Soviet Union made the social position of women part of its international cultural diplomacy. They were presented as educated, socially active participants in Soviet public life.
Surely just a coincidence that the CIA then paid Steinem to attend the 1959 and 1962 festivals, where she would have been exposed to this new model for women. And that she was doing so just as Washington was also increasingly focused on competing with this new Soviet economic model.
And surely it’s just another coincidence that President John F. Kennedy established the President’s Commission on the Status of Women in 1961, chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt – or that JFK himself had been impressed by women in important positions in the USSR, according to his own brother, the late Senator Ted Kennedy.
Steinem’s Playboy Bunny exposé showing the exploitation of women in Hugh Hefner’s “gentlemen’s” clubs came just a year after one of the festivals, in 1963. The same year that the USSR was also sending a woman to space, while America was sending women to get butt-slapped by some pervert for a paycheck.
Don’t think that the CIA noticed or really cared that much about what women were doing in the workforce at home and abroad? They were actually kind of obsessed with it. To the point of collecting for their files a 1965 congressional report pointing out how women were everywhere in the Soviet workforce, and that “the party and Government have succeeded in altering social custom and public attitudes toward the employment of women.”
In 1963, the CIA found that “by 1959 about 80 percent of Soviet physicians and almost 75 percent of teachers, economists, and planners were women,” in a report concerned with Soviet leadership potential.
In 1974, three years after Steinem had nationally launched the political women’s issue magazine, ‘Ms.’, and become synonymous with the women’s liberation movement, Washington’s Rand Corporation think tank was still churning out research on women’s roles in science and technology in the USSR vs. America.
The Soviets had already understood the value of putting women to work, educating them, and showcasing them as evidence of social progress to the rest of the world. Hardly surprising that it wasn’t long before Washington understood the competitive value of offering its own version.
Steinem entered the American establishment’s Cold War contest with Russia over competing models of modernity at precisely the moment when the status of women had become part of that ideological battlefield.
At the perfect time, she waltzed in through a door that was just begging to be opened by the American establishment. One that had already been flung wide open by Soviet men and women.

Far-right AfD wins key German state election but falls just short of majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:17:39 UTC
01:17:39 KST

The populist, far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has surged to a resounding victory in a crucial state election in Germany, but fell just short of winning a majority in its quest to form the country’s first far-right state government since the second world war.
The party of Germany’s unpopular chancellor Friedrich Merz, the Christian Democrats (CDU), slumped to a disastrous result in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
AfD’s candidate for governor, Ulrich Siegmund, said “we have written history” and the party had a clear mandate to govern. He told public broadcaster ARD that voters had sent a signal that “things cannot carry on like this”. “A very good campaigner for us in this election campaign was Friedrich Merz,” Siegmund said.
AfD was seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature to govern alone and overcome the so-called firewall of mainstream parties’ refusal to work with the party. AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classed as “rightwing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency.
Final results showed AfD falling three seats short, with 39 lawmakers in an 83-member parliament. Siegmund, 35, said it would not engage in “games” such as a minority government. But it was not evident how its divided opponents could assemble any stable government without it.
AfD won 43.8% of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin.
That was far ahead of Merz’s CDU , which polled 17.2% – losing about half its support – and won 15 seats. The centre-left Social Democrats polled 9.3%, the Greens 8.9% and the Left party 8.6%, winning eight seats apiece.
The BSW party, which has said it would not elect either Siegmund or incumbent Sven Schulze as governor but criticises the “firewall” against AfD, took 5.3% and five seats.
Participation in the election was at a record high of 76.5%.
Addressing jubilant supporters after exit polls had been published, Siegmund said his party was ready to reach out to all powers that strove for political change.
“We extend a hand to all democratic forces that wish to pursue better policies,” he said, adding that themes such as migration and domestic security were not up for debate.
The CDU described its result as “bitter” but said it would not back down from its refusal to rule together with AfD, which the far-right party has also ruled out.
Franziska Hoppermann, general secretary of the CDU, called it a “defeat overall” for the Christian Democrats. “And it is also a defeat for all those who have borne responsibility in the democracy in Saxony-Anhalt over the past 35 years,” she added, in reference to the difficult post-communist era.
She ruled out any discussion over Merz’s future, which analysts have suggested will increasingly become a topic of debate after his party’s defeat. In one recent poll, only 9% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt said they were satisfied with Merz’s politics.
Alice Weidel, AfD’s co-leader, said the result gave her party a “clear government mandate” and that it would “talk to all the parties” to work out a strategy as to how AfD could rule.
About 1.7 million people were eligible to vote in the east-central state.
Final polls had shown AfD to have about 40-41% of support, and the party appears to have almost doubled its 2021 result of 23.7%.
The number of undecided voters in advance of the vote was much lower than at previous elections, polling showed.
The small state has been governed since 2002 by Merz’s conservative CDU, together with two smaller parties.
The Saxony-Anhalt election had been seen as the biggest test yet for Merz, who is very unpopular, along with his government, a coalition with the SPD. Merz has thus far failed in his promises to reset Germany’s struggling economy or stop the rise of the AfD, which has been making regular and steady gains since it entered parliament in 2017 and is now the Bundestag’s leading opposition party. Irregular immigration has reduced since Merz has been in office, but not to an extent that has appeased the average voter.
In national polls, the CDU has also been overtaken by the AfD, which has its eyes on victory at the next federal elections in 2029 or 2033.
If the AfD manages to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt, Siegmund has promised to immediately start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the building of new windfarms.
He wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think Modern” to “Think German”, and to reintroduce the singing of the German national anthem in schools.
Siegmund also sought in the campaign to capitalise on a mood of “ostalgie”, or nostalgia for communist East Germany, and to tap into discontent among east Germans. He has made repeated references to a rise in foreigner-related crime, even as the crime rate has fallen dramatically. AfD is pro-Kremlin, urging a stop to support for Ukraine and pushing for Ukrainians to no longer receive refugee status.
Siegmund turned up to vote on Sunday morning with his wife, riding an East German-era moped in the party colours, which was also a prominent prop during the election campaign in rallies across the state. In a statement in front of the polling station, he voiced his optimism that the party would achieve “45%, and some”, and saying he wanted to “build bridges”.
Tensions before the election were high, with a considerable police presence and a number of demonstrations taking place across the state. Thousands of opponents of the AfD gathered in the state capital, Magdeburg, on Saturday, for a “festival of democracy”.
On Saturday evening, a message beamed on to the facade of Magdeburg Cathedral read: “We do not abandon what we love. True love of the homeland is not the AfD.”
The bishop of Magdeburg, Gerhard Feige, in an address to a gathering of churchgoers, warned against forces “that want to sow discord, stoke mistrust and fear”. He drew parallels with history, warning that a democracy has the potential to abolish itself. “Not everyone who votes or is elected democratically is a democrat,” he said.
The German Economic Institute has warned of the far-reaching consequences for the German economy, in Saxony-Anhalt and beyond. It said the AfD’s immigration policy would be “calamitous” for the state, which has an ageing, dwindling population and is heavily dependent on foreign workers.
Critics have also warned that an AfD-run state, due to the Kremlin-friendly stance of the party, could leak sensitive information to Russia. The AfD has dismissed such claims. It has said it would seek to reform the domestic intelligence service, calling it biased.

Iran touts military response as US maintains blockade, hits tankers

Iran touts military response as US maintains blockade, hits tankers
Tehran says the time for proportionate retaliation is over after a US strike on Iranian tankers inside the blockade line.
Tehran, Iran – The United States continues to rely on a mix of military force and economic sanctions against Iran, which has so far only prompted authorities in Tehran to consider more forceful responses.
The US Central Command (CENTCOM) released video on Saturday showing three Iranian crude oil tankers being hit – one off Kharg Island, Iran’s main oil export hub, another near Jask and a third in the Gulf of Oman. Two were “permanently disabled”, while a third sank after extensive bombing, CENTCOM said.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iran President Pezeshkian calls for unity as US ramps up economic pressure
- list 2 of 3US says it hit Iran oil tankers accused of helping ‘regional proxies’
- list 3 of 3US, Iran engaged in tanker war: Where is the months-long conflict headed?
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) later aired video of its own, showing explosives-laden projectiles crashing into multiple ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
“Aggressor US must know that it has no way but to leave the region and stop its malignance,” the IRGC said in a statement on Sunday. It added that a US-built sea drone was hit while trying to enter Iranian waters in the vital waterway, through which one fifth of the world’s oil and gas passes in peacetime.
The IRGC also said on Sunday it had fired several ballistic missiles towards a US aircraft carrier and another warship that are part of the network of vessels imposing the months-long naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports. Both vessels sustained some damage and fled, said the IRGC, although there was no immediate evidence of a successful hit and CENTCOM said the attacks were “evaded”.
The IRGC said it considered the acknowledgement by the US that missiles were launched towards its warships as “live evidence of the enemy’s strategic defeat and proof” of the force’s “offensive capabilities”.
Speaking during a private meeting of parliament members on Sunday, Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Tehran has inflicted “significant blows” to US bases across the region to the “frustration” of leaders in Washington.
“The Americans have surely understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end and our recent strikes against aggressor bases was only a start,” said Ghalibaf, who is also Iran’s chief negotiator with the US.
Any further attacks against Iranian interests will be met with “faster, heavier and more painful” strikes from Iran, he warned.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the US attacks on Iranian ships illegal and a “war crime” that runs counter to the United Nations Charter.
Who is the blockade hurting?
US and Iranian officials provide different readings of what is transpiring after months of disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the naval blockade imposed since mid-July.
The administration of President Donald Trump says more vessels have transited the strategically important waterway over recent weeks under US guidance, despite threats and attacks from Iran, with traffic allegedly nearing pre-war levels on some days. That account is countered by Iranian authorities, which say the strait remains closed.
The US military said about 90 commercial vessels have been redirected as part of the blockade, with several more disabled or boarded.
Crude oil exports from the Middle East during August were down 39 percent since the January and February baseline of 18.5 million barrels per day (mbpd), according to TankerTrackers. It said the current deficit is now 7.2mbpd, down from 12.4mbpd in May.
“Although most may recover in the coming months, Iran’s exports of 1.68mbpd (baseline number) may likely remain at zero for the foreseeable future; depending on any agreement,” the maritime intelligence company posted online on Sunday.
Iranian authorities have confirmed that they have been unable to get crude oil past the US warships imposing the blockade.
But they pointed out it does not equal a total halt to exports, with President Masoud Pezeshkian saying late last month that up to 90 million barrels of oil were exported during the brief period that the memorandum of understanding signed with the US in June was in effect.
Some of the oil is kept in floating storage outside the blockade, allowing Iran to gradually sell it at a discount to its main oil customer, China, despite US sanctions.
Washington is counting on those supplies running out in the foreseeable future.
“There’s probably only about 30 million barrels of Iranian crude oil left that China hasn’t bought,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Sunday. “So that will run out soon and there will be no problem with China buying because they have no product.”
Bessent again hailed the “one-two punch” of the blockade and sanctions as part of what the Trump administration has branded Operation Economic Outcast, aimed at reducing Iran’s trade with neighbours and further isolating 90 million Iranians.
Iranian authorities have not said how much longer they expect to be able to sell oil amid the US onslaught, nor have they elaborated on whether they are exploring potential alternative routes.
But experts have said that while overland and rail routes can move limited refined products, fuel oil and liquefied petroleum gas towards Afghanistan, Iraq, Central Asia and beyond, they cannot offer a viable and scalable replacement for the volume transported by very large crude carriers through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s Economy Ministry on Sunday established an “economic war headquarters” to counter the pressure, as the country deals with one of the world’s highest inflation rates, unemployment, energy imbalance and a host of other deep-seated issues.
But IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi suggested that the US was taking several times more economic damage from the war and blockade than Iran.
“If the US wants to deal one dollar in economic damage to Iran, it may deal several dollars’ worth of costs and damages to itself,” he said, pointing to lowered US strategic energy reserves and decreased aluminium exports from the region as examples.

German far-right AfD wins by a landslide in Saxony-Anhalt but falls short of majority

The far-right Alternative for Germany party surged to a major victory in a regional election on Sunday, but fell a little short of winning a majority in its quest to form the country’s first far-right state government since World War II.
The German far-right party AfD has taken a commanding lead in Sunday's Saxony-Anhalt vote, but could not secure enough seats to form a majority.
Final results showed AfD receiving 43.8% of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin. However, falling three seats short, with 39 lawmakers in an 83-member parliament.
Meanwhile, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the party of Germany’s unpopular leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, slumped to a disastrous result in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, with only 17.2% of the vote, and won 15 seats.
The centre-left Social Democrats got 9.3%, the Greens 8.9% and the Left Party 8.6%, all winning 8 seats apiece.
“We have written history,” said Ulrich Siegmund, the anti-migration, Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany’s candidate for governor, and added that the party now has a clear mandate to govern. The 35-year-old politician told public broadcaster ARD that voters had sent a signal that “things cannot carry on like this.” He said that “a very good campaigner for us in this election campaign was Friedrich Merz.”
Turnout was very high at 77.8%. AfD appeared to have won over many people who didn’t vote at all five years ago.
The result could reshape political landscape
The result could significantly reshape the political landscape in eastern Germany, with the AfD emerging as by far the strongest force in the new state parliament.
Siegmund said AfD would not engage in “games” such as a minority government, although it wasn’t evident how its divided opponents could assemble any stable government without it.
A first state government would mark the biggest achievement in the anti-immigration party’s 13-year history, arriving amid widespread public frustration with a national government struggling to revive the country’s sluggish economy.
Whether or not the AfD ultimately takes power, the result delivers a setback to Friedrich Merz, whose centre-right party has led Saxony-Anhalt for 24 years.
Unlike many of its European neighbours, modern Germany has yet to see a far-right or right-wing populist party head a national, state, or major city government.
The AfD is the largest opposition party in Germany’s federal parliament, drawing its strongest support from the less prosperous states of the former communist east, including Saxony-Anhalt.
Its regional branch in Saxony-Anhalt is among several designated as a proven right-wing extremist group by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, which cites members' denigration of migrants from Muslim-majority nations, among other concerns.
The party frequently promotes "remigration"—a controversial term referring to the mass deportation of immigrants—while its leader in a neighbouring state appealed two convictions for knowingly using a Nazi slogan.
The AfD strongly rejects all allegations of extremism, maintaining that such labels are politically motivated.
Germany’s states have extensive powers
Germany’s 16 states wield extensive powers, particularly in managing internal security and running the education system.
Ulrich Siegmund has outlined his top priorities as launching "a deportation offensive" and eliminating incentives for migrants to come to Germany and "exploit our social system." He also aims to initiate the lengthy process of withdrawing Saxony-Anhalt from the regional public broadcasting network, citing concerns over "disinformation."
In education, the regional branch of the AfD advocates for permitting homeschooling, which remains illegal across Germany. The party pledges to prohibit schools from officially displaying the rainbow flag and to mandate the inclusion of the national flag.
Furthermore, the party opposes taxpayer funds being "given away" to Ukraine and promises to push for lifting sanctions against Russia, though foreign policy decisions fall strictly outside state jurisdiction.
The influence of Saxony-Anhalt—one of the smaller states in a country of 83.5 million people—remains limited, controlling just four of the 69 total votes.

Wages in manufacturing grew faster than the average in Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:14:30 UTC
01:14:30 KST

By Orsolya Soosaar, Economist at Eesti Pank.
Data from Statistics Estonia show the average gross monthly wage rose in the second quarter by 5.5% to 2243 euros. Wage growth slowed in the private sector, while the collective agreements signed last year meant it was faster in the public sector in education, healthcare and public administration. The rise of 6.8% in the minimum wage from the start of April boosted the growth in wages that are below the average, while the growth in wages above the average slowed.
Recovering growth in the economy has supported growth in exports, and the improved performance of industry stands out in the wage data because of wages rising faster than the average in manufacturing and construction. Employers are again looking for additional staff, and that is supporting growth in wages and is reflected in a rise in the number of vacancies, especially in construction. The average wage in those sectors fell relative to the average in the economy during the recession, and it is now climbing back.
The labour force survey run by Statistics Estonia shows that unemployment was at 6.6% in the second quarter of 2026, and there were an estimated 10,000 fewer people out of work than a year earlier. The number of people in employment was also lower at the same time though, meaning that unemployment fell because labour force participation declined. Participants in the labour force are those who are in employment and those who are unemployed but are actively looking for work and are ready to start work within a short time.
Labour force participation may have fallen partly because the number of jobs on offer has been low for a long time and competition for vacancies has been tight. Equally, the change this year in the conditions for receiving unemployment benefits may have reduced the motivation for those who were previously not in the labour market to register as unemployed, and so may have affected their search for work. People who had not recently been in employment, such as those who had been studying full-time, at home with children, or caring for relatives, earlier had the right to receive unemployment benefits, but the basic level of unemployment insurance that has replaced those benefits requires them to have been in work previously.
Source: eestipank.ee

Exit polls: Germany’s far-right AfD holds clear lead in Saxony-Anhalt election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:12:36 UTC
01:12:36 KST

BERLIN — Germany’s far right claimed its biggest electoral success since World War II in Sunday’s regional vote in Saxony-Anhalt, with the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party advancing to the cusp of genuine power for the first time.
The state election is seen as a key test of whether the anti-immigrant, Russia-friendly AfD — now comfortably the most popular party in the EU’s biggest economy — can turn its electoral strength into a position in government.
The party itself is candid that it sees the eastern region of Saxony-Anhalt as a blueprint for its national ambitions, using the slogan: “It begins here.”
Advertisement
“We’ve made history. We’re taking back our country. It starts here in Saxony-Anhalt,” Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s candidate for regional premier, said at a victory event in the city of Magdeburg where a crowd chanted his name — “Uli, Uli” — in unison.
With almost all of the ballots counted, the AfD was set to win some 44 percent, a landslide on high turnout which would give it 39 seats in the regional parliament — just shy of the 42 seats needed to rule outright.
The political haggling over whether the AfD can wield power is now likely to center on whether it can come to an arrangement with the BSW, a populist-left party founded by a former member of East Germany’s communist party. The alternative is to persuade lawmakers from other parties to defect.
Sunday’s election is a catastrophe for the Christian Democratic Union of Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Its support crashed to less than 18 percent — a devastating implosion from the 37. 1 percent it scored in 2021.
The success of the AfD in this small state of just 2.1 million inhabitants has even sparked speculation about a potential Kanzlertausch, or chancellor swap.
Siegmund argued the result was a direct signal to Merz.
Advertisement
“Of course, it’s also a message directed at Berlin … Each day of having this man in the chancellery is one too many. That’s how people in Saxony-Anhalt see it, too.”
By 10 p.m., Merz was conspicuous by his absence, not having appeared to address the result, which is widely seen in Berlin as a turning point in the country’s post-war history.
Electoral math
The electoral arithmetic of whether the AfD can govern is still coming down to the wire.
The AfD’s national co-leader Alice Weidel immediately hailed a “historic result” and said the party had “a very clear mandate for governing.”
But Siegmund will now need to determine whether he can drum up support from members of other parties — even on an individual basis — to take him to the 42-seat majority.
Weidel said her party “always has an outstretched hand” for coalition partners. Siegmund also said he was willing to cooperate with other members of the legislature either as “a caucus or an individual representative.”
Advertisement
The most likely partner is the populist BSW party of Sahra Wagenknecht, which has denounced the “firewall” of mainstream parties against the far right as antidemocratic, and looks set to have four lawmakers. But the AfD has also made overtures to CDU members to peel off and join forces.
The BSW has proposed installing a “nonpartisan” premier to lead the state government with “shifting alliances” in parliament. But the AfD is unlikely to agree to such an arrangement; it appears more probable that the BSW could ultimately help the AfD’s lead candidate take power on a more informal basis.
Tino Chrupalla, the AfD’s other national co-leader, predicted the AfD would only get stronger if the other parties united against it to keep it out of power.
“Our position is clear. If the others think they know better and that this election result isn’t a sign of things to come, then they should go ahead [without the AfD], but the next election result will then be 50 plus,” he said.
Body blow to Merz
The outcome is a bruising blow for the CDU, which has governed the region over the past 24 years. CDU General Secretary Franziska Hoppermann called it a “very difficult result” and an “overall defeat” for the Christian Democrats.
Sven Schulze, the current prime minister of Saxony-Anhalt, also conceded the severity of the defeat, particularly since turnout appeared to be very high.
Advertisement
“The winner of the election, the AfD, is now the strongest force in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt, and we in the CDU will have to deal with this result,” he said.
That four in 10 voters in Saxony-Anhalt supported the AfD — even though the state’s intelligence agency has designated its local branch a right-wing extremist organization, and members of lead candidate Siegmund’s inner circle have reportedly belonged to an organization modeled on the Hitler Youth — underscores the widespread distrust in mainstream parties, the media and public institutions in eastern Germany, a region under communist rule during the Cold War.
The party achieved its best result since its founding in 2013 by vowing to deport migrants with a “remigration offensive,” to push for closer relations with Moscow — including by bringing back school exchange programs with Russia — to remove rainbow flags from schools, and to introduce a “baby welcome grant” of €2,000 for the first two children and €4,000 for each additional child. The party also pledged to reform school curricula to reduce material on Germany’s Nazi past in an effort to end what some of its politicians call a “guilt cult.”
However, the party’s success was apparently due less to its own pledges than to voters’ rejection of mainstream parties, particularly Merz and his conservative bloc. Only 9 percent of voters in Saxony-Anhalt approve of Merz’s performance, according to an ARD exit poll.
Saxony-Anhalt is the German state with the lowest average net income, and economic anxiety — over declining industry and rising energy costs — was a major factor motivating voters. Some 70 percent said they were “greatly worried” that rising prices would prevent them from paying their bills, according to an ARD survey, while 58 percent feared they would be unable to maintain their standard of living.
Surveys show that the AfD also leads in the eastern state of Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania, where voters go to the polls on Sept. 20. In Berlin, a traditionally left-wing capital where voters cast ballots the same day, the AfD is also performing strongly with around 18 percent support.
The Saxony-Anhalt result surpasses the AfD’s previous breakthrough in the eastern region of Thuringia, where it won 32.8 percent of the vote in 2024. After that election, the CDU was reduced to forming a minority coalition with left-wing parties.

Germany’s far-right AfD wins key Saxony-Anhalt election by landslide
BERLIN – Germany’s far-right AfD won a landslide victory in a key regional election on Sept 6 in the former communist east, a result seen as a stinging rebuke for Chancellor Friedrich Merz, but looked set to miss out on an absolute majority to govern alone.
“We have made history today,” said a jubilant Ulrich Siegmund, the 35-year-old lead candidate of the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany party in Saxony-Anhalt state, as the vote count continued.
The AfD won 44 per cent, more than doubling its support, and far ahead of the around 18 per cent for the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of Merz, according to projections by public broadcasters ARD and ZDF.
The CDU’s state premier Sven Schulze called the outcome “a severe blow”, but said he will stay on as caretaker leader during what could be a long and painful process towards a new state government.
All major parties have agreed on a “firewall” of non-cooperation with the AfD, whose state branch is categorised as “right-wing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency.
The AfD’s national co-leader Alice Weidel – who has long condemned the “firewall” concept as undemocratic – praised her party’s result as “sensational” and said the party had “received a very clear mandate to govern” in Saxony-Anhalt.
However, it remains far from clear who will eventually rule, as the AfD gained just less than half of parliamentary seats.
The CDU had hoped to cobble together a multi-party coalition to cling to power, but would still lack a majority even if it teamed up with the centre-left Social Democratic Party, Greens and the far-left Die Linke.
The AfD meanwhile may hope to win the support of the small pro-Russian BSW party – a leftist group that is tough on immigration, and which was expected to just scrape into Parliament with 5 per cent.
Weidel said that “naturally, a government scenario involving the BSW is very interesting for us”.
A first-ever AfD state government would be a shock for many in Germany, which has been at pains to atone for its dark history of World War II and the Holocaust and so far kept extremist parties at bay.
“I am personally appalled by this election result,” said Josef Schuster, president of the Central Council of Jews.
The spectre of a far-right state government drew thousands of the AfD’s opponents to a rally on Sept 5 in the regional capital Magdeburg, with banners saying “life is better without Nazis”.
“I’m very worried,” demonstrator Laura Saalfeld told AFP, fearing a change in atmosphere.
“Far-right sympathisers will show themselves more openly on the streets,” she said.
Radical agenda
Siegmund has ambitions to become state premier and lead a political revolution from Saxony-Anhalt that would propel the party to national victory in 2029.
On the campaign trail, Siegmund – a former entrepreneur with a sharp undercut hairstyle and a huge social media following – has been mobbed by adoring fans, many wearing T-shirts bearing his likeness.
The party has tapped a sense of nostalgia for communist East Germany as well as lingering resentment about an enduring wealth gap with the west decades after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall.
In line with the sometimes defiant sense of local “Ossie pride”, Siegmund has often ridden the iconic local Simson bike, including to the polling booth Sept 6 in his home town of Tangermuende.
While Siegmund has been dubbed the friendly face of the AfD, his campaign promises have been radical, including targeting irregular migrants with a “remigration and deportation offensive” from day one.
The party’s anti-“woke” agenda also includes vows to replace LGBTQ pride rainbow flags at public schools with the German standard, and to lessen the emphasis on the Third Reich in history teaching.
The German Economic Institute has warned that the AfD’s immigration policy would be “ruinous” for Saxony-Anhalt, which is highly reliant on foreign-born workers, especially in the health sector.
The AfD win heaps pressure on Merz, who has vowed to reboot a stagnant economy and restrict irregular immigration, but has seen his party beaten by the AfD in national surveys too.
“The result is even worse than what opinion polls had suggested beforehand,” wrote Holger Schmieding of Berenberg bank.
“This will most likely trigger a period of serious and potentially noisy soul-searching within the CDU.
“A major reason for the AfD success seems to be that the federal government under Merz has become deeply unpopular.” AFP

Germany's far-right AfD hails big victory in east, but falls short of majority
- Published
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) has won a decisive victory in Germany's eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of mainstream rivals. Preliminary results show it has fallen short of an outright majority, but the AfD says it has won a mandate to govern.
The far-right AfD secured 43.8% of the vote, with the conservative CDU on 17.2%, according to the state election commission's interim results.
Charismatic leader in the state, Ulrich Siegmund, said it was "sensational" and they wanted to start governing as soon as possible.
No far-right party has won control of a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing, local education and culture.
Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35.
He along with joint national leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla were overjoyed as exit polls revealed they were on track to score more than double the party's result in 2021.
- Katya Adler: Europe wrestles with impact of AfD's historic regional gains 
  - Published1 hour ago
Commentators and political opponents spoke of the outcome as a watershed and break with the past. Main TV channel Das Erste cancelled its legendary crime drama Tatort to focus on what the result meant.
"This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," Siegmund told supporters. "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal."
US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the German TV projection on his Truth Social platform, and then Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev took a screengrab of Trump's post and praised a "historic win for the pragmatic AfD".
Dmitriev had earlier praised the Russia-friendly AfD as "the party of hope and reason, co-operation truth and hope for Germany". Ahead of Germany's federal election last year, US Vice-President JD Vance endorsed the party, in a move criticised in Germany as political interference.
Polish centre-right Prime Minister Donald Tusk saw the result very differently, saying "in Poland only idiots and traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD".
The AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament instead of the 42 needed for an outright majority, although that is unconfirmed by the preliminary results.
Without enough seats to form a majority government, Ulrich Siegmund has so far refused to lead a minority government, even though the party's national leaders see it as a possibility.
"If necessary there'll just be new elections, then we'd just get 50 or 55%," said Siegmund, while saying he was prepared to work with individual MPs or a party.
The spotlight now falls on the left-wing populist BSW, which scraped into parliament but is set to win five seats and could help Siegmund come to power. The BSW is also tough on migration and backs importing Russian gas, and it has kept the door open to working with the AfD.
A crowd of supporters at the AfD election night party HQ erupted in cheers as the projections came up on the screen.
A short while later, people burst into singing Germany's national anthem.
"We have made history in this state," Siegmund said. His opposite number in the CDU, Sven Schulze, conceded victory as he watched the conservative vote slump by more than half on the previous election.
"This was an extremely tough and intensive election campaign," said Schulze, adding that his party would have to deal with the result.
Germany's centre-left SPD described the outcome as "truly dramatic" and national leader Lars Klingbeil, whose party is in government nationally with the CDU, described the outcome as a "signal to Berlin" and he was adamant that they would hear it.
The anti-migration AfD stands for Alternative für Deutschland. It has not only dominated the election campaign, it is emerging as the dominant force in the result and its supporters believe they are on the march.

Other parties refuse to go into coalition with the AfD, operating a Brandmauer or firewall aimed at keeping the far right out of government. In Saxony-Anhalt, the BSW has offered to co-operate with the AfD on some issues if it gets into the state parliament.
The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states.

Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally. Far-right AfD wins vote in Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state: Exit polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:07:08 UTC
01:07:08 KST

German far-right AfD wins Saxony-Anhalt election, falls short of majority
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has won the election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, according to preliminary results.
AfD won 43.8 percent of the vote, according to preliminary official results. That is more than twice the 17.2 percent for the incumbent centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU), led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
“We have achieved exactly what we wanted to achieve,” said AfD’s lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund. “We have made history in this state.”
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel also hailed the “historic” result, which has given the far-right party a clear mandate to govern, though it was not immediately clear whether it would be able to form a government.
Merz did not make a statement on Sunday evening on the election results. The German leader left the CDU’s head office, the Konrad-Adenauer-Haus, after 10pm local time (20:00 GMT).
“The reality is the AfD has got the lion’s share of the votes in this election, according to the exit polls. But the question is: is it enough to get them control of the state? Right now, we cannot say for sure,” reported Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane from Magdeburg in eastern Germany.
The latest projections gave the AfD 39 of the state parliament’s 83 seats, leaving it three short of the 42 needed for an absolute majority in the state parliament in Magdeburg.
Siegmund said he wanted to extend a hand to all parties willing to bring about a fundamental political transformation in the state. However, the AfD will not bend to other parties’ will, he stressed.
The AfD has never participated in a governing coalition in Germany’s 16 states, nor in its federal government, as all other mainstream parties refuse to work with it, a policy infamously known as the “firewall”.
Tino Chrupalla, the AfD’s national co-leader, claimed the result showed that voters had rejected the governing coalition’s policy.
The mainstream parties “were voted out, or rather, the voters delivered a clear verdict, and I can only encourage them to recognise that the ‘firewall’ has been definitively rejected by the voters today,” Chrupalla told broadcaster ARD.
Saxony-Anhalt’s AfD branch has been classified as a confirmed right-wing extremist organisation by the state’s domestic intelligence agency, a designation the party rejects as politically motivated.
Blow to Merz’s authority
Sunday’s result is another blow to the authority of Merz, whose popularity has declined as his coalition government struggles to revive growth in Europe’s largest economy.
His centre-right CDU came a distant second. Incumbent Saxony-Anhalt state premier Sven Schulze congratulated the AfD and acknowledged that the result had hit his party hard, saying, “We’re going to have to live with this result”.
Schulze later said he did not intend to cooperate with the AfD, although he initially declined to give a clear answer when asked whether the CDU’s firewall would remain in place.
The projected parliamentary arithmetic would make forming a government exceptionally difficult. Schulze could attempt to assemble an alliance involving several parties, though the CDU has traditionally ruled out formal cooperation with both the AfD and the Left (Die Linke) party.
AfD has tapped into a sense of nostalgia for communist East Germany, as well as lingering resentment about the enduring wealth gap with the west decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989.
In line with the sometimes defiant sense of local “Ossie pride”, Siegmund has often ridden an East German-produced Simson Schwalbe bike, including to the polling booth on Sunday in his hometown of Tangermunde, with his wife in tow.
While Siegmund has been dubbed the friendly face of the AfD, his campaign promises have been radical, including targeting undocumented migrants with a “remigration and deportation offensive” from day one.
AfD’s agenda
The party’s anti-“woke” agenda also includes promises to replace LGBTQ pride rainbow flags at public schools with the German standard and to change history teaching to lessen the emphasis on Hitler’s Third Reich.
To replace migrant workers, the AfD wants to lure back German expatriates, while offering “baby bonuses” for families to reverse the shrinking population in the small state of 2.1 million.
The German Economic Institute has warned that the AfD’s immigration policy would be “ruinous” for Saxony-Anhalt, which is highly reliant on foreign-born workers, especially in the health sector.
Others have voiced fears that an AfD-run state security apparatus could leak sensitive information to Russia, which Moscow could use to destabilise Germany.
The Kremlin “makes no secret of the fact that the AfD is the most important instrument for destabilising Germany for [Russian President Vladimir] Putin,” Thuringia state Interior Minister Georg Maier told the Handelsblatt daily newspaper.
