US envoys meet Putin: What’s behind latest diplomacy on Russia-Ukraine war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:00:16 UTC
00:00:16 KST

US envoys meet Putin: What’s behind latest diplomacy on Russia-Ukraine war?
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner meet Putin in Moscow and head to Kyiv as part of Trump’s new efforts to broker an agreement.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have held talks with President Vladmir Putin in Moscow, in what appears to be new efforts by the Trump administration to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that the envoys were bringing “a proposal to end the war” – Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II – and a senior Russian official said it was an “important peacemaking visit”.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Witkoff and Kushner will travel to ‘end’ Russia’s war in Ukraine: Trump
- list 2 of 4Trump sends envoys to Russia, Ukraine with new peace plan
- list 3 of 4At least 5 killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine as US envoys visit Moscow
- list 4 of 4US envoys arrive in Kyiv for Ukraine war talks after meeting Putin
Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and Witkoff, the US special envoy, are expected to arrive in Kyiv on Sunday, reviving diplomacy when both countries have escalated attacks. Both Moscow and Kyiv announced a three-day ceasefire to coincide with the latest trip.
So what’s behind the latest initiative by the US envoys and will it help end the war?
What was the outcome of the meeting?
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said the high-level talks were “highly useful” and lasted for more than three hours, according to Reuters.
Witkoff and Kushner “outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement,” said Ushakov, without providing any further detail, but added that the talks had been “substantive, very frank and constructive”.
Videos show Putin meeting the US envoys in the famous Red Drawing Room at the Kremlin on Saturday and telling his guests that the situation they are exploring “is, of course, not an easy one”.
The question remains whether Russia is willing to compromise, said Al Jazeera correspondent Yulia Shapovalova from Moscow. “Moscow demands that Ukraine not join NATO and hand over four Ukrainian regions to Russia, including territories not controlled by Russian forces.”
In September 2022, Putin proclaimed the annexation of four partially occupied Ukrainian regions – Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia. The move was not recognised by the international community, including the UN. Ukraine has refused to cede territory to Russia.
The Trump administration has ruled out a seat for Ukraine at NATO – which Russia has opposed. Trump had initially been critical of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, but has since mended ties after berating the Ukrainian leader in the Oval Office in February last year.
In August, Trump met Putin in Alaska, but the summit failed to reach a deal to end the war.
Why are the US envoys in Moscow?
Witkoff and Kushner have been involved in a number of diplomatic talks, including the Iran war, the so-called ceasefire agreement between Hamas and Israel and the Ukraine-Russia war.
Witkoff was appointed as the special envoy to the Middle East and later assigned the task of helping end the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Kushner also played a major role in the 2020 Abraham Accords that saw a number of Muslim countries recognise Israel. The initiative has been criticised for prioritising Arab-Israeli normalisation without addressing the question of a Palestinian state.
The details of the latest Ukraine peace plan are unclear, but Trump reportedly said last week, “we have an idea for peace”, without providing any additional details.
US officials from the National Security Council, State Department and the Treasury were also part of the delegation. The presence of Treasury official Gene Lang, who oversees US sanctions policy, including on Russia, indicates that the ongoing financial, economic and trade sanctions on Russia might have been part of the discussions in Moscow.
The Trump administration has ramped up sanctions on Russia aimed at forcing it to end the war. The Iran war has, however, diverted Trump’s and global attention away from the Ukraine-Russia conflict.
The Iran war has also strained transatlantic ties as Trump has accused his European and NATO allies of not helping him in efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran has used as leverage in talks. He has also been critical of NATO allies for not sharing the burden of collective defence, particularly against Russian threats.
NATO members from Europe have since stepped up their spending and offered to provide security guarantees to Ukraine after a deal is signed with Russia.
The latest push comes amid deadly Russian missile and drone attacks on Ukraine, while Kyiv has stepped up drone attacks on Russian energy sites.
What is Witkoff and Kushner’s next stop?
They have arrived in Kyiv for their first visit to meet President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
It was their second visit to the Kremlin this year and the eighth since the start of the war.
Experts say Ukrainians are sceptical of the US envoys.
“The view in Ukraine [is] that Witkoff, and to some extent Kushner, are most susceptible to accepting Russia’s narrative,” said Alexey Muraviev, a senior research fellow of defence and strategic studies at Edith Cowan University in Australia.
Witkoff told Putin that the US president had sent his best wishes and thanked him for the limited ceasefire during the delegation’s visit. The special US envoy was also recorded telling Putin that “we will have all these incredible stories and memories, and yours will be right at the top of it all”. The Russian president conveyed his gratitude to Trump and said Moscow would do its utmost to ensure the safety of the mediators.
The choice of words and tone won’t sit well with Ukrainians, explained Al Jazeera correspondent Audrey McAlpine from Ukraine’s capital, Kyiv.
While the visit there is seen as significant, the interaction between the envoys and Putin is an indication of “that familiarity between Witkoff and Putin”, she said.
Where the war stands now?
Russia and Ukraine announced a halt in attacks on each other’s capitals until Monday. The no-shoot policy is to ensure the envoys travel to the talks.
However, attacks have been reported in other cities in both the warring countries. At least seven people were killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine, while a Ukrainian drone attack killed one person in Russia’s Belgorod region.
In recent months, the two sides have intensified drone strikes, killing dozens. Ukraine’s production of low-cost, long-range drones has increased the number of attacks on industrial and logistical sites deep within Russia.
“There are growing concerns about the level of Ukraine’s resilience given the collateral damage that the Russian attacks have caused to Ukraine’s infrastructure ahead of the incoming winter,” Muraviev said, while pointing out that Putin is looking for a more long-term strategic deal.
Recent drone incidents reported in a number of European countries have raised suspicions that Russia is responsible, although no proof has been published. They included a failed drone explosion at Germany’s Leipzig airport and a fire at a drone factory in Poland.
Why is Trump pushing for a new deal now?
The US president has said that tens of thousands of people are dying on both sides every month due to the Ukraine-Russia war. During his re-election campaign in 2024, Trump said he would end the war within 24 hours, but that deadline has been revised several times.
He has hosted Putin in Alaska and held talks with Zelenskyy several times but has failed to find an agreement to end the war.
Recent steps by the Trump administration are interpreted as an attempt to revive relations between the US and Russia after months of stalled diplomacy.
CIA director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow last month to meet with Russian intelligence officials and the US invited Russia’s Finance Minister, Anton Siluanov, to a recent G20 meeting. His attendance was criticised by several European countries who refused a group photo with the Russian diplomat in protest.
Trump is expected to meet Putin next in November during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China, according to media reports. Russia’s Deputy Foreign Minister, Sergei Ryabkov, said on Sunday that Moscow has not ruled out a trilateral meeting between the Russian, Chinese and US presidents, the TASS state news agency reported.
Trump’s latest diplomatic push comes as the Iran war remains deadlocked and the Ukraine-Russia conflict has turned into a war of attrition. The war with Iran has become hugely unpopular domestically ahead of the crucial midterm elections in November. If Trump’s Republican party loses its majority in Congress, it would become extremely hard for the president to push his agenda.
A peace agreement in the longstanding war in the coming weeks could be a major boost for him ahead of election day.

Shutting down the office bore is one thing – but can you use the same tactics in everyday life? | Polly Hudson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
15:00:08 UTC
00:00:08 KST

The last thing you need in a meeting that could have been an email is attachments. Sadly, it’s sod’s law that there’s one oblivious person in every work gathering who raises extra, unnecessary queries using as many words as possible, and holds everybody up. Now, Forbes magazine has helpfully supplied three phrases business leaders can use to stop rambling questions from hijacking or lengthening proceedings, without embarrassing the hijacking lengthener.
But obviously it’s not only the office where we encounter those seemingly hellbent on derailing interactions, so can we steal Forbes’ gameplan for boring chat in real life?
Many conversations are DOA, too dull to rescue, but others – at a party, the school gates, a random bump-into – can be going fine until a third party ruins it by asking for or providing superfluous details that stymie the story. Sometimes you’re not married to that party, so you can’t give them a Paddington hard stare or pinch them. What does Forbes advise?
“Phrase one: route the tangent somewhere else. Say, ‘Let me pause you there. That’s worth discussing, but it’s more than we can cover here … Send me the rest, and I’ll follow up after the meeting.’” Clearly too formal for a casual natter, but there’s still gold in them thar hills. “I’d love to hear all about this when there’s time – text me later,” may be the most artful get-out-of-chat-free card ever played. Next?
“Phrase two: close a question you’ve already answered. Say, ‘We covered that earlier, so I’m going to keep us moving.’” Bit brutal, so IRL maybe reply, “But, anyway …” and then steer the convo in the direction you want to go (presumably towards the exit).
And finally: “Phrase three: give the floor to someone else. Say, ‘I want to make sure we hear from people who haven’t spoken yet. Let’s take the next question from someone new.’” It was good while it lasted, but unfortunately every technique has its limits. There’s no way of saying this, whether in the pub or at the conference room table, that won’t be loudly and clearly received as STFU.
Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

More than 140 killed amid Houthi offensive in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
14:58:52 UTC
23:58:52 KST

Breadcrumb
Toll from Yemen clashes passes 300 as civilians flee homes
The toll from days of fighting between government forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in southwest Yemen climbed past 300 on Sunday, as hundreds of families fled their homes to escape the violence.
Two military officials with the Saudi-backed government forces told AFP that 84 of their troops were killed between midday Saturday and early Sunday morning, mostly in missile attacks. Four Houthi military sources said 57 rebel fighters were killed in the same period.
Families fleeing fighting in Maqbanah and Jabal Habashi in Taiz governorate in Yemen's southwest took refuge at Al-Bareen camp for the internally displaced on Saturday.
Days-long clashes have erupted in Yemen over control of a gateway to the Red Sea in the deadliest fighting in the Arabian Peninsula country since a 2022 ceasefire between the two sides collapsed in July.
Beginning on Thursday, the Houthis launched an offensive aiming to cut off the government-held port city of Mokha, under fire for weeks, and advance towards areas bordering the Bab al-Mandab chokepoint at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
According to an AFP tally compiled using various military and medical sources from both sides of the conflict, more than 300 combatants and some civilians have been killed since the start of the Houthi assault on Thursday.
One military official with the internationally recognised government based in Aden said fighting had subsided in the early hours of Sunday morning.
The military official said government "forces were able to establish positions for themselves north of Hays after advancing in the area", referring to a frontline district less than 30 kilometres inland from the Red Sea coast.
But the official added the Houthis had advanced west of Taiz, south of Hays, in their push towards the Bab al-Mandab.
With Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz to commercial ships, the Bab al-Mandab chokepoint has gained importance as a transit route for oil from Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest exporter of crude.
In July, a fragile truce between the Houthis and Yemen's government fell apart after the rebels welcomed an Iranian plane to the capital Sanaa, setting off a spate of attacks.
The fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and government troops supported by US ally Saudi Arabia signals the emergence of a new front in the wider Middle East war, which broke out in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
The Houthis have also announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and have begun targeting its ships and territory.

At least 1,370 physicians left Israel between 2023 and 2025, following Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's judicial overhaul, nearly double the number who left during the same period a decade earlier, according to a new Tel Aviv University study published Sunday.
The study was conducted by Prof. Itai Ater of the Coller School of Management, who heads the Economists for Democracy forum; Prof. Nittai K. Bergman, head of the Berglas School of Economics; and Doron Zamir, a doctoral student at the Coller School of Management.
The group has already published several reports documenting increased emigration since 2023, particularly among academics, engineers and other highly skilled professionals.
"Economists have been warning since 2023 about the departure of highly skilled workers as a result of the government's policies," Ater told Haaretz.
"It began in the context of the judicial overhaul and has only worsened since Hamas' October 7 attack, the war and the disparities between those serving and those not serving [in the military]. We economists warned that citizens who can leave would do so. The documents we published seek to determine whether these warnings were justified."
The study uses the Central Bureau of Statistics' definition of an emigrant who has left Israel. Under this definition, physicians are considered to have emigrated if, during the first year after their departure, they spent more than 270 days outside Israel and, since their departure, have not spent more than three consecutive months in the country.
The researchers also limited the analysis to people who had lived in Israel for at least three years before their departure. This was intended to exclude immigrants who arrived in Israel following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Some have argued that many of these immigrants have since left the country, potentially distorting the emigration figures.
Because many physicians eventually return to Israel, for example, after completing their residency, the researchers also accounted for returnees. After adjusting for these groups, the study found that Israel lost an average of 255 physicians per year during the period examined, five times the annual average of the previous decade.
To provide a clearer picture of the trend, the researchers examined emigration rates among physicians aged 45 and older, those who have generally completed their residency and are expected to train the next generation of doctors in Israel.
The study found a worrying trend in this group as well: between 2023 and 2025, one in five physicians who emigrated was at least 45 years old, compared with one in seven during the previous decade.
An analysis by medical specialty shows that among ear, nose and throat, dermatology, and ophthalmology physicians, specialists who are already in high demand in Israel, 6.2 percent of those working in these fields left the country during the period examined (116 physicians). Among physicians in these specialties under the age of 60, the figure rises to 9.4 percent.
Another concerning figure involves surgeons: 188 surgeons left Israel during this period, representing 6 percent of all physicians working in the field, and 8.8 percent of those under the age of 60.
A breakdown by district shows that most of the physicians who left had lived in the Tel Aviv District, where 5.4 percent of physicians emigrated, compared with just 1.5 percent of physicians who lived in West Bank settlements.
The data on physicians under the age of 60 comes alongside a report published by the Finance Ministry last week, which found that in the coming years, approximately 24 percent of specialist physicians working in Israel's public hospitals will be approaching retirement age.
It also found that about 25 percent of physicians currently working in Israel have already passed retirement age and continue to work because of the shortage of doctors.
Atar concludes that what is particularly troubling is not the current situation, but the trend revealed by the study.
"The big question is what will happen after [the election in] October. If the trend doesn't change, the numbers we are seeing now will become much more painful," he said.

Ukrainian Drones Hammer Major Russian Oil Refinery, Knocking Out Key Gasoline Unit

Ukrainian Drones Hammer Major Russian Oil Refinery, Knocking Out Key Gasoline Unit
Ukrainian drones struck the Ryazan Oil Refinery in Russia overnight on September 6, hitting a key processing unit used in the production of high-octane gasoline components and triggering a fire at the facility.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Analysis of footage from the attack indicates that the drones targeted the refinery’s Izomalk-2-LIN-800 low-temperature isomerization unit. Videos published by the open-source monitoring channel Exilenova+ showed a fire burning inside the refinery complex following the strike.
The Izomalk-2 unit processes low-octane pentane-hexane fractions into high-octane components used to produce automotive gasoline, including fuel meeting Euro 5 environmental standards.
Ryazan regional governor Pavel Malkov confirmed that a fire had broken out at an industrial facility following the drone attack, without identifying the site.
“Debris caused a fire at one of the enterprises; according to preliminary information, there were no casualties. Emergency services are working at the scene,” Malkov said.
Other sections of the Ryazan refinery have also been hit repeatedly. Previous strikes targeted its ELOU-AVT-3, ELOU-AVT-6, and AVT-1 crude-processing units. Satellite imagery from August 3 indicated that two of the refinery’s four primary crude-processing units had been disabled.
The Ryazan Oil Refinery, owned by Russia’s Rosneft, is one of the country’s largest refining facilities, with an annual processing capacity of approximately 17 million tonnes of crude oil.
The facility produces gasoline, diesel, aviation fuel, and other petroleum products. Its infrastructure also includes hydrocracking, catalytic reforming, vacuum gas oil hydrotreatment, and other processing systems.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces struck Russian military infrastructure in the Bryansk region, hitting a radar station, an electronic warfare system, and a relay supporting a MESH communications network, according to Ukraine’s General Staff.

Delhi building collapse: 3 dead, 6 rescued; 'will spare no one', CM Rekha vows action - top developments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
14:46:10 UTC
23:46:10 KST

The eyewitness said the collapsed building was called ‘Hostel Daze’
NEW DELHI: Six people were killed and five were rescued after a five-storey boys' paying guest (PG) accommodation collapsed in southwest Delhi's Satya Niketan area on Sunday, officials said. Rescue operations were under way to search for any remaining people trapped under the rubble.The collapse involved a building known as 'Hostel Daze', which was being used as a boys' PG. An adjacent building also collapsed, according to eyewitnesses.JPN Apex Trauma Centre (AIIMS), on late Sunday, informed that it received 10 patients from the Satya Niketan building collapse. Four were brought dead, while one critically injured patient later succumbed. Three are admitted and undergoing treatment, one underwent limb surgery, and one with minor injuries was discharged after observation.
3 killed among 9 rescued as rescue operation continues
The AIIMS Trauma Centre said eight injured people were brought to hospitals following the incident. Seven were taken to the AIIMS Trauma Centre, while one was admitted to Safdarjung Hospital. Two of those brought to AIIMS were declared brought dead.The death toll later rose to three, with authorities confirming that six people had been rescued from the rubble.
Two National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) teams were deployed at the site, while two additional teams were kept on standby, NDRF Inspector General NS Bundela said. Rescue teams were working in coordination with the State Disaster Response Force, Delhi Fire Service and other agencies.
Eight fire tenders on spot
The Delhi Fire Service received information about the collapse at around 1.30 pm, following which eight fire tenders and multiple rescue teams were rushed to the spot. Police also cordoned off the area as rescuers searched through the debris.Eyewitnesses said several students were believed to be inside the building when it collapsed. A local resident claimed the PG had around 15 rooms, with two to three students staying in each room, and that around 35 to 40 students were residing on its upper floors.Residents said many students were inside their rooms because it was Sunday. Several locals joined the rescue operation, removing debris with their hands and whatever tools were available.
Basement construction work under scanner
Residents alleged that construction or repair work was under way in the basement and that water had accumulated there. A local resident who has lived in the area for around two decades claimed the building's foundation was weak.
Another resident said he had been inside the building shortly before the collapse and managed to get out minutes before the structure came down.The adjacent building was also reportedly leaning after the collapse, raising concerns about the safety of nearby structures.
Students from several states among residents
Residents said most students staying at the PG were from Kerala, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh and attended colleges including Motilal Nehru College, Atma Ram Sanatan Dharma College and Sri Venkateswara College.One resident said students were paying around Rs 12,000 per bed at the accommodation. Residents also raised concerns about the condition of buildings in the congested locality, where several residential properties have reportedly been converted into student PG accommodations.
CM Rekha Gupta visits collapse site
Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta visited the site and reviewed the ongoing search and rescue operation. Emergency teams continued clearing the rubble and searching for anyone who may still be trapped."No one will be spared," she says.
The Rekha Gupta-led Delhi government has ordered a magisterial inquiry into the incident and directed that an FIR be registered against the building owner, the chief minister’s office (CMO) said.The decision was taken following an on-site review and a preliminary assessment of the incident, the CMO said.“Following an on-site review and based on the preliminary assessment, the chief minister has ordered a Magisterial Inquiry of the incident and an FIR against the building owner,” the CMO said.
It added that those found responsible for the incident would be held fully accountable and face the strictest provisions of the law.
PM Modi expresses condolences
Prime Minister Narendra Modi expressed condolences over the deaths in the Satya Niketan building collapse and prayed for the speedy recovery of those injured. He said authorities were working at the site and assisting people affected by the incident.

Mediterranean Sea now at spa temperature, daily average 28.54°C on 13 August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
14:41:44 UTC
23:41:44 KST

On 13 August the Mediterranean averaged 28.54°C, its highest level since comparable records began in 1940, Aemet reports, capping a summer with the warmest July on record at sea and in mainland Spain.
Surface waters across the Mediterranean Sea reached an average temperature of 28.54ºC on 13 August, the highest recorded since at least 1940, Spain's State Meteorological Agency reported on Sunday.
Aemet itself noted on social media that throughout almost the whole of August the sea was breaking daily temperature records, one after another, with barely any respite.
The warning comes just weeks after Mercator Ocean International, which implements the Copernicus marine service, confirmed that July had already been the hottest month ever measured in the Mediterranean. The average that month was 27.07ºC, with a margin of uncertainty of ±0.27ºC, beating the previous maximum, set in July 2025 (26.68ºC), by four tenths of a degree.
Mercator Ocean's comparison series begins in 1993, meaning that both bodies, despite using different methods and reference periods, concur in describing a sea that has entered a thermal regime not seen before.
This pattern has been in place for months
Data from late June were already pointing that way. Aemet (source in Spanish) warned at the time that Mediterranean temperatures had reached levels more typical of the second half of August, when the sea is usually at its warmest.
At the start of the summer, temperatures rose to 2.6ºC above normal, to the point that the sea exceeded the average usually seen in mid-August while it was still June, an anomaly the agency itself described as exceptional.
On a planetary scale, the phenomenon is not confined to the Mediterranean. July 2026 was the month with the highest global ocean surface temperature in the entire record, with an average of 21ºC between 60º north and 60º south.
Across the Mediterranean basin, 27% of the sea experienced its warmest July since 1993 and around 70% of the surface ranked among the four hottest Julys ever measured, ruling out the idea that the record can be explained by just a few exceptional locations.
It is important to stress that the sea-temperature record cannot be singled out as the direct cause of the high temperatures recorded on land, as many different factors come into play in the atmosphere. It can, however, alter conditions along the coast: water releases heat more slowly than the land surface, so a Mediterranean this warm makes it harder for temperatures to fall at night, increases humidity and leads to hotter nights near the shore.
The build-up of energy in the sea also affects ecosystems. Prolonged marine heatwaves subject organisms adapted to specific thermal ranges to considerable stress and can alter species distribution, increase mortality and change the functioning of entire coastal communities.
With the figure recorded on 13 August, the Mediterranean has once again surpassed the record it had set only a few weeks earlier, in a summer which, on land and at sea, keeps breaking its own records.

US President Donald Trump has criticised the alleged exchange-rate gap between the Canadian and US dollars, calling the "imbalance" unacceptable.
"Canada's (currency) Dollar imbalance with the US is unacceptable," Trump wrote on his social media platform Truth Social on Sunday. "It has been that way for years - but no longer!"
Trump did not elaborate on what he meant by the remark.
The Canadian dollar has historically been weaker than its US counterpart for most of the past 15 years. The long-term average stands at about $1 to 1.24 Canadian dollars.
Since 2015, the currency has mostly traded between 1.20 Canadian dollars and 1.45 Canadian dollars against the greenback. It only reached or exceeded parity during part of the 2007-2012 commodity boom, when the Canadian dollar was stronger than the US dollar.
Dollar-for-dollar retaliation
The US dollar currently trades at around 1.38 Canadian dollars, meaning one Canadian dollar is worth roughly 72 US cents.
A weaker Canadian dollar makes Canadian goods cheaper for US buyers and US goods more expensive for Canadian consumers. Trump has repeatedly criticised the trade gap with Canada amid an ongoing trade war between the two neighbours.
Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered negotiators to return home from Washington.
The US subsequently moved to impose 50 percent tariffs on key Canadian goods. Carney has vowed dollar-for-dollar retaliation starting September 8.
It remains unclear whether Trump plans to take any action regarding the currency gap. The White House has not issued further details on the president's remarks.

Xinhua Headlines: High-speed rail link injects new vitality into revolutionary sites of China's Long March
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
22:40:32 CST
23:40:32 KST

NANCHANG, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- As the train pulled out of Ruijin Station and wound through rolling hills, 67-year-old Liu Ying leaned against the window, softly humming a melody she had known since childhood -- one that evokes the spirit of the epic Long March that shaped modern China more than 90 years ago.
Her grandfather, Liu Jinchang, was among the more than 86,000 soldiers of the Central Red Army who set out on the Long March in October 1934. He never returned.
On Sunday morning, the high-speed train G3998 departed from Ruijin City in east China's Jiangxi Province, bound for Yan'an City in northwest China's Shaanxi Province, linking the two revolutionary sacred sites by high-speed rail for the first time. The journey, which used to take up to 22 hours with multiple transfers, now takes just about 11 hours on the 1,857-km route.
Liu never met her grandfather, but she spent years tracing his footsteps. In 2014, while visiting a memorial park in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, she found his name etched among more than 1,000 fallen soldiers from her hometown of Yudu County, Jiangxi. Tears streamed down her face.
"My grandfather set out from Ruijin, but he never made it to Yan'an. Today, I'm following the route he took northward, finishing the journey he couldn't complete and seeing the Yan'an he never got to see," Liu said.
FROM FOOT TO TRACK
Ruijin and Yan'an are both landmarks in China's revolutionary history. Located in eastern and northwestern China respectively, they are separated by a straight-line distance of over 1,300 kilometers, yet bound together by the Long March. More than 90 years ago, the Central Red Army set out from Ruijin and marched 12,500 kilometers through countless trials and perils to reach northern Shaanxi.
The new rail line serves as a vital artery connecting eastern China with the city clusters in the northwest. It has forged an important corridor for economic exchange and created an efficient and convenient bridge for domestic and international travelers to visit the two major revolutionary sites of the Long March in person, and to gain a deeper understanding of China's journey from hardship to rejuvenation, said Wang Tao, a researcher at the China Executive Leadership Academy, Yan'an.
The train is an ultra-long cross-line high-speed service, pieced together across seven railway sections and traversing the provinces of Jiangxi, Hubei and Shaanxi. Previously, no direct train or flight connected the two cities, requiring passengers to transfer at least twice. The new service has cut travel time from up to 22 hours to about 11 hours, said Ye Ronggen, an official with China Railway Nanchang Group Co., Ltd.
At the end of 2025, the Xi'an-Yan'an high-speed railway opened, formally integrating Yan'an into the national high-speed rail network. On June 30, 2026, the Xi'an-Shiyan high-speed railway began operations, completing the full Wuhan-Xi'an high-speed corridor. With these high-speed links now seamlessly connected, the distance between northwestern and central China has been sharply reduced, and a direct high-speed rail passage between Ruijin and Yan'an has been opened.
On board the high-speed train on Sunday were dozens of descendants of Red Army veterans, like Liu Ying, each carrying their family's memories and stories as they headed toward the same destination.
"Grandpa walked the entire Long March in straw sandals. Today, I'm taking the high-speed rail to follow in his footsteps, to see Yan'an with my own eyes," said Wang Wanping, a descendant of Red Army veteran Wang Rushen, clutching his grandfather's old photograph and a commemorative medal. Inspired by his grandfather's teachings, Wang Wanping has devoted himself to education for many years and has taught at a remote primary school in Ruijin.
Wu Jiancai, deputy secretary of the Party branch of the Xi'an-Yan'an high-speed Railway Project Department, China Railway 21st Bureau Group Co., Ltd., had participated in the construction of both the conventional Xi'an-Yan'an railway and the high-speed line.
He said that while the routes' length and speed have changed, the drive to build roads through mountains and bridges across waters has remained unchanged. Once his current project wraps up, he said, he plans to take the high-speed train from Yan'an to Ruijin to see for himself the monumental changes the railway has brought to the old revolutionary base areas.
NEW ROUTE, NEW PROSPECTS
No sooner had Yu Qiumei, deputy director of Ruijin's bureau of culture, radio, television and tourism, learned of the new direct high-speed rail service to Yan'an than she picked up the phone to call her counterparts in the northern city.
On Sunday, Ruijin sent a delegation of red education institutions, travel agencies, hotel operators and scenic spot managers north for inspection, and on Monday, Yan'an would send its own delegation south to Ruijin via the high-speed train to sign a framework cooperation agreement.
"Revolutionary bases joining hands for development is seriously compromised if transport links are inadequate," Yu said. She recalled her 2022 trip to Yan'an, which involved a train to Nanchang, a flight to Xi'an, and then a connecting drive. The journey took an entire day. Now, she said, one can enjoy the scenery all the way and arrive in Yan'an just by nightfall.
The bureau also plans to hold promotional events in major cities along the route, including Wuhan and Xi'an, to boost red tourism in the city.
Song Xuelin, deputy director of Ruijin's development and reform commission, suggested using tourism as a starting point, with cooperation extended to industry, rural revitalization and talent exchange. The train is transforming a transport link into a flowing economic and cultural tourism belt, Song added.
Over the years, the Chinese government has continuously increased support for the old revolutionary base areas and steadily improved the transportation backbone network. Ruijin and Yan'an have both developed integrated, multi-modal transport networks covering aviation, high-speed rail and expressways, achieving a historic transformation in their transport landscapes.
Ruijin, once a landlocked place with no access to rivers or the sea, now has an operational airport, a functioning inland port, and high-speed trains passing through, allowing investors from the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area to arrive by rail.
Yan'an, situated on the Loess Plateau, has seen its transportation upgrade and tourism industry boosted by high-speed rail. In the first half of this year, Yan'an Railway Station handled 2.329 million passenger departures and 2.327 million arrivals, both up by over 30 percent year on year.
Red-themed study tours, Party-related exchanges, family visits and business travel between the old revolutionary bases in southern Jiangxi and northern Shaanxi have been growing increasingly close, with demand for point-to-point direct services rising steadily. The railway authority will further optimize capacity deployment to facilitate a faster flow of passengers, goods and information between the two cities, according to China Railway Nanchang Group Co., Ltd. ■

Major Chinese financial enterprises announce plans to boost core capital
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
22:40:24 CST
23:40:24 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Eight central financial enterprises, including the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC), on Sunday unveiled plans to replenish their capital, with the funds to be used to strengthen their core Tier 1 capital.
The eight enterprises are set to raise or receive a combined 360 billion yuan (about 53.11 billion U.S. dollars).
Experts said the capital replenishment is a forward-looking policy measure, which is expected to further strengthen the financial institutions' sound operations, enhance their ability to withstand risks and improve their capacity to serve the real economy.
Agricultural Bank of China (ABC) and the ICBC announced plans to raise up to a combined 260 billion yuan through A-share issuances to designated investors to replenish their core Tier-1 capital.
ABC said in a filing with the Shanghai Stock Exchange that it plans to issue A-shares to China's Ministry of Finance (MOF), China National Tobacco Corporation and its relevant subsidiaries, with total proceeds of up to 160 billion yuan.
After deducting issuance expenses, the bank will use all proceeds to replenish its core Tier-1 capital. The final fundraising amount will depend on the issuance plan approved by regulatory authorities, according to ABC.
ICBC said separately that it plans to raise up to 100 billion yuan via an A-share issuance to the MOF, China National Tobacco Corporation and related subsidiaries.
The bank said it will use the net proceeds entirely to replenish its core Tier-1 capital. The capital increase will be implemented after the bank completes the required internal and external approval procedures.
Core Tier 1 capital, the highest-quality form of bank capital used to absorb losses, serves as a key buffer against financial risks. If a bank raises more core Tier 1 capital, it generally has more room to expand lending while maintaining regulatory capital ratios.
The planned capital replenishment comes as China has been moving to strengthen the capital base of major state-owned financial institutions. The 2026 government work report proposed issuing 300 billion yuan in special treasury bonds to help major state-owned commercial banks replenish capital.
Also on Sunday, the Export-Import Bank of China said the MOF will inject 30 billion yuan into the bank to better support its policy-finance mandate and service major national strategies, while China Export & Credit Insurance Corporation said it will receive an injection of 10 billion yuan.
China's finance ministry will also provide fresh capital to four major Chinese insurers in moves aimed at strengthening their capital positions, solvency and risk resilience, according to statements released Sunday. ■

Geopolitical risks prompt Türkiye to revise economic targets
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
22:40:08 CST
23:40:08 KST

ANKARA, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Türkiye has raised its inflation forecasts and lowered growth and tourism revenue projections in a new economic roadmap, as heightened Middle East tensions add uncertainty and complicate efforts to curb still-high inflation.
The Medium-Term Program for 2027-2029, unveiled Sunday by Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz, puts Türkiye's year-end inflation forecast for 2026 at 28.4 percent, up significantly from the previous projection of 16 percent.
The program lowered the 2026 growth projection to 3.3 percent from 3.8 percent, while the tourism revenue forecast was reduced to 65 billion U.S. dollars from 68 billion dollars.
The revisions come against a backdrop of heightened tensions in the Middle East, which have increased uncertainty over energy prices, tourism flows, trade and broader global economic conditions.
"The global economy is entering a new period in which predictability has declined. Geopolitical risks and uncertainties have increased," Yilmaz said at a press conference in Ankara.
Yilmaz stressed that the war in the Middle East involving the United States, Iran and Israel since the end of February was estimated to have added 7 percentage points to inflation this year.
Yet the latest inflation figures indicate that Türkiye's disinflation process has continued despite the more challenging external environment. Annual consumer inflation eased to 31.51 percent in August from 31.75 percent in July, according to the latest official data.
Yilmaz highlighted the progress made since inflation peaked at 75.5 percent in May 2024, saying that it had entered a "marked downward trend" under the policies implemented since then.
For policymakers, the external environment creates an additional layer of uncertainty. Türkiye is heavily dependent on imported energy, meaning a prolonged escalation in the Middle East could feed into domestic costs through energy and transportation prices.
Tourism is another area exposed to regional tensions. The sector is an important source of foreign currency and employment, and weaker international travel to Türkiye could affect both service exports and the country's external balance.
Istanbul-based economist Mustafa Sonmez said the revised targets appeared to recognize that the final stage of disinflation could take longer than previously expected.
"The important point is that the downward trend in inflation has not been reversed despite the geopolitical shock," Sonmez told Xinhua. "But maintaining that trend will become more difficult if energy and transportation costs remain volatile," he said.
Analysts said the revised growth forecast also reflects the balance policymakers face between continuing to bring down inflation and maintaining economic activity.
Senol Babuscu, a finance expert and scholar at Ankara's Baskent University, said the new program should be viewed against the wider external environment.
"Geopolitical developments will be one of the key variables for Türkiye's economy in the coming months," Babuscu told Xinhua. "Energy prices, tourism and the exchange rate could all be affected, making the disinflation process more sensitive to external shocks," he warned. ■

Bosnian Serbs strengthen ties with Israel amid tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
14:37:40 UTC
23:37:40 KST

Bosnian Serbs strengthen ties with Israel amid tensions
Opening of Israeli commerce office in Banja Luka deepens ties between Republika Srpska and Israel, raising concerns about Bosnia’s wider political implications.
The Israeli Chamber of Commerce last week opened an office in Banja Luka, the seat of government of the Bosnia and Herzegovina entity of Republika Srpska, in a move officials said would “further strengthen” the two sides’ ties.
The opening comes when Israel faces growing international criticism due to its genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, including by the Sarajevo-based Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the other main political entity within Bosnia.
But in Republika Srpska, Israel has enjoyed strong support since the start of the war on Gaza in October 2023. Milorad Dodik, the entity’s former president and effective leader, has frequently expressed pro-Israeli views positioning Republika Srpska as a key ally of Israel in the Balkans.
Following the outbreak of the Gaza war, Dodik said that Republika Srpska fully supports Israel’s right to self-defence, while the Palace of the Republic in Banja Luka was illuminated with the colours of the Israeli flag.
Dodik, who last year was stripped of his post and banned from holding political office for six years. That was after being convicted for refusing to comply with the decisions by the international envoy overseeing the peace deal that ended Bosnia’s 1990s war. He has opposed initiatives for the international recognition of Palestine. In August 2025, he said “a state that does not exist in reality cannot be lawfully recognised”.
Speaking at the opening ceremony in Banja Luka on Thursday, Dodik highlighted the political and historical ties between the Serb and Jewish people and what he described as their similar “suffering”.
“We have shown that we can, under impossible conditions and in an environment that is historically speaking hostile, preserve our identity and our holy word, which is freedom,” said Dodik.
Israel’s Ambassador in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Galit Peleg, said the office in Banja Luka is aimed at connecting businesses and to promote “investment cooperation“ between the two sides, without offering details.
“At a time of protests and threats in Sarajevo, the Office of President Milorad Dodik offered us a beautiful building in Banja Luka,” Geleg said at the ceremony, referring to the pro-Palestine demonstrations in Bosnia during the war on Gaza.
Dodik said Republika Srpska will create a support programme for new technologies from Israel, without disclosing details. Similarly, Republika Srpska authorities have touted the possibility of a significant Israeli investment, without providing any information.
The office’s president is Amir Gross Kabiri, an Israeli businessman, industrialist and investor who in recent years has become one of the most prominent figures in Bosnia’s economic and political life. He became known to the country’s wider public after his company, a subsidiary of the M.T. Abraham Group, an international conglomerate and investment group, signed a contract in 2020 to lease the facilities of the collapsed Mostar aluminium giant Aluminij.
After signing the agreement on the office opening, Ana Trisic Babic, the acting director of the Office for International Cooperation of the Republic of Srpska, said the entity and Israel “have long nurtured friendly relations”, which she linked to “the historical experiences of the two peoples and the challenges they face”.
She added that the authorities of Republic of Srpska view Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s support for the opening of the office as a confirmation of those relations.
Rescued from bankruptcy?
Davor Gjenero, a Zagreb-based analyst with extensive knowledge of political affairs in the Western Balkans, said the office opening will give Republika Srpska’s authorities an opportunity to alleviate the entity’s significant financial problems, including rising debt.
He said Republika Srpska “is facing a kind of bankruptcy and any kind of economic activity with Israel can be also part” of its strategy to address the issue.
Gjenero also highlighted the “connection” between the policies of Dodik and Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, which he described as a potentially “dangerous” development amid rising tensions in Bosnia.
“This could also be a sign that centrifugal processes are taking place, which could pose a serious threat to the unity and sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina,” he said.
Gjenero argued that the cooperation between the Republika Srpska and Israel, along with the growing cooperation between Serbia and Israel – particularly in the military sector – could further increase tensions in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
He said “any activity” by the Republic of Srpska “without coordination with Sarajevo can be a serious problem for Bosnia and Herzegovina in its dialogue with the European Union”, as the country seeks EU membership.
“Also, any kind of making Dodik stronger is dangerous for relations between Sarajevo and Banja Luka and internal relations in Bosnia and Herzegovina.”

Lee Chang Dong's Possible Love Is a Delicate Drama of Love and Longing in Anxious Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Lee Chang-dong’s delicate yet sturdy drama Possible Love—premiering here at the Venice Film Festival, hitting theaters Oct. 23 and streaming on Netflix Nov. 6—is a movie about figuring out how to function in the world. If that description seems confoundingly vague, Lee’s movie is not. It shows us a world where people feel lost after losing their livelihood, where individuals strive to connect with others despite differences of class and temperament, where tenderness ultimately has more power than arrogance. It’s a movie with a gentle, generous spirit.
Lee opens the picture with a funeral, or, rather, a small family piling into their car to get to the funeral venue. Wife and mother Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon) wonders if she’s wearing the right dress, and the shoes she has chosen, a pair she hasn’t worn in a long time, are already pinching her feet. Her husband, Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), says little—so little that it’s clear he’s filled with dread over whatever awaits him at this upcoming, obviously unhappy social event. Their extremely quiet young son (Jung Seop) sits in the back seat, amusing himself by dangling an empty chip bag out the window like a windsock. “It’s flying,” he says, just before letting it go—he’s not the only one feeling the oppressiveness of that car ride.
It’s never expressly spelled out who this funeral is for, but we can intuit that it’s one of Ho-seok’s former work colleagues. It turns out that Ho-seok is one of many workers who not so long ago lost his job at a large corporation, SP, and he hasn’t yet recovered, either financially or emotionally. Mi-ok is doing the best she can—she holds down a menial factory job—but her husband’s depression and excessive drinking is getting to her. By chance, in the funeral home parking lot, she meets a handsome stranger, Sang-woo (Zo In-sung), who moves his very expensive car when Mi-ok believes her wedding ring, having slipped off her finger, has rolled beneath it. It turns out that Sang-woo’s wife, Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-Jong), is making a documentary about, as she puts it, “the personal lives of laborers.” Ye-ji is thrilled to have found Mi-ok and Ho-seok as subjects—she’s particularly interested in the melancholic Ho-seok, who, she believes, could be the dramatic key her project. But she and Mi-ok also genuinely like each other and strike up a friendship. Possible Love traces the tangled dynamics between these four characters, while also flirting with uncomfortable questions about the moral quandaries that can arise in any filmmaker-subject relationship.
Mostly, though, Possible Love traces the ways people come to care for one another, either platonically or romantically. Ye-ji and Mi-ok quickly come to think of themselves as sisters. Though Ye-ji has married well, she doesn’t come from a privileged family—her father ran a dry-cleaning establishment—and she has some sense of Mi-ok’s money worries and feelings of insecurity. At an early meeting, where Ye-ji outlines the aim of her proposed documentary to Mi-ok, she leaves the table momentarily, and Mi-ok snaps a picture of the elegant backpack she’s left behind. Then she uses a Google-image search to find out the brand. It’s made by Loro Piana, and quite obviously beyond Mi-ok’s means. That's just one example of how Lee explores simple human wants, desires, jealousies. We often can't help wanting things we can't afford, especially when they've already been stamped by the approval of someone we admire.
Lee has dedicated the film to the memory of Krzysztof Kieślowski’s Dekalog 10; he has said he was particularly struck by the commandment “Thou shalt not covet.” As humans, we often like nice things, but what we really need is a way to keep a roof over our head and food on the table. Possible Love explores the desperation that can strike when we can’t meet those basic needs. Sang-woo, cocksure and a little clueless, spends much of the movie on the phone making business deals. Meanwhile, Ho-seok suffers quietly, as if encased in a bubble of isolation. Mi-ok loves him, but she’s frustrated with him; no wonder she’s drawn, perhaps romantically, to sexy and stalwart Sang-woo. The movie’s most potent scene occurs late in the film when, with Ye-ji’s camera rolling, Ho-seok finally lets his guard down: Ye-ji may be getting the footage she set out for, but has she earned it honestly? Sul Kyung-gu is sensational here. If the character he’s playing is key to Ye-ji’s movie-within-a-movie, he’s also Possible Love’s anguished beating heart.
Lee’s 2018 noir mystery Burning was, what we used to call in the days before the pandemic, a surprise art-house hit. An art-house hit today may not mean the same thing as it did then, given how much the cinema-going audience has shrunk in less than 10 years. It’s hard to predict whether Possible Love will find a similarly enthusiastic audience. This is perhaps a more plainspoken movie than Burning; its moral questions are fairly easy to identify and parse. But at a time when more people worldwide are worrying about hanging onto gainful employment, even as a relatively small handful of people control the majority of the world’s wealth, the dramatic pull of Possible Love may be even greater than that of Burning. Sometimes it’s a relief when a movie captures undercurrents of anxiety that, in our daily lives, we find difficult to put into words. With Possible Love, it’s as if Lee has taken our unspoken feelings and handed them to his actors. With words and gestures, with tentative smiles and flashes of anger, they show us fears and worries we might be feeling ourselves, possibly galvanizing us to face them.

PayPal layoffs hit Israel as payment giant restructures global operations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
14:35:01 UTC
23:35:01 KST

American payment services giant PayPal is laying off 70 employees in Israel from its local workforce of 300 as part of a restructuring announced in May by the company’s new CEO Enrique Lores.
The cut will hit the Tel Aviv development center, which develops artificial intelligence systems to analyze transactions in real time, detect fraud, prevent money laundering, and monitor the company’s user experience and mobile applications.
Lores’ global efficiency plan involves structural changes and includes a major reduction in the company’s workforce, including at the management level, as it shifts its focus to AI integration.
It will see data scientists, software engineers, and product developers laid off.
Structural changes at PayPal
When the restructuring was announced, Bloomberg said that the plan would involve laying off 20% of the company’s workforce, over 4,500 employees, and saving around $1.5 billion over the next few years.
Other locations hit by the restructuring plan include Ireland (164 layoffs), India (200 layoffs), and PayPal’s headquarters in San Jose, United States (251 layoffs).
PayPal was quoted in local media as saying that the cuts were part of the previously announced changes and are “designed to simplify our global operations and put the company on a path to long-term growth.”
“Decisions of this kind are not easy, and we are fully aware of their impact on our employees. We are committed to standing by them and providing them with full support during this period of change,” PayPal was quoted as saying.
The company said in April that it would also split its business operations into three divisions: product payments, consumer financial services through Venmo, and cryptocurrency payments.
The Financial news website reported that the company will also be closing its 10-year-old venture team, which has backed over 80 companies across three funds totaling more than $850 million.
PayPal had bought several Israeli companies and recently acquired Cymbio, a Tel Aviv commerce tech company, for an estimated hundreds of millions of dollars.
PayPal Ventures first invested in Cymbio in 2022.

Conference of European Rabbis launch seven point manifesto to combat antisemitism in the EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
14:34:46 UTC
23:34:46 KST

The Conference of European Rabbis (CER) launched a seven-point manifesto in Brussels last week, demanding that European governments move beyond physical security measures and dismantle the ideological and financial infrastructure driving rising hostility against Jewish communities.
The manifesto, titled “A Call to End the Violent Hatred,” was presented at the Representation of the Free State of Bavaria to the EU before a gathering of politicians, policymakers, and journalists.
Opening the launch event, CER President Chief Rabbi Pinchas Goldschmidt warned against accepting the heavily fortified state of Jewish institutions as an enduring reality. “Almost every Jewish school and synagogue in Europe sits behind guards, steel barriers, and concrete blocks,” he said. “Jewish children are growing up believing this is normal. It is not.”
He added, “The test is not whether Jewish communities can survive behind concrete barriers but whether Jewish life can flourish openly, safely, and with dignity.”
Sharp escalation in violence across the continent
The manifesto highlights a sharp escalation in violence across the continent, pointing to incidents such as the torching of four Hatzola Northwest ambulances outside a synagogue in a London suburb, an explosive attack on a synagogue in Liège, a car torched in Antwerp’s Jewish quarter, a targeted Jewish school in Amsterdam, the fatal shooting of two worshippers in a Manchester synagogue on Yom Kippur 2025, and a stabbing spree in Golders Green.
The document also notes that hate marches have filled European capitals for three years, while European security services and courts have linked Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to proxy attacks and plots against Jewish citizens.
Detailing the strategy to counter these threats, the manifesto outlines seven core policy proposals.
The first proposal calls to train and certify religious leaders, demanding that faith leaders arriving from abroad meet minimum language proficiency requirements and possess a basic understanding of democratic rights and responsibilities.
It requires institutions to implement training from a curriculum covering religious freedom and Holocaust remembrance, alongside giving authorities the power to revoke visas, licenses, or permits from clerics who incite hatred or glorify terrorism.
The second focuses on exposing and blocking extremist funding to stop money that spreads hate. It calls for transparent registers of major foreign donations to religious institutions, thorough investigations into funding linked to extremist states or organizations, the removal of charitable status from bodies promoting antisemitism or radicalization, and the freezing of funding streams connected to hate.
The third aims to strengthen oversight of religious institutions, ensuring that places of worship and faith-based charities are subjected to standard external audits regulated by a recognized authority to prevent them from becoming centers of radicalization.
The proposal includes inspecting educational materials and staff when concerns arise, coordinating intelligence between law enforcement and regulatory bodies, and closing down institutions that repeatedly promote violence or hatred.
The fourth stipulates that every religious institution should appoint a trained community safeguarding officer responsible for monitoring hate incidents and warning signs, maintaining clear reporting procedures, liaising with police and civil society, and ensuring safeguarding is embedded within daily community life.
The fifth addresses the digital space by pointing to online platforms as incubators of radicalization. It urges communities to be educated about extremist content while demanding that the EU Digital Services Act (DSA) be expanded to ensure strict and swift regulation against incitement. It requires technology companies to promptly remove incitement and strengthens cooperation between governments and platforms.
Zero tolerance for hate on the streets
The sixth demands zero tolerance for hate on the streets, emphasizing that public demonstrations must not become vehicles for antisemitic intimidation. The framework calls for the prosecution of individuals inciting violence and promoting terrorist groups, holding event organizers accountable when incitement recurs, banning organizations that repeatedly glorify terrorism, and enforcing the law without fear or favor.
The seventh proposal calls for the creation of a European Register of Responsible Institutions to build trust between communities and wider society by establishing a public framework that recognizes congregations and organizations committing to these standards and promoting best practices across faith communities.
The manifesto concludes with a stark warning to policymakers, emphasizing that a continent unable to protect its Jewish citizens from violent hatred can no longer claim to uphold human dignity, the rule of law, democracy, or freedom.

Bennett unveils B’Yachad election slate with Lapid at No. 2 and five women ranked in the top 10
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
14:33:51 UTC
23:33:51 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel Elections
- Bennett unveils B'Yachad slate: “The best team for repairing Israel”
Bennett unveils B'Yachad slate: “The best team for repairing Israel”
Lapid is ranked second and five women enter the top 10 as the new political alliance finalizes its election lineup
B'Yachad party chairman and Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett unveiled his candidate list for the upcoming elections on Sunday, confirming a political alliance with Yesh Atid leader Yair Lapid just one day before the deadline for filing electoral slates with the Central Elections Committee.
Bennett will head the joint ticket, with Lapid taking the second position. Former Transportation Ministry director-general Keren Turner is ranked third, followed by Yesh Atid lawmaker Meirav Ben Ari and former Communications Ministry director-general Liran Avisar Ben-Hurin.
The slate brings together experienced parliamentarians, former senior public officials and figures with military and municipal backgrounds.
Retired Maj. Gen. Noam Tibon is placed sixth, while former Yesh Atid ministers and lawmakers Meirav Cohen, Ram Ben Barak, Naor Shiri, Vladimir Beliak and Yorai Lahav Hertzanu also appear among the top 20.
Announcing the list, Bennett described it as a team assembled to “repair the State of Israel.”
“After hard work and thorough selection processes, today we are presenting the best team for repairing the State of Israel,” Bennett said.
“The compass I set before my eyes two years ago, when I began working on the plan to repair Israel, is clearly reflected in our Knesset list: doers, men and women who know how to enter the Knesset and the government ministries, and repair.”
Bennett called the slate the strongest and most capable electoral team Israel has seen in decades.
“Personally, this is the best and most effective list to have run for the Knesset in the last generation,” he said. “This is a list that reflects the existential need for Israel’s future: people who work hard, fast and at the highest possible level.”
“Remember them well,” Bennett added, “because they are the ones who will lead the great change, very soon.”
- Naftali Bennett
- Yair Lapid
- Keren Turner
- Merav Ben Ari
- Liran Avishar Ben-Horin
- Noam Tibon
- Michal Hirsch Negrin
- Eitan Ginzburg
- Meirav Cohen
- Yonatan Shalev
- Brura Naim-Arman
- Ram Ben-Barak
- Amir Strugo
- Naor Shiri
- Nisan Ze’evi
- Vladimir Beliak
- Orly Harel
- Yorai Lahav-Hertzanu
- Shahar Varon
- Yasmin Sacks-Friedman
The unveiling follows weeks of upheaval inside Yesh Atid, where several prominent figures, including Mickey Levy and Meir Cohen, announced that they would not seek reelection. The departures came amid expectations that the merger with Bennett would leave Lapid with only five or six realistic positions for Yesh Atid representatives on the combined slate.
Lapid released a separate 15-member Yesh Atid candidate list on Saturday.
Lapid acknowledged the personal and political cost of reshaping his party ahead of the alliance.
“The process of building the list that we went through is unprecedented,” he said. “This is the saddest, but also the most inspiring moment I have experienced since entering politics.”
“I have no intention of pretending that everything is fine,” Lapid continued. “This process broke my heart more than once. I hated every moment, but I love these people more than ever. They are my friends; they are my family. There has never been, in the entire history of Israeli politics, a process like this.”
The final ranking offers the clearest picture yet of how Bennett and Lapid intend to divide influence within their new political partnership. It also signals their effort to present the alliance as an experienced, governing alternative—one built around administrative competence, security credentials and a promise of national renewal.
With the filing deadline approaching, attention will now turn to whether the Bennett-Lapid partnership can remain united through the campaign and convert its prominent roster into electoral momentum.

Russia&apos;s Ryazan oil refinery has completely halted operations following a strike by FP-1 drones.

Russia's Ryazan oil refinery has completely halted operations following a strike by FP-1 drones.
Kyiv • UNN
The Ryazan oil refinery completely halted operations following a strike by the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
The Ryazan oil refinery has completely ceased operations after being struck by long-range FP-1 UAVs operated by the Ukrainian Defense Forces. This was reported by Fire Point, the company that manufactures the attack drones, according to UNN.
Details
The company said that nearly four months ago, on May 15, the Ryazan refinery came under a large-scale attack, as a result of which almost all of its primary oil-processing units were damaged. Repairs to some of the units lasted more than three months, after which the refinery resumed processing.
But today, September 6, Fire Point drones once again visited the Ryazan oil refinery. As a result of the attack, the facility completely halted operations to carry out repairs. And it appears that this time it will also be for a long while
Earlier, Fire Point, the company that manufactures the attack drones, reported that Ukrainian forces had struck the Ryazan oil refinery using long-range FP-1 UAVs. The company also added that the strike hit the largest primary oil-processing units at the Ryazan refinery.
The strike was also confirmed by the General Staff of Ukraine. According to the General Staff, during the night of September 6, the Defense Forces struck the Ryazan refinery, the "Rostov-on-Don" airfield, and three air-defense facilities in russia.
Additionally
The Ryazan oil refinery is one of the largest oil-processing enterprises in russia. Its designed capacity is approximately 17 million tonnes of oil per year (about 4.9% of the total volume of oil refining in russia).
The refinery is part of the structure of "Rosneft." The facility has repeatedly been hit and attacked by Ukrainian Defense Forces drones (in particular, in May, July, and September 2026). Previous attacks caused significant damage to processing units, prolonged shutdowns of primary and secondary oil processing, and fires on the refinery's premises.
Previously
Following strikes by the Defense Forces, the operations of "LUKOIL-Nizhegorodninefteproekt" LLC and "NOVATEK-Ust-Luga" in russia were halted.

Mosque in Belgium vandalised with swastikas, hateful messages

A mosque in northern Belgium has been vandalised with swastikas and hateful messages, while dog faeces were left outside its entrance.
The vandalism at the Tawfieq Mosque in Schelle, Antwerp province, was discovered by mosque board members on Friday morning, Belgian public broadcaster VRT reported on Sunday.
Swastikas and hateful messages had been painted on the mosque’s door and windows, while dog faeces were scattered in front of the building.
“We were extremely shocked when we discovered the message, the swastikas and dog faeces at our centre,” the board said.
Officials photographed the damage before cleaning the building ahead of Friday prayers and filed a complaint with police against the unknown perpetrators.
‘Muslim hatred in its purest form’
Local police confirmed the incident, saying they were taking it seriously and had launched an investigation to identify those responsible.
Muslim Rights Watch Belgium described the attack as “Muslim hatred in its purest form,” stressing that it should not be treated as an isolated act of vandalism.
“This is not an isolated case of vandalism or an act of ‘troublemaking,’ but a disgusting and explicit expression of Muslim hatred,” the group’s chairman, Mohamed Amin Chaib, said.
The organisation said it would also file a complaint and urged authorities to strengthen security around mosques.

Iran defeat Vietnam at AFC U20 Asian Cup 2027 qualifier
TEHRAN – Iran finished runners-up in Group C of the AFC U20 Asian Cup China 2027 Qualifiers after coming from behind to defeat hosts Vietnam 3-1 on Sunday.
Vietnam took the lead in the 41st minute when Nguyen Quoc Khanh was played through on goal by Dau Hong Phong before beating Iran goalkeeper Amimahdi Maghsoudi with a shot at the near post.

The visitors completed their comeback in the 63rd minute when Mahan Beheshti calmly converted a penalty to put Iran 2-1 ahead.
Iran then sealed the victory deep into stoppage time, with Abolfazl Zadeh Attar making no mistake from the spot in the 95th minute to complete the 3-1 win.
The result saw Iran finish second in Group C, while Vietnam were beaten on home soil despite taking an early lead.

EU chief von der Leyen heads to Greenland in show of support for the island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
14:21:24 UTC
23:21:24 KST

Speaking at the World Economic Forum's annual meeting in Davos this year, von der Leyen said the EU was working on a "massive European investment surge" in Greenland in a bid to ramp up Arctic security.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is visiting Greenland on Sunday and Monday as the bloc signals its continued support for the island amid US President Donald Trump's repeated calls for the United States to acquire it.
As part of the visit, von der Leyen is expected to sign a joint declaration between the EU and the Danish autonomous territory on Monday.
Since his return to the White House in January last year, Trump has claimed the US needs to take control of Greenland for its "national security," arguing that either China or Russia would otherwise seize the island.
Von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa issued a joint statement in January in which they highlighted the importance of "territorial integrity and sovereignty" and said the EU stood "in full solidarity with Denmark and the people of Greenland."
Speaking at the World Economic Forum's annual meeting in Davos this year, von der Leyen said the EU was also working on a "massive European investment surge" in Greenland in a bid to ramp up Arctic security.
The Commission has proposed allocating €530 million to Greenland under its budget for the 2028–2034 period, which it said reflected its "growing geostrategic importance in the Arctic."
The Financial Times reported that von der Leyen is set to announce an additional €200 million in funding for the island during her visit.
In May, Trump's special envoy to Greenland, Jeff Landry, said it was time the US "puts its footprint back" on the territory.
Landry, who is also the governor of Louisiana, made the comments during a trip to the territory, his first since his appointment to the special envoy role in December 2025.
Speaking from Greenland's capital, Nuuk, Landry told Agence France-Presse: "I think that you're seeing the president talk about increasing national security operations and repopulating certain bases in Greenland."
"Everyone that I've talked to in Greenland would love to see the US repopulate those bases," he continued, adding that the territory "needs the US."
In January, the leaders of five political parties in Greenland’s parliament released a joint statement with a clear message to the US.
"We do not want to be Americans, we do not want to be Danes; we want to be Greenlanders," it read.
The US is reported to have had 17 military facilities and more than 10,000 troops on Greenland at the height of the Cold War. It currently operates just one base on the island, the Pituffik Space Base - the US Department of Defense's northernmost installation.
Pituffik is used for missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance missions, according to the US Space Force.

Ukrainians have been allowed to submit claims for loss of employment due to the war

Unknown Publisher

Ukrainians have been allowed to submit claims for loss of employment due to the war
Kyiv • UNN
The Register of Damage has opened a category for compensation for lost earnings due to the war. Claims are submitted through the Diia portal.
Ukrainians who lost their jobs and income because of the war can now submit a claim to the international Register of Damage through "Diia." This was reported by the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration, according to UNN.
Details
The International Register of Damage Caused by the Aggression of the Russian Federation against Ukraine has opened a new category, A3.4, "Loss of Paid Employment," for claim submissions. Individuals who worked as employees or were self-employed and were deprived of their source of income due to losing their jobs as a result of the armed aggression of the Russian Federation against Ukraine may submit a claim in this category. The new category provides an opportunity to record claims for compensation for earnings that a person was unable to receive due to war-related job loss
In addition, according to the available data, a separate category, A3.5, "Loss of Private Entrepreneurship," already exists in the Register for individual entrepreneurs who lost income due to Russian aggression.
All claims to the Register are submitted through the "Diia" web portal. Currently, 30 claim categories are open to individuals and legal entities, as well as state authorities and local self-government bodies.
To remind you
In Ukraine, 94,267 unemployed people have been officially registered, with the largest numbers in Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv and Poltava regions. Employers are experiencing an acute shortage of skilled workers, drivers and doctors.
