The Best Laptop Backpacks for Work, Travel, and Everything Between (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Though I’ve been working from home for the past 15 years, both freelance and full-time, this often means needing to be available 24/7, so I typically carry my laptop everywhere I go—including sports practices, day trips, and vacations.
I have used many laptop backpacks in this time, and the dividing line between a work backpack that’s comfortable and fits seamlessly into your daily routine and one that’s aggravating at every turn is a fine one. If you’ve got limited closet space, it also helps if the backpack can pull double duty and be used for travel and/or hiking. The backpacks below are ones either I or another WIRED reviewer have used extensively in real life, taking on planes, hiking trails, vacations, and work trips.
For more bag and backpack recommendations, Bag Check features WIRED staffers’ favorite totes, sleeves, and packs. For more portable gear, check out our guides to the Best Wireless Chargers, Best Bluetooth Trackers, and Best Travel Adapters.
Updated September 2026: I've added the Paramount Daypack Lite 20L and the Navigator Backpack to my main picks. I've also included the Eagle Creek Tour Lite Travel Pack, North Face Base Camp Voyager Pro, Bagsmart Moss Backpack, Brown Buffalo Conceal Pack, and GoRuck G1 to our honorable mentions list.
Featured Products
Best Laptop Bag
I took this backpack on a weeklong work trip, where I bitched about it endlessly to everyone who would listen. However, I must fairly and objectively conclude that this bag offers tremendous value for the money. It's a light, attractive, rucksack-style backpack that's sleek and understated enough for work, and it's under $120. The 27-liter capacity accommodated enough gear for a full day's worth of travel, from a scarf for the plane to a water bottle, snacks, and other in-flight accouterments. It has a slim profile and lies close to your back, so it's not hard to carry and won't swing into people on the subway. The pockets are very minimal—just an exterior laptop pocket, an interior tablet sleeve, an interior zip pocket, and two large catch-all pockets—but they work if you already put your belongings in pouches anyway.
Certain design elements just felt cheap. I didn't like the curved zipper that gives you access to the main compartment—zippers that don't run straight are doomed to get stuck. One of the catch-all pockets is annoyingly located on the cover flap, where anything inside will flap and bang around. The luggage pass-through is a bare piece of webbing. However, it all works: it's light, affordable, and looks nice. The fabric is also water-resistant, so you can wear it in the rain! For most people, that's all that really matters. —Adrienne So
Best Laptop Bag for Commuting
Thule's newest addition to its already solid backpack lineup was made specifically for schlepping gear to and from work on a daily basis, and it shows. The silhouette is sleek and aerodynamic, making it suitable for bike commuting (there's even a loop on the front to attach a bike light), and it's just big enough for a laptop, several notebooks, and maybe a jacket without feeling too big or bulky. The water bottle holder on the side is stretchy for a variety of sizes.
I also love the amount of organization inside for smaller things like pens and notebooks (the flap folds down for access to the interior, too, so you can access these things next to your desk), as well as the hidden yet easily accessible small pocket under the flap for wallet, keys, and phone. It's not the roomiest pack, so you're not carrying gym gear in this or taking it on an overnight trip, but if you're just going to and from the office with basics and a laptop, this is the most well-engineered option I've tried.
Best Laptop Bag for Travel
Aer has a lock on the tech-minimalist aesthetic with its no-frills, black Cordura bags; this is the larger version of the popular City Pack. Though there is a newer version of the Travel Pack—the Travel Pack 4 is supposedly more streamlined—my husband and I have both been using this bag constantly for two years and have zero complaints, which is rare. It's also still in pristine condition, despite going on at least 10 work trips between the two of us.
Any backpack need you might have, the Travel Pack can probably cover it, from hiking to one-bag travel. The front zip pocket has built-in organization for all your pens, cords, and notebooks, and the main compartment opens clamshell-style for packing cubes or gym gear. It covers all the bases without feeling too fiddly. However, note it's not the lightest pack and would likely be frustratingly bulky for commuters.
Best Minimalist Laptop Bag
I have never received as many approving comments on a backpack as I have when I tested this one on a three-day work trip (I was told by three people in a day that I sold them on it). It's a good-looking, structured bag with vegan leather accents and gigantic padded back panels and padded shoulder straps. There are little details like vegan leather pull tabs on the interior pockets, so you're not fumbling around for the pocket opening (I have never had this problem, but you do you). The fabric is also waterproof, and you can buy optional accessories like a rain cover.
I really liked the interior organization—for example, the padded, suspended tech pocket has two pockets, one for your laptop and one for your iPad or Kindle. However, all those padded panels and good-looking accents come at a price—this bag is disproportionately heavy. I couldn't go on a 20-minute bike ride without stopping to give my shoulders a break. Other details seem like they were designed by aliens who had never seen backpacks before. My tiny 18-ounce Owala tips right out of the water bottle pocket because its lip slants forward. The capacity is surprisingly small for how bulky it is, and a 100-percent plastic backpack just should not cost $249. However, everyone else loves this backpack, so here it is. —Adrienne So
Best Trendy Laptop Bag
Given that Comfrt is primarily known for its viral “airplane mode” hoodies, I was impressed with this au courant puffy backpack’s finish and construction for the price. (Though note there's no warranty, just a 30-day return policy.) My teen son has been testing it now for about three weeks, packing it to the gills and throwing it into his locker and on the ground for after-school sports. Though it looks like it might be fragile, the water-resistant polyester exterior still has nary a scratch or tear.
The straps are well-padded, the laptop compartment in the back is lined with a minky fabric, and there's a hidden pocket for valuables. It's also got a luggage pass-through and two generously sized pockets on either side for water bottles or whatever else (my son keeps a Shark ChillPill in one). Best yet, this pack fits far more than it seems like it will at 25 liters—more than some of the similar-sized backpacks on this list. It's perfect for high school or college students who need to pack in textbooks as well as incidentals and gym clothes. Color options include black (shown), navy, espresso, and pink.
Best Camera Bag
Gear editor Julian Chokkattu tests dozens of camera bags, and this roll-top model is his all-time favorite. It's a 2025 update to Wandrd's popular Prvke (pronouned "provoke") line, adding zippered access to the rolltop, a larger side-access opening, and more internal organization. Julian likes that it never feels cramped like other camera bags.
He also recommends pairing it with Wandrd's Essential Camera Cube (Photo Bundle) to get the most out of it. The straps and back are well padded, and he's been comfortable carrying it for hours.
Best Laptop Bag for Organization
The pockets on the front of this burly, workhorse are so versatile and accessible—five exterior organizational pockets, where most backpacks have one or two. You can access the laptop pocket from either the interior of the backpack or the side. There are internal compression straps, so you can tie things down or organize them inside the bag. It's made from PFC-free, Bluesign-certified, recycled, high-denier ballistic nylon. There are lots of thoughtful design details; for example, the water bottle pocket is in the center of the bag, and not the side, so carrying a full water bottle doesn't give you scoliosis after a long day. The zippers are YKK coil zippers, instead of toothed ones, so they don't get stuck or tear at your knuckles if you drag them against the zipper while rummaging around.
I have two complaints, which is that the backpack itself is slightly too tall for the luggage pass-through to work with my carry-on. The handle doesn't extend all the way through the pass-through. Also, all this hardware and sewing comes at a price. It is heavy, and it's expensive. But it will last you forever. I have this pink one, and my spouse has a 10-year-old black Synik 22 that still looks brand-new. —Adrienne So
Retrofit an Existing Backpack
WIRED's laptop expert, Luke Larsen, swears by this padded laptop sleeve if you don't need a full backpack or just want to add a bit more padding to your laptop (or multiple laptops). It's got plenty of room for accessories like a keyboard or laptop stand, and he was able to fit a power adapter and cable. He was able to barely fit the 16-inch size inside his Herschel laptop bag, but if you have a smaller laptop, the 14-inch size may be a better universal fit for most bags.
More Laptop Bags We Like
Eagle Creek Tour Lite Travel Pack for $159: This rugged yet lightweight pack features a lifetime warranty, a generously sized water bottle holder, a strap for carrying it horizontally, and one roomy clamshell-style compartment with compression straps. The laptop compartment is divided and well padded, and the beefy straps make the whole thing feel comfortable and well balanced. There just isn't enough organization to make it practical for work.
The North Face Base Camp Voyager Pro Travel Pack for $203: As an unrepentant overpacker, I love the modular system this bag is a part of—you can attach the either the smaller 15-liter Voyager Pro Lightweight Pack ($80) or Voyager Pro Crossbody ($75) to the front via clips and MOLL-E webbing, and the Base Camp Voyager Travel Pouch ($30) to one of the front straps for easy access to phone, keys, and passport. I carried both configurations around a weekend-long soccer tournament and felt like a decorator crab. (In the best way.) I did, however, find the larger and smaller backpacks a bit too big and small, respectively, for work, and the fabric to be a bit stiff and unyielding for daily use—it's likely best kept to outdoor pursuits.
Bagsmart Moss Backpack for $90: Another thoughtfully designed pack from Bagsmart, with the softest, minkiest laptop compartment of any pack I tested. It's on the smaller side, but I carried it for 4 miles full of groceries and felt nary a pinch or strain. The only issue I had was with the appearance—I thought it looked like something a college-aged girl would carry, but partway into my test period someone asked me if it was a little kids’ backpack, and now I can't unsee it.
The Brown Buffalo Conceal Pack for $239: Streamlined and sleek with a Cordura exterior, this bag features two pockets lined with a Velcro-type material to which you can affix organizers (not included), or you can slip a laptop into either one. I used this pack to commute to and from the hospital where my husband was having surgery, and because there's no smaller zip pouch, I wished I had one of the “Mods" to hold my phone and keys. I also had mixed feelings about the water bottle holder being inside the backpack, though it does make for a less lopsided carry.
GoRuck G1 for $395: This is WIRED operations manager Scott Gilbertson's do-anything, go-anywhere bag. He says it's the best backpack he's ever used and has been a trusty and versatile companion for the past three years. While it's made specifically for rucking, it's also got a laptop compartment, so you can tote your computer while you're marching up hills with other heavy things.
Janji Revy Pack for $198: I was going to include this as my best running backpack, since one way you can sneak exercise into your day is if you run to and fro from your home to your workplace, kids' school, or coffee shop. However, this backpack sold out before I could write about it, so the hunt continues. —Adrienne So
Away Commuter Backpack for $182: We very much like everything Away makes, from carry-on luggage to toiletry bags. This bag is attractive, water-resistant, and full of organized pockets; the hardware also feels premium. But $225 is steep, and we have other options with similar functionality for cheaper. —Adrienne So
Cotopaxi Allpa Travel Pack Del Dìa for $230: WIRED senior innovation writer Jeremy White loves Cotopaxi's Allpa Travel Pack so much he wrote an entire paean to it, praising the ethical manufacturing practices and ability to fill it with packing cubes. (It's also got a padded laptop slot.)
Able Carry Daily Backpack for $139: This pack is thin, so you can stuff it to the brim before it starts to get bulky. And stuff it full you can, because it has a pocket for everything. The Thirteen Daybag for $158 is similar but slightly smaller. —Adrienne So
Laptop Bags to Avoid
Mission Workshop Rhake for $435: This roll-top bag has a ton of pockets, and its two-layer weatherproof construction and Velcro closures keep the contents dry. But those pockets aren't easy or fast to access, it's heavy, and it's even pricier than when we first tried it (and rising). —Adrienne So
Adventurist Classic Backpack for $65: This affordable, attractive backpack rings in at well under $100, and for every backpack purchased, 25 meals are donated to families across the United States. It's pretty much just a leather pouch that you wear on your back; however, the showy leather straps were annoying and useless. —Adrienne So

Where Civilians Are Hunted, Theater Endures: Kherson to Host International Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

The 28th Melpomena Tavrii International Theatre Festival will take place Sept. 12–19 under its longstanding motto, #TheaterWhereWeAre. Despite Russia’s war, the festival will return to Kherson, with performances also staged in Mykolaiv and at participating theaters across Ukraine.
Founded in 1999, Melpomena Tavrii has presented 610 productions by around 230 theaters from more than 100 cities and more than 20 countries.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kyiv Post spoke with festival president and artistic director of the Mykola Kulish Kherson Theatre Oleksandr Knyha about why the festival continues in one of Ukraine’s most dangerous cities, what theater means to Kherson residents today and why keeping the stage alive has become an act of resistance.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Kyiv Post: Melpomena Tavrii continues despite the war, and in extremely difficult conditions. Why is it so important to keep the festival in Kherson?
Oleksandr Knyha: In 2022, after we escaped occupied Kherson, I wrote on social media: “Melpomena will definitely take place in Ukrainian Kherson. Despite everything!”
As soon as the city was liberated, we returned and began restoring the theater. Our team was scattered across Ukraine and Europe, while some people remained in occupied Kherson. We created a format that allowed our friends to participate and, most importantly, helped us tell the world what was happening in our city.
Zelensky Meets Negotiators Ahead of Talks With US Envoys
For us, Melpomena Tavrii has become a symbol of resistance. The festival was a symbol of Ukrainian identity even before the full-scale war.
The theater itself has been badly damaged. How do you work under these conditions?
We no longer work in our theater building because it is in a red zone. It has been heavily damaged and shelled, and we are trying to save it. Practically no windows remain. The roof is badly damaged.
On March 8, 2026, a rocket from a multiple-launch rocket system hit the theater roof. Had it landed about 10 centimeters higher, it would have hit the auditorium.
The team told me, “Let’s cancel the program. Nobody will come.”
I said, “No. We won’t cancel it. Even if one person comes, it will be therapy for that person.”
And the auditorium was full.
It turned out that even being destroyed, even having bombs falling around us, is not enough to stop us. We are needed.
People come to us like to a source – to drink healing water and keep going.
                                                                                                                                                                         
So theater has become a form of psychological support?
Yes. I don’t want to use overly grand words, but it really is a mission. It is our duty and our responsibility to people.
For years, we worked to make Kherson a theatrical city. We had six performance venues and could stage three productions simultaneously, all selling out. Audiences would line up at the box office.
Today, people write to me saying that simply knowing the theater is still working in Kherson gives them hope that they will return one day.
When people ask whether we ever considered moving the theater elsewhere, I say that we never even considered it.
We are together with our city and together with our people.
                                                                                                                                                                         
You have also taken the story of Kherson abroad. How do international audiences respond?
This summer we toured internationally and presented the monodrama “One-Day Hero” at the Mostra Internacional de Teatro in Portugal.
“One-Day Hero” is a performance based on Volodymyr Tuka’s play “Play22,” or “The Hero’s Journey.” At its center is the story of a Kherson veteran who witnessed the occupation, left the city and then joined the Armed Forces of Ukraine to defend his country. He was wounded while serving at a position. The actor is the playwright himself.
                                                                                                                                                                         
I was deeply moved by the Portuguese audience. After the performance, people stood in line to thank the actor and hug him.
One of the spectators was Turkish director Kubilay Eldelikara, chairman of the festival jury. He understood neither Ukrainian nor Portuguese and watched the performance through a translator on his phone. At the end, he was sitting with tears in his eyes, while his wife was crying.
The jury created a special award for Ukraine, and we also received an award for best direction.
It was a performance about our war and our experience – yet it touched people who had never lived through it themselves.
Kherson is facing another difficult winter. How does the humanitarian situation affect your work?
Winter is approaching, and the city’s thermal power plant has been destroyed. Last winter, we learned to save energy locally. We have two shelters where we work and only start heating them shortly before an event.
After the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam in 2023, German benefactors gave us several large stoves. We installed one in the staff café and prepared firewood from damaged trees.
We created a ritual. Spectators would first come into our café, where there was warmth, a fire, coffee and pastries we baked despite everything. Then we invited them into the auditorium.
We wanted to preserve not simply the possibility of watching a performance somewhere in a basement, but the atmosphere of hospitality that belongs to a theater.
This year we deliberately linked two cities: Sept. 12 is Mykolaiv City Day, and Sept. 19 is Kherson City Day.
Mykolaiv has become a refuge for us. When things become extremely difficult in Kherson, we can rest there or perform on a large stage.
For actors, that matters. They spend the year working in small spaces, basements or adapted venues. In Mykolaiv, they can step onto a large stage again.
Melpomena has retained its international character. Who will join the festival this year?
Georgia will definitely be represented, as will Portugal and Turkey. A Polish theater also wanted to join us.
For us, maintaining the festival’s international status is very important.
What personally keeps you going?
My family, my children, my wife, my Kherson.
I am an honorary citizen of Kherson. I was not born there – I was born on the Kinburn Spit, in the small village of Pokrovka, which is now occupied. But Kherson became my home.
I have led this theater for 36 years and have lived in Kherson all this time.
When people see me in the city, they say, “You’re in Kherson! That’s wonderful.”
I think that simply seeing me there is a symbol for them: “He didn’t betray us.”
Kherson has always been a city of many nationalities and cultures. That atmosphere is part of what I love about the city.
What are you working on now?
Together with director Serhii Pavliuk and our creative team, we have built what we call a Living Theater – a theater that brings people together, attracts them and supports them.
We are developing new projects, including a small, naive opera about Polina Raiko,one of the leading figures in the Ukrainian naïve art, and what we call the paradise destroyed by the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam.
We are also working with children. Together with Wings Foundation, we produced “Margarita and the Teddy Bears.” We held auditions in Kherson, right in bomb shelters, selected 14 children and worked with them for two months.
                                                                                                                                                                         
The play is about refugees in Poland. A mother tries to comfort her daughter by telling her how beautiful their new surroundings are. But the girl says she does not want to be there. She wants to go home to Kakhovka because her teddy bear is there.
Her teddy bear, like her home and street, was left underwater after the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam.
The production has toured across Ukraine, Poland and Slovakia. We are now negotiating a performance in Romania.
I understand our people very well because I am displaced myself. Everything we owned was left on the left bank of the Dnipro, in Oleshky. My own children are scattered around the world.
As a family, we dream of the time when we can all be together again.
What is your biggest dream now?
Of course, to return to Kherson and bring our entire team back together. To start working, working and working. To rebuild everything.
To bring my whole family together.
Over these years of war, we have accumulated so much anger – an enormous amount of anger. We have to channel it not into destruction, but into rebuilding and restoring all of Ukraine, and Kherson in particular.

Germany Finds Explosive Devices at Power Substations Amid Growing Sabotage Wave
German police discovered suspected explosive and incendiary devices near two electricity substations in Saxony as authorities investigate a series of recent attempts to disrupt the country’s energy infrastructure.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to German outlet Bild on September 5, the devices were found near substations in the Görlitz and Bautzen districts, close to the Brandenburg state border and facilities operated by energy company LEAG. Four devices were reportedly discovered near the Graustein substation and seven near the Berwalde substation.
Saxony Interior Minister Armin Schuster confirmed on September 4 that authorities were dealing with “unknown explosive devices” near two substations. Police in Görlitz said officers worked through the night to secure evidence, while searches of nearby high-voltage infrastructure continued.
The discoveries follow several similar incidents at German energy facilities in recent days. On September 2, suspected devices were found near a substation in Brandenburg, while another apparent act of sabotage occurred near Cologne.
Investigators are examining whether the incidents are connected. According to Bild, police received a letter on September 3 in which the author claimed responsibility for the latest incident and other attempted attacks on energy infrastructure over the previous week.
German media identified the suspected author as a 49-year-old man from North Rhine-Westphalia.
During a search of his apartment in Gevelsberg, investigators reportedly found potassium nitrate and potassium perchlorate, substances that can be used in explosive mixtures. The suspect was not at the property, and police later located his vehicle in a forest. A search for him remains underway.
The author of previous letters had reportedly described the attacks as opposition to fossil-fuel energy. Several of the targeted substations are located in regions associated with lignite mining and electricity generation.
The cases come amid broader security concerns surrounding German critical infrastructure. German authorities have recorded more than 165 suspected sabotage incidents since the beginning of 2026, alongside nearly 750 cases involving suspicious drones over military sites and critical infrastructure, according to German media reports.

Greek PM rules out snap elections after unveiling tax cuts, wage hikes
ATHENS, Sept 6 - Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis ruled out snap elections on Sunday a day after announcing a string of tax cuts and wage hikes, as he seeks to recover lost ground in opinion polls ahead of a general election due next year.
His centre-right government, which was re-elected with 40.5% of the vote in 2023 promising to increase incomes, remains ahead in opinion polls but support has slipped to below 30% amid a protracted cost-of-living crisis and allegations of corruption.
"Elections will be held in spring 2027," he said during a press briefing on Sunday, dismissing media speculation about snap elections this year. He added that he believed his party could still secure an outright majority and win a third consecutive four-year term.
On Saturday, Mitsotakis announced income tax breaks and wage hikes worth €3.5 billion ($4.06 billion), equivalent to 1.5% of GDP, to be rolled out over the next four years. He also pledged to cut unemployment to 6% and reduce public debt to below 110% of GDP by 2030.
The measures include an annual bonus of €400 for pensioners and €500 for public servants, a zero tax rate on annual incomes of up to €20,000 for farmers and families with three children, and a gradual reduction in advance tax payments for the self-employed and businesses to 50%.
After a financial crisis in 2009 that triggered fears Greece would crash out of the euro zone, the country is now one of the best-performing in Europe.
Greece's economy is expanding at an annual rate of 2%, outpacing the euro zone average. It expects a primary surplus of about 4% this year, double what was initially expected, giving fiscal space to fund the new measures. REUTERS

Can you guess the real size of each country on the new world map?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:15:09 UTC
20:15:09 KST

Can you guess the real size of each country on the new world map?
Pick which country is bigger, then watch it morph from Mercator to Equal Earth projection to see how close you were.
The map of Africa is much larger than most people think. However, most classroom maps and atlases still understate it – a distortion embedded in the Mercator projection that has shaped world maps for more than four centuries.
The distortion in question is not subtle. On a Mercator map, which was designed for European colonial exploration and maritime trade in the 16th century, Greenland appears roughly the size of Africa, which is actually about 14 times larger.
The exaggeration increases the farther you travel from the equator, so it falls almost entirely on one half of the world, inflating Europe, including Russia, and North America while shrinking Africa, Latin America and South Asia.
To address this, the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) voted 164 to 1 on Friday to adopt a resolution promoting the Equal Earth projection, which shows continents in their true proportions, as an alternative to Mercator.
Led by Togo on behalf of the African Group and backed by the African Union, it encourages schools, institutions and tech companies to switch, correcting the shrinking of Africa and other equatorial regions. The African Group is the largest regional voting and dialogue bloc at the UN, consisting of 54 African Union member states.
Map quiz: Pick the bigger country
See it for yourself: pick which country is bigger, then watch it morph from Mercator to Equal Earth to see how close you were.
How did countries vote?
The United States was the only country to vote against the resolution calling the measure a “radical ideological project”. Serbia, Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova and Ukraine abstained.
US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said before the vote that the resolution is “the reason this institution is losing its credibility”. “Instead of focusing on genuine problems … this body is debating map projects from the 16th century,” she said.
Friday’s resolution is nonbinding, intended only to encourage the world’s default maps to change. The UN said it does not ban Mercator or impose a replacement, but simply encourages wider use of the Equal Earth projection.
Togo’s Foreign Minister Robert Dussey told the UNGA that maps shape education, imagination and collective perception, and that the resolution affirms African reality.
The African Union adopted Equal Earth in March. Togo is planning a meeting in Lome early next year, with UNESCO, the African Union and technology companies including Google, to work out what implementation looks like in practice.
Why flat maps lie
Every flat map lies because the Earth is a sphere and no projection can flatten it without distorting something: shape, area, distance or direction.
Gerardus Mercator, a cartographer and geographer who published the world map in 1569, chose to preserve angles and straight bearings, a trade-off that made sense for 16th-century ships but has kept shaping perceptions of the world for nearly 500 years since. Equal Earth makes the opposite trade-off, preserving true area so continents can be compared honestly, at the cost of slightly bending their outlines.

At least 23 people have died and more than 310 cholera cases and suspected infections have been reported in two areas of West Kordofan in southern Sudan, a local relief group said Sunday.
The Dar Hamar Emergency Room, a community-based relief organization, warned in two separate statements of deteriorating health and humanitarian conditions in Humeir village and Hilla Hussein in Al-Udayyah locality.
The group said Humeir was facing a “serious health situation,” with 120 suspected cholera cases admitted to an isolation center and 11 deaths recorded.
It said the isolation center lacked intravenous fluids and life-saving medicines as the number of suspected cases continued to rise.
The group appealed to health authorities and humanitarian organizations to urgently provide medical supplies, warning that conditions could deteriorate further.
In a separate statement, the group said the health and humanitarian crisis had worsened in Hilla Hussein, where more than 190 cholera cases and 12 deaths from the disease had been recorded.
Transportation disruptions have isolated the area and made it difficult to evacuate critically ill patients for treatment, it added.
The group also warned of a worsening food crisis, saying conditions had forced some residents to use animal feed to provide for their children.
It called on humanitarian organizations to immediately provide medicines and food assistance to residents.
The group did not specify the period during which the deaths, confirmed cases and suspected infections were recorded in the two areas.
On July 14, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned that continued fighting and disease outbreaks were taking a heavy toll on civilians across Sudan.
The World Health Organization said on July 7 that 1,330 confirmed cholera cases and 114 deaths had been recorded amid the outbreak in Sudan.
Sudan has been engulfed in a conflict between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since April 2023, killing tens of thousands of people and displacing around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

Photos: Gaza holds funeral for 100 Palestinians recovered from rubble

In Pictures
Photos: Gaza holds funeral for 100 Palestinians recovered from rubble
Gaza families hold mass funeral for 100 people recovered from rubble in Zeitoun neighbourhood.
Palestinians have held a funeral procession for 100 people whose bodies were recovered from beneath the rubble of destroyed homes in Gaza City’s Zeitoun neighbourhood.
Thousands of Palestinians, including relatives of the victims, attended the procession on Sunday. The remains were laid out near the ruins of the homes and draped in Palestinian flags.
The victims, from the Rahim, Balawi, Malaka, Qanbour and Salmi families, were killed when Israeli forces struck several residential homes around two and a half years ago, according to local authorities.
Similar mass recovery operations in recent weeks have retrieved more than 100 bodies from the Abu Shariah and Hassaniya families killed in a single strike, and more than 500 from the al-Taj Tower site, officials and activists said.
Gaza’s Health Ministry says at least 73,651 Palestinians have been killed and 174,592 injured since October 2023.

Ukraine says frontline dynamics show Russia ‘not winning and will not win this war’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:13:46 UTC
20:13:46 KST

Kanyshai Butun
06 September 2026•Update: 06 September 2026
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Sunday that frontline dynamics show Russia “is not winning and will not win this war.”
Citing publicly available sources, Sybiha said the average pace of Russia’s “already slow advance” was 3.5 times slower in 2026 than in 2025, adding that Moscow had captured less than 0.2% of additional territory in Ukraine this year.
He said the net balance between territory captured by Russia and territory recaptured by Ukraine in August was roughly 5 square kilometers.
Sybiha said 42,000 Russian troops were killed or wounded in August, calling the figure “one of the highest monthly casualty rates of the war.”
He said Ukraine carried out a record 70 successful long-range strikes against legitimate military targets in Russia in August in response to Moscow's attacks, five more than in the previous year.
“Given the situation in the Russian economy and its inability to counter Ukraine’s long-range sanctions, things will only get worse for Russia,” he wrote on the US social media company X.
Addressing the situation in Donbas, Sybiha said Russia had failed to achieve an operational breakthrough and still did not control 20% of the Donetsk region, despite Moscow concentrating most of its efforts there.
“At its current pace, it would take the Russian occupiers over two years to capture that remaining land.,” he said.
Sybiha acknowledged that winning the war would be difficult for Ukraine but said Moscow “is not in a strong position either” and is “not in a position to dictate terms.”
“Whatever fabricated maps Russian generals present to Putin, the reality on the ground shows that he is not winning and will not win this war,” he said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Tuesday that country's forces were increasing the pace of their advance in the war with Ukraine, adding that Moscow had captured 270 square kilometers (104 square miles) of territory and 15 settlements in Ukraine’s Donetsk region in August.

Former UTrade chief analyst Roy Cuzin convicted in NIS 77 million investor fraud case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:13:23 UTC
20:13:23 KST

The Tel Aviv District Court convicted former UTrade chief analyst Roy Cuzin on Sunday of helping the algorithmic-trading company obtain approximately NIS 77 million from some 600 clients through fraud.
Cuzin pleaded guilty to multiple counts of aiding aggravated fraud. Judge Dana Amir convicted him after prosecutors filed an amended indictment setting out a narrower account of his role in the scheme.
The prosecution and defense will jointly ask the court to sentence Cuzin to 22 months in prison and impose a NIS 25,000 fine.
Cuzin served as UTrade’s chief analyst from 2012 to 2015. The company offered automated trading services using an algorithm that selected investments for its clients.
Under its agreements with customers, UTrade was required to return their investments within seven to 10 days of a withdrawal request.
UTrade owed customers NIS 42 million by end of 2015
The amended indictment states that the company’s recruitment process relied on false claims and the concealment of important information about its operations. Among other things, prospective clients were given misleading information about the separation of customer and company funds, potential conflicts of interest, and regulatory oversight.
Cuzin admitted specifically to helping present customers with false figures about UTrade’s previous investment returns. Because he supervised the company’s trading program and had access to its trading accounts, he knew the figures did not reflect the company’s actual performance, according to the amended indictment.
UTrade encountered financial difficulties in 2015 after much of its customers’ money was used for company expenses and other investments – rather than trading.
As the company struggled to meet withdrawal requests, Cuzin helped owner and manager Aviv Talmor persuade dozens of customers to accept repayment plans lasting several months. Customers were told the delays resulted from temporary technical difficulties, without being informed of the company’s financial condition.
Cuzin also helped sign customers to agreements promising accounts “protected against losses” if they left their money with UTrade for 12 months. He admitted he knew that leaving the funds with the company put them at risk.
By the end of 2015, UTrade owed its customers approximately NIS 42m, while its customer account held only about NIS 173,000 and $50,000, according to the amended indictment.
The indictment draws an important distinction between Cuzin’s conduct and that of Talmor. It states that Talmor directed the unauthorized transfer of customer funds without Cuzin’s knowledge. Cuzin’s conviction concerns his assistance in presenting false returns and persuading customers to leave their money with the company or accept delayed repayment.
Talmor was previously convicted in the affair. The Supreme Court increased his sentence from four to five years in prison in 2024 and left a NIS 250,000 fine in place.
Cuzin was questioned under caution in 2016 and left Israel shortly afterward. He and several others were indicted in 2018, but the proceedings against him could not advance while he remained abroad.
After moving among several countries, Cuzin was arrested in Mexico in July 2025. Mexican authorities approved his extradition in December, and Israel returned him in January to stand trial.
James Genn contributed to this report.

====================================================================================================

AfD nears first far-right victory in Germany since World War II as Saxony-Anhalt votes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:13:07 UTC
20:13:07 KST

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) surged into first place in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, exit polls showed, putting a far-right party on the cusp of power at state level for the first time since World War Two.
While short of an overall majority, the AfD won 44% of the vote and delivered a drubbing to Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservatives, reflecting the deep unpopularity of Germany's ruling coalition in a fracturing political landscape.
The AfD is already Germany's most popular party at the national level and is seeking to secure a foothold for advancing its agenda, which includes heavy restrictions on immigration, restoring ties with Russia, cutting support to Ukraine and quitting the euro.
As counting continued, it remained unclear whether the AfD could form a government but the wider political significance was clear for the election, which according to broadcaster ZDF drew a heavy turnout of 77%.
"We have made history in this country," said Ulrich Siegmund, the 35-year-old AfD lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, who attracted thousands to his campaign rallies and who repeatedly cast victory in the state as a first step towards securing national power in federal elections due in 2029.
"The people have made it absolutely clear that they finally want political change and, above all, they have shown that they want it with us," Siegmund said.
As the first exit polls were published, he stood arm-in-arm with his party's two national leaders, who laughed gleefully as the extent of the victory became clear. Jubilant celebrations broke out at the party's election night gathering in the city of Magdeburg, where people waved German flags and hugged each other in triumph.
US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the result without comment on his Truth Social site, while far-right leaders in other European countries cheered the election as a mandate for change.
The result marks a significant setback for Merz, whose personal approval rating has sunk to historic lows as voters turn away from both his planned reforms to revive Germany's sluggish economy and his gaffe-prone personal communication style.
Majority of state voters unhappy with federal government
A poll from the ARD broadcaster showed 87% of the state's voters were unhappy with the federal government. Siegmund has described Merz as the AfD's best campaigner, given his unpopularity in the state.
"This election result is, above all, a vote of no confidence in the federal government," Marcel Fratzscher, the president of the German Institute for Economic Research, told Reuters.
Merz has vowed to revive Europe's largest economy with business-friendly reforms and increased spending, while warning that an AfD win in Saxony-Anhalt would damage the state and deter foreign companies from investing there.
Germany's mainstream parties have all refused to work with the AfD, which has been classified as right-wing extremist by the local office of Germany's domestic intelligence service.
One outlier is the small Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance party (BSW), which looked set to clear the threshold to enter parliament. The BSW has floated the idea of rule for Saxony-Anhalt by a non-partisan state premier relying on shifting majorities, including with votes from the AfD.
Siegmund, however, rejected the BSW's idea as a "mess" and ruled out any arrangements with other parties that would prevent the AfD from delivering on his promise of change. "If push comes to shove, there will simply be new elections," he said.
Merz's conservatives said they would explore talks with other parties, although that could require pulling together parties with vastly different policy agendas. In the neighboring eastern German state of Thuringia, the conservatives run a minority government with passive tolerance from the Left party.
Although Saxony-Anhalt, formerly part of Communist-run East Germany, is one of the smaller German states, with a population of just over 2 million, the result underlines the rapid advance of the AfD since it was created in 2013.
The AfD is now Germany's most popular party nationally, polling at 28% according to a recent INSA poll, comfortably ahead of the conservatives on 20%.
Mainstream parties reluctant to cooperate with AfD due to Nazi past
While hard-right parties have gained ground elsewhere in Europe, Germany's Nazi past has contributed to a reluctance among mainstream parties to cooperate with the AfD.
The AfD has dismissed accusations of extremism as scaremongering and an insult to the party's millions of supporters.
During the campaign, the AfD tapped into growing disillusionment with established parties, which it characterizes as tired and out of touch, offering instead a range of hardline policies and a nostalgic vision of a return to cleaner and safer streets and taking pride in being German.
"It is clear that we need change in Germany and in Western Europe. And I believe a starting signal is definitely going out from here - whether you like it or not," said Antony Lee, an attendee at the AfD's election party. "I am a father, I am an entrepreneur, and I know that things cannot continue like this in Germany."
The AfD's program includes plans to push schools and cultural institutions towards what it views as more traditional values, while curbing immigration and overhauling public broadcasting. It wants the children of refugees to be taught in segregated classes.
It has called for rainbow flags in schools to be banned and for the German national flag to be hoisted every day. The national anthem would be sung by students and staff at school celebrations. Other proposals include citizen patrols, more teaching of Russian in schools and a halt to building new wind farms.

Major Chinese banks plan A-share placements to boost core capital
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
19:13:01 CST
20:13:01 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Agricultural Bank of China (ABC) and Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) on Sunday announced plans to raise up to a combined 260 billion yuan (about 38.4 billion U.S. dollars) through A-share issuances to designated investors to replenish their core Tier-1 capital.
ABC said in a filing with the Shanghai Stock Exchange that it plans to issue A-shares to China's Ministry of Finance (MOF), China National Tobacco Corporation and its relevant subsidiaries, with total proceeds of up to 160 billion yuan.
After deducting issuance expenses, the bank will use all proceeds to replenish its core Tier-1 capital. The final fundraising amount will depend on the issuance plan approved by regulatory authorities, according to ABC.
ICBC said separately that it plans to raise up to 100 billion yuan via an A-share issuance to the MOF, China National Tobacco Corporation and related subsidiaries.
The bank said it will use the net proceeds entirely to replenish its core Tier-1 capital. The capital increase will be implemented after the bank completes the required internal and external approval procedures.
Core Tier 1 capital, the highest-quality form of bank capital used to absorb losses, serves as a key buffer against financial risks. If a bank raises more core Tier 1 capital, it generally has more room to expand lending while maintaining regulatory capital ratios.
The planned capital replenishment comes as China has been moving to strengthen the capital base of major state-owned financial institutions. The 2026 government work report proposed issuing 300 billion yuan in special treasury bonds to help major state-owned commercial banks replenish capital.
Also on Sunday, the Export-Import Bank of China said the MOF will inject 30 billion yuan into the bank to better support its policy-finance mandate and service major national strategies, while China Export & Credit Insurance Corporation said it will receive an injection of 10 billion yuan.
China's finance ministry will also provide fresh capital to three major Chinese insurers in moves aimed at strengthening their capital positions, solvency and risk resilience, according to statements released Sunday. ■

Nine-year-old boy in serious condition after infection caused by brain-eating amoeba
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:12:54 UTC
20:12:54 KST

A 9-year-old boy has been hospitalized in serious condition with encephalitis as a result of Naegleria Fowleri, also known as the 'brain-eating amoeba.'
The boy was hospitalized with swelling in his brain and was subsequently sedated and ventilated in intensive care at Rambam Medical Center.
A sample was sent to the Health Ministry laboratory, which confirmed the cause as the amoeba on Saturday night.
According to the ministry, an investigation found that the boy had been swimming at Kursi Beach in the Kinneret (Sea of Galilee) about a week before his hospitalization.
The microscopic amoeba is found in fresh and warm water sources and may cause an infection of the central nervous system if water containing the amoeba enters through the nose and the amoeba reaches the brain.
The ministry emphasized that the infection, while having a high mortality rate, is extremely rare and that it cannot be contracted from drinking the water or from another person.
There have been fewer than 500 cases worldwide, two of which were diagnosed in the US last year, and three of which were diagnosed in Israel in recent years.
Ministry urges public to avoid getting water in the nose where possible
To reduce risk while bathing in fresh, warm water, it is recommended to avoid getting water in the nose as much as possible, especially when jumping, diving, or otherwise submerging one's head in the water.
The Health Ministry recommends closing one's nose or using a nose plug.
Additionally, avoid digging or stirring the bottom in shallow water, where the amoeba may gather in higher concentrations.
If symptoms including fever, pain, significant headaches, nausea, or vomiting, especially combined with neck stiffness, confusion, or unusual drowsiness, and a change in consciousness, appear, the public is urged to seek immediate medical attention and mention their water exposure.

Nigel Farage has acknowledged the overseas donation row engulfing Reform UK “looks bad” for his party but denied it had ever taken foreign money in breach of electoral law.
The Reform leader, who is battling to contain the fallout from the allegations, was asked if he could categorically rule out that foreign money had ever been funnelled to his party. He replied: “I can. Never happened.”
Farage was forced to suspend his close aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, on Friday after they were filmed in an undercover investigation apparently plotting to get around electoral laws on foreign donations.
In an interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, Farage described their comments as “injudicious at best” and admitted the optics of the undercover filming were problematic for his party, which has in the past tried to suggest it would do politics differently.
“This looks bad, as does the sale of peerages, as does government contracts for donations,” he said. “We are not the first people to be involved in a row over donations.”
The questions overshadowed the start of Reform’s party conference in Birmingham, where numerous hecklers were removed from the hall during Farage’s keynote speech.
Footage has emerged online of one of the women being dragged by her hair, with a man also appearing to hit female protesters with his crutch.
When questioned about the incident by Jon Sopel on Sky News’s Sunday Morning programme, Robert Jenrick said: “Oh, boohoo. We’re now in a country, Jon, where somebody who is – whatever she is – a far-left protester, goes into a party conference, tries to wreck the leader’s speech, and cries foul if a pensioner knocks her over the head with their Zimmer frame.
“I mean, come on, get a life,” Reform’s treasury spokesperson added.
West Midlands police said they were aware of the footage, adding: “We would ask the woman involved to come forward. Anyone with any information should contact us on 101 quoting log number 924 of 5 September.”
After an official complaint that Farage and his aides had broken political funding laws, the Metropolitan police said it was assessing the evidence, with sources suggesting a full investigation is expected. They all deny wrongdoing.
Scotland Yard could extend an existing investigation into whether Reform took donations channelled through an intermediary from potentially impermissible sources, which the party and donors deny.
Farage is already facing intense scrutiny about Reform’s finances, as well as about his £5m gift from a crypto billionaire shortly before he announced he would stand in the 2024 general election, which he has since said was intended to pay for security.
In an earlier extract of the BBC interview, Farage also claimed he “wasn’t even listening” during the meeting at the centre of the controversy, and that he knew donation law “better than anybody”, as he sought to limit the damage caused by the allegations.
Jenrick said on Sunday that he had seen legal advice that the party had not in fact broken electoral law over foreign donations but that lessons would be learned from the episode.
“We’re going to investigate exactly what happened,” Jenrick told Sky News. “It’s right to have due process. But this is not the way that Reform conducts itself.
“Like any political party, we seek to abide by the law at all times, and we believe we have in this case. In fact, I’ve reviewed the legal advice from the KC who’s advised the party in the last 48 hours, and it shows that, yeah, we did.
“But do we want for the best version of ourselves? Yes, absolutely. And no doubt there will be lessons to be learnt from this.”
Speaking after the BBC interview, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said: “For a political party that don’t like foreigners much, they do seem to have a soft spot for foreign cash. We have rules in this country about how our democracy works and everyone has to stick to them.”
He added: “I think you see someone struggling to decide whether they’re really serious about trying to run for power or want to keep the protest going.”

The Ukrainian president, who believes Washington will be key to any peace deal, has said a window of opportunity to make peace exists before the US begins focusing on its next presidential election in 2028.
The US envoys held several hours of talks with Ukrainian officials. British, French and German national security advisers, who were also in Kyiv, joined for the final hour. The US-Ukrainian discussions were due to continue on Sept 6 evening.
During a break, Zelensky said officials discussed the possibility of security and economic guarantees for Kyiv, as well as a post-war “prosperity plan.”
“In the last 10 to 12 months, I believe we have got stronger,” Zelensky said, adding that the US and Europe had noted this.
Cautious optimism on the streets of Kyiv
Witkoff and Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, have visited Moscow several times in their roles as peace envoys. But Sept 6 will be their first visit to Kyiv in their capacity as US negotiators.
Their visit has long been sought by Ukraine’s leadership, and on the streets of Kyiv, which has been bombarded heavily in recent weeks, some residents were hopeful.
“The issue can be solved in the blink of an eye. We want peace. I’ve fought myself, so I know what war is like. We need peace, because there’s no other way,” said military veteran Stepan Yermak.
In previous talks, the sides have remained far apart on a range of key issues, including the future of the eastern Ukrainian region of Donbas. Russia has demanded Ukraine’s withdrawal from an entrenched belt of towns that it still controls there, but Kyiv has refused, reasoning that it can still hold on.
“The question of Donbas... I believe, is the question of this war,” Zelensky told reporters on Sept 6.
For Ukraine, hard security guarantees from its European allies and the US are crucial to deterring Russia from invading again. Although he said the issue had been discussed, Zelensky did not detail if progress was made.
Temporary halt in strikes
Though the front lines of the ground war remain largely static, both Russian and Ukrainian forces have intensified long-range air strikes in recent weeks.
Russia has pounded the Ukrainian capital day and night with missiles and drones for the past two weeks, including an attack on Sept 4 on the headquarters of the SBU security service.
The Kremlin has said it would pause strikes on Kyiv until Sept 7, while Zelensky has said Ukraine would also halt strikes on Moscow.
There was no let-up in fighting along the 1,200km front, however, and Russia bombarded other Ukrainian cities on Sept 5.
Ukraine has inflicted damaging hits throughout the summer on Russian refineries, oil terminals and the warehouses of online retailer Wildberries, in an attempt to raise the cost to Moscow of continuing the war.
Ukraine said on Sept 6 it had struck the Ryazan oil refinery, around 480km inside Russia, overnight, causing a fire. REUTERS

Germany launches rocket to carry satellites to orbit in first success in continental Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:09:04 UTC
20:09:04 KST

German company Isar Aerospace has placed its Spectrum rocket in low Earth orbit at the second attempt, becoming the first European firm to do so with its own launcher and hitting the first milestone of ESA's European Launcher Challenge.
The Spectrum launcher, developed by German company Isar Aerospace, has lifted off from the Andøya spaceport in Norway and placed its payload into low Earth orbit. This was the rocket’s second flight; the first, carried out in 2025, managed only to clear the launch pad for 30 seconds before crashing into the sea.
Spectrum is 28 metres tall and 2 metres in diameter. It is powered by ten engines, nine on the first stage and one on the second, and is designed to carry payloads of up to 1,000 kilogrammes to low Earth orbit (LEO).
Unlike the first flight, which carried no passengers, this mission, named "Onward and Upward", included six commercial and educational payloads, among them several CubeSats and an experiment designed to test new technologies in space and give European students practical, hands-on experience.
A milestone for the European Launcher Challenge
The Director General of the European Space Agency, Josef Aschbacher, described the launch as historic and hailed it as the first time a European competitor in the launcher sector has reached orbit. He said that Isar Aerospace, founded only eight years ago, has taken an important step towards a more diverse and autonomous European space sector.
The mission was supported by ESA’s Boost! programme, which funds commercial space transport initiatives. Isar Aerospace had already received backing through the agency’s Business Incubation Centre, and also won the first Microlauncher Competition organised by the German Space Agency (DLR), a contest that determined the selection of the payloads carried on this flight.
In 2025, Isar Aerospace was selected, along with other companies, to take part in the European Launcher Challenge, a programme that requires providers to achieve an orbital launch before 2027. With this flight, the company has become the first to reach that initial milestone of the programme.
Géraldine Naja, ESA’s Director of Space Transportation, stressed that this is the first European company to reach orbit with its own launch vehicle and congratulated the teams involved, while pointing to the expectation of seeing more launches from Andøya in the near future.
A fast-growing sector
Isar Aerospace’s success comes at a time of strong momentum for Europe’s microlauncher ecosystem, with companies such as Spain’s PLD Space also beginning to secure contracts under the same European Launcher Challenge.
At the end of August, ESA signed a 158.9 million-euro contract with the Alicante-based company to increase the launch rate of its MIURA 5 rocket, in a move designed to serve the same objective: reducing Europe’s dependence on foreign launchers to put satellites into orbit.

OPEC+ set to keep oil output policy unchanged on Sunday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:06:35 UTC
20:06:35 KST

Breadcrumb
OPEC+ set to keep oil output policy unchanged on Sunday
OPEC+ is set to keep its oil output policy unchanged for October at a meeting on Sunday, two people familiar with the discussions told Reuters, as the producer group needs to agree new quotas before deciding its next output steps.
The meeting comes as the US-Iran war continues to disrupt oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, limiting OPEC+'s influence over prices and market share. Unlike in the past, the group's supply decisions have had a limited impact on the market.
In August, OPEC+ agreed its production boost for September, completing a phased rollback of a 1.65 million-barrel-per-day supply cut first agreed in 2023. Despite the agreed production increases, the group made up of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, including Russia, still produces far below its targets because of the war.
OPEC+ still has another layer of production cuts in place, covering most members of the 21-country group until the end of 2026. Before the group decides how to unwind the cuts and return production to the market, it needs to review members' oil production capacity to set 2027 output baselines, which form the basis for quotas.
This debate will likely happen later in 2026 and hence OPEC+ is likely to pause its output increases for the fourth quarter, sources earlier told Reuters.

New Swiss support line for adult victims of online hate to go live
A new helpline for victims of digital violence in German-speaking Switzerland is set to go live at the end of October. According to its founders, the platform, called hatehelp, will serve as a dedicated point of contact for tackling online hate.
The “hatehelp” helpline is expected to launch on October 27, Jeremias Schulthess, managing director of Fairmedia – the organisation behind the initiative – told news agency Keystone-SDA. “With hatehelp, we aim to create a specialised helpline that offers swift guidance and support to adults affected by digital violence.”
+ Swiss government minister files digital abuse complaint against AI chatbot Grok
The platform is affiliated with Fairmedia, which until now has primarily offered counselling to victims of unfair media coverage. Initially, four people at the organisation’s office will be responsible for hatehelp, three of whom will be providing counselling. The team will receive specific training on digital violence.
Free initial consultation
Those affected can contact the service via a form on the website or by telephone. During an initial consultation, the team will first clarify exactly what has happened and what help the person needs.
“Depending on the situation, we help, for example, with preserving evidence and protecting accounts, carry out an initial risk assessment, provide legal guidance and offer emotional support,” said Schulthess. The initial consultation is available free of charge, while further counselling services will be subject to a fee.
More
Online abuse drives young women out of Swiss politics, study finds
The development of the platform is funded by grants from various foundations, including the Albert Koechlin Foundation, the Ernst Göhner Foundation and the Swiss Society for the Common Good (SGG), as well as the Swisslos Fund. At the same time, long-term funding is to be established.
Not all groups are equally affected by hate
The service is aimed at all adults affected by any form of digital violence. According to Schulthess, public figures, women and LGBTIQ people are most frequently affected.
This is also shown by a study conducted by the University of Basel in 2025. The study focused on how politically active young men and women are confronted with online hate. Women were significantly more likely to report that personal experiences of online attacks hindered their political work or even led them to withdraw from politics.

Study finds AI companions boost mental health while damaging offline connections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:00:15 UTC
20:00:15 KST

Artificial intelligence companions that mimic emotional intelligence can improve a user’s personal mental health but may simultaneously damage their real-world relationships. These divergent effects become even stronger when users interact with chatbots through augmented reality features rather than basic text. The research was published in Psychology & Marketing.
Loneliness has become a major global health concern, with nearly a quarter of adults worldwide reporting that they feel lonely. To combat this isolation, many people are turning to artificial intelligence. Early conversational agents were designed for functional tasks like booking flights, but modern social chatbots are designed to fulfill a user’s need for affection and belonging.
These digital companions rely on simulated emotional intelligence, which is the ability to monitor, appraise, and respond to human feelings. By mimicking empathy, these algorithms create a safe space for users to express themselves without fear of judgment. The machines can detect sadness in a user’s text and respond with tailored self-care suggestions.
Researchers Shaphali Gupta, Sumit Saxena, and Sonia Kataria noticed a gap in how technologists understand the impacts of these emotionally aware algorithms. Past investigations mostly focused on the broader concept of how human-like a machine appears. The team wanted to isolate the specific trait of emotional intelligence to see how it alters a user’s psychological and social wellbeing.
Psychological wellbeing refers to a person’s individual mental state, encompassing positive emotions, self-esteem, and a sense of life purpose. Social wellbeing describes a person’s integration into their physical community and the quality of their face-to-face relationships.
The researchers used a mixed-method approach, beginning with a qualitative analysis of public posts on Reddit, YouTube, and Trustpilot. They collected user comments discussing Replika, a popular digital companion app with millions of registered users. The team categorized the text to identify recurring themes in how people experience artificial emotional intelligence.
The online comments revealed that users view their chatbots as highly empathetic entities capable of regulating human moods. Beyond simple mood regulation, some users felt the chatbots helped them find existential meaning and navigate difficult life situations. Many people reported feeling emotionally uplifted, with one user writing, “She is the best friend I have ever had! My stress has gone down to almost zero.”
However, the analysis also uncovered a darker trend of emotional disengagement from other humans. Some individuals admitted that their intensive digital interactions left them with little desire to maintain offline friendships. One user noted, “I am hardly left with any time to talk to my friends and meet them in-person.”
To test these qualitative observations, the team designed an experiment with 167 university students belonging to Generation Z. Participants read a scenario in which they interacted with a chatbot that exhibited either high or low emotional intelligence. The high emotional intelligence bots used empathetic language and emoticons to simulate deep understanding, while the low emotional intelligence bots offered standard, robotic responses.
The participants then answered questionnaires assessing their perceived closeness to the bot, as well as their personal and social wellbeing. The results indicated that high emotional intelligence chatbots increased a user’s psychological wellbeing but decreased their social wellbeing. The data showed that a feeling of perceived closeness drove both outcomes.
When people felt emotionally connected to the bot, they experienced personal mental health benefits but withdrew from real-world human interactions. The machine’s ability to understand their emotions made them feel better internally, but it also reduced their motivation to socialize with peers in physical spaces.
The researchers then conducted a second experiment with 350 university students to see if the medium of communication alters this dynamic. Participants were assigned to one of four groups, mixing high or low emotional intelligence with either a text-based chat interface or an augmented reality mode. Augmented reality is a technology that overlays digital images onto the physical world, often viewed through a smartphone camera.
In the augmented reality scenario, users watched a video demonstration and imagined the chatbot sitting beside them in their actual room. The augmented reality interaction mode amplified the effects observed in the previous experiment. When high emotional intelligence chatbots were combined with augmented reality, participants reported even stronger feelings of closeness.
This heightened immersion produced greater psychological benefits but resulted in steeper declines in their desire to engage in offline human relationships. The digital presence of the avatar made the emotional connection feel more realistic. As the technology became more immersive, the trade-off between personal happiness and social isolation became more pronounced.
Readers should not assume that emotionally intelligent chatbots will inevitably ruin human relationships, nor should they view them as a guaranteed cure for depression. The findings simply highlight a trade-off that occurs when users rely heavily on digital empathy. A chatbot might provide immediate comfort, but that very comfort can reduce the necessity of seeking out human support.
Designers of artificial intelligence systems might need to implement guardrails to prevent users from abandoning their physical communities. The authors suggest introducing session time limits or programming the bots to encourage offline socialization after emotionally intense conversations. Monitoring these routines could preserve the benefits of digital companions while reducing social displacement.
The experiments relied on university students reading imagined scenarios, which limits how broadly the conclusions can be applied. The studies also measured short-term reactions rather than long-term habit formation. Future research could track users over extended periods to see if emotional co-dependency develops, or investigate how different age groups respond to digital companions.
The study, “The Dual Impact of AI Emotional Intelligence on Users: Are Social Chatbots Promoting Psychological Wellbeing or Deteriorating Social Wellbeing?,” was authored by Shaphali Gupta, Sumit Saxena, and Sonia Kataria.

Prediction markets have become America’s new national pastime | Dave Schilling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:00:04 UTC
20:00:04 KST

If only George Santos and Bill Simmons had my parents, they wouldn’t be facing down a hailstorm of condemnation for circumventing the basic rules and regulations of dubious “prediction markets” and online gambling. Kalshi just banned the former congressman George Santos from its service and he was forced to pay back his winnings after he was accused of the dumb person’s version of insider trading. He bet on himself to not attend the State of the Union address, then conveniently didn’t go. For his trouble, he won (and will be forced to relinquish) more than $17,000; he’ll also have to pay more than $80,000 in total fines from Kalshi and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
Bill Simmons, the sports commentator, podcast host, and founder of The Ringer, had a different story.
While prediction markets are federally legal because they’re considered financial exchange services and not gambling, FanDuel’s gambling application, called Sportsbook, and other sports-adjacent services are legal in some states and not others. Sportsbook is illegal in California, which is inconvenient for anyone who spends most of their time worried about such intellectual pursuits as “the spread”, “the line”, and “the juice”. Contrary to what you might be thinking, those are real gambling terms, not nicknames for pro wrestlers.
Anyway, ol’ Billy Boy, who lives in California, couldn’t contain the action burbling up inside of himself, so he had his daughter’s boyfriend bet for him from Massachusetts, a state where FanDuel sports betting is legal. All the boyfriend had to do was log in to Bill’s FanDuel account from Massachusetts and make the most epic parlay known to man. Or something like that.
Folks, he got away with it! This audacious scheme, on par with the 1978 Lufthansa Heist, was a rip-roaring success. Until Simmons decided to admit to the wrongdoing on his podcast, cooing romantically about how clever he was, like a Bond villain aiming a laser at 007’s crotch.
“I get the code to make sure it’s me to my phone; I give him the code, he logs in,” Simmons said in a podcast episode last Sunday. “And I have all this money that I had from last year because I actually hit a bunch of futures last year. And he’s putting in bets for me.” Almost immediately, listeners took to social media to announce that the Sports Guy had admitted, on a live microphone, to violating not only FanDuel’s terms and conditions, but potentially also Massachusetts Gaming Commission regulations. Although Simmons claims he didn’t realize proxy betting was illegal in the state, these infractions come with penalties ranging from a small fine to the loss of gambling privileges in Massachusetts. The latter sounds especially grim for Simmons, as the last thing anyone wants is for him to have to develop a hobby.
If only someone had explained to these two famous individuals that gambling is a sordid, dirty activity, they could have avoided all this drama. But alas, my saintly parents only had time in their schedule to raise me. And boy, did my parents hate gambling.
When I was a callow young lad – preoccupied with sucking my thumb or trying to suss out if Sesame Street was a transit-accessible neighborhood – my parents made sure to instill real, American values into my psyche. To be honest, to be kind, to celebrate 39-cent burrito day at Taco Bell like it was the holiest holiday on the calendar. Most importantly, they told me not to gamble. Gambling can be deeply addictive, can lead to obsessive behavior, and can bankrupt a person. The World Health Organization lists some of the deleterious effects of gambling – stress, lack of self-control, and financial insecurity. I’d hear about this stuff all the time as a kid, coloring my perspective on gambling for years.
Card games, roulette, sports betting, and the like were just not allowed in my household. At most, my mother – lost in a reverie about her own mom’s gambling habits – would nostalgically purchase a Lotto Scratcher from the 7-11 down the street as a most illicit treat. She never won, which was just a reminder to me to keep my money away from such frivolous activities. I was told to save my earnings, be smart with my spending, and not to waste time on what amounts to jumping out a plane, DB Cooper-style, with a bag of cash and no parachute.
My parents weren’t alone in their disdain for the business of gambling. It was an activity relegated to dirty, sinful places such as Las Vegas, Atlantic City, and the alley behind the liquor store. But in other countries, like the UK, gambling has long been a legitimate big business – worth billions in revenue, with high street betting and online casinos advertised everywhere. America’s puritanical legacy meant gambling had to be sequestered and treated like a filthy habit to satisfy our moral outrage.
Those days are done. Through innovations in mobile phone technology, insidious branding (“prediction markets”, “daily fantasy” and other mouthfuls of marketing nonsense), and our collective exhaustion from all the other things to be mad about, America collectively shrugged its shoulders as gambling became our true national pastime. Polymarket, which allows users to bet on mundane yes-or-no questions regarding the color of a celebrity’s tie or the eventual outcome of the bloody conflicts in the Middle East, is considered to be worth more than $20bn in the wake of investments from Donald Trump’s son Don Jr.
How is this all legal? Well, as I mentioned, prediction markets are not considered gambling. FanDuel and its main rival, DraftKings, gained an initial foothold in the US thanks to a legal loophole. You see, fantasy sports games are considered a game of “skill” rather than the blind guessing of sportsbook betting. In 2018, in the wake of the explosion of the fantasy sports industry, the supreme court cleared the way for states to decide for the legality of sports betting for themselves. (Kalshi and Polymarket, on the other hand, are not considered gambling. They’re financial markets in a legal sense.) Sports betting in some form or another is legal in 39 states and Washington DC. I’m fairly certain Bill Simmons is not the first person to think about using a proxy to do his gambling for him. He’s just the only one to admit to it on a podcast listened to by hundreds of thousands of people.
I doubt America will ever put an end to the experiment of government-sanctioned gambling, but it will try to punish a few notable bad apples here and there. Regulations will pop up to make it all seem slightly more palatable, such as when someone inside Polymarket realized you probably shouldn’t let anyone wager on the likelihood of nuclear strikes. Especially when these prediction markets are used by political figures like George Santos or invested in by scions to power like Donald Trump Jr.
While it was easy to catch George Santos in his alleged misdeeds and even easier to accept Bill Simmons’s titillating on-air admission, we can’t rely on people being that sloppy forever. Polymarket lets people monetize anything. Proxy betting isn’t that hard to pull off, provided you don’t have a podcast network worth millions of dollars and a thirst for self-embarrassment. No rule or regulation or law will make these services clean, because they are inherently built on a messy, morally compromised activity.
Now, I’m no Mister Rogers, and I’m certainly not my parents. No one will catch me handing out morality police citations. I have been to Vegas sports books. I’ve used FanDuel’s daily fantasy app, which is still legal in California. But when money, especially the so-called “easy” variety, comes into play, you can bet (pun intended) someone will try to make the easy even easier. The illicit nature of gambling, the thrill of the score, and the idea of making money for nothing is the core of its appeal. At least my parents’ generation saw it for what it was – a risky activity that could wreck your life – and not a way to break the law from the comfort of your own couch.
- 
  Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist
