Fatah Central Committee secretary-general reveals Hamas talks in Turkey, doubts elections - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:01:38 UTC
19:01:38 KST

Jibril Rajoub met with Hamas leaders Khalil al-Hayya and Zaher Jabarin in Turkey two weeks ago, the secretary-general of the Fatah Central Committee confirmed to the Hamas-affiliated Quds News Network on Friday.
According to a source who spoke with the Palestinian Press Network, Rajoub also met with mukhtars, or clan leaders, from the Gaza Strip in an effort to potentially create his own alliance ahead of the election.
Rajoub told Quds that he doubted the Palestinian Legislative Council elections scheduled for November would go ahead, though he called for a meeting of all Palestinian factions to develop a roadmap for national dialogue and reform with Egyptian support.
Rajoub said such a meeting would renew legitimacy for the Palestinian political system, arguing that Palestinians are currently facing an impasse that has evolved into an existential threat. Renewed Palestinian unity, he said, would be an essential step toward establishing a Palestinian state.
Hamas meets with multiple Fatah officials
Yoni Ben Menachem, a senior researcher at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs, told The Jerusalem Post that Hamas has met with several Fatah officials in recent weeks and has found a foothold among those disappointed by Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas’s attempts to position his son as his successor.
The officials, who reject Yasser Abbas as a potential new president, are considering new alliances with Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad as a way to signal their disappointment with Abbas and pressure him to prioritize Palestinian interests over his personal aspirations, Menachem continued.
Menachem also agreed with Rajoub’s assessment that Abbas would again postpone the long-delayed elections, saying he had been warned that doing so would be a “dangerous gamble” for Fatah, given that Hamas won a majority of the seats in the last PLC election in 2006, securing 74 seats. Hamas has since mounted a new campaign to win over Abbas’s critics, Menachem said.
Beyond unity, Rajoub said the Palestinian political focus should be on addressing the refugee crisis, unifying the Palestinian approach toward Israel and defining a pluralistic and democratic national identity.
That unified approach toward Israel, he argued, should center on confrontation rather than normalization, with “popular resistance” representing the most effective way to handle the conflict with Israel.
However, opposing factions that have engaged with Hamas recently told The Post that it was becoming more widely understood that violent campaigns against Israel had not been successful and that it was more effective to focus on combating “the occupation” through diplomacy.
Rajoub also advocated for political, judicial, security, administrative and financial reforms, as well as changes to the Palestinian curriculum. He said it was also necessary to address the “issue” of payments to Palestinian prisoners and their families, who receive financial assistance from the Palestinian Authority under a system that critics have long said ties payments to the length of a prisoner’s sentence in an Israeli prison.
The PA has struggled to maintain the payments in recent months amid US pressure and Israel’s withholding of tax revenues. Palestinian Media Watch has reported that Palestinians who carried out attacks against Israeli and American citizens and now live outside the territories have continued to receive payments, while recipients inside the territories have reported delays.
Rajoub advocates for PLO strength
Rajoub also said that the Palestinian Liberation Organization must remain the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people. He argued that the biggest mistake made by the Palestinian political system was allowing the PA to become dominant over the PLO.
His comments come as the FDR faction appears to be gaining influence within Fatah. Rajoub rejected the possibility of former Fatah leader and current FDR leader Mohammed Dahlan returning to the Palestinian political sphere, though Dahlan also met with Hamas’s leadership only weeks ago and has been pushing for renewed Palestinian unity across the factions.
Menachem explained that Hamas was building support with as many high-profile players as possible, seeing the PLC elections as an opportunity to “rehabilitate themselves” from the military failure in Gaza through a democratic success.

====================================================================================================

The way to Jerusalem: A modern-day pilgrimage in the land’s ‘diverse embrace’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:01:28 UTC
19:01:28 KST

Four Christians, three Jews, four languages, six days, and 111 kilometers from Jaffa Port to Jaffa Gate.
That’s how Michigan resident Jody Bernat, 67, summed up the parameters of the modern-day pilgrimage she and her husband, John Belsher, took last spring under the leadership of The Way to Jerusalem (W2J).
“We were two Taiwanese women, a gentleman from Catalonia, a man from West Virginia, an Israeli woman, and John and me. With a variety of language barriers and fitness levels, we needed to find a group pace and a way to communicate,” she recalls.
“Sometimes it was gestures, glances, knowing looks. Sometimes we walked in silence. Often, we sang, and many times we exchanged views on life,” Bernat says.
Led by an English-speaking guide, the pilgrims bonded through their shared exploration of the places, people, and cultures they encountered along the route.
“Our stays in Christian monasteries, Arab villages, and Jewish quarters were all part of the landscape that outsiders rarely see or understand in the diverse embrace of this powerfully beautiful land,” Bernat says.
“The Ethiopian restaurateur, the man selling flowers on the street, the market bustling as Shabbat approached – all the people living day to day in this region who want to live simply, peacefully, and in harmony,” she continues, describing her impressions.
If ancient pilgrimages were about holy sites, religious ritual, forgiveness, and redemption, modern pilgrimages are about personal growth and connection with people and places, say W2J co-founders Yael Tarasiuk-Nevo and Golan Rice, both secular Jewish Israelis who formerly worked in El Al security.
“It can be an inner spiritual experience or even a culinary or social experience. It’s different for each type of person. We give a platform for Jews, Christians, Muslims, or non-believers to experience what they want on their pilgrimage to Jerusalem,” Rice says.
Tarasiuk-Nevo adds that meeting residents and hearing their stories is key. “Pilgrimage has always been a community journey, even in biblical times. People would journey with you, and others would host you. You’ll have good food, a warm shower, and a comfortable bed at the end of each day of your journey.”
‘We went on faith’
Bernat recalls that the military escalation with Iran earlier in April made getting to Israel complex and expensive. Yet the stress of those difficulties dissolved when they arrived at Jaffa Port.
“It was quite profound to see where the [ancient] ships came in with pilgrims like us, making their way to Jerusalem. For a moment, we were voyageurs from centuries past, with the same desires and the same uncertainty of what we would encounter as we embarked on this journey,” Bernat says.
“We walked in a calm week – a surprise to all who begged us not to go to a war zone,” she notes. “We went on faith.”
Faith was the primary pull for W2J pilgrim Suju Ellen Chen, 55, of Taitung, Taiwan.
“I am an Evangelical Christian. Over the past seven years, I have traveled to Israel three times. Twice, I came with church groups during the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot),” Chen says.
“In 2023, I came for Shavuot and joined a gathering of intercessors from around the world who had gathered at the Southern Wall to pray for Israel,” she adds.
After October 7, Chen yearned to gain a deeper understanding of the region’s modern history and reality but waited until the Gaza conflict simmered down.
“Toward the end of 2025, I came across a post by a Taiwanese YouTuber called Israel Mega about W2J’s first international pilgrimage group. I signed up almost without hesitation.”
For Chen, the first highlight of the itinerary was Rishon Lezion, where she learned about the influence of the Rothschild family, the origins of Israel’s flag and national anthem, and the stories of the early settlers scrambling for water and other essential resources.
“Even before the establishment of the State of Israel, there were people who clearly knew who they were and understood that they were building a home in the Promised Land. This continuity of identity and its connection to the land deeply moved me,” she says.
“Every place we visited along the way allowed me to experience Israel personally and to discover a country that is vibrant, resilient, remarkably diverse, and open-hearted,” Chen notes. “We often pray for Israel, but we do not necessarily truly know the people we call ‘our family in Israel.’”
According to her, “This pilgrimage allowed me, for the first time, to hear their voices, share their spaces, and begin to see Israel not simply as a place we pray for, but as a people and a land we are called to know.”
The shared multifaith encounters of the diverse pilgrims drew them close, Chen continues. “We were so different from one another, yet somehow, we were able to walk this road together without offending or excluding one another.”
The power of modern pilgrimage
This effect is exactly what W2J’s founders hoped to achieve.
“In building W2J, we had our own pilgrimage journey,” Tarasiuk-Nevo reflects.
In October 2021, Rice completed his first of three pilgrimages along the Camino de Santiago, a European network of walking and cycling routes frequented annually by half a million people for fitness, history, or personal growth. He started writing a book about his experiences.
In July 2022, after his final Camino de Santiago trek, he met with his former El Al coworker at a café. Tarasiuk-Nevo, then managing social projects for the Bat Yam Municipality, agreed to help with his book.
Their discussion turned to the power of modern pilgrimages.
“Why did Golan [Rice], a nonreligious Jew, start to cry along the Camino de Santiago? We tried to understand what this was about,” Tarasiuk-Nevo recalls. “We realized it was the human encounters.”
“We are not businesspeople or tourism executives, but we felt a mutual call to start a pilgrimage route to Jerusalem. We just came with a dream that W2J can make a real change,” she says.
Funding the project out of pocket, they conducted research and started a closed Facebook group for Israelis to explain their idea and recruit trial participants.
“At the beginning, we were aiming for Spanish-speaking people from Europe because they know the Camino de Santiago. But we knew that the local community had to be engaged in this,” explains Tarasiuk-Nevo.
“In January 2023, we made the first pilot journey with Israelis,” says Rice. “We started with six people at Jaffa Port and ended with more than 50 at Jaffa Gate because each day more people joined us.”
In September, they registered W2J to Jerusalem as a nonprofit association. “The only way this dream will last is if it’s not beholden to any agenda,” Tarasiuk-Nevo notes. “Israel has always been a place of conflict, and that’s our reality. This pilgrimage is above conflict and politics; it gives another point of view.”
The first organized group, Pioneer Pilgrimage, took place in May 2025 and was led in Hebrew by a certified tour guide trained by W2J. The second one followed in October 2025. Itzik Albachari, an Israeli participant in the first Pioneer Pilgrimage, coordinates the Hebrew-language treks.
Global Pioneers
Bernat inspired the inaugural English-speaking Global Pioneers pilgrimage in April.
She had completed the 500-mile Camino de Santiago across Spain for her 65th birthday and found it empowering, she says.
“But in each town we were encouraged to go to Mass in the local churches. As a Conservative, fairly observant American Jew, I had wished there was something that had more of my Jewish history. I thought maybe there might be a Camino de Santiago in Israel. So I searched and came across The Way to Jerusalem. I wrote to [Tarasiuk-Nevo] and asked if it was possible to go on this journey.”
With Bernat’s welcome persistence, the founders made it happen despite the linguistic, religious, and cultural differences among their international clientele.
“Each pilgrim speaks a different language and eats different food,” Rice says. “Without W2J, they probably wouldn’t meet. Suddenly they’re walking together for seven days to the same places. Yet each translates that place individually. They are very excited by the stories in each place.”
“We ask local people along the way to tell their stories. We don’t edit those stories,” Tarasiuk-Nevo adds. “If someone in Rishon Lezion wants to tell the story of Zionism and the first synagogue, if the shawarma vendor in the Ramla Market wishes to tell the story about his family there, we enable them to do so. We work hard to ensure that every encounter will be a good encounter.”
When the Global Pioneer group arrived at Jaffa Gate, Rice says, “They were crying because the adventure culminated in one place called Jerusalem. This is a powerful way to bring people together and give them an opportunity to express their journey in any way they want.”
Bernat comments that although she lived on a kibbutz for a summer, visited Israel several times with her family, and has children living in Tel Aviv, “I was not expecting to feel the immense heart-and-soul response that overcame me as we marched into Jerusalem with our awesome guide, Alon.”
Chen adds, “As I have been reflecting on this journey, I have increasingly realized something very simple: I now have friends in Israel. Real relationships are beginning to grow between us.”
Pilgrimage of light on Hanukkah
Most of the W2J pilgrimages, which are not kosher or Sabbath-observant, are conducted in Hebrew and geared to locals.
The next Global Pioneer trek in English is planned for December 5-12, paralleling the eight days of Hanukkah, the festival of lights.
Dubbed the First Pilgrimage of Light, this journey from Jaffa Port will culminate in Jerusalem with a nighttime tour of hanukkiot illuminating the windows of the Old City.
“A lot of Jews and non-Jews from abroad are excited about this, wanting to share and experience this together, the reality of this holiday in Israel,” Rice says.
Details are available on W2J’s website, thewaytojerusalem.org/general-5, or write to mail@thewaytojerusalem.org
W2J Global Pioneer: A travelogue
Below are excerpts from Jody Bernat’s travelogue from her Global Pioneer pilgrimage this past year, April 30-May 5.
Day 1
Our pilgrimage began early this morning in Jaffa. The seven pilgrims and our guide, Alon, walked to Jaffa Port, where original pilgrims once arrived in the Holy Land by sea.
Our journey took us through the busy streets of Tel Aviv and briefly through a sandy route to Rishon Lezion. We got our pilgrim credential stamped in several locations. Along the way, we saw a powerfully moving memorial tree garden for the victims of October 7.
We visited the Museum of the History of Rishon Lezion, where the Israeli flag was first created, the national anthem was written, and the first all-Hebrew school was launched. We checked into the Raphael House Hotel and made our way to an authentic Ethiopian restaurant where we met up with the creators of the Way to Jerusalem, Yael and Golan.
Day 2
We walked to a synagogue where a cantor sang a prayer for us. It was so beautiful. His great-grandfather was the rabbi there. The lay leader was surprising: Yael’s husband, Gad. We walked on to Be’er Ya’acov and then into Ramle, where we visited an ancient water source, and we all paddled in the water.
We came upon a man selling flowers. He offered us cold water and then allowed our guide to put a sticker on his store for the W2J. We walked through a local market that was bustling with people shopping for Shabbat.
Day 3
We left Ramle and made our way into the countryside. The path was rugged and the scenery beautiful. Golan and Yael organized a wonderful rest stop with drinks and snacks just before we climbed up to the Tel Gezer lookout. This site is where, thousands of years ago, civilizations built upon one another, including King Solomon’s.
We are walking history. From here we headed to the Monastery of Our Lady of the Seven Sorrows (the Trappist Abbey) in Latrun, where we were greeted by one of the monk-padres, attended Mass (chanted in French), and ate dinner in the courtyard. They made us a special dish that was created for the pope. The women slept in a spacious house next to the church bell – no sleep for me!
Day 4
We left the Trappist Monastery early and climbed up to an old cemetery with a nearby dome that had incredible acoustics. We sang a few songs there. We kept climbing hills for hours and stopped for a picnic hosted by Yael and Golan in the forest.
The rest of the day was spent climbing up and up and up into Abu Ghosh, where we visited the Saxum Visitor Center, which depicts religious history.
We climbed up some more to the Benedictine monastery. The monks cooked us a fabulous dinner – they are French and have the cuisine touch! Father Olivier came and talked with us about life, love, and being a monk.
Day 5
We attended early morning prayer at the 12th-century Benedictine monastery church. After a quick breakfast, we set off along beautiful pathways, climbing toward Jerusalem. We stopped for a picnic snack with W2J guide Miri and climbed up to an old ruin near Nataf. It’s believed to be perhaps an olive oil production ruin.
We continued climbing up to Sataf – panoramic views of the Judean Hills. We had lunch at the amazing café before making our way down the steep ancient stone steps on the Israel National Trail, then began to ascend again to Ein Kerem.
At the Franciscan monastery, Yael and Golan greeted us with a gift of limoncello liqueur made by the Benedictine monks. Dinner tonight was by the Italian Franciscan monks. Tomorrow we make our way into Jerusalem.
Day 6
The majority of the morning we walked up and up and then more up on a path toward Jerusalem. Construction blocked the path just before entering the city, causing us to maneuver over big rocks to a memorial for a Righteous among the Nations who saved many Jews when the Nazis marched in.
[When] we arrived at the Jaffa Gate, Yael and Golan and a Tourism Ministry representative greeted us. They stamped our credentials, gave us our certificates, and then escorted us to a private tour in the Tower of David.
We gathered for an emotional farewell, collected our belongings, and made our way through the market to the Western Wall. A powerful and amazing week of wonder. It was not an easy walk, but one that was worth the long miles and hours on the trail.
The experience is profound. One hundred and eleven kilometers from Jaffa Port to Jaffa Gate. We did it!!!

Egyptian broadcaster and influencer sentenced to death after gang, drug convictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:01:24 UTC
19:01:24 KST

An Egyptian television presenter and social media influencer was sentenced to death by hanging after being convicted of belonging to an organized crime gang that imported chemical substances used to manufacture and traffic illegal drugs.
Sara Khalifa, 39, was convicted along with 11 other members of the criminal organization after authorities uncovered drug laboratories hidden in two apartments in Egypt’s capital. Khalifa, who has 2.5 million followers on Instagram, is best known to the Egyptian public for hosting the popular crime program “Mission Impossible.”
Khalifa’s role in the trafficking network was uncovered after armed police forces seized more than 750 kilograms of synthetic drugs, along with raw chemicals, weapons, and ammunition, during raids last year on two apartments in Cairo.
According to reports in Egypt’s state-owned newspapers Al-Ahram and Akhbar Al-Youm, the gang was convicted of establishing a criminal organization specializing in obtaining materials used to produce drugs for the purpose of trafficking them, as well as possessing firearms and ammunition without a license.
The gang was also accused of manufacturing synthetic drugs after importing raw materials from outside the country.
Prosecutors told the court that Khalifa, who also owns a plastic surgery clinic and an event production company, effectively financed the cartel and traveled abroad to communicate directly with international crime bosses.
The prosecution presented 20 testimonies, alongside a range of digital evidence, including recorded conversations and incriminating video footage.
Khalifa disputes allegations, verdict subject to appeal
Khalifa strongly denies the allegations against her, and the verdict is currently subject to appeal. When questioned by the judge in September of last year about her alleged involvement in the case, she claimed that she had never seen drugs until she was filmed next to them at the offices of the local anti-narcotics authority.
The death sentences of the network’s members were approved and officially announced on Saturday, after the case was referred for the nonbinding opinion of Egypt’s Grand Mufti, a step required by law in death penalty cases in the country.
Of the 28 defendants who stood trial, 12 were sentenced to death by hanging, nine were sentenced to life imprisonment, and seven others were acquitted.
In addition to the death sentence, Khalifa and several other defendants were sentenced to five years in prison in a separate case involving the kidnapping and physical assault of a young man.
All 12 individuals sentenced to death have the legal right to appeal their sentences before Egypt’s Court of Cassation.

Returning to the mountain: A Rosh Hashanah homecoming in Safed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:01:06 UTC
19:01:06 KST

I turned 44 on a summer morning in the Galilee, standing in an alley so narrow I could touch both walls at once.
I had come back to this city before, on various occasions over the years, but this was my first time as a travel photojournalist. I arrived with a new kind of curiosity, ready to listen, explore, and seek. I came carrying the lens I had built over these past two years: an eye trained on the landscape’s opportunities for wellness and healing.
Something is fitting about doing this now, in the weeks preceding Rosh Hashanah, when the Jewish calendar is a reminder of a 500-year enigma of how does a person, or a people, start over again?
Safed does not let you forget that it has done this before. In the 16th century, after the expulsion from Spain, refugees climbed this same mountain carrying anguish that had nowhere else to go, and built the intellectual and spiritual capital of the Jewish world.
Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote the Shulhan Aruch here. Rabbi Yitzhak Luria, Ha’Ari, reshaped Jewish mysticism from a study house a few alleys away from where I stood on my birthday. Rabbi Shlomo Halevi Alkabetz composed the “Lecha Dodi” hymn here, sung to this day in synagogues worldwide as part of Friday night services.
What I found on this trip was a living industry of healing, conceived by people who deliberately chose this mountain, and who have spent decades turning old stone into a place where broken things get put back together.
I made The Way Inn my base for the weekend, and from its stone courtyards I set out to explore the rest of the city’s healing landscape: Livnot U’Lehibanot; the artists who came here and never left; and the kitchens keeping the Old City’s table warm.
I came to this story as a journalist and left it thinking hard about my own restlessness, and about why anyone carrying a hard year should put Safed on their list before the New Year begins.
The Way Inn: A sanctuary of 10 lights
To understand The Way Inn, you must first experience its physical embrace. Stepping off the busy roads of Safed and walking down a quiet stone alleyway, you enter an exquisite, 10-room boutique inn, where beautiful suites are spread out over terraced stone courtyards.
The entire property is crafted with extraordinary attention to detail; everything, from the tiles to the furniture, is handmade by local artists.
On the rooftop, a panoramic view of Mount Meron stretches out before you, offering a front-row seat to the region’s legendary sunsets.
The rooftop is a space designed intentionally to feel like a sanctuary, an idyllic setting for intimate family events, small group gatherings, deep healing, and romantic getaways.
This sanctuary is the creation of Genine Gita Barel and her husband, Rony Barel. Genine, who made aliyah after working at the Israeli Consulate in New York, was on a spiritual journey in India when she met Rony, a professional chef.
Their shared path eventually led them to Safed in 1998, where they bought their first house, which Rony lovingly restored with his own hands.
They began hosting groups for gourmet meals in their home, prepared by chef Rony, and did that for 15 years, cultivating a reputation for exquisite food and warm hosting, before deciding to expand.
To bring their vision to a grander scale, they bought the neighboring properties, spending three years renovating four historic stone buildings into a single hotel structured around the 10 sefirot, the Kabbalistic emanations that map the flow of divine energy.
Each of the 10 rooms is dedicated to a specific sefirah and styled in its corresponding color and energetic character, ensuring that no two rooms feel alike.
The premier double suite, Tiferet (Balance and Beauty), is bathed in warm gold tones and features a private balcony overlooking the majestic mountains.
Netzah (Endurance) is dressed in calming blues, with a headboard hand-painted by a local Safed artist and a deep soaking tub.
Malchut (Kingship), the largest room, was once the Barel family’s own home and now comfortably accommodates families or groups of six to seven guests.
Keter (Crown), representing the highest spiritual level, is decorated with custom glass lamps made by local artist Sheva Chaya.
True to its ethos of mindfulness and healing, there are no televisions anywhere on the property. This deliberate choice is designed to pull guests out of what Genine calls the “autopilot” of modern life, replacing screens with a nightly, 45-minute natural light show as the sun sinks behind the Galilean hills.
Guests gather in the Womb Room, the hotel’s warm, enveloping lobby stocked around the clock with black coffee and herbal tea, which hosts workshops, live acoustic music, and the spontaneous, deep conversations that only happen when phones are put away.
A highlight of the property’s physical healing is its authentic Turkish hammam, and I can attest that this was the most memorable physical treatment I have had on any assignment.
Tucked behind an antique wooden door imported from Indonesia, the steam-filled hammam offers a deeply restorative experience.
The treatment begins with a traditional Kessa scrub on heated stone benches, an intensive, full-body exfoliation that gets the blood moving and lets tense muscles finally breathe.
What follows is a therapeutic swing between hot and cold water, which resets the pulse and dissolves the low-grade stress of modern life. I left feeling, quite literally, lighter than when I had walked in.
This capacity for deep healing extends far beyond individual vacationers. During the war, Genine and Rony turned the inn into a refuge, hosting a fully funded, free-of-charge retreat for bereaved women, mothers, widows, and sisters who lost loved ones in the fighting.
The hotel’s terraced, private courtyards allowed the women to relax in intimate, safe circles and share their grief, supported by sound-healing sessions and astrology readings led by Genine, who has practiced astrology for the past 20 years.
The hotel is built to hold up to 36 guests, providing a holistic infrastructure for larger groups and family events, but for Genine, intimate connection remains the goal. As she describes it, the space succeeded because “people were able to form small, intimate groups in a calm, relaxed way and to share with one another.”
To Build and Be Built: Livnot U’Lehibanot
If The Way Inn taught me what Safed’s healing looks like when it is built by love and patience, Livnot U’Lehibanot taught me what it looks like when it is built by hand.
Fifty-two years ago, a young American Jew named Aharon Botzer arrived in Safed and bought a crumbling ruin in the Old City. He married Miriam, and together they began welcoming strangers for Shabbat meals in their home.
That custom became the foundation of the organization Livnot U’Lehibanot, whose name translates as “to build and to be built.”
As one longtime member of the team put it to me, Aharon is still “stopping people in the alleyway and bringing them in for Shabbat meals. To this day, that is the foundation.”
The idea behind the organization is almost surprisingly simple, and that is exactly why it works: when a person spends the day doing physical labor with their own hands, something in them gets repaired at the same time.
Over the decades, the organization’s work has taken many shapes, from hosting meals on Shabbat to running long-term volunteer programs for young Jews from the Diaspora who experience Israel through rebuilding and community service.
What Livnot’s team eventually uncovered beneath its own building floor was almost unbelievable: an entire buried Jewish neighborhood dating to the city’s 16th-century golden age. Subsequently recognized as a National Heritage site, the team dug the tunnels that now let visitors walk through that hidden quarter.
Inside those excavated passages sits the part of the visit that stopped me cold: a 500-year-old heated mikveh, its waters warmed by an ancient oven built into the floor beneath it.
Local tradition holds that this may be the very mikveh where Ha’Ari himself once immersed, a story anchored to a historical letter from Ha’Ari’s mother to Rabbi Hayim Vital, asking him to watch over her son, who suffered from arthritis. This detail explains why a hot bath would have mattered so much to him.
Standing over that ancient floor, I understood something about this mountain: healing tourism has been its purpose for 500 years, long before anyone gave it that name.
Elsewhere in the tunnels, a sound-and-light installation walks visitors through the four elements of Kabbalah – fire, air, water and earth, closer in spirit to a wellness retreat than a museum tour.
One of its most striking features is a holographic presence that guides visitors through the underground chambers, a presentation designed in part by Aharon’s son Eliezer, who tragically died recently in an accident. Walking through this amazing exhibition, built into the earth his father once dug out by hand, I felt like I was standing near something still breathing.
Young adults coming to Livnot keep discovering that healing experience. Arriving through programs such as Birthright, Masa, and Hillel, Livnot’s volunteers combine hands-on rebuilding work with hiking, touring, music, Jewish learning, and a comprehensive Shabbat experience that staff members describe as one of the most powerful parts of a participant’s time in Israel.
Even meals carry something of the place’s history, with fresh bread baked in an on-site 16th-century oven. As mentioned in his book Jewish Pride, Livnot helped inspire Michael Steinhardt’s vision for Birthright nearly three decades ago, and today Livnot raises funds to continue bringing that experience to a new generation.
Since October 2023, when the Galilee itself became a front line, Livnot’s volunteers have gone out to physically rebuild shelled and evacuated communities such as Menara, Malkiya, Dafna, Avivim and Kiryat Shmona.
But their mission of restoration spans the entire country. Starting in December 2023, Livnot’s teams spent a year and a half on the Gaza border, establishing a continuous healing presence in hard-hit southern communities and kibbutzim.
In Nahal Oz alone, what began as raw, emotional volunteer work, clearing debris, painting, and restoring burned-down bedrooms, evolved into a highly professional reconstruction operation, bringing together teams of professional Israeli builders with volunteer cohorts from across the Diaspora.
Impressed by their efficiency and care, the kibbutzim began employing Livnot’s teams as official project managers and builders.
As one team member recalled, “At a certain point, they started taking us on as project managers, even really paying us... like contractors. Yes, at the lowest possible wage, and we even donated [our own resources], but still, they paid us.”
Ultimately, Livnot repaired about 30 damaged homes in Nahal Oz, before bringing its refined building expertise back to the northern front, where it recently completed the restoration of a home struck by an anti-tank missile in Avivim.
For founder Aharon, this crisis work is the natural extension of the philosophy he established 46 years ago.
“Our core principle is to let Jews be a part of physically building the Land of Israel,” Aharon explains. “It does something to you.... When you do physical labor with your hands, you build up yourself as well.”
The artists who turn sound into light
Safed’s spiritual economy runs on more than hospitality. It runs on artists who came here looking for something else and never left.
Avraham Loewenthal grew up in Michigan and studied art in Chicago. He came to Israel for a six-month artist-in-residence program in Arad, and as it was drawing to a close, he visited Safed for a single Shabbat. He fell in love with the city and never left, and it was here that he met his wife, who is from Baltimore. That Shabbat was 30 years ago.
In his Old City studio, Safed Gallery of Mystical Art, built into a two-level structure, Avraham has spent decades on a project that sounds like science fiction and turns out to be pure Kabbalah: he runs the four traditional shofar blasts – tekiah, shevarim, teruah, and tekiah gedola, representing the four letters of God’s name – through sound-mapping software, then converts the resulting frequency patterns into digital paintings on canvas.
His work leans heavily on triangles, which he explains through the Kabbalistic Tree of Life and its three pillars, right, left and center, standing in for three states of consciousness: joy and gratitude, brokenness and grief, and the integrated, whole heart that understands that both belong to the same person.
In one extraordinary piece, he painted 288 triangles representing the 288 sparks of divine light scattered at the moment of Creation, which every person is tasked with gathering and repairing. His work can be seen at www.kabbalahart.com.
A short walk away, in a stone home purchased in 1980 and restored by hand, David Friedman has lived and taught since 1979. Whereas Avraham works in sound and color, David works in breath and geometry.
He teaches visitors to hear the Hebrew letters alef, mem, and shin as elemental forces – air, water, and fire – and leads a simple breathing meditation built around the two letters that together form the word “shem,” one of God’s names: the exhale forms the sound of the shin, lips open, and the inhale forms the sound of the mem, lips closed.
Breathe the two together, David says, and a person is quite literally calling the divine presence into themselves with every breath. It is a small, physical practice I found myself repeating on the walk back to my room.
A few turns down the cobblestone labyrinth, this connection between breath and Creation reaches its physical limits at Sheva Chaya’s studio, Safed Glass.
Established in 2005 by American-born artist Sheva Chaya, the studio centers on a roaring 2,000-degree flame where solid glass liquefies into a glowing, honey-like substance.
For Sheva Chaya, the intense focus required to manipulate the molten glass is an active practice of mindfulness, but its true soul is the breath.
She points to a midrash comparing God’s creation of Adam, blowing the soul of life (nishmat hayim) into him, to a glassblower.
The breath traveling from deep within the lungs to shape the vessel serves as a stunning physical metaphor for the ongoing miracle of life.
At the core of her work is tikkun, the Kabbalistic repair of brokenness. Taking the fragile, shattered shards of glasses broken under wedding huppahs, Sheva Chaya melts them down in her flame to fuse them into a single, resilient mezuzah.
“When the fire is there,” Sheva smiles, “the brokenness itself becomes part of the beauty.”
This philosophy of finding light in the shards carried her through the Second Lebanon War in 2006, when she painted 20 vibrant canvases under fire to keep her thoughts anchored in goodness.
Today, as the current war silences Safed’s alleyways, she holds fast to that same resilient optimism, believing this difficult quiet is merely setting the stage for a new spiritual growth in the North.
We spent an afternoon with Hana Karo, a 30-year Safed resident who directs the organization Ruach Tsfat, “Spirit of Safed.”
Hana lays out a map of the four holy cities of the Land of Israel, matched to the four elements: Tiberias is water, Hebron is earth, Jerusalem is fire, and Safed, highest in the mountains, is spirit.
Local tradition holds that the air in Safed runs clearer than the air in Jerusalem, and that this clarity is part of what draws people here looking for revelation rather than money.
Hana told us something I haven’t forgotten: people who come to Safed rarely come to make money, and the ones who try usually leave disappointed. What they are looking for, she said, is some internal point that can finally develop from the inside – a retreat, a rest, a stillness, that lets a person shed the noise of work and traffic and finally touch the ground again.
Hana also explained the color that gives Safed’s alleys their signature look. The blue washed over doorframes and synagogue walls carries two explanations locals tell in the same breath:
One explanation ties it to the thread of techelet woven into a prayer shawl, white for purity and blue for holiness and heaven.
The other, older and more folkloric, holds that demons cannot rest in the sky, only on unclean ground, so when they look down and see a town painted the color of the sky, they assume there is nothing there to land on and keep flying.
A table set from the fire: The flavors of the Old City
No healing city runs on spirit alone, and Safed’s kitchens carry as much of its story as its synagogues do.
Our first stop was a small stand in the Old City alleys, across from the historic Beit HaKahal site. The stand, run by Ronen, is known simply as Ronen HaTeimani.
Dressed in traditional Yemenite clothing, Ronen prepares lehuh, a soft Yemenite flatbread, stuffed here with local Safed cheeses and topped with spicy s’hug he grinds in a stone mortar.
It is street food, and it anchors the city’s culinary story to its archaeology, a few steps from history that predates the dish by centuries.
For a fuller meal, Bashert, operating out of the Beit Mendis building, is the city’s hangout for meat lovers.
Kosher lemehadrin, the restaurant is led by chef Yoni Tuvul, was founded by Asher Roth, and its name, meaning a match ordained from above, hints at its pitch: a place where a slow-smoked brisket, cooked for 12 to 18 hours, tastes like something meant to happen. Its parve desserts round out a meal that feels both indulgent and kosher.
Bashert shares its building and kitchen roots with Beit Mendis, a full catering operation that can produce 50 to 1,500 portions across the North and runs a Thursday-and-Friday food fair, with more than 100 salads, 50 meat dishes, cholent and fish spread out for a city getting ready to rest.
And for a smaller, sweeter stop, we kept circling back to Bella and Jacqueline, a bakery tucked into the Old City’s Artists’ Quarter, turning out warm baked goods worth the detour, the kind of stop that rewards no plan beyond walking until the smell pulls you in.
What the mountain remembers
I keep returning, in my notes from this trip, to something Hana said almost in passing: Safed ripens the soul.
I did not fully understand that sentence until we were on our way home, replaying the hammam, the tunnels, the sunset from a hotel balcony named for a Kabbalistic emanation, and the quiet confidence of everyone I met that this particular mountain has been doing this work for 500 years and has no plans to stop.
I was born in this city, and it took me 44 years to come back and actually look at it. That gap gave me a birthday spent in a place built, quite literally, out of the belief that a person or a nation can be broken all the way down and still be built back up, stone by stone, breath by breath, guest by guest.
It is a good idea to carry into a new year, maybe the oldest idea Safed has.■

A concert, not a political rally

Scientists discover previously unknown brainwave chains that organize memory during REM sleep
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:00:21 UTC
19:00:21 KST

A recent study in rats suggests that during the rapid eye movement (REM) phase of sleep, the brain uses repeating chains of rapid electrical waves to organize and replay memories in a highly specific manner. These high-frequency brainwave chains appear to foster communication between different brain regions and help regulate activity in the memory centers of the brain. The research was published in eLife.
Memory consolidation is the biological process of turning fleeting recent experiences into stable long-term memories. This process heavily relies on the interaction between two major brain areas. The hippocampus is a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the brain that initially records new memories, while the prefrontal cortex is a region at the front of the brain responsible for complex thinking and long-term storage.
While scientists have long known that sharp electrical waves coordinate memory replay between the hippocampus and the cortex during deep non-REM (NREM) sleep, how REM sleep contributes to this dialogue remained murky. For instance, a 2016 study covered by PsyPost demonstrated that during deep sleep, sharp-wave ripples in the hippocampus dictate slow brainwave rhythms in the cortex to drive memory replay.
More recently, a 2024 study indicated that rapid ripples of electricity originating in the prefrontal cortex during NREM sleep actually suppress hippocampal activity. Other research, such as a 2012 study, found that REM sleep adjusts the overall excitability of hippocampal neurons.
The new study connects these threads by exploring how rapid-fire brainwave chains in the prefrontal cortex during REM sleep organize a distinct replay of memories and regulate hippocampal brain activity. The research, led by Justin D. Shin and Shantanu P. Jadhav, aimed to determine exactly how prefrontal and hippocampal dynamics differ during high-frequency electrical events across both NREM and REM sleep stages.
“Decades of research has established the role of reactivation in hippocampal and cortical regions of the brain during NREM sleep,” Jadhav, a professor in the Department of Psychology and the Volen Center for Complex Systems at Brandeis University and head of the Jadhav Lab, told PsyPost. “REM sleep stages, which are typically associated with dreaming, are known to be important for memory consolidation, but whether and how memory reactivation occurs in REM sleep is still unknown and debated.”
“The motivation for our study was to address this gap,” Jadhav explained. “We used spatial learning tasks in rodent models to investigate memory reactivation in REM sleep, and its relationship to NREM sleep reactivation, to shed light on sleep memory processes.”
To investigate this, the scientists monitored the brain activity of 10 adult rats as they learned a spatial memory task. The rats navigated a W-shaped maze to receive rewards, an activity that requires active communication between the hippocampus and the prefrontal cortex. During the learning phase and the subsequent sleep sessions, the researchers continuously tracked the animals’ brain activity.
They surgically implanted arrays of microelectrodes, known as tetrodes, into both the prefrontal cortex and the CA1 region, a major subfield of the hippocampus that serves as a primary output zone for memory signals. This allowed the team to record both the broad electrical rhythms of the brain and the firing patterns of individual neurons. Using the ratio of different brainwave frequencies, the researchers categorized the rats’ sleep into NREM and REM stages.
During NREM sleep, the prefrontal cortex produces brief, rapid bursts of electrical activity known as ripples. The researchers noticed that these NREM ripples triggered massive, synchronous bursts of firing among prefrontal neurons. During REM sleep, the researchers detected similar rapid events, which they termed high-frequency oscillations (HFOs).
Unlike the single bursts seen in NREM sleep, REM HFOs tended to occur in repeating chains. These chains repeated roughly every 130 milliseconds, a timing that perfectly aligns with a slower, steady brain rhythm called the theta wave, which is highly active during REM sleep.
The neuron firing patterns during these REM HFO chains were highly structured. Instead of the massive bursts of widespread activity seen in NREM sleep, the overall background noise of the prefrontal cortex quieted down. Against this suppressed background, specific small groups of neurons fired in sparse, sequential patterns. This indicates that the prefrontal cortex replays memories in a much more precise and orderly sequence during REM sleep.
“A particularly surprising finding was that neural reactivation in REM sleep is organized differently compared to NREM sleep,” Jadhav said. “REM reactivation was sparse, involving smaller specific subsets of neurons in cortical regions, and temporally extended, lasting on the order of ~1 second. In contrast, NREM reactivation occurs in bursts of activity lasting ~100 msec.”
During these REM HFO chains, the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus showed increased synchronization in the theta frequency range. The REM HFO chains also engaged a specific subset of neurons in the hippocampus. Interestingly, these were the exact same hippocampal neurons that were most strongly silenced during the prefrontal ripples of NREM sleep.
By tracking these specific hippocampal neurons over time, the researchers observed that they gradually increased their baseline firing rates across the sleep session. This provides evidence that the alternating stages of NREM and REM sleep work together to adjust and tune the excitability of memory circuits. The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which similarly found that memory consolidation during REM sleep relies on sparse, highly coordinated neural replay, though that study focused on fear memory rather than spatial learning.
“Our results show clear qualitative as well as quantitative differences in memory reactivation patterns in REM vs. NREM sleep in cortical-hippocampal regions,” Jadhav noted. “These findings suggest new mechanisms for how the two major sleep stages, NREM and REM sleep, together reactivate memories of daily experiences for selectively storing and integrating long-term memories.”
To better understand the biological mechanics driving these differences, the researchers built a computational model of the brain network. They focused on acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter that is highly concentrated in the brain during REM sleep but practically absent during NREM sleep.
“The study also included a modeling component, in which we were able to replicate the experimental results of distinct reactivation patterns in REM and NREM sleep using a model cortical network, based on known differences in the amount of a specific neuromodulator called acetylcholine,” Jadhav explained.
When the model simulated the low acetylcholine levels of NREM sleep, a small input triggered widespread, explosive bursts of neural activity. But when the model simulated the high acetylcholine levels of REM sleep, the network became more restrained. The high acetylcholine limited the spread of activity, perfectly recreating the sparse, sequential firing seen during the actual REM HFO chains.
There are a few things to keep in mind regarding this study. The researchers could not directly link these REM-specific memory replay events to behavioral improvements on the spatial task. Future studies using tasks known to heavily depend on REM sleep might be necessary to map these brainwaves directly to learning outcomes.
“Our study provides phenomenological evidence for distinct physiological signatures of reactivation in REM and NREM sleep, but we have yet to show a direct link between this novel form of REM reactivation and memory consolidation,” Jadhav clarified.
Moving forward, the research team aims to test this direct link. “A major long-term goal is to establish that this REM reactivation process is required for memory consolidation, and dissect the complementary roles of REM and NREM sleep reactivation in long-term memory storage,” Jadhav stated. “Indeed, how these two sleep stages work together to mediate memory consolidation is a major outstanding question in the field.”
Additionally, the researchers could not perfectly separate REM sleep into its more granular sub-stages, known as tonic and phasic REM, because they did not record the rats’ eye movements. The data was also collected over a few hours rather than a full 24-hour cycle, which means the study did not capture how these sleep dynamics might shift over a full day and night.
“A second major line of research is to investigate the role of neuromodulators, chemicals in the brain which are largely responsible for the vastly different activity signatures seen in REM and NREM sleep,” Jadhav added.
The study, “REM sleep prefrontal high-frequency oscillation chains mediate distinct cortical – hippocampal reactivation patterns compared to NREM sleep,” was authored by Justin D. Shin, Michael Satchell, Paul Miller, and Shantanu P. Jadhav.

Chinese food vendor sparks ‘camera bullying’ debate after vloggers portray her as ‘evil granny’
Some content creators claim ‘there is no privacy in public places', lawyers clarify that people do not forfeit personal rights by being visible
A 92-year-old snack vendor from southwestern China has sparked a debate over online exploitation after vloggers deliberately provoked her to produce sensational videos presenting her as an “evil granny.”
This case mirrors a similar “camera bullying” incident last November, where tourists filmed an elderly woman from the Yi ethnic group in traditional clothing on a train, despite her apparent discomfort.
“Camera bullying” refers to the act of filming individuals without their consent to garner online views, with critics highlighting the potential emotional damage it can cause.
This issue transcends China’s borders. On TikTok, some teenagers have popularised the “flip the camera” prank, which involves pretending to ask strangers for help filming them before secretly turning the camera around to capture the passers-by’s awkward reactions.
The recent controversy revolved around grandmother Xue, a vendor in Chengdu, Sichuan province, who sells egg-baked pancakes on the street after losing her son to illness. Her determination has garnered support from local residents.

The company described the work in a post captioned “Golden hour. Live fire. Mothership operations with 75th Ranger Regiment, U.S. Army.” Petrel said the AERO Sky also functioned as an airborne relay node during the exercise, keeping command-and-control links active for units operating beyond direct line of sight.
According to the company, the system requires a single operator, can launch within minutes, integrates with the Android Team Awareness Kit mapping software used across the military, and can route communications across mesh networks, satellite links and LTE cellular connections depending on what’s available in the field. Petrel’s post did not specify how many strike drones the aircraft carried during this exercise or confirm whether any were released against a target.
This is the second publicly disclosed Army evaluation of the AERO Sky this year. The Defence Blog reported in April that Petrel had validated the aircraft alongside the 101st Airborne Division during a live-fire exercise at the Joint Readiness Training Center at Fort Polk, Louisiana, where the drone deployed armed first-person-view attack drones directly from the air. The newly disclosed work with the 75th Ranger Regiment appears to combine that same strike-mothership configuration, carrying FPV drones as payload, with the aircraft’s communications relay function, two of three mission sets, alongside logistics, that Petrel has said the aircraft is designed to handle.
The AERO Sky is a Group 3 unmanned aircraft, a category covering drones larger than small quadcopters but still light enough to be moved and operated without heavy support equipment. The aircraft has an 11-foot wingspan, a maximum takeoff weight of roughly 100 pounds, and a payload capacity between 30 and 50 pounds, depending on configuration, with six to eight hours of endurance. It combines vertical takeoff and landing with fixed-wing flight, letting it launch without a runway while still flying efficiently enough for extended missions. Petrel builds the airframe from a blend of carbon fiber and balsa wood, materials the company has said keep the unit cost around $90,000 and allow the aircraft to be assembled in about four minutes.
Petrel Technologies was founded by CEO Jacob Stonecipher and Chief Operating Officer Chris Rothe, a former Green Beret. The company originally operated under the name Sustainable Skylines, building drones to tow advertising banners over Miami Beach, before the founders pivoted the business toward military applications and emerged from stealth in February.

America’s 911 System Is Dangerously Out of Date
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

“911, what is your emergency?”
For the millions of Americans who have dialed 911, these are the familiar and comforting words we hear upon placing the call. It is the question that guides us through a moment of chaos or crisis, the linchpin to saving lives and protecting health.
But in recent years, an increasing number of 911 callers have heard something a little different:
“911, where is your emergency?”
It is very nearly the same question, but the slight change underscores vast differences in people’s experiences seeking help in an emergency. In an era when parents can monitor their children’s movements in real time, and ride-share drivers know the precise corner to stop, many Americans may be surprised to learn a sobering truth: the 911 professionals who answer the phone are often unable to automatically pinpoint a caller’s precise location, and cannot always rely on callers themselves to provide it.
The extra time it takes to figure out exactly where to send help, even if it’s a few extra seconds, costs lives. But the United States has let our 911 emergency response system languish for decades, failing to make the necessary investments to bring it into the digital age. That inaction should be unacceptable to every American. Upgrading 911 technology should be a national priority, and Congress must provide sufficient funding to ensure it works in every community.
When America’s 911 system launched in 1968, it was built to serve people calling from landlines at fixed locations. Callers were tracked using address directories that listed the location of the phone they were calling from. As a result, emergency personnel could be dispatched almost immediately. It made sense, and it worked fast.
Nearly 60 years later, we are living in a completely different era. In 2024, more than three-quarters of 911 calls came via either cellphones or Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) and other wireless voice services. Since some states do not break down calls by service type, that number is likely even higher. By contrast, only about 7% came from landlines. In many states, landlines now account for less than 5% of 911 calls. That number is likely to decline further in the years ahead.
Our current 911 system isn’t built for this. Often, a 911 professional can trace a call only to the cell tower that received it, which can be a fair distance from a caller’s exact location. As many as 20% or more of calls are traced to the wrong tower. Unlike apps like Google Maps or Life360 that can continuously track a phone’s precise location, 911 call takers must rely on carrier data when the call was first made. Updates come in 20- to 30-second intervals. If the call needs to be transferred, this process must start from scratch. This wastes precious time. It is especially hard in rural areas, where towers can be few and far between, or dense locations like high-rise apartments.
Asking “where is your emergency” may sound like an easy fix, but that incorrectly assumes a caller can always answer the question. Callers may be in an unfamiliar location. They may be navigating imminent danger, such as an intruder or attacker, that prevents them from sharing. They may give the wrong address, or they may move locations from the moment a call is placed to the time help arrives. Even the emergency data that may be stored in a person’s cell phone for precisely such a circumstance can’t be accessed by call takers or dispatchers.
Simply put, our nation’s 911 system is rapidly becoming obsolete.
Past attempts to fix these errors have failed. The ENHANCE 911 Act, enacted in 2004, authorized up to $250 million in annual federal grants to help states upgrade their 911 systems. But those appropriations were never made. Other funding opportunities for states wound up being far smaller. Ultimately, the legislation was not reauthorized by Congress, and national funding efforts dried up. In recent years, federal funding for 911 upgrades has ground to a halt.
Congress should right this wrong by fully funding NextGen 911 services, which would provide 911 professionals and Emergency Communications Centers with the life-saving information they need—such as accurate location information—to do their jobs. Thirty-eight states have pledged to upgrade to NextGen 911. If fully implemented, 911 would shift from an analog relic to an Internet Protocol-based system. That would allow for more advanced communication technologies, including receiving 911 “calls” via text or video, that would be especially useful for 911 callers who are either unaware of or unable to share their location. It would also help callers with disabilities, such as people who are deaf or hard of hearing, access the system as well.
Full NextGen 911 rollout nationwide is estimated to cost approximately $15 billion. The cost of inaction is far higher. Fixing access to location data would free up 911 professionals to rapidly triage calls. It would also mean a quicker and more accurate on-scene response, helping callers and emergency personnel alike.
When 911 launched, cell phones did not yet exist, and America’s emergency response system is still largely stuck in that bygone era. This is an emergency of our own making, and it is fixable. Our leaders must answer the call for help.

Iran war likely to drag on for another six months, ex-US defense secretary warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

Donald Trump’s war with Iran is likely to drag on for another six months, Leon Panetta, the former US defense secretary, has warned, as the US president struggles to find his way out of the controversial conflict.
Panetta declared in an interview that the war with Iran – launched by Trump over six months ago – risks becoming another “forever war in the Middle East”, with no clear end in sight.
“It’s no mystery that the United States and Iran are caught in a terrible stalemate, in which there really are very few options available to bring this war to an end,” said Panetta, who also served as CIA director under Barack Obama, suggesting the conflict is on course to become “another failed war” in the Middle East “like Iraq and Afghanistan”.
“I think the likelihood is this war is going to continue for another six months without being resolved,” he added.
Panetta spoke to the Guardian days after the US army secretary, Dan Driscoll, abruptly resigned, departing amid the conflict, following reports of tensions with the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, over a series of firings.
US service members “are going to war at a time when there’s tremendous turmoil at the Pentagon, in the command structure, which really creates a sense that there’s nobody in charge”, Panetta, who served as defense secretary from 2011 to 2013, added. “And I just think that, whether it’s Iran, or whether it’s our adversaries, they’re now looking at the United States, and see weakness in terms of our ability to be able to really implement our military capability of defending our country.”
He said: “My biggest concern right now is we live in a very dangerous world, with the primary threats coming from China, from Russia, from North Korea, and from terrorism, and yes, from Iran as well. But what I’m concerned about is that we’re sending a message of weakness to our primary adversaries.
“And while they continue to meet and support each other in this axis that’s been created, I think they look at the United States as being particularly weak right now, and that’s a horrible message to send at a time when we’re facing those kinds of threats.”
In a statement, the Pentagon insisted it was “firing on all cylinders” under Hegseth’s leadership.
“The premise that the Department is in disarray is completely baseless and an insult to every dedicated professional and warfighter in this building who comes to work every day to defend this nation,” the chief Pentagon spokesperson, Sean Parnell, said. “This is what reform looks like.”
The White House was also contacted for comment.
In March, just three weeks after the US and Israel launched their military operation in Iran, Panetta told the Guardian he believed Trump was stuck between a “rock and a hard place” as he weighed whether to expand the war in a bid to eliminate Iran’s leverage over the strait of Hormuz, or “just simply walk away and declare victory”, despite the risk of perceived failure.
Earlier this week Panetta said he “absolutely” believed Trump remains in that position. “He’s boxed himself in,” he said.
Trump now has three options, according to Panetta. The first would be to walk away and “admit that it’s a failed war”, something Panetta finds it difficult to see Trump doing.
The second would be to draw out the current “stalemate, with periodic attacks going back and forth, tit for tat”, and both sides attempting to “avoid the startup of a more dangerous war” while refusing to either negotiate or surrender.
That approach, Panetta believes, would produce “what all parties feared”: another protracted war in the Middle East.
The third option, he said, would be for the US to take control of the strait of Hormuz, and remove Iran’s “most dangerous leverage point” over the US, “which is the ability … to close and disrupt” the global trade chokepoint.
“So the president either steps up and does what’s necessary to open up the strait of Hormuz, or, as I said, he just continues to play … this game of pretending that somehow he’s winning a stalemate when the fact is he’s not,” Panetta said.
Asked if he believed the war is “winnable” for the US, Panetta replied: “It’s only winnable if there is a dramatic change in the attitude of the United States that makes clear that the objective, the primary objective by the United States at this point in time, is to reopen the strait of Hormuz.”
He also argued that Trump has damaged his credibility by repeatedly erroneously claiming that a deal to end the war is imminent, and that the strait of Hormuz is open.
“So the real question is, is he going to make a decision to actually deliver?” Panetta asked. “For a lot of reasons, right now, he’s caught in the worst of every world because not only does he not have credibility, but any threats he makes are totally ignored.”
Earlier this week, JD Vance told reporters that he would not describe the current military conflict with Iran as a “war”. And asked whether he expected the conflict to be over by November’s US midterm elections, the vice-president replied: “I think the reality is I don’t know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians.”
Panetta told the Guardian he believes many Americans have “lost faith” in Trump’s “ability to handle this war”, pointing to recent polling that he said found that a majority of Americans believe that conflict with Iran was a mistake and are against it.
He also said he hopes the Pentagon and Trump’s broader administration learn from what happened with the extremely long deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln, which arrived in Thailand this week after a record-breaking deployment supporting US operations against Iran that lasted more than 260 days without a port visit, amid reports of deteriorating living conditions and mental health aboard.
“Bottom line is, you do not deploy people endlessly into a war zone without making some kind of plans for rotation,” Panetta said.
“So it’s not just that the war is going badly – I think there’s also kind of a lack of trust in our military as to whether or not they are properly supporting our men and women who are putting their lives on the line.”

Game on: November elections kick into high gear with control of Congress in the balance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:00:02 UTC
19:00:02 KST

When voters went to the polls in the 2022 midterm elections, all the ingredients were there for Joe Biden’s allies to suffer a wipeout. The president was unpopular, inflation was high and historical trends predicted voters would take out their frustrations by ending the Democratic party’s control of Congress.
But when the ballots were tallied, the gains Republicans expected to make did not quite materialize. They had won the House of Representatives, but only by a slim margin, while Democrats had expanded their majority in the Senate and built up their strength in state legislatures.
Four years later, those very same factors are present once again as Republicans prepare in the 3 November midterms to defend the Senate and House majorities they won two years ago, when voters elected Donald Trump president. Like Biden before him, the president is unpopular and inflation is still high, though not as high as it was under his predecessor. And though he and his allies insist otherwise, there are few reasons to believe Trump can beat the historical trend of voters using midterm elections as an opportunity punish the party holding power in Washington.
“The out party, typically speaking, is frustrated or even angry at what has happened during the previous two years, and they’re itching to register their disagreements and discontent, and 2026 is going to be no exception,” said Bill Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington who previously advised Democratic presidents.
Campaigning is set to intensify following Monday’s Labor Day holiday, a milestone in election years that marks roughly two months until voters head to the polls. Recent public opinion surveys have shown Democratic candidates for House and Senate seats are either ahead of their opponents or in close contention, and major election forecasters have moved their ratings of key races in the party’s favor.
But Republicans appear to have an advantage in one important realm, and that’s cash. Though some Democratic candidates like the Georgia senator Jon Ossoff and James Talarico, who is running for a Senate seat in Texas, have posted strong fundraising figures, Trump’s Maga Inc Super Pac has $400m that could be deployed to help his allies, while his erstwhile ally Elon Musk has $50m in another Super Pac, which began spending in favor of some Republican candidates last week.
Republican-led states have likely limited to some degree the party’s losses in the House by redrawing congressional maps, with the help of a recent supreme court ruling, despite efforts by Democratic-led states to retaliate.
“I’ve been saying this over and over, but Republicans are going to defy history in 63 days and we’re going to hold this House majority,” the House speaker, Mike Johnson, recently told reporters.
A little over a year after the September 11 attacks, George W Bush’s Republican allies were able to expand their majorities in the House and Senate in the 2002 midterms, but most other elections have been unpleasant to terrible for the party in power.
Bill Clinton lost both chambers in 1994, and Bush suffered the same fate in 2006. In 2010, Barack Obama famously described the major losses suffered by Democrats in his first midterm election as a “shellacking”. Democrats lost control of the Senate four years later. In 2018, Trump’s Republicans lost the House, even as they built up their Senate majority.
Biden’s first and only midterm – 2022 – stands out for the deus ex machina that appeared in the form of the supreme court’s decision in Dobbs v Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned Roe v Wade and ended the constitutional right to abortion.
“It was very clear that women were more energized than usual, and that young people were more energized than usual because of one thing: the Dobbs decision. That’s what really changed the direction of the election,” said Larry Sabato, whose Sabato’s Crystal Ball was among the forecasters that in advance of the vote predicted two dozen Democratic losses that year in the House.
The pummeling did not come to pass: the GOP netted nine House seats to give them a tiny majority in the lower chamber, while Democrats expanded their control of the Senate by a single seat, and all their incumbents won re-election.
Though Trump was out of office during that election, he endorsed and campaigned with Republican candidates and was frequently in the news for his myriad legal troubles. But without actually being on the ballot, congressional Republicans weren’t able to benefit from his popularity, as they would in the 2024 elections. Democrats, meanwhile, seized on Trump’s continued power in the GOP to rally voters opposed to the then former president, boosting themselves in key races, said Aaron Hitefield, a political science professor at Mississippi State University who studied the 2022 election.
“Trump rhetoric benefits Democrats electorally and motivates voters, while not equally motivating Republicans,” he said. “This isn’t necessarily anything new; we always have a surge and decline comparing a president’s party in the presidential election year versus a midterm, but it is particularly more pronounced with Trump.”
Now back in the White House, Trump’s profile is as high as ever, and he recently announced plans for an unusual midterm convention later this month in Dallas where he’ll personally pitch voters on keeping Republicans in control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency.
It’s a tall order – with a majority no bigger than three seats, many things would have to go right for the GOP to hold the House. Winning the Senate is expected to be tougher for Democrats, because the party must capture at least three seats in states Trump won two years ago, including several that elected him by double digits.
Control of either chamber would let Democrats block Trump’s legislative agenda and give their lawmakers subpoena powers they can use to investigate his administration.
Party leaders have centered their pitch to voters on the issue of affordability, arguing that the president’s attack on Iran, imposition of tariffs on trading partners, refusal to extend tax credits for Affordable Care Act health plans and cuts to the social safety net have all driven prices higher.
“Life has gotten far too expensive in this country, and Republicans don’t give a damn about it,” the Democratic House minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, told reporters last week.
Recent polls of the generic ballot – an important indicator of sentiment in congressional elections – have shown that Democrats have an edge of between three and eight percentage points. But the trend isn’t unanimous. This week, a Harvard CAPS-Harris Poll taken in August showed Republicans with a slight advantage among likely voters.
In Washington, the House reconvened last week after a five-week recess, but Johnson opted to cut its schedule for September short by two weeks, which will give representatives the opportunity to return home to campaign.
But though it is typical for electioneering to intensify in the 60-some days before the election, Galston believes voters’ perceptions are “baked in”, with the only lingering question being which party can get more of their supporters out to vote.
“A lot of people have already made up their minds,” he said. “Especially for Republicans, the question is not so much whether they’re going to cross party lines and vote for Democrats, although I think some will, but whether they’ll get out of bed on election morning.”
There, the Democrats appear to be ahead. An Economist/YouGov survey from the final weeks of August showed Democratic voters with a six percentage point lead in enthusiasm, higher than it was earlier in the summer.
“It’s hard to get excited about a presidency that has been defined by a complete failure to get prices under control, coupled with a war that is looking increasingly like a fiasco,” Galston said.
