Councils in England and Wales accused of excessive fees to run outdoor classes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
09:00:01 UTC
18:00:01 KST

At 6am on the beach at Westgate-on-Sea in Kent, Angela Brier-Stephenson used to meet a small group of about 10 people for yoga.
The class lasted 45 minutes and participants paid what they could.
Thanet council told her she would need to pay £1,200 a year as part of its seasonal licensing scheme. She has not run the class for the past two summers as a result.
Councils across England and Wales require hundreds of pounds in fees, dozens of pages of paperwork and first-aid certification from people running small, free or donation-based exercise classes in parks and on beaches, according to a new report published by the Campaign for Freedom in Everyday Life.
The report, titled Banned from the Beach: the Crackdown on Outdoor Community Sport, documents how licensing schemes first aimed at commercial personal trainers and bootcamps in the early 2000s now also apply to even small community gatherings, including a qigong class of seven people, and a mother-and-baby choir.
Josie Appleton, the director of the Campaign for Freedom in Everyday Life, said: “The fees bear no relation to any money these classes make and are frequently far larger than the cost of running the scheme.”
Thanet brought the fee down to £300 for fitness activities before the 2026 season. “The licensing process allows the council to ensure that all current regulations are met. When an individual or organisation provides a service to the public that involves payment or donation, regardless of pricing structure, it remains a commercial activity,” a council spokesperson said. “All commercial operations require licences when trading on publicly owned land. Fees are set by business type and location and started at £300 for fitness activity in locations such as Westgate-on-Sea.”
In Bristol, Julia Turner is resisting a £100 fee to run her £8-a-session, BYOB (bring your own baby) choir. “I am leading classes for new mothers in parks which have no clean working facilities; there are no bandstands to keep us dry and there is no way to reserve a spot. I would be happy to pay a one-off fee for the council to check my risk assessments but other than that, what are we actually paying for?” she said.
Turner has staged a flash-mob singing demonstration inside City Hall. But she admitted that running the choir, which began as a passion project, was at risk of becoming “too difficult to bother with”.
Also in Bristol, Chloe Broomby said the fees had made it impossible to run her weekly, donation-based qigong classes on the Downs.
“I don’t make much money; some weeks I only had seven people turning up,” she said. “It really was for the joy of it.”
Ailie Tam, who has taught community yoga in St George Park in Bristol for six years, was happy to continue running her classes at an occasional loss when only one or two people turned up. But she too has stopped the sessions since fees were introduced.
Bristol city council said its scheme included discounted rates of up to 75% for small businesses and charitable organisations.
“Licensing helps to ensure that businesses operating in these important public spaces are appropriately insured and act responsibly,” said Stephen Williams, a councillor and the chair of the public health and communities policy committee. “The licence fees cover the cost of administering the scheme, with any surplus money reinvested into maintaining and improving our city’s parks.”
Appleton’s report identifies 19 councils with licensing schemes for outdoor exercise that also apply to free or donation-based classes. The councils, she said, used a range of legal mechanisms, from events-licensing schemes designed for large events, and others designed for commercial personal trainers in the early 2000s, to Victorian park bylaws.
In the London borough of Richmond, running an unlicensed exercise class is a criminal offence – enforced by a private contractor, Parkguard, which issues fixed-penalty notices.
“Our enforcement officers will seek to engage constructively and support park users in understanding and complying with regulations, using formal enforcement action only where necessary and proportionate,” said a council spokesperson. “Where an organised activity makes regular use of our parks, it’s reasonable that it makes a contribution towards managing and maintaining them.”
Councils say they need to know who is using public land and to ensure activities are safe.
In the London borough of Waltham Forest, a free outdoor fitness class was stopped mid-session by two park rangers. A council spokesperson said: “We ask for a small fee and completion of forms to provide vital information – even for free events – to ensure compliance with safeguarding and health and safety policies, and to help contribute to maintenance costs.”
In Swansea, officials initially proposed charging Helen Wilson £24.15 a session for the free or donation-based weekly beach yoga classes she had been running for more than a decade. After hundreds of messages of support and a petition, the council withdrew the charge, saying the fees were to ensure public space was used in a safe way and that it had initially understood the classes to be commercial.
Wilson said: “I think they saw it as an opportunity to make money and if that jeopardised what I was offering, then so be it.”
Tam believed the main issues was that “the people being pushed out of parks by these fees are the very people helping to make those spaces more valued, cared for and actively used by their communities”.

Aged 41, I’m back at my secondary school – but this time they’ve let me in the staffroom | Nell Frizzell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
09:00:01 UTC
18:00:01 KST

You know those dreams when you’re back at school? And you’re sitting at a desk reading a GCSE exam paper? Only you don’t recognise anyone around you? Well, I am living that dream. Because, at the age of 41, I have gone back to school. And not just any school. I have gone back to my own secondary school. Only this time, I am allowed in the staffroom.
That’s right: a short 25 years after walking out of those concrete and carpeted halls, the smell of polyester jumpers and canteen chips heady on the early summer air, I am back. But now I’m training to be a teacher.
To some extent, this was inevitable due to the logistics of my life. Despite a few lessons, I have never learned to drive (my instructor asked my mum out on a date and things got so awkward so quickly I have never really been behind a steering wheel since). I also have small children at nursery and primary school nearby, which meant that I had to beg my training scheme to place me at a school I could easily cycle to.
But as I sit beneath the very ceiling tiles I once knew as intimately as the freckles on my own arm, I also wonder if this was somehow destined. If I, as someone who loved school, was raised by a teacher, and married a teacher who was himself raised by a teacher, was always going to join the family business. Or if, like one of those eels that swims all the way from the silty bed of some Essex river out to the Sargasso Sea to spawn, only for its larvae to wriggle all 10,000 salty kilometres back home, I have been slowly making my way back to school since I left.
It is undeniably odd to find myself walking across the playground on which I first tasted Um Bongo, and heard the name the Strokes, and hid my first love bite under a sticky layer of foundation. As I hustle to a safeguarding meeting, or am escorted by my mentor to pick up my new printing code, I can’t help but remember treading that same route at 15, wearing a skirt I’d sewn myself out of wetsuit material (I stretched the definition of our school uniform back then until the seams screamed), or with the initials of the boy I fancied written in ballpoint pen on the inside of my thumb, or on the way to my last ever chemistry lesson.
I’m also far from the only person I know hole-punching their way into a new career after decades in the arts, media or what we used to laughingly call “the creative industries”. I can count at least four former journalists from my contingent retraining as English teachers, another who is well on their way to qualifying as a plumber, a DJ working as a midwife, and a fair crop of writers, poets and journalists working towards jobs as therapists.
The old story used to be that ambitious people worked as teachers for a few years and then went into creative fields – Romesh Ranganathan, Philip Pullman, Joanne Harris, Greg Davies and so on. But it seems to me that publishing, music, broadcasting and all the rest are now losing scores of mid-career artists to the world of education and other public services. Or rather, if you’re lucky, the ambition to press your thumb on to the surface of the world, through writing or performing, one day gives way to a far greater urge: to unfurl the thousands of brilliant minds coming up behind you.
I am genuinely as excited about reading Macbeth with a group of teenagers on plastic moulded chairs, as I ever was about speaking to a bookshop full of paying attenders. I am thrilled at the prospect of being able to dissect a novel over weeks in a classroom, rather than in minutes on the radio. I am delighted to be back in my old assembly hall, taking notes on a lined page, only this time with grey hairs, and two children down the road, and two decades of life in my rucksack.
And this time I don’t even need to bring in my PE kit.
- 
  Nell Frizzell is a journalist and author

Political scientist explains why Russia keeps Ukraine under constant shelling
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:56:44 EEST
17:56:44 KST

Political scientist explains why Russia keeps Ukraine under constant shelling
Kyiv • UNN
Russia has stockpiles, produces and receives missiles and drones, so massive attacks may continue for weeks. Expert Stanislav Zhelikhovskyi links the escalation to pressure on Ukraine and elections in the Russian Federation.
Russia may continue massive attacks and prolonged air-raid alerts in Ukraine. Journalist Stanislav Zhelikhovskyi, a political scientist specializing in international affairs, told a UNN journalist more about how long the Russian Federation's new tactics may last and why the escalation is taking place now.
Details
According to the expert's assessment, Russia has stocks of missiles and drones, continues to produce them, and additionally receives weapons from other countries. Therefore, it is still too early to talk about the rapid end of the current wave of attacks. However, certain periods of calm are possible.
I think that in the coming days, perhaps weeks, the Russian Federation will be able to do this, because it cannot be ruled out that it has accumulated a certain number of munitions, missiles, drones, and so on. And it is terrorizing [Ukraine] for as long as it can. I do not rule out that this could continue right up until the so-called parliamentary "elections" in Russia
Moscow is trying to pressure Ukrainians
The expert notes that Russia's capabilities are not limited to accumulated stockpiles. Instead, Moscow continues to produce missiles and drones and also receives certain types of weapons from abroad. According to him, this makes it possible to maintain the strikes even after using some of the accumulated resources.
In addition to the stockpiles they have, there is also the production of missiles, drones, and other capabilities. Russia imports weapons, including those same ballistic missiles. We can mention North Korea here. And therefore, this means that it has additional capabilities to strike Ukraine and carry out massive strikes
According to the political scientist, the duration and intensity of the attacks may vary depending on Russia's available resources. However, in his opinion, it is unlikely that they can be stopped completely in the near future. He also draws attention to Russia's preparations for the autumn-winter period.
There may be certain periods of calm if, for example, Russia really does not have enough jet-powered "Shaheds" or something else. Although, judging by the information available, they currently have enough options to continue this terror. In addition, we must also understand that Russia is preparing for the autumn-winter period
In addition to their military objective, the strikes also have a psychological dimension, in the expert's view.
I think that the more or less obvious reasons are that Putin wants to break the Ukrainians, to force them to agree to the ceasefire terms that we all know about, first and foremost the territorial aspects. Evidently, it is important for him to gain control over all of Donetsk and Luhansk regions
Also, according to Zhelikhovskyi, the current attacks are causing Ukraine not only human losses, unfortunately, but also economic damage. This concerns the impact on businesses, the energy sector, and the operation of various life-support systems.
Here, it is worth being patient, and the state of Ukraine needs to do everything possible to defend itself more effectively against such attacks, because they cause significant damage. First, this is a threat to human lives and health, and second, it is material damage to businesses, the Ukrainian economy, the energy sector, and so on
The attacks may be linked to the "elections" in Russia
The political scientist separately draws attention to another possible political calculation by the Kremlin. In his opinion, Putin may be interested in Ukraine carrying out large-scale retaliatory strikes against major Russian cities ahead of the so-called "elections" to the State Duma, so that he could then use this in Russian propaganda.
Putin, I think, would like Ukrainians to strike back, especially if we are talking about large Russian cities such as Moscow, St. Petersburg, and some others. And in this way he wants to demonstrate to his citizens: look, the Ukrainians are enraged at us; they are killing and destroying
In the expert's opinion, the Kremlin may use such strikes to accuse Ukraine of escalation and increase support for the pro-government party.
Support for "United Russia" would mean that citizens were thereby also voting for tougher measures against Ukraine, including new mobilization measures. And thus, in effect, the elections would turn into a kind of referendum for Russians—whether they support the war or not
The political scientist believes that the number of attacks may fluctuate, but air raid alerts will most likely remain regular. This particularly concerns Kyiv and the capital region.
I think that it may, but not by very much; after all, there are also certain limitations on these capabilities in Russia. That is, they may be either in the quantity they currently have, or increase or decrease slightly, but the regularity may continue
The expert assumes that the current situation may continue until the "elections" in Russia, that is, until September 20.
There will not be a single day without an alert, at least in Kyiv and some other cities. And one way or another, these attacks will be serious and have consequences. This may continue at least until the "elections" to the State Duma, and afterward it will become clear from the situation what Putin will want to do

Ukraine Blinds Russian Defenses in Bryansk, Hitting Radar, EW System and MESH Network

Ukraine Blinds Russian Defenses in Bryansk, Hitting Radar, EW System and MESH Network
Ukrainian forces struck several Russian military systems in Russia’s Bryansk region, including a radar station, an electronic warfare complex, and a relay supporting a MESH communications network.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s General Staff on September 5, the strikes were carried out on September 4 and targeted military infrastructure at three separate locations across the region.
A Russian radar station was hit near Kartushino, while an electronic warfare system was targeted in the area of Pogar. Ukrainian forces also struck a MESH network relay in Zlynka, the General Staff said.
The General Staff did not identify the specific models of the radar or electronic warfare systems involved, meaning their exact capabilities and value cannot yet be independently assessed.
Radar stations are used for tasks ranging from airspace surveillance and target detection to supporting air defense and other military operations. Electronic warfare systems can be employed to detect, disrupt, or suppress radio communications, navigation signals, and drone control links.
The MESH relay represents a different part of the communications infrastructure. In a mesh network, individual nodes can relay data between one another rather than relying exclusively on a single central communications point.
Such architecture can extend communications coverage and provide alternative routes for data if individual links are disrupted. The General Staff did not specify which Russian MESH system was targeted or what units it supported.
Ukrainian forces also struck a repair facility used by a Russian military unit in Sokolohirsk in the temporarily occupied Luhansk region.
“The extent of the damage is being clarified. Work on the enemy’s key military targets continues. More to come!” Ukraine’s General Staff said.
Earlier, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said its Group 13 unit struck a Russian Bastion coastal missile system in temporarily occupied Crimea, a platform capable of launching both Onyx and Zircon missiles.

Border Police officer’s final hours: new details emerge in deadly Netanya shootout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:49:45 UTC
17:49:45 KST

The investigation into the death of Border Police Sgt. David Hoyer Amrani, who was fatally shot after opening fire in Netanya’s Kiryat Hasharon neighborhood, is still in its early stages, with new details emerging about the minutes leading up to the deadly encounter.
Ynet has learned that because police officers were involved in the shooting, the case is expected to be transferred in the coming hours or days to the Justice Ministry’s Police Internal Investigations Department. Amrani’s funeral is due to take place Sunday at the Even Yehuda cemetery.
Amrani, 20, was shot by police and Border Police personnel after officers said he opened fire in the area. He was initially listed in critical condition and later died of his wounds. No one else was injured.
Before the confrontation, Amrani was seen carrying an M16 rifle. Officials initially suspected he might be suffering from combat trauma, but the Defense Ministry’s Rehabilitation Department said he had not been treated there for post-traumatic stress disorder and was not known to the system as a PTSD patient.
Amrani enlisted for compulsory service in the Border Police in August 2024 and served in the West Bank, including in Hebron after completing his training. People who knew him said there was nothing in the days before the incident that suggested what was about to happen. They said he had even ironed and prepared his clothes for another workweek before leaving home with his weapon.
According to testimony collected at the scene, Amrani spent roughly 20 minutes moving between residential buildings while firing bursts into the air. Police who arrived initially identified him as an armed suspect without knowing the circumstances and reportedly feared a possible terrorist attack.
Witnesses said that at one stage Amrani advanced toward officers while continuing to fire into the air. A gunbattle then broke out and he was shot. He later died of his wounds.
Neighborhood resident Avigail Cohen told ynet that the shooting went on for an extended period and sent residents scrambling for cover.
“There were lots of shots and it took the police time to arrive,” she said. “He was shooting into the air. People went into safe places. We were in the garden with my little sister, everything was calm, and then we saw people panicking. We started hearing bursts of gunfire.”
“We went up into buildings, into people’s apartments,” she added. “He started moving toward our area and we hid in the apartment of a wonderful woman. It lasted something like 20 minutes.”
Her brother Harel said he first heard gunfire from the direction of the stadium.
“I saw him reach my building. He barricaded himself there,” he said. “I reported all the details to the police and ran to my room to get my weapon, to be ready. He looked lucid. He just moved between the buildings and fired into the air.”
The new details are also raising questions about whether there were warning signs that were missed before the shooting.
Attorney Idan Kleiman, chairman of the IDF Disabled Veterans Organization, told Ynet that he understood Amrani had previously asked to be transferred to another sector.
“That is a warning light,” Kleiman said. “If someone had taken it seriously and asked ‘why?’ we might have reached the stage of support and treatment. There has to be a very clear address, a phone number, for every soldier and member of the security forces, and treatment has to begin as soon as distress appears.”
“In his case there was a warning sign, and unfortunately the system apparently did not pick it up,” he added.
Kleiman warned that similar cases could recur if security personnel are not identified and supported earlier.
“I think we are on the edge of an abyss,” he said. “Israel knows how to find its fighters when it wants them to go out to the battlefield, but it also has to know how to find them when they come back and take care of them.”
“We will not be able to prevent everything. There will unfortunately be tragedies, but we have to make an extraordinary effort to care for these brave fighters and save as many as possible.”

US envoys head to Kyiv after talks with Putin
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
11:49:45 EEST
17:49:45 KST

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are due in Kyiv on Sunday for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy after spending more than three hours with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, as Washington seeks a route towards ending the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin and White House described Saturday’s meeting in positive terms but disclosed few details.
The White House said the meeting covered “substantive plans for next steps” and said further details would emerge in the coming weeks.
Witkoff and Kushner will now present the results of their Moscow discussions during their first wartime visit to the Ukrainian capital.
Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov said the US representatives presented several ideas on possible routes towards a settlement. He did not disclose their contents. Ushakov described the discussions as useful and frank and said the meeting also covered economic relations between Russia and the United States.
“The talks went beyond a mere exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis,” Ushakov said. He said the delegations discussed economic questions and possible joint Russian-US projects.
The lack of detail left no public evidence of a change in the positions that have divided Moscow and Kyiv through previous rounds of diplomacy.
Putin told the US delegation that Russia remained confident about achieving its military objectives. According to Ushakov, the Russian president also repeated Moscow’s demand that negotiations address what the Kremlin calls the “root causes” of the war.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Russian forces occupy about one-fifth of Ukrainian territory. The ground front stretches for about 1,250 kilometres, with limited territorial changes despite months of fighting.
Moscow has continued to demand Ukrainian territorial concessions. The Kremlin said on Friday that Putin stood by terms he set out two years ago, including Ukrainian withdrawal from four regions claimed by Russia and an end to Kyiv’s plans to join NATO.
Ukraine rejects those demands and has refused to surrender territory that remains under its control.
A person close to the Kremlin told Reuters before the latest diplomatic mission that Putin intended to continue military operations until Russian forces had taken the remaining Ukrainian-held areas of the Donetsk region. The source said Putin believed Russian forces would achieve that objective by the end of 2026. Western military analysts cited by Reuters dispute that timetable because of the rate of Russian advances.
US President Donald Trump sent Witkoff and Kushner to Moscow after saying on Friday that Washington had prepared a proposal intended to end the war. Trump did not disclose its terms.
Putin thanked Trump for his diplomatic efforts when he welcomed the two representatives at the Kremlin.
“The situation is, of course, not simple,” Putin said in remarks shown on Russian television. He asked the envoys to pass his greetings and thanks to Trump before the closed meeting began.
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that he had already spoken with Witkoff and Kushner and was prepared for further discussions.
The diplomatic activity comes alongside continued missile and drone attacks.
Russian strikes on Saturday killed at least seven people, according to Ukrainian officials. Five people died in an attack on a factory in the Dnipro region, while strikes in the Kyiv area also caused deaths. Other attacks damaged buildings in southern and central Ukraine.
Zelenskyy said Russia had also struck airports in Kyiv and Boryspil before the US delegation’s expected arrival. He described those attacks as a Russian response to the possibility that the envoys would travel to Kyiv.
Ukraine’s airspace has remained closed to normal civilian traffic since the full-scale invasion began, and foreign delegations have generally entered the country by train.
Russia has agreed to suspend attacks on Kyiv for three days during the US visit. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin ordered the pause to protect the delegation.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine would refrain from strikes on Moscow through Monday.
“Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
The temporary arrangement applies to the two capitals. No broader ceasefire has been announced.
Long-range attacks have increased in recent months. Russia has sent missiles and drones against Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, while Ukraine has targeted Russian military sites, oil refineries, terminals and other infrastructure.
A Russian strike on Friday hit the headquarters of Ukraine’s SBU security service. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have disrupted fuel supplies and contributed to higher domestic fuel prices.

'Security zone'

Hezbollah has not commented on the announcement or confirmed that Israel has captured the site.
Also this week, the International Committee of the Red Cross facilitated the transfer to Lebanon of five people detained by Israel.
Israel and Lebanon began direct negotiations after the latest hostilities erupted, with fresh talks expected this month, though no date has been announced.

Ukraine Abstains as UN Backs Equal Earth Map Showing Crimea Separate From Ukraine

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:48:00 UTC
17:48:00 KST

Ukraine abstained during a United Nations vote on the adoption of the Equal Earth world map projection after the depiction showed the temporarily occupied Crimean peninsula separated from the rest of Ukrainian territory, the Permanent Mission of Ukraine to the UN announced.
The Equal Earth map depicts Crimea in a distinctly lighter shade than mainland Ukraine, while also distinguishing it from the color used for Russia. Other sovereign territories subject to Russian occupation – such as regions within Georgia and Moldova – did not receive distinct cartographic demarcations on the map.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukrainian lawmaker Kira Rudik stated that the altered depiction directly drove Ukraine’s decision to abstain from the resolution, which was initiated by the West African nation of Togo. “In 2026, the UN should not need a reminder: Crimea is Ukraine. Shame,” Rudik wrote.
                                                                                                                                                                         
In an official statement, Ukraine’s Permanent Mission emphasized that while Kyiv supports efforts to eliminate historical distortions concerning the relative scale of continents – particularly across Africa and the Global South – the cartographic representation of occupied Ukrainian territory constitutes an unacceptable violation of the UN Charter and international law. Ukrainian diplomats noted that prior negotiations with the draft resolution’s sponsors failed to produce a compromise text.
Analysis: Pro-Russia AfD Eyes First German State Government as Support Surges
“Such a misinterpretation could open a Pandora’s box, effectively facilitating abuses and distortions of the political map of the world,” the mission stated.
“It is regrettable that while correcting grave historical injustices of the past and finally addressing the horrific consequences of colonialism, particularly in Africa, we may simultaneously create new and no less serious problems, opening the door to misinterpretations and creating ambiguity that runs counter to the interests of every member state.”
The Equal Earth map projection was originally designed in 2018 as an equal-area pseudocylindrical projection to more accurately represent the true relative landmass of continental land areas, notably correcting the disproportionately shrunken scale of the African continent common to traditional Mercator projections.
Previous United Nations friction
The cartographic dispute follows recent diplomatic friction at the United Nations regarding allied declarations on the war.
On Aug. 24, 50 nations endorsed a joint statement at the UN marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence, condemning ongoing Russian strikes and demanding a full, immediate, and unconditional ceasefire. However, the US declined to co-sign the declaration, which was presented by Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen.
The stance reflected earlier instances in which Washington refrained from endorsing specific Ukrainian-backed UN declarations. In late May, the US did not join a statement condemning Russian threats of systematic strikes against Kyiv, following a similar decision in late 2025 regarding a document characterizing Moscow’s aggression as an “unprovoked war.”
Russian UN Ambassador Vasily Nebenzya dismissed the August ceasefire appeal, characterizing international efforts to halt the conflict along existing frontlines as attempts to impose a freeze that are “doomed to fail.”
Nebenzya insisted that Moscow would reject any agreement that compromises its perceived security interests, arguing that diplomatic progress remains impossible without acknowledging what he termed the “situation on the ground.”

Excavations begin at Hadrian’s city
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:47:32 UTC
17:47:32 KST

AA Photo
Archaeological excavations have begun at Hadrianoi, an ancient city founded by Roman Emperor Hadrian on the southern slopes of Mount Uludağ.
Traces of Hadrianoi, a city founded by Roman Emperor Hadrian in 123 A.D. in what is now the northwestern province of Bursa’s Orhaneli district, are being uncovered through archaeological excavations.
The excavations are being carried out across an area of approximately five decares under the leadership of the Bursa Museum Directorate, under the scientific supervision of Professor Derya Şahin, a faculty member in the Archaeology Department of Bursa Uludağ University’s Faculty of Arts and Sciences.
The excavations aim to precisely locate the ancient city of Hadrianoi, which Roman Emperor Hadrian founded in 123 A.D. in an area where he hunted on the southern slopes of Mount Uludağ, and to reveal the historical importance of the region.
Bursa Museum Director Ahmet Türkmenoğlu told state-run Anadolu Agency that Orhaneli, one of Bursa’s oldest districts, has been inhabited since the Roman period.
Noting that the existence of a city called Hadrianoi in the district has long been known, Türkmenoğlu said: “Following an earthquake, Roman Emperor Hadrian came to Anatolia to inspect the area and particularly toured what we call the regions of Mysia and Bithynia. During this journey, he visited İzmit and İznik and then traveled toward Erdek. As he passed through this area, he stopped at the foothills of Mount Uludağ and presumably founded a city here, naming it Hadrianoi. Why did he establish it here? Because Hadrian was very fond of hunting, and this area was quite ideal for hunting.”
Türkmenoğlu said there was also a road in the area that had been actively used since the Roman period.
“This road passes through Harmancık and leads to Kütahya and Balıkesir, and it is still in use today. The city was established along this road. There are also thermal springs in the region. They may have been used at the time as well. In fact, there are many reasons why the city could have been established here,” he said.
HH A completely untouched landscape
Emphasizing that historical sources also document the foundation of Hadrianoi in 123 A.D., Türkmenoğlu said archaeological excavations had therefore begun at the site.
He noted that the team first had to conduct extensive clearing work.
“Because we entered a completely untouched landscape. After completing the clearing work, we realized that we were inside a huge, monumental structure. It may be an agora, a marketplace, or perhaps a gymnasium, an educational complex. We will learn this as we excavate,” he said.
Türkmenoğlu said the excavation is currently being carried out by a five-person team.
“The point we are excavating is very close to the entrance of the monumental structure, particularly its main wall. We first want to reach the floor of the structure. The findings we obtain there will shed light on the site and help us uncover the structure. This will also allow us to determine its architectural layout,” he said.
He added that other parts of the site would be excavated over time.
“Within such a monumental structure, as we continue excavating, we may naturally encounter sculptural works, particularly in the lower sections. The structure is visible today. Although the exterior walls have collapsed, in many places we can clearly see the walls and architectural elements in situ, meaning in their original positions,” Türkmenoğlu said.
He added that the archaeological excavations and subsequent work at the site could create an important destination for cultural tourism in Türkiye.

World’s most powerful lightning-chasing satellite joins China-Nepal flood relief efforts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:47:12 UTC
17:47:12 KST

World’s most powerful lightning-chasing satellite joins China-Nepal flood relief efforts
The Fengyun-4C’s storm-tracking abilities could provide vital early warnings about extreme weather events during the rescue operation
China is using the world’s most powerful geostationary weather satellite to track severe thunderstorms over Nepal and deliver real-time intelligence as the two countries continue search and rescue operations following last month’s devastating glacier collapse.
The Fengyun‑4C satellite – launched last December and now positioned 36,000km (22,000 miles) above the equator – carries a Lightning Mapping Imager (LMI) that captures 500 frames per second, sifting through 30 gigabits of data every second to pinpoint individual lightning strokes.
That processing power, engineers say, is equivalent to playing 30 high-definition films a second and spotting every traffic light in each one.
In the hours after the glacier disaster struck on August 26, Beijing set up a cross-border emergency monitoring observation mechanism, according to state news agency Xinhua.
At the core of that response is the LMI’s continuous animation, which gives meteorologists a sharp, frame‑by‑frame view of lightning activity inside severe storms.
Combined with the Fengyun‑4C series’ cloud animations, convective initiation data, rainfall estimates and precipitation measurements from the Fengyun‑3G satellite, the system allows forecasters to track regional rainfall and weather changes in real time.
As the most obvious sign of extreme weather, lightning can reveal where storms are intensifying, how fast they are moving and when they might unleash flash floods, landslides or destructive winds.

UIPM integrates Obstacle World Championships into Beijing's city vibe
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:44 CST
17:41:44 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- As the UIPM 2026 Obstacle World Championships concluded at Beijing's Universal CityWalk on Sunday, UIPM President Rob Stull and Secretary General Shiny Fang described the event as a successful example of integrating competitions into urban settings.
It marks the second consecutive year the obstacle worlds is held in Beijing. Last year, the National Olympic Sports Center hosted the first edition after obstacle was incorporated into modern pentathlon.
"I was very happy with the previous venues. They were beautiful and well-organized. But this venue [Universal Studios] is really about entertainment, and that is the difference," Stull said. "Universal is such a worldwide known brand. Out of a sports venue, and get into a themed park. For everybody, it's a great opportunity."
At the 2024 Paris Olympics, many events were held at the iconic urban sites, including the Palace of Versailles and the Eiffel Tower.
"We saw what could be done in terms of these iconic sites. It was really cool and highly successful for everyone. We took some inspiration from the Paris Games, absolutely," said Stull.
As a new discipline within modern pentathlon, obstacle will replace equestrian and make its Olympic debut at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.
"The next Games in Los Angeles is a very different setup. Los Angeles doesn't have locations like Paris, but we have Hollywood," Stull said. "Modern pentathlon is in the urban cluster. It's about 3x3 basketball, skateboarding, BMX freestyle, to name a few. These are whole youth things with urban vibes."
This year's five-day Obstacle World Championships features the 100m individual, 400m individual, 4x100m relay, 3km individual and 3km team competitions, while U11 and U13 groups are introduced to the 100m and 3km events.
"For the young kids in Asia, they have their typical sports such as table tennis and badminton. Normally, we think these types of things like the obstacle run is more for western people. But the truth is that every kid has a nature. When they see the obstacles, they just want to overcome all these," said Fang. "That is why we try to encourage more children and teenagers to participate in this challenging event."
According to the UIPM calendar, the Obstacle World Championships will also take place in Beijing in the next two years.
"We will be happy to come back here at the Universal Studios, but we don't have an answer yet. Not only the Universal Studios but also other famous places could be considered as well. I believe we have more opportunities next year," said Fang. ■

Chinese literature finds growing readership in Russia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:38 CST
17:41:38 KST

by Xinhua writers Vladislava Chugueva, Zhang Chaoqun
MOSCOW, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Literature from China is finding an increasingly receptive audience in Russia, with works by Chinese authors gaining popularity and attracting growing interest from local publishers.
At the ongoing 39th Moscow International Book Fair, where China is the Guest of Honour, more than 2,000 titles and nearly 5,000 copies of China-themed books are on display as part of the Guest of Honour program themed "Reading China."
For Russian publishers, the growing appeal of Chinese literature has created new opportunities to introduce a wider range of Chinese works to the market.
Eksmo, one of Russia's largest general-interest publishing houses, has become a key publisher of translated Chinese-language works.
Eksmo editor Daria Shpakovskaya told Xinhua that books set in ancient China are particularly popular among young Russian readers.
"It doesn't matter whether it's fantasy or not. The men in robes, the women in beautiful costumes, the intrigue, the complicated relationships -- that's what makes it great. It's something new, and that's what really draws people in," she said.
The rising appeal of Chinese literature has also been fueled by the rising presence of Asian animation, television series and games in Russia.
"Interest in China is now fashionable, and even though I'm no longer young, I see that the children of my friends are immersed not in European culture, but in Asian culture," said Andrey Chernikov, an international copyright specialist at Eksmo.
Shpakovskaya said that through literature, television and visual arts, Russian readers are gaining a better understanding of Chinese culture, which helps foster closer cultural exchanges between the two countries. She noted that many young Chinese people are also choosing to study in Russia.
"We are very pleased that the Chinese side has also become interested in the Russian market. There is a real cultural exchange. We are interested in their literature, and they are interested in ours," she said.
Eksmo also publishes Russian-language editions of novels by Chinese writer Mo Yan. The editions have gained popularity in the Russian market, with stylish cover designs to attract younger readers.
Shpakovskaya added that young readers are drawn to Mo Yan not only because of his reputation as a renowned Chinese writer, but also because his works feature diverse narrative styles and explore a wide range of themes.
Staff at the publishing house said that while Mo Yan is regarded as a major literary figure, the modern presentation of his works has helped bring his writing to a younger generation.
"Mo Yan's readership consists not of teenagers, but rather of new-adult audiences," Shpakovskaya said. "Still, many dedicated fans of Asian literature and members of fandom communities are willing to take on his dense and complex works." ■

China Focus: Overseas visitors look beyond landmarks to experience everyday China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:22 CST
17:41:22 KST

TIANJIN, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Wearing a pair of mixed reality glasses, Ugandan content creator Kaziro Grace Mukisa found himself standing among Beijing's old streets, where virtual figures from the ancient Chinese myth "Classic of Mountains and Seas" appeared to emerge from the pages of the book and blend into the real world around him.
He reached out repeatedly, adjusting his view and interacting with the digital images floating in front of him.
"You could see animated characters appearing alongside real-life scenes. It was very vivid and immersive," Mukisa said at the 2026 China Culture & Tourism Industries Expo in north China's Tianjin Municipality, which concluded on Sunday.
Around the expo, technology is giving visitors new ways to engage with Chinese culture.
At the four-day event, visitors encountered a wide range of emerging tourism experiences. Humanoid robots performed on stage, a robotic horse walked steadily along a simulated mountain trail, and a robot chef prepared food. Visitors could also immerse themselves in traditional Chinese crafts, including New Year paintings, porcelain making and the inside painting of snuff bottles.
Sri Lankan tour guide Amila was drawn to a camping vehicle displayed at the expo. After stepping inside and carefully examining its space and facilities, he said the vehicle was a fresh experience for him and offers many more possibilities when traveling.
Amila, who has visited China many times over the past two decades, said he had witnessed improvements in tourism services and infrastructure.
"China has rich historical and cultural heritage as well as diverse natural landscapes. I love visiting museums in different places and exploring World Heritage sites," he said, adding that services such as online ticket booking, facial recognition entry and smart audio guides have made travel more convenient.
In Tianjin, some overseas visitors are looking beyond the city's best-known attractions, choosing mountain homestays or wandering through local neighborhoods instead.
Tuane van der Merwe from South Africa recently traveled to the city's Jizhou District with her parents, choosing a mountain homestay instead of popular urban attractions. Surrounded by nature, they could view the Great Wall from their accommodation.
"Here, you can see the city and nature together as one," Tuane van der Merwe said. "It's just amazing."
Another travel blogger, Billy, explored Tianjin's neighborhoods, focusing on ordinary scenes rather than famous landmarks: breakfast shops filled with morning aromas, people walking along the Haihe River and conversations echoing near bridges at dusk.
For him, these everyday moments revealed another side of the city.
Such experiences are emerging as China's inbound tourism continues to grow. A recent economic impact study by the World Travel & Tourism Council showed that international visitor spending in China reached 135 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, up 10.5 percent year on year, exceeding the global average growth rate of 3.2 percent.
Meanwhile, easier entry policies have given international travelers more options. Since China optimized its transit visa-free policies in December 2024, inbound travel facilitation measures have continued to take effect. Data from the National Immigration Administration showed that China recorded 22.91 million inbound foreign visits in the first half of this year, up 20.4 percent year on year. Of those, 77.7 percent were made under visa-free entry facilitation policies.
Olesia Razumnaia, general manager of Sunmar Travel Agency in Russia, said overseas tourists were increasingly shifting from simply visiting attractions to experiencing local culture and daily life, with more interest in immersive and experiential travel.
China is responding by developing more diversified tourism products. The country's tourism development plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) calls for creating themed tourism products featuring food, traditional crafts, history and culture, technology experiences, wellness, study tours, festivals and shopping.
"Tourism is not only a bridge for cultural exchanges and closer connections between peoples, but also an important window for presenting a real, multidimensional China," said Wang Wei, vice president of the China Association of Travel Services and senior vice president of Trip.com Group.
Richard Matuzevich, senior manager of the External Liaison Department of the World Tourism Cities Federation, said China's diverse tourism experiences allow visitors to discover a more complete and modern picture of the country.
"A first visit is about getting to know China. A return visit is about experiencing China," he said. ■

Australian housing affordability hits record low in 2026: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
16:41:12 CST
17:41:12 KST

CANBERRA, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- Housing affordability in Australia deteriorated to a record low in the 2026 financial year, with elevated home prices and higher mortgage rates substantially reducing households' borrowing capacity, a report finds.
A typical-income household earning about 125,000 Australian dollars (about 90,000 U.S. dollars) a year could afford to buy just 12 percent of homes sold nationwide, the lowest level on record and below the previous low of 14 percent in the 2008 financial year, according to the report released Saturday by realestate.com.au.
Affordability is particularly challenging for low-income households. Those earning 76,000 Australian dollars annually could afford to buy just 2 percent of homes sold in the past year, essentially locking them out of the housing market, the Housing Affordability Report said.
The decline came following the Reserve Bank of Australia's three consecutive interest rate hikes in February, March and May to dampen inflation, the report noted.
Higher borrowing costs more than offset income growth and softening home prices toward the end of the financial year. As a result, housing affordability has declined nationwide, it said.
Affordability declined in all states in the 2026 financial year, with South Australia becoming the country's least affordable state, overtaking the state of New South Wales, the report showed.
A median-income household in South Australia could afford just 7 percent of homes, with the state capital Adelaide's median home value reaching 940,000 Australian dollars, it said. ■

17:40:35 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin held more than three hours of "highly useful" talks on Saturday with two U.S. envoys seeking a deal to end the Ukraine war, a Kremlin aide said, but he gave no indication of any breakthrough.
The aide, Yuri Ushakov, said Americans Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner "outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement." Ushakov did not say what these ideas were.
He said Putin had told the pair that Russia was making "real progress" on the battlefield and was confident of achieving its goals, while stressing the necessity of addressing "all the root causes of the conflict."
These are statements that Moscow has made repeatedly since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Russia's smaller neighbor in February 2022. Both sides have intensified long-range air strikes in recent weeks while the front lines remain largely static.
Putin praises Trump's efforts
A White House official told Reuters the talks had been "substantive" and that next steps would be announced in the coming weeks.
There was no comment from Witkoff and Kushner, who were visiting Moscow for the first time since January on behalf of President Donald Trump. They flew out of Moscow soon after the talks and are due to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Kyiv on Sunday.
"The talks went beyond a mere exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis. Economic issues and potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in some detail," Ushakov said. "Overall, one can say that the negotiations were timely and highly useful for both sides."
Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev posted on X that the meeting had been an "important peacemaking visit." He and Ushakov were both present at the meeting.
The Russian president praised Trump's efforts to end the war.
"Understanding that he is entering a difficult situation, he nevertheless does not stop his efforts to help bring about a settlement and to make his contribution to resolving the Russian-Ukrainian conflict," Putin said in televised remarks at the start of the talks.
Trump suggested on Friday that the U.S. had a fresh proposal aimed at ending the war but did not elaborate.
Putin promised to ensure the safety of the U.S. negotiators. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said earlier that Putin had ordered the Russian military not to strike Kyiv for three days because of their trip.
A vast gulf in positions
Over the previous 10 days, Russia pounded the Ukrainian capital day and night with missiles and drones, including an attack on Friday on the headquarters of the SBU security service.
Ukraine has inflicted damaging hits throughout the summer on Russian refineries, oil terminals and warehouses of online retailer Wildberries, in an attempt to raise the cost to Moscow of continuing the war. Zelenskiy said Kyiv was prepared to refrain from strikes on Moscow through Monday.
Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on how to end the war, the deadliest in Europe since World War Two.
A person close to the Kremlin, speaking before reports emerged of the trip by Trump's envoys, said Putin was still intent on capturing more territory.
"There is no chance of reaching an agreement regarding the front line until Putin finishes securing the remaining part of the Donetsk region," this person told Reuters, adding that the Kremlin leader was confident — based on reports from his commanders — that this would happen by the end of the year.
Western military analysts see such a possibility as remote, given Moscow's slow rate of progress. Ukraine has refused to surrender land it has successfully defended at huge cost, and rejects such terms as tantamount to surrender.
The Kremlin said on Friday the position that Putin set out in a speech two years ago — that Ukraine should cede the entire territory of four regions claimed by Russia and abandon its plan to join NATO — was "unshakeable."

Giant mechanical elephants open Taipei Arts Festival

2026-09-06

17:40:10 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Three giant mechanical elephants took over the streets of Taipei’s Shilin District on Saturday, with crowds peaking at about 100,000 for the opening of the 2026 Taipei Arts Festival.
The free outdoor performance, titled “Trois Elephants Passent…” (“Three Elephants Pass…”), was staged by French street theater company Compagnie Oposito in collaboration with Taiwanese performers.
The three mechanical elephants, each nearly 5 meters tall, were accompanied by performers, musicians, and large mechanical birds as they traveled along Jihe Road toward the Taipei Performing Arts Center.
The procession began at 7:14 p.m., a time chosen to reference 1914, when Taipei’s first zoo was established. The approximately one-hour parade was followed by a stage performance outside the performing arts center, per a press release.
Horns and heavy drumbeats accompanied the elephants as costumed performers moved through the streets alongside the giant machines. The production combined street theater, music, and visual spectacle, temporarily turning the area into an open-air theater.
The Taipei Department of Cultural Affairs said crowds along the parade route reached about 100,000 at the event’s peak. The department described the performance as an opportunity to transform Taipei into a “city theater without a roof.”
The turnout also created difficulties for spectators. Some people complained online about crowded viewing areas, long waits, and problems moving through the area, per China Times.
Organizers recommended that people attending Sunday’s performance use alternative viewing locations if they could not find a suitable position along the route. The performance was also scheduled to be livestreamed on the Taipei Performing Arts Center’s YouTube channel from 7:14 p.m. to 8:45 p.m.
Sunday’s parade was scheduled to begin at 7:14 p.m. at the Shin Kong Life Insurance Shilin Education Center and proceed to the Taipei Performing Arts Center plaza.
Traffic restrictions were planned around the route. Jihe Road between Zhongzheng and Wenlin roads was to be closed during the performance, with drivers advised to use Chengde Road, Zhongshan North Road, or Wenlin Road as alternative north-south routes, per Liberty Times.
Compagnie Oposito, founded in 1982, is known for large-scale street performances and urban festivals. The production was inspired in part by images of animals traveling through Taipei’s streets when the city zoo moved from Yuanshan to Muzha in 1986.
The 2026 Taipei Arts Festival will continue through Oct. 25 with performances and cultural events across the city.

Russia is failing to export its new grain harvest in time and is losing export revenues - intelligence

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06

Russia is failing to export its new grain harvest in time and is losing export revenues - intelligence
Kyiv • UNN
In August, Russia’s grain exports fell 2.5-fold. In September, wheat shipments could decline by another 52.1–62.5%.
russia has faced problems exporting grain from the new harvest. In August, its shipments fell 2.5-fold, while in September wheat exports may drop by more than half again. This is reported by the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
russia is failing to ship out grain from the new harvest in time. From August 1–20, exports fell 2.5-fold, to 1.4 million tonnes, while wheat exports fell 2.6-fold. In September, wheat exports may decline by a further 52.1–62.5%, to 1.8–2.3 million tonnes—the lowest level since 2010. Excess grain is driving down the domestic market. Over the week, prices for wheat, barley, sunflower and soybeans fell by 3.3–8.5%, and over the year by more than 40%
In addition, according to available information, on August 28 Rostov Region, which accounts for nearly 10% of russia’s harvest, introduced a state of emergency due to problems with grain exports.
the kremlin is responding by preparing state purchases, concessional loans, subsidies and loans secured by unsold crops. The cancellation of the export duty and compensation for expensive shipments to alternative ports are also being considered. This will not solve the problem. Up to 70% of russia’s grain exports passed through southern ports, while alternative routes lack sufficient capacity. Transporting grain to the Baltic Sea adds $30–50 per tonne, making exports even less profitable
According to the intelligence service, the problems have already affected major agricultural companies. Net profit at the russian agricultural holding Rusagro collapsed by 99% in the first half of the year—from 4.8 billion to 55.88 million rubles.
The state is effectively paying for grain to remain in storage. Concessional loans will not create demand, subsidies will not increase port capacity, and cheap money will not replace broken logistics. If exports do not recover, stocks will grow, prices will fall, and the losses will be shifted onto the budget and banks of the russian federation
Previously
Due to the shutdown of ports in Rostov Region, grain that cannot be exported has piled up. Wheat exports have fallen to their lowest level in 16 years.

Vast new archaeological site opens in Geneva
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:34:21 UTC
17:34:21 KST

Vast new archaeological site opens in Geneva
The grand opening ceremony for the new Saint-Antoine archaeological site (SaSA) delighted the public on Saturday in Geneva. Located beneath the Théodelinde Esplanade, this space, covering nearly 1,000m², showcases exceptional remains spanning two millennia of history.
“There was already a large crowd at the opening,” said Cindy Dulac, the manager of SaSA. Many local residents, curious visitors and families came to explore this new site, which has taken years of work to complete.
Its story began in 2010 during the redevelopment of the esplanade, when some exceptional archaeological remains were discovered. The site was then subjected to meticulous excavations between 2012 and 2015. Given the significance of the heritage finds, the authorities decided to protect them and make them accessible to the public.
More
Why Switzerland is an archaeological treasure trove
A project with a budget of CHF14.5 million ($18 million) was subsequently approved. The extensive construction project began in September 2023 and was completed recently.
Two thousand years of history
Three skylights provide natural light to highlight the historical periods on display. Even without descending into the site, it is possible to see part of the excavations from the new esplanade. Entry is via one of the skylights. Visitors descend a few steps to immerse themselves in two millennia of Geneva’s history.
The temperature is pleasant (22.5C) and the light soft. Visitors can wander around a 1st-century Gallo-Roman settlement, a necropolis containing over 300 graves used between the 3rd and 13th centuries, and part of the 5th-century funeral church of Saint-Laurent. There are also remains of 16th-century fortifications.
Further research
One skeleton is of particular interest to visitors. “It is that of a woman who was between 25 and 50 years old at the time of her death,” explained the guide. She shows no signs of having suffered any violence, he added. This is the only skeleton on display to the public. The others are being kept for further research.
More
A sensational Swiss discovery thanks to volunteers: archaeology for all
The SaSA is also designed as a scientific platform. There is still much research to be carried out on the remains that have been discovered, said Dulac. Scientists will be invited to take up residencies. A cultural space is open for contemporary artists to hold temporary exhibitions.
The opening celebrations continued until late Saturday afternoon. Younger visitors were able to try their hand at archaeological excavations, using spades and trowels in large containers. The official part of the event took place on Friday evening in the presence of officials from the canton and the City of Geneva.

Why China’s shrinking population may be a blessing, not a curse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:30:07 UTC
17:30:07 KST

Alex Lo has been an SCMP columnist since 2012, commenting on China and international affairs.
There is little in common between Daron Acemoglu and Xi Jinping. As a strong advocate of the Western model of liberal democracy, Acemoglu, co-recipient of the 2024 Nobel Prize in economics, may be considered the ideological opposite of the Chinese president.
But on a crucial point about China’s future, the two may, strangely, be on the same page: an across-the-board introduction of cutting-edge technology may enhance productivity and maintain economic growth. It may counteract the negative impact of drastic population decline in the decades ahead.
While that may be an emerging consensus among economists and other social scientists, it still runs counter to the popular narrative that a rapidly greying China is doomed. The official figures released in January, for example, set off alarmism. China’s population fell by 3.39 million last year to just over 1.4 billion – a fourth consecutive decline and the steepest so far. Births dropped by 17 per cent to 7.92 million, the lowest since records began in 1949. Roughly 323 million Chinese, close to a quarter of the population, are now over 60.
The reaction was swift and familiar: China will grow old before it grows rich, its workforce will hollow out, its pension system will buckle, its ascent will end.
Some concerns are warranted. If 2.1 children per woman is the population replacement rate, then those countries with the lowest birth rates – China at 0.63, Japan at 0.6, and South Korea at 0.46 – are projected by 2050 to experience population declines of 20-30 per cent relative to 2023; their share of the population aged 65 and over to reach 30-40 per cent; and older workers (aged 45 and over) to comprise 60 per cent of the labour force.
02:58
What might China do to address its record low birth rate and declining population?
But that’s not the whole story. In fact, much of it is missing, and the alarm has outrun the analysis. “What if the historical evidence tells us that collapsing birth rates, paradoxically, are good for the economy,” economist Joeri Schasfoort asks in his YouTube channel, “because they force companies to innovate?”

Zionist Home-The Reservists chairmen Chili Tropper and Yoaz Hendel on Sunday announced they would pursue "separate political paths," while stressing that their ideological partnership and decades-long friendship remain intact.
Later on Sunday, Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party announced that Tropper will be given sixth place on its party list for the elections.
In a joint statement, the two recalled more than 20 years as neighbors and friends, sitting alongside one another in synagogue and serving together for several years in the reserves.
“We both chose to try to serve the public through the political arena as well,” they said. “In some cases together and in all other cases separately, but with a very similar ideological outlook.”
The statement came less than two months after Tropper and Hendel announced that they would run together in the upcoming Knesset election, seeking to create what they described at the time as a significant new Zionist political force.
Their party had failed to pass the electoral threshold in recent polling, along with a group of other small right-wing parties that have recently emerged, which have been informally termed "the third bloc."
“In recent weeks, we established Zionist Home-The Reservists together, with a clear goal: establishing a Zionist government, and making an effort for it to be as broad as possible,” the two said.
They added that the party had succeeded in establishing “an important and significant place” for itself and attracting many supporters.
“However, faced with the complicated political reality, each of us made a personal decision,” Tropper and Hendel said.
Hendel in contact with parties to form bloc, spox. tells 'Post'
Meanwhile, Hendel is now in contact with all the parties in the third bloc regarding an alliance for him to join, his spokesperson told The Jerusalem Post after the announcement of the split.
Among the parties in the third bloc is MK Benny Gantz's Blue and White. There have been reports that Gantz has been considering adding various figures to his list, such as former justice minister Ayelet Shaked, who quit political life in 2022.
Party slates must be finalized and registered this week in order to be eligible for the October 27 election.
If small parties run in the elections and ultimately fail to cross the electoral threshold, the votes that went toward them will not be counted.
Hendel confirms agreegment with economist Yaron Zelekha
Following his split from Tropper, Hendel announced that he would run jointly with Yaron Zelekha, an Israeli economist and political figure who heads the New Economic Party, which has also consistently failed to cross the necessary electoral threshold required to enter the Knesset in past elections.
The two said they had agreed on a set of basic principles, including joining only a Zionist government and demanding that a universal conscription law be passed before a government is formed.
Earlier in the day, Hendel had been in contact with all the parties in the third bloc regarding an alliance for him to join, his spokesperson told The Jerusalem Post after the announcement of the split.

Cherkasy Oblast, Poltava Oblast, and Sumy Oblast were also attacked, but no significant damage was reported.

Markets will be closely watching balance of payments data, industrial production figures and, in particular, the Turkish Central Bank’s interest rate decision this week.
The Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is scheduled to meet on Sept. 10 to decide on the policy rate.
According to Zeynel Balcı, research director at Meksa Yatırım, the prevailing market expectation is that the central bank will leave its policy rate unchanged at 37 percent on Sept. 10, while year-end interest rate expectations stand at 35 percent.
However, Balcı said a rate-cut surprise could not be ruled out in light of the resumption of weekly repo auctions and the credit packages announced for tradesmen and manufacturers, which he said could be viewed within the framework of an easing of monetary tightening policies.
According to Balcı, a possible rate cut would likely be perceived positively by Borsa Istanbul, particularly by bank stocks, as the banking sector is among the most interest rate-sensitive segments of the market.
“If the rate is left unchanged on Sept. 10, expectations will likely shift to the Oct. 22 meeting. This could have a short-term negative impact on the stock market,” Balci said.
The central bank is scheduled to release July balance of payments data on Sept. 11, while the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) will publish July industrial production figures on Sept. 10.

Russian-Israeli historian Artyom Kirpichenok was detained at Ben Gurion Airport on suspicion of espionage linked to Iran, according to reports in Russian media.
The opposition news outlet Meduza reported over the weekend that Kirpichenok, who holds both Israeli and Russian citizenship but lives in Russia, was arrested after arriving in Israel. According to the report, investigators suspect him of contact with a foreign intelligence operative and involvement in influence activity directed against Israel.
His lawyer, Inna Labedinskaya-Katz, told the Russian newspaper Izvestia that the case involves several espionage-related charges whose details are classified. “This is the most serious type of offense concerning harm to state security,” she said.
Family members told Meduza that the allegations were false and stemmed from Kirpichenok’s ties to Russia. At the same time, relatives said they understood that investigators suspected him of contact with an agent connected to Iran or Lebanon.
Kirpichenok, 51, was born in St. Petersburg and immigrated to Israel in the 1990s. He studied at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and later returned to Russia, where he has lived since 2005.
Over the years, he has become a vocal critic of Israel and Zionism. His books include A People’s History of Israel, which deals with the history of Palestine and the establishment of the Jewish state, and Israel: The Road to Catastrophe, which examines Israeli domestic and foreign policy through a historical lens
The Iran connection also appears in Kirpichenok’s travel history. Izvestia reported that he visited Iran several times despite being an Israeli citizen. In 2018, he reportedly spent about two weeks there and documented the trip extensively on social media.
His relatives argued that those visits had not previously triggered action by Israeli authorities. They said Kirpichenok returned to Israel several times after traveling to Iran without being questioned about the matter.
Labedinskaya-Katz said Kirpichenok was arrested by the Shin Bet and is being held in a secure wing. She also alleged that he complained of harsh treatment during interrogation, including sleep deprivation, constant lighting in his cell, being forced into uncomfortable positions and questioning under pressure and threats.
Those allegations have not been independently verified.
Supporters in Russia have since formed a campaign demanding his release and are collecting signatures for petitions to be sent to Israeli consulates in Moscow and St. Petersburg.
The group claims Kirpichenok had been invited to Israel to lecture at a conference and now suspects the invitation may have been a trap.
Former Russian lawmaker Darya Mitina has also expressed concern that Kirpichenok could become a bargaining chip in relations between Israel and Russia.

With two days remaining before Israel’s election lists close, Chili Tropper and Yoaz Hendel announced Sunday that they will not run together, as Tropper moves closer to a possible alliance with Gadi Eisenkot.
Ynet has learned that talks between Tropper and Eisenkot have advanced, and the assessment within the anti-Netanyahu bloc is that if Tropper ultimately decides to merge with another party, it will be with Eisenkot. Tropper has made preserving places for members of his faction a priority, and a deal with Eisenkot could secure realistic slate positions for Shira Shapira and Elisaf Peretz.

Hendel, who joined forces with Tropper after the latter left Blue and White, will not be part of the move. His next political step remains unclear, although he has recently held separate talks with Benny Gantz.

“We have more than 20 years of being neighbors, friends, sitting next to each other in synagogue and several years of reserve duty together,” they said. “We both chose to try to serve the public through politics as well. In some cases together.”
“In recent weeks, we established Zionist Home-Reservists together, with a clear goal: forming a Zionist government, and an effort for it to be as broad as possible. Facing the complicated political reality, each of us made a personal decision. Even those who look very hard will not find any bad blood.”

The competition over Tropper also reflects a wider struggle inside the anti-Netanyahu bloc. Both Eisenkot and Naftali Bennett have sought to bring him into their camps, in a contest that is about more than simply adding another recognizable political figure.
A Tropper-Eisenkot deal could strengthen Eisenkot’s claim to leadership of the bloc and potentially reopen the contest between him and Bennett over who will lead the opposition camp into the election. Despite differences in polling, other parties in the bloc, including Yisrael Beytenu, have yet to fully accept Eisenkot’s leadership.
The expectation that Tropper may ultimately choose Eisenkot rests partly on Yashar’s greater ability to offer viable slate positions to Tropper’s allies.
Tropper is still weighing other possibilities, including running independently with possible connections to Gantz or Ayelet Shaked, but those scenarios are currently considered less likely.

With voters in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt heading to the polls on Sunday, tensions are mounting within the governing Christian Democrats over their possible coalition options.
Three days before the election, Friedrich Merz’s CDU was trailing well behind the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) at just over 20%. Polls put the AfD as high as 43%.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
That would make the AfD by far the strongest force in the state parliament. Yet the party currently appears unlikely to win an absolute majority, leaving open the question of whether it can translate an electoral breakthrough into executive power.
Its lead candidate, Ullrich Siegmund, has ruled out entering a coalition and says he wants the AfD to govern alone.
The CDU, led by incumbent Minister-President Sven Schulze, is facing a dilemma of its own. One of his current coalition partners, the liberal FDP, is unlikely to clear the threshold for returning to the state parliament.
The projected numbers also appear to rule out a majority coalition with the SPD and Greens.
Schulze could, nevertheless, seek to form a minority government with the support of the Left Party, which is expected to emerge as the third-strongest political force.
Speaking to journalists last week, Schulze said neither AfD nor Left Party ministers would have a seat at his cabinet table. The wording was notable for what it did not exclude: a CDU-led minority government tolerated by the Left from outside the coalition.
Lithuania to Launch Integrated AI Drone Defense System
A similar arrangement is already in place in neighbouring Thuringia, another east German region, where CDU Minister-President Mario Voigt has been governing for almost two years with a government dependent on votes from the Left Party in the state parliament.
But replicating such an arrangement in Saxony-Anhalt would collide with a long-standing CDU red line.
A party “incompatibility” resolution adopted at the CDU’s 2018 conference rules out cooperation with both the AfD and the Left, which has roots in the Party of Democratic Socialism, itself the successor to East Germany’s ruling Socialist Unity Party (SED).
While Schulze has left a narrow path towards toleration by the Left, the CDU district executive committee in the Harz region has issued a position paper explicitly rejecting exploratory talks, coalition agreements or tolerance arrangements that would depend on Left Party support.
“We are aware of the paper in question, and it was circulated as a handout at the most recent meeting of the CDU district executive committee in Harz. The district executive committee will not consider its substance until its next meeting,” CDU Secretary-General Mario Karschunke told Euractiv.
Until that discussion takes place, it is explicitly a contribution to the debate, which is, of course, something every party member is entitled to make“, he added, while insisting that no position of the CDU Harz district branch or of the CDU in Saxony-Anhalt can be inferred from it. “If we started publicly commenting on every single opinion expressed within our party, we would probably have little time for anything else.”
Shortly afterwards, the chairs of the Christian Democratic Employees’ Association (CDA) in Saxony-Anhalt, Berlin, and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania issued an election appeal explicitly ruling out both the AfD and the Left Party.
Within the AfD, they argued, “far-right positions are socially acceptable”, and the party is “hostile to Europe and friendly towards Putin”.
“Equally clearly, the Left Party, which is the successor to the SED, whose rule was responsible for a lack of freedom and suffering in the GDR and which today openly promotes antisemitism, cannot be a partner for Christian Democratic politics,” the paper stated.
The appeal was also co-signed by Sepp Müller, deputy chairman of the CDU parliamentary group in the Bundestag. Müller, who hails from Dessau in Saxony-Anhalt, has repeatedly spoken out against any form of cooperation with either the AfD or the Left Party.

Türkiye plans 30-year privatization of Bosphorus bridges, highways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:17:00 UTC
17:17:00 KST

AA Photo
Türkiye has adopted a new decision regarding the privatization of two state-operated Bosphorus bridges in Istanbul, along with highways, ring roads and connecting roads.
Under the new framework, the bridges, highways and ring roads will not be privatized as a single package but may be offered either together or separately.
A presidential decree published in the Official Gazette on Sept. 5 expanded the privatization program covering the Bosphorus (15 July Martyrs) Bridge and the Fatih Sultan Mehmet Bridge, as well as four highways, to include the Nigde-Pozanti Motorway, the Gaziantep Ring Motorway and the Caglayan Junction-Yenisehir Junction section of the Bursa Ring Road.
Under a 2010 decision, the bridges and highways were planned to be privatized as a single package through the transfer of operating rights for a period of 25 years from the date of physical handover.
The latest presidential decision introduced three key changes. The bridges and highways may now be privatized either as a whole or in separate groups, while the operating period has been extended to 30 years.
In a written statement on the decision, the Privatization Administration (OİB) emphasized that efforts concerning the highways and bridges operated by the General Directorate of Highways and included in the privatization portfolio do not involve the sale of public assets.
The administration said the model is based on transferring operating rights for a specified period while ownership remains with the state.

Indian refiners accounted for roughly 60 per cent of that volume, energy analytics firm Vortexa said in a report.

The scheduled easing of Russia’s diesel export ban from September 1 may not quickly restore supplies, with Ukrainian drone strikes continuing to disrupt refineries and export infrastructure. Vortexa recorded 32 refinery attacks across July and August.
The Perm refinery, with capacity of 2,60,000 barrels per day, was left operating at only about 28 per cent of its crude distillation capacity after an attack, while no diesel cargoes have left Tuapse since a May strike.The US supplied about half of Europe’s seaborne diesel imports from outside the region in August, at around 5,20,000 barrels per day. But shipments fell from nearly 5,40,000 barrels per day in the first half of August to about 3,50,000 barrels per day in the second half.
