The student loan scam looking to dupe already anxious students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
06:00:57 UTC
15:00:57 KST

You are about to start university and can’t wait but then you receive a worrying text message. It is a few days before the first student loan payment is due to land in your account and apparently someone has tried to alter your bank details.
“Our records indicate that your bank details on your student finance account were changed on Friday 16th. If you did not do this please contact us immediately,” says the text.
You click on the web link in the message and go to what you think is the website of the Students Loans Company (SLC), the government body that administers loans and grants. You log in to check that everything is OK, put in your bank details and the screen says: “Thanks for confirming.” But what you have done is supply this important information to criminals.
Acting quickly, the scammers then use your log-in details to access your real account and change the bank account so that your student loan payment is diverted to them.
The government is making a fresh push to raise awareness of this fraud as the new academic year starts.
This month, about £2.6bn is being paid out in maintenance support to 1.1 million students. The first of three loan payments will be deposited in the accounts of students in England and Wales. Students from Northern Ireland and Scotland get their loan instalments every month.
In the last academic year, £519,000 was lost to scammers who defrauded 168 students, according to the SLC. More than 1,100 people had their details changed but in most cases the fraud was stopped before money was lost.
What the scam looks like
Scammers are using several methods including text message, email or phone calls to target students.
The messages can claim that a payment is at risk because bank details need to be updated. Or it may say that an account has been closed unless the student acts immediately to log in to their “account” through the link provided.
The link supplied in the message leads to a clone of the SLC site and students are asked to input their details.
“It’s a race against time because the criminals then use those details to log into our genuine site to change the bank account on the genuine student account to divert the maintenance loan payment before we spot it,” said Alan Balanowski, the risk director at SLC.
Criminals know that billions of pounds will land in students’ accounts this month and have timed their approach to coordinate the fraud with a sense of urgency that people may not get their money when they need it. This is a common tactic used by criminals to get people to act in haste.
What to do
Be aware of when you could be the target of scams – September, January and April are the months when the student loan instalments are paid in England and Wales.
SLC says it won’t ask you to confirm personal or financial information by email, text or on social media. Don’t click on any links provided, instead log in to your account through the Gov.uk website.
Students are also urged to not publicise when they are getting their payment by refraining from putting it on social media.
SLC says that it does not provide services through WhatsApp and won’t initiate contact on social media. So immediately be suspicious if you are contacted in either of these ways.
Any fraudulent emails can be sent on to report@phishing.gov.uk while scam text messages can be forwarded to 7726.
If you suspect your account has been compromised, change the password immediately and contact SLC. Victims should be able to get a replacement payment so there is no financial loss to them.

====================================================================================================

‘Fabulous museums and no queues’: five of the best under-the-radar city breaks in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
06:00:57 UTC
15:00:57 KST

Nantes, France
As dilemmas go, it’s an unusual one: saddle up a giant squid or board a submersible for a voyage to the bottom of the ocean. In the end, I find myself drawn to a fierce-looking merhorse and tentatively take the reins. High above, my daughter glides by on a flying fish, metallic fins flapping, while her Dad is battling stormy seas at the helm of a huge conch shell. A ride on the Carrousel des Mondes Marins (marine worlds carousel) – a three-storey steampunk merry-go-round inspired by Jules Verne’s novel Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea – is one of the highlights of a visit to Nantes. A surreal fairground ride, a work of art and a homage to the city’s most famous son. It’s also a lot of fun.
On the banks of the Loire, 30 miles from the Atlantic ocean, Nantes is a city whose fortunes were built on the sea. As a young boy growing up near the docks in the 1830s, Verne dreamed of being a ship’s captain, but it wasn’t to be. Instead, he embarked on a series of journeys of the imagination, channelling his wanderlust into novels such as Around the World in 80 Days and Journey to the Centre of the Earth. The last of Nantes’ shipyards closed in the 1980s, but Verne’s unique vision provided the inspiration for a radical art and regeneration project, Les Machines de l’Île, that has breathed life into the abandoned quays and warehouses of the Île de Nantes, the river island that was home to the city’s docks.
This is now the stomping ground of the Grand Éléphant, a 12m-high mechanical pachyderm that carries passengers on tours of the island, spraying bystanders with water from its trunk. I’d seen photos but nothing prepares you for the thrill of turning a corner and seeing the real thing lumbering towards you. You can learn about the magic behind the machinery at the nearby Galerie des Machines, where the creators bring a mechanical menagerie of strange creatures to life.
The Verne connection also inspired the name of the city’s summer arts festival, Le Voyage à Nantes, which transforms streets, parks and public spaces into an open-air art gallery from July to September. Our visit coincides with the festival’s opening weekend, and the squares and avenues of the elegant Graslin district are busy with DJ sets, food stalls and people checking out the new artworks. In the Place Graslin, a beautiful square built – like much of Nantes – from chalky-white tuffeau stone from the Loire valley, some kind of cataclysmic eruption has been conjured up in front of the opera house. Huge ammonites appear to have been forced up from beneath the earth, engulfing cars in a mountain of rubble, their doors wide open, radios playing, as though abandoned in haste.
Just yards away, children are playing in the dancing water fountains of the square, while the white-aproned waiters of art nouveau brasserie La Cigale weave through the pavement tables delivering seafood platters to diners unfazed by the apocalyptic scene before them. Titled Fossil Opera, the artwork is a commentary on consumerism and the fleeting nature of human endeavour, and is one of about a dozen site-specific installations that have appeared in the city, as if by magic.
Even outside the summer months, there is plenty to discover in France’s sixth largest city. Each year, a handful of the festival installations are selected to become permanent fixtures, which has resulted in an impressive collection of contemporary public art, from Les Anneaux, a series of 18 giant steel rings on the Quai des Antilles, which frame views of the Loire and light up at night, to Tadashi Kawamata’s Belvédère de l’Hermitage, a viewing platform inspired by a swallow’s nest, which juts over a sheer cliff.
All of these cultural highlights, old and new, are linked by the Ligne Verte, a 12-mile (20km) green line painted on the pavement. We follow the trail through the Passage Pommeraye, an exquisite 19th century glass-roofed shopping arcade; past the imposing Château des ducs de Bretagne, a moated 15th-century castle; stop off at the excellent Musée d’arts de Nantes, which houses an impressive collection of international art spanning seven centuries; and finish up at the peaceful Jardin des Plantes, a charming (and free) botanical garden which is home to a handful of modern art installations and a good cafe. From here it’s a short stroll to the Lieu Unique, a cultural space and concert venue in the factory that once produced the city’s beloved buttery LU biscuits.
And there’s more to come. The Jardin Extraordinaire is a newly created garden and climbing wall in a disused granite quarry in the Bas‑Chantenay district. The exotic planting, waterfall and paddling pools were inspired by descriptions in Verne’s novel, The Mysterious Island. The nearby Chantenay docks have been colonised by studios, music spaces and the Little Atlantique Brewery, housed in a 19th-century former oil mill. Opposite the quarry, a derelict industrial building is being transformed into a new riverside cultural hub, the Cité des Imaginaires, which will eventually provide a home for an expanded Jules Verne museum. It’s an ambitious project: creative, unconventional and looking to the future. I’m sure Jules Verne would approve.
Joanne O’Connor
The trip was supported by Le Voyage à Nantes. Oceania Hôtel de France, just off the Place Graslin, has air‑conditioned doubles from €101 room-only
Winter’s Journey, a seasonal festival of concerts, temporary light installations, artworks and gastronomic events, runs from 21 November to 3 January.
Basel, Switzerland
Unless you’re a professional who makes their way to the Art Basel fair every year, chances are Switzerland’s third largest city will have passed you by – or rather you will have passed it by. Basel is one stop before Zurich on the fast train from Paris, but to whiz through would be a mistake. For art and design lovers, it is the perfect city to explore on a long weekend.
Basel bills itself as “the city of art and culture on the Rhine”, and it lives up to its boast. Stroll around the charming old town and marvel at the cathedral before enjoying a cold beer at one of the many cafes. If temperatures soar, you might want to join local people with a dip in the Rhine.
Once you’ve done all that, you need to engage with the area’s art offerings. Within the city, the Kunstmuseum holds more than 300,000 works spanning eight centuries, with big hitters such as Monet, Van Gogh and Warhol, while Museum Tinguely is home to the work of the idiosyncratic Swiss sculptor Jean Tinguely and his dada-esque machines.
But the two real draws are on the outskirts of the city. Fondation Beyeler in the suburb of Riehen is home to an impressive collection of modern and contemporary art, and always has a blockbuster exhibition (currently Pierre Huyghe) to check out. A short bus or train ride across the German border in Weil am Rhein is the Vitra Design Museum, home to one of the world’s largest permanent exhibitions of modern furniture design.
Before you admire the furniture collection, take a walk around the campus, where you can marvel at the main museum building designed by Frank Gehry; the Vitra Schaudepot – which houses the furniture collection – designed by Herzog & de Meuron; Zaha Hadid’s former fire station; and Tadao Ando’s conference centre. There is a beautiful garden by the Dutch designer Piet Oudolf, and the recently added Doshi Retreat for a moment of quiet reflection designed by the Indian architect Balkrishna Doshi, his first completed project outside India and the last he worked on before he died in 2023.
That’s half the day gone, so time to head inside. In lots of ways, exploring the Schaudepot is like walking through a giant doll’s house, with the rooms filled with instantly recognisable furniture icons from the 19th century to today, including works by Verner Panton, Le Corbusier, Alvar Aalto and Charles and Ray Eames. The museum also puts on temporary exhibitions. And if all of that has exhausted you, head to the VitraHaus Café, which serves a delicious lunch.
Max Benato
The Volkshaus, a boutique hotel in the old town, has doubles from 152 swiss francs (£138) room-only
Lübeck, Germany
Unless you’ve read Buddenbrooks, Thomas Mann’s epic family saga, you may not have heard of Lübeck. But in the middle ages, this port city in Germany, 70km north-east of Hamburg, was one of the richest and most powerful places on Earth. Today, despite the best efforts of the RAF to destroy it in 1942, it remains a beautifully intact medieval gem.
The old town is a Unesco world heritage site. It sits on an island in the centre of the city, encircled by the rivers Trave and Wakenitz, and the water is a good place to start exploring. My boyfriend and I hired an electric boat (€49 for up to six people) and spent an hour circumnavigating and gazing at its distinctive seven church spires.
Back on dry land, we set off on a guided walking tour, starting at the imposing – if wonky – Holsten Gate. We took in the five red brick churches the spires belong to (two have doubles), and climbed one of them, St Petri’s viewing tower, for a panoramic view. We also stopped at the 800-year-old town hall on the marketplace.
But just as fascinating was what lies behind the gothic splendour. At one time, there were 180 hidden alleyways and courtyards threaded through the old town, and about 80 remain. These labyrinthine lanes were built behind wealthy merchants’ mansions to house the poor. Today, the restored cottages are sought-after and the flower-filled, cobbled alleys are charming to explore.
To better understand Lübeck’s past, we visited the European Hansemuseum in the old castle monastery. It tells the story of the Hanseatic League, the powerful trade network that stretched from England to Russia and gave Lübeck (“the Queen of the League”) its wealth in the middle ages and its status as a free city state right up to 1937.
In a nearby palace, the Museum Behnhaus Drägerhaus displays 19th- and early 20th-century German and European art, including work by Edvard Munch, who visited Lübeck and painted its salt warehouses. Just round the corner is the Günter Grass-Haus, where the writer regularly stayed (he died in Lübeck in 2015).
We visited in June during the HanseKulturFestival, when the quarter around St Jakob’s church was full of live music stages, food stalls and outdoor bars. The next festival isn’t until 2028, but there are annual museum, theatre and literature nights, and popup live music in the summer.
Lübeck has three natural open-air swimming areas, one on the island. And the seaside isn’t far away – we had a day trip to Travemünde, a historic resort town with miles of sandy beach, taking a scenic river ferry there (90 minutes) and a 20-minute train back.
In town, the medieval Schiffergesellschaft (Seafarers’ Guild) is now a traditional Hanseatic restaurant, with long communal tables. Alongside North Sea fish and Holstein meat dishes are vegetarian versions of labskaus, a sort of hash.
Sadly, we couldn’t visit Buddenbrookhaus, the museum dedicated to the novel, as it is being renovated. It is expected to reopen in 2030 – which gives you plenty of time to read Mann’s 864-page doorstopper. Like Lübeck itself, it is worth the effort.
Rachel Dixon
The trip was provided by germany.travel and luebeck-tourismus.de. Accommodation was provided by Liho Lübeck, doubles from £73 room-only
Parma, Italy
Parma is just far enough off Italy’s main travel routes to discourage the huge crowds of tourists that flood the likes of Venice and Florence. Most travellers reach this tranquil Italian gem by flying into Milan or Bologna, followed by an hour’s train ride. It is definitely worth that extra effort, as I discover a city that ticks every box for a weekend getaway: fabulous museums and frescoed churches without long queues or the need to book a timeslot in advance; friendly, affordable trattorie and osterie showcasing a feast of local food and wines; and, if you time it right, the chance to catch an opera composed by locally born Giuseppe Verdi in the intimate Teatro Regio.
The historic centre of Parma is small and easily explored on foot, taking me past an array of architectural masterpieces. I kick off at the grand Piazza Duomo, dominated by the imposing 900-year-old romanesque cathedral. Everyone’s eyes are drawn up to the ornate cupola, decorated with a captivating illusionist fresco by local Renaissance artist Antonio da Correggio. Next to the cathedral stands the early gothic Battistero, an octagonal baptistery whose bare, minimalist exterior contrasts with an incredible explosion of colours from the 13th- and 14th-century paintings that cover the interior. Then, tucked away behind the Duomo, I come upon the entrance of the medieval Monastero di San Giovanni Evangelista, whose cloisters and garden are a peaceful oasis. Entry to the monastery and cathedral is free.
Parma’s big must-see is the monumental Palazzo della Pilotta, a baroque complex of palatial museums, a library and remarkable 400-year-old theatre, all included in a single €18 entry ticket. Just by the Parma river that slices the city into two, the palazzo was built by the Farnese family, whose patronage created most of the city’s Renaissance monuments. The Teatro Farnese, made almost entirely of wood, is rarely used as a venue today, but a visit remains an incredible experience. I leave most sightseeing time, though, for the Pilotta’s landmark Galleria Nazionale di Parma, a treasure trove of old master paintings. It may not quite rival the collection of the Uffizi, but I enjoy the chance to just turn up without booking in advance and quietly appreciate works by Leonardo da Vinci, Fra Angelico, Canaletto and Tintoretto without being surrounded by crowds.
Sightseeing is only part of Parma’s attraction, however, as this is one of Italy’s food capitals. I walk into the rustic, raucous OsteMagno bar, where everyone is tucking into tagliere – wooden boards piled with razor-thin slices of cured ham, the famous prosciutto crudo di Parma, artisan salami and crumbly aged parmigiano reggiano cheese, accompanied by a glass of the local’s favourite tipple, fizzy red Lambrusco wine, which is a lot more drinkable than I expect.
This is not a city to seek out chic, gourmet restaurants, but rather one of the many traditional trattorie such as Da Antonia, whose eponymous owner has overseen the cucina for more than 50 years, or the 120-year-old Trattoria Corrieri, serving up generous plates of homemade pasta for less than €15.
John Brunton
Palazzo Dalla Rosa Prati has doubles from €80 room-only
Santander, Spain
Often dismissed as little more than a ferry terminal – somewhere to stop overnight if you want to take your dog to Europe or lower your carbon footprint – the port city of Santander is undergoing something of a cultural renaissance. It’s already blessed with a spectacular bay facing the Cantabrian mountains, wide sandy beaches, grand, colonnaded plazas and superb food, but the opening of new art spaces and museums in the coming months will put the Cantabrian capital firmly on the weekend-break map.
Leading the way on 8 September is Faro Santander – a new cultural centre in a grand historical building housing a 1,000-piece art collection belonging to Banco Santander, including works by Velázquez, Goya, Titian, Rubens and Picasso. Different parts of the collection will be shown at different times.
With its ornate white facade facing the bay, the Pereda building was previously the bank’s headquarters, but has been transformed into a striking, 21st-century museum space by Pritzker prize-winning British architect David Chipperfield.
Santander’s moment in the spotlight will extend into 2027 when Madrid’s Reina Sofia Museum opens its first outpost, set in a similarly grand neo-Renaissance building just a few metres away from Faro Santander. The museum will house the Archivo Lafuente, with paintings, sculptures and manuscripts, including major collections on dadaism and the Spanish civil war, as well as art from Spain, North America and Latin America.
Faro Santander and Archivo Lafuente will form two points on a kind of “art triangle”, along with architect Renzo Piano’s 2017 Centro Botín contemporary art centre just over the road. With a bijou but impressive permanent collection, including works by Matisse, Juan Gris, Joaquín Sorolla and Mark Rothko, the Centro Botín sits on the waterfront like a giant, stilt-mounted, 60s alarm clock sawn in half.
Spaniards cottoned on to Santander’s charms long ago, and the seafront is lined with elegant fin-de-siècle villas built when well-heeled Madrileños discovered that the city’s Atlantic breezes were the perfect respite from the Spanish capital’s infernal summer. More than 100 years later, while Britain was experiencing its own heatwave, I followed their lead. Temperatures were in the balmy high 20s as I ambled past toddlers building sand castles and teenagers frolicking in the surf on El Sardinero beach, just 15 minutes by bus from the city centre.
The centre itself is wonderfully walkable and there’s an unhurried, laid-back vibe in the streets, grand plazas and narrow alleys near the gothic cathedral, lined with bars serving pinchos – the Cantabrian equivalent to tapas.
After tucking into tender, grilled squid, laced with gutsy garlic and olive oil, at Mesón Rampalay on a leafy square, I spent a fascinating couple of hours at Mupac – the Museum of Prehistory and Archaeology of Cantabria, just a few minutes’ walk away from Faro Santander.
The museum, which is home to one of Spain’s most important prehistoric collections, features excellent interactive displays, and in 2027 it is moving to a brand new, multimillion-euro building. By next year, it seems, Santander will be not just the capital of Cantabria, but a capital of culture too.
Eddi Fiegel
The trip was provided by Faro Santander. Abba Santander, near the Centro Botín, has stylish doubles from €66 room-only

The exhibition showcasing the work of Hungarian painter Sándor Pinczehelyi in Pécs is open to visitors until 8 November 2026 at the M21 Gallery in the Zsolnay Cultural Quarter.
A retrospective exhibition of the oeuvre of 80-year-old Sándor Pinczehelyi has opened at the M21 Gallery in the Zsolnay Cultural Quarter in Pécs. Long before the Iron Curtain came down, the artist was already combining Soviet totalitarian insignia with the symbols of Western affluence.
The exhibition features 150 works by the Munkácsy Prize-winning artist, who has been named Artist of Merit and Artist of Excellence, offering a comprehensive selection spanning six decades of his career.
"In European art circles I am known as someone who, in the earlier socialist period, worked with symbols such as the hammer and sickle, the paving stone and the star. One such piece is my iconic work with the hammer and sickle you can see here. There is virtually no art book dealing with that period in which this work is not reproduced."
Divided into nine thematic sections, the genre-spanning exhibition guides visitors from his earliest works to the present day through photographs, paintings, spatial sculptures, prints and enamel pieces. Alongside well-known works, visitors can also see pieces that have never been published before. The exhibition also presents works that were shown at the exhibitions in Turin and Berlin.

Chinese military university urged to revise AI course to ‘educate for war’
Proposal sees mapping out defence scenarios as better preparation for future officers involved in intelligent warfare
Researchers from the National University of Defence Technology’s College of Intelligence Science and Technology outlined their proposal in the July issue of the journal Defence Industry Conversion in China.
The initiative comes as China seeks to cultivate more military personnel with the technical skills to use artificial intelligence (AI) in future warfare.
As global militaries explore the use of AI in planning, training and combat, the technology is also changing what the troops need to learn, with China aiming to train forces capable of applying emerging technologies to armed operations.
The researchers said case studies in the existing AI course lacked sufficient “military flavour” and needed to be redesigned to better serve the practical needs of “educating for war”.
The university introduced “Principles and Practice of Artificial Intelligence” as a tailored course for non-AI science and engineering graduate students in its 2022 autumn semester.

Netanyahu races to finalize Likud election slate amid growing party tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:58:45 UTC
14:58:45 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is racing to finalize Likud’s Knesset slate before Tuesday night’s filing deadline, as internal pressure mounts over his remaining appointments and uncertainty persists over possible last-minute recruits and political alliances.
Likud Secretariat members were informed Saturday night that Netanyahu wants to convene the body Tuesday, just hours before the 10 p.m. deadline for submitting candidate lists for the 26th Knesset. The meeting is expected to approve any remaining candidates Netanyahu chooses to add to the slate.
The timing has heightened tensions inside Likud. Ministers, lawmakers, activists and local party officials are pressing Netanyahu not to make additional appointments unless they offer a clear electoral advantage, with some candidates already pushed significantly lower on the list following the party’s primaries.
Netanyahu has so far secured places for Defense Minister Israel Katz and Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar near the top of the slate, as well as for Likud Central Committee chairman Haim Katz and businessman Oren Dobronsky. Several additional places remain available for potential recruits or political deals before the deadline.
One name recently floated is Dr. Keren Assayag, a lecturer and breast cancer researcher who recently met Netanyahu. After initially expressing reservations about entering politics, party figures now believe she may be willing to join Likud, though it remains unclear whether she would receive a realistic position on the slate or simply endorse the party publicly.
Netanyahu has also sought to use the remaining flexibility to encourage broader cooperation on the right. He had hoped to bring retired Brig. Gen. Ofer Winter into an alliance involving Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism and Moshe Feiglin’s Identity party, which have already joined forces.
Winter, however, has repeatedly rejected merger proposals and, according to several reports, also turned down offers of reserved places on the Likud slate. If those efforts fail, Netanyahu is expected to unveil new candidates instead, a move that could reignite tensions inside a party still unsettled by its contentious primaries.
The dispute is particularly sensitive because reserved appointments can push candidates elected in the primaries into significantly lower positions. Some who initially finished near the start of the second group of 10 candidates have already fallen into the third after reserved places were inserted.
That has prompted lawmakers and ministers to mobilize activists, branch chiefs and local officials in an effort to persuade Netanyahu not to use every appointment available to him. Netanyahu is aware of the pressure, but the decision to convene the Secretariat indicates he intends to keep all options open until the final hours.
The scramble inside Likud is part of a broader rush across Israel’s political system as parties prepare their final election slates.
Naftali Bennett is expected to present the list of his Beyachad alliance Sunday night while continuing efforts to recruit Chili Tropper. The emerging slate, which includes figures from Yesh Atid, currently contains more candidates than polling suggests will win seats.
Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Lieberman is also expected to unveil his party’s list Sunday. The party has been polling at around 10 seats, while Lieberman has recruited several new candidates in recent weeks, particularly figures associated with liberal religious Zionism and active military reservists.
Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar! party has emerged in polls as Netanyahu’s leading challenger, is due to present his slate Monday. “I’m talking to everyone,” Eisenkot said over the weekend. “We’re preparing more surprises for the next three or four days.”
A possible alliance between Eisenkot and Bennett also remains in play. Neither has confirmed that talks are advancing, but both stopped short of ruling out such a move when questioned at a Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth conference last week.
Tropper remains another potential piece in the final round of maneuvering, with the possibility that his Zionist Home-Reservists faction could join either Bennett or Eisenkot before Tuesday night’s deadline.

Hungary begins hunt for corrupt regime's billions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:54:00 UTC
14:54:00 KST

Hungary begins hunt for corrupt regime's billions
September 6, 2026
Asset recovery — it sounds bureaucratic but behind this phrase is one of the most important campaign promises made by Hungary's new government.
Hungary's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, and his Tisza party want to retrieve funds and assets that went — in some dubious ways — to the family of ousted Hungarian leader Viktor Orban or his allies, various oligarchs, or frontmen. The new government wants those funds back for state use, and it also plans to hold the beneficiaries accountable under law.
Billions of euros were stolen or diverted and, if social media is to be believed, many Hungarians want to see the individuals responsible behind bars. Magyar has talked of a sum of around €60 billion ($70 billion), though other estimates suggest the real amount could be three times that much.
Orban, allies lived lives of luxury
Observers say the success or failure of the asset recovery will almost certainly influence the future of Magyar and the Tisza party.
The huge sums of money are linked to images of decadent luxury under Orban. The former Hungarian prime minister's family, party members, and friendly oligarchs lived on luxury estates, flew in luxury jets, vacationed on luxury yachts, and repeatedly won billions worth of public contracts.
Orban-affiliated entrepreneurs, artists, academics, and journalists were also generously supported with public funds for years. Often their main qualification was loyalty to the former prime minister.
Those lifestyles contrasted with the lives led by Hungarians in poverty, the image of neglected public infrastructure, poor conditions in schools and hospitals, and the exodus of many young Hungarians from the country, as well as a huge deficit in the state budget, some 7.5% of Hungary's national income. These contrasts explain why there is such a popular desire for justice.
It's been almost four months since the new Magyar government took office and anti-corruption actions have officially started.
At the end of July, the new government established the National Asset Recovery Authority, or NVVH — a sort of "super institution" with very broad powers and independence.
Hungary hasn't had an authority like this in its modern history. The way state assets were privatized in the 1990s after communist rule was problematic, as it often was elsewhere in the former Soviet bloc. When Orban first came to power in 2010, there was a half-hearted attempt to address the corruption of the previous government under Ferenc Gyurcsany, but it came to nothing.
This time, things are meant to be different.
The NVVH will investigate where public funds flowed and how assets like real estate were used. Although no specific date has been set, the investigations will primarily focus on the Orban government's time in power, so dating back to 2010. The authority is also meant to make sure this cannot happen again, and will look into how public funds and assets are to be used in future.
The NVVH has both policing and prosecutorial powers, so it can investigate cases and bring charges. The authority is accountable to Hungary's parliament.
Controversy around new anti-corruption body
But the creation of the NVVH has not been without controversy.
Late last week, parliament appointed Anna Unger, 46, a political scientist at Eotvos Lorand University in Budapest, to head the new anti-corruption and asset recovery body. Unger is an expert on political systems, democratic institutions, and party financing and was chosen out of almost 100 other applicants in a process with several stages.
Some were surprised at Unger's appointment, as she wasn't really a public figure. Her research has included political corruption but she's not a recognized expert on the topic, nor is she a lawyer. Observers had expected a lawyer or an anti-corruption expert to get the job, somebody like Miklos Ligeti, head of legal affairs at Transparency International Hungary since 2012.
Ligeti also applied for the job but is reportedly being considered for a position as a deputy director. Unger will have four deputies with different duties and responsibilities. Katalin Tasnady, a well-known prosecutor with around two decades of criminal law experience, was made the NVVH's deputy chief of investigations.
Government representatives said Unger had presented a comprehensive political vision for the agency's work. During her parliamentary hearing, she said that under Orban, Hungary saw more than just what one might call classic corruption. An almost feudal system had prevailed, she argued. That was why in addition to restitution and asset recovery, the system had to be thoroughly investigated and exposed so that it would never happen again, Unger said.
No justice in next 6 years?
Unger caused the biggest upset when she said it would be folly to expect legally binding verdicts in any major corruption cases during the NVVH's first six-year term.
Robert Puzser, a popular commentator and personality on social media, called Unger's statement "devastating." Voters had given Magyar "unprecedented power to hold the country's plunderers to account," he said on Facebook, and if Hungarians had to wait more than six years, it could cause the collapse of this new government.
The new prime minister himself reacted angrily to critics who said the NVVH should have had a lawyer at its head.
"Nobody promised people they could vote for the leader of the NVVH as if it was a [reality TV] casting show," he wrote on Facebook. Plenty of experts thought Unger was absolutely suitable for the job.
In a podcast on the 24.hu media outlet, political science Gabor Torok surmised that the way that the NVVH had been established indicated that it would be a "strong political institution" that aimed to come to terms with the recent past.
Torok said the public expects the Tisza party to thoroughly reckon with the old system, and the new government will only be able to maintain the public's trust if it doesn't look like the "culprits of the previous order" are getting away with their past crimes, he said.
This article was originally written in German.

Germany's far-right AfD eyes historic state victory in Saxony-Anhalt election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:52:06 UTC
14:52:06 KST

Germany's far-right AfD eyes historic state victory in Saxony-Anhalt election
Germany's anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany party is aiming to become the first far-right party to take power at a state level since World War II as voters in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt head to the polls Sunday. However, a failure to secure an absolute majority may see the politically isolated party struggle to form a government.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Voters in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt will go to the polls on Sunday in a closely watched election that could see the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) become the first far-right party to take power at a state level since World War II.
Under the smiling and telegenic 35-year-old leader Ulrich Siegmund, the party has been polling comfortably ahead for months, and there is a genuine chance the AfD could take an absolute majority on Sunday evening – particularly if several smaller parties fail to clear Germany's 5 percent threshold to enter parliament.
Polls opened at 8am local time (06:00 GMT) and some 1.7 million voters have until 6pm (16:00 GMT) to cast their ballots, with first projections expected shortly after.
The AfD's key campaign promises include a "remigration and deportation offensive", a ban on LGBTQ pride rainbow flags at public schools and an end to new wind farms.
Read moreGermany: Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, the ideologist behind the AFD’s plans in Saxony-Anhalt
Germany's domestic intelligence agency considers the AfD chapter Siegmund represents as "right-wing extremist" with links to ethno-nationalist groups and think-tanks.
Siegmund was present at a 2023 secret meeting near Berlin where extreme right-wing activists discussed a radical "remigration" plan to forcibly expel millions of people with a migration background from the country.
Sunday's vote is being closely watched as a barometer for the government of the deeply unpopular Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has attempted to chip away at the AfD's popularity by taking a tougher line on irregular migration and security.
Recent surveys place the AfD at just over 40 percent, followed by Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) at 23 percent.
An absolute majority would allow the AfD to bypass mainstream parties' efforts to keep the party blocked out of power by refusing to work with it under a longstanding "firewall" policy.
Achieving an absolute majority is a high bar to clear in Germany's proportional electoral system, which was designed in part to encourage coalition governments and make it difficult for one party to rule alone.
If the AfD falls short of an outright majority, a CDU-led administration under incumbent state premier Sven Schulze is the most likely outcome, though the exact shape of any coalition would depend on which parties enter.
Weeks of coalition talks could follow Sunday's vote.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
'What we have started here can no longer be stopped'
For the AfD, the Saxony-Anhalt election is a stepping stone towards its larger ambitions of securing national power in the next federal election scheduled for 2029.
"No matter the outcome of tomorrow's election, we have already made history," said Siegmund at a final rally on Saturday evening.
"Because what we have started here in Saxony-Anhalt – what is currently sweeping across all of Germany – can no longer be stopped," he told the crowd in Saxony-Anhalt's capital, Magdeburg.
The AfD has long tapped into lingering resentment in Germany's East about an enduring wealth gap with the West decades after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall.
Many state-owned enterprises were shuttered following the absorption of the communist German Democratic Republic by the West, sparking large-scale unemployment and population flight, especially by young women.
Decades on, wages and savings remain lower on average, most big business is still based in the west, and eastern Germans – one fifth of the population – are under-represented in politics.
Even if the AfD emerges as the frontrunner on Sunday, though, the party would struggle to enter government due to the firewall.
Such a result opens the prospect of complex coalition negotiations, dependent on which parties can hit the 5 percent hurdle.
Polls show one of the CDU's current coalition partners, the liberal FDP, falling short, while the other, the centre-left SPD, is under 10 percent.
The small far-left anti-immigration BSW, the only party that has not ruled out a coalition with the AfD, is also likely to miss out.
For Schulze, who is favoured in polls as voters' top choice for leader, combining with the SPD and Greens might not be enough for a majority, but the CDU has ruled out a coalition with the far-left Left Party that could help it reach that threshold.
One option could be a minority government led by Schulze that would depend on passive tolerance from the Left – a model used in the neighbouring eastern German state of Thuringia.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AFP)

Serbia Is Not a Russian Province, and Lavrov Has No Right to Decide Its Future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:52:00 UTC
14:52:00 KST

On Sept. 3, at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Sergey Lavrov said: “Out of inertia, countries continue; our Serbian friends and now our Armenian colleagues are seeking to join the EU.” He added that he was confident “this desire will disappear very soon.”
There is neither friendship nor respect for Serbia in those words. What they reveal instead is an old Kremlin reflex: treating countries it deems close to Russia as places where Moscow is somehow entitled to interpret their interests, judge how serious their decisions are and predict when they will abandon them. Lavrov was not commenting on a passing decision by a Serbian government. He reduced Serbia’s entire strategic course to a temporary weakness from which, in his view, the country will eventually recover, and such contempt deserves an answer stripped of diplomatic euphemism.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Sergey Lavrov has no right whatsoever to decide what Serbia should want, how long it is permitted to want it or where Serbia belongs. Vladimir Putin has no such right either, nor does a state that has demonstrated its understanding of sovereignty by sending tanks across the internationally recognized borders of another country.
Serbia is not a Russian province, not Moscow’s political property, and not a country over which the Kremlin possesses some historical, moral, or political title. Nobody in Moscow has been given a mandate to treat Serbia as part of a Russian sphere of influence, to dismiss its foreign-policy choices as a temporary mistake, or to decide how much independence Serbia may exercise before Russian interests take precedence. Serbia owes Russia neither its future nor its foreign policy, neither its alliances nor its right to decide where it belongs. Any attempt by the Kremlin to behave as though Serbian independence ends where Russian interests begin is not friendship, but imperial arrogance.
British Journalist: In Ukraine, the Nation, Not Its Leaders, Drives History
If Serbia wants to negotiate membership in the European Union, that is Serbia’s decision. If Serbia one day decides to abandon that course, that decision must also belong to Serbia. A Russian foreign minister cannot announce in advance that a sovereign country will soon “get over” its own policy, as though Serbia were merely passing through a phase that Moscow expects eventually to cure. That is not the language of an equal relationship between sovereign states, but of political guardianship that Serbia has granted to no one.
The arrogance is all the more grotesque because it comes from today’s Russia, a rogue state that attacked Ukraine, seized parts of its territory and attempted to alter internationally recognized borders by force. Russian armed forces and authorities have committed war crimes in Ukraine. The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry has documented willful killings, attacks on civilians, unlawful confinement, torture, rape, and the unlawful transfer and deportation of children. The UN has also documented the widespread and systematic torture of Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees held under Russian control, as well as executions of captured Ukrainian soldiers. Russian attacks continued to strike Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure throughout 2026, and in July the monthly number of civilians killed reached its highest level since May 2022.
None of this is incidental background to Lavrov’s remarks about Serbia. It is the record of the state he represents and of the aggression he has spent years defending before the world.
Ukraine has already lived through the consequences of the doctrine behind Lavrov’s contempt for Serbia’s choices. Moscow spent years insisting that it understood Ukraine better than Ukrainians themselves, that it knew where Ukraine belonged, which alliances it was entitled to pursue, and how real its independence could be if its chosen direction conflicted with Russian interests.
When political pressure failed to secure obedience, the Kremlin resorted to force. Russian troops entered Ukraine, occupied its territory, destroyed its cities, and, through annexation, attempted to turn the spoils of war into Russian land. In occupied areas, Russian authorities imposed Russian citizenship, Russian law, and the Russian education system, while people considered disloyal were subjected to intimidation, detention, torture, deportation, and forced displacement.
This is the ultimate destination of a policy that begins with the belief that a neighboring or “friendly” country does not possess the full right to choose against Moscow’s wishes.
Among the most repugnant elements of Russia’s occupation policy has been its treatment of Ukrainian children. Russian authorities have transferred children from Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine to the Russian Federation and to other areas under Russian control, in numerous cases separating them from the families and communities to which they belong. The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia’s Commissioner for Children’s Rights, for the war crime of unlawfully deporting and transferring Ukrainian children. Putin is therefore the president of a state waging a war of aggression and a man subject to an international arrest warrant over crimes involving children taken from the occupied territory of another country. Against that record, Lavrov’s presumption that he can pronounce upon Serbia’s future is not merely offensive; it is obscene.
Lavrov is no peripheral figure in this regime, and there is no reason to indulge the fiction that he is simply a professional diplomat carrying out somebody else’s policy. He has been Russia’s foreign minister since 2004 and is one of the longest-serving senior figures in Putin’s system. He was foreign minister when Russia went to war with Georgia, when it annexed Crimea, when it tore into Ukrainian sovereignty in Donbas and when, in 2022, it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Throughout those years, his role has been to give diplomatic vocabulary to what Russian power does on the ground: aggression recast as defense, occupation dressed up as historical correction, and another country’s freedom of choice portrayed as a threat to Russian security. Lavrov understands perfectly well what the UN Charter means, what internationally recognized borders mean and what the prohibition of aggression means. That knowledge does not diminish his responsibility; it makes his role more damning. He has spent years consciously representing and defending a policy that has brought war, occupation and war crimes back to Europe.
In 2022, the European Parliament recognized Russia as a state sponsor of terrorism and as a state that uses terrorist methods, citing deliberate attacks and atrocities against Ukrainian civilians, the destruction of civilian infrastructure and other grave violations of international and humanitarian law amounting to war crimes. Describing today’s Russia as a rogue state is not rhetorical inflation. It is an entirely fitting description of a government that has trampled the fundamental rules of the international order while demanding the protection of those same rules for itself. The Kremlin insists that Russia’s borders are inviolable while changing Ukraine’s borders by force, invokes sovereignty whenever it wants to keep others out of Russian affairs and discards the sovereignty of its neighbors when their policies cease to suit Moscow. That double standard has left dead civilians, devastated cities, and occupied land in its wake, and Lavrov consequently has no political or moral standing from which to prescribe the limits of any other European country’s freedom of choice.
His phrase “our Serbian friends” sounds all the more cynical for that reason. Serbia is useful to the Kremlin as a “friend” only for as long as it refuses to impose sanctions on Russia, allows space for Russian political influence and keeps European Union membership sufficiently distant for Moscow to treat it as unfinished and ultimately unattainable business. Whenever Serbia reaffirms EU membership as a strategic goal or supports the territorial integrity of Ukraine, Moscow explains those decisions away as the product of Western pressure, a failure by Serbia to understand its own interests or, as Lavrov now puts it, mere “inertia” that will soon pass. That has nothing to do with a relationship between equals. It is an expectation of political obedience.
Serbia has been a candidate for European Union membership since 2012 and has conducted accession negotiations since 2014. The process has lasted far too long and has been burdened by mistakes in Belgrade, slow reforms and the indecision of the European Union itself, but all that belongs in a debate between Serbia and the EU. Lavrov has no place in that debate. Serbia may change its policy, alter the pace of negotiations or even change its ultimate objective, but it can do so only through its own sovereign decision. There is no Russian veto over Serbia’s European future, however much the Kremlin might wish otherwise.
The deepest insult in Lavrov’s statement is not his contempt for the European Union, but his assumption that Serbia still belongs to a category of countries to which Moscow feels entitled to explain what they really want. The Kremlin has never received a mandate from Serbian citizens to determine the strategic direction of their country. No episode of diplomatic alignment between Moscow and Belgrade gives Russia any claim over Serbian sovereignty. Russia holds no title deed to Serbian foreign policy and possesses no historical license to invalidate Serbia’s decisions whenever they displease the Kremlin. If Moscow understands friendship as an entitlement to Serbian obedience, the problem is not some supposed Serbian failure to appreciate Russia, but Russia’s refusal to accept Serbia as a fully independent state.
Putin’s Russia possesses neither the political nor the moral authority to lecture Serbia about its future. The boundary the Kremlin must accept could hardly be clearer: Russian state power ends at the borders of the Russian Federation, beyond which lie other countries, other peoples and decisions that belong to neither Putin nor Lavrov. That includes Serbia’s right to decide for itself whether it will one day become a member of the European Union. Serbia does not have to prove the depth of its European commitment in order to state the obvious fact that Moscow will have no say in that decision. It need only behave as a sovereign country and answer Sergey Lavrov’s prediction in the only terms appropriate for a man speaking on behalf of a rogue state that has already written its claim to decide the future of other nations in Ukrainian blood: the Kremlin must keep its hands off Serbia.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

UK’s largest carmaker to axe thousands of jobs – media

UK’s largest carmaker to axe thousands of jobs – media
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has confirmed plans to cut jobs as Britain’s largest carmaker struggles with rising costs, falling sales, and the impact of US tariffs, with The Times reporting that up to 4,000 positions could be eliminated.
JLR has faced mounting pressure from US tariffs, which have made its British-built vehicles more expensive to sell in the US despite London securing a reduced 10% rate. The impact has been particularly significant given that North America is the company’s largest market. Its troubles were compounded by a major cyberattack last year that forced it to halt production for several weeks.
JLR’s revenue fell by nearly 10% in the quarter ending in June, while pre-tax profit plunged by more than two-thirds to £109 million ($147 million). According to The Times, chief executive PB Balaji is under pressure from JLR’s Indian owner, Tata Motors, to cut costs.
In a statement to media, JLR said it “must adapt to evolving global market conditions” while seeking approximately £1.7 billion ($2.3 billion) in savings over the next two years and lowering its annual break-even point to 300,000 vehicles.
JLR said it is “opening a voluntary redundancy program” for salaried and management staff.
Employees were reportedly informed on Friday. The Times reported that up to 4,000 positions could be eliminated over the next two years, although JLR has not confirmed the number.
JLR directly employs around 34,000 people at sites in the West Midlands and Merseyside and supports an estimated 120,000 jobs across Britain’s automotive supply chain.
European carmakers have been reducing their workforces amid weak demand, rising costs, and growing competition from lower-cost Chinese manufacturers. Volkswagen this week approved another 50,000 job cuts by 2030, bringing its planned global workforce reduction to approximately 100,000. Its Porsche subsidiary is set to eliminate another 5,000 positions by 2035.
Germany’s car-manufacturing crisis has also been compounded by high energy costs since the country lost access to much of the cheap Russian pipeline gas on which its industrial economy had long relied following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume has separately cited US tariffs and intensifying Chinese competition among the pressures weighing on the company’s competitiveness.

Trump's approval rating falls to record low — Financial Times poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:44:14 UTC
14:44:14 KST

LONDON, September 6. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump's approval rating has dropped to a record low in a survey conducted by the British company Focaldata for the Financial Times, with only a third of US voters approving of his performance at the White House.
According to the study, only 33% of respondents supported Trump's current political course, compared to 35% a month earlier. At the same time, his support among Republican voters fell to 72%, which is also an anti-record in FT polls.
It is noted that the overwhelming majority of respondents rejected Washington's trade policy and the tariffs imposed by the Trump administration, linking them to the rising cost of living for US citizens. Two-thirds of voters believe the US economy is moving in the wrong direction, with another 57% saying that Trump's administration policies have negatively affected their financial well-being. Furthermore, 56% of survey participants expressed dissatisfaction with the latest trade tariffs on Canada, voicing concern over a possible further increase in prices for consumers.
FT also noted a decline in Trump's level of support as a political ally, as 46% of respondents believe that the current president is making the upcoming midterm congressional elections more difficult for the Republican Party. Another 47% stated their unwillingness to support a candidate publicly endorsed by Trump.
The poll was conducted from August 28 to September 1 among 1,914 registered voters, with a margin of error of approximately 2.6 percentage points.

The US rejected a claim by Malaysia’s opposition Islamist party that Washington once sought to influence the country’s choice of political leadership, calling the allegation false.
“The United States has never sought to decide Malaysia’s political leadership,” US embassy in Malaysia Charge d’Affaires David H. Gamble Jnr said in a statement on social media on Sunday. “Any account to the contrary is false.”
Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS) president Abdul Hadi Awang said at the Islamist party’s annual congress on Saturday that a US ambassador once asked the party whom it would propose as prime minister if it took power.

He said the then-US ambassador had requested to meet him and he attended with former PAS secretary general Mustafa Ali.

Colombia vows crackdown after deadly drone swarm attack (VIDEOS)
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has vowed to step up operations against armed groups after a drone swarm attack on a military compound killed three soldiers and injured four others.
The assault comes as Colombia is grappling with what has been described as its worst wave of violence in a decade. In August, an explosion outside a police station in Cucuta injured 11 officers and killed a police dog. Earlier this week, a car bomb outside another police station in the northeast killed one civilian and injured 11 others.
The latest attack occurred on Friday night at the El Trapiche military post in Ocana, in the northeastern department of Norte de Santander, according to Colombian authorities.
At least 20 UAVs were used in the assault, AFP reported. Explosives dropped from the drones struck barracks and other parts of the base before a firefight broke out. Two soldiers died at the scene and a third passed away after receiving medical attention. A Colombian Air Force helicopter was also hit by shrapnel.

Ukraine’s drone forces say they hit 58,465 Russian targets in August, nearly 1,900 a day. Three named campaigns did the strategic damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:31:45 UTC
14:31:45 KST

Ukraine's drone forces say they struck 58,465 Russian targets in August, an average of nearly 1,900 a day. The tally is up almost 9 percent on July and more than double January's, and it included 54 vessels of Russia's shadow fleet, 33 air-defense systems, and 168 energy nodes, Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert "Madiar" Brovdi reported on his Telegram channel.
The volume matters less than where some of it lands. Cutting power to occupied Crimea and the south is meant to blind Russian air defense, much of which runs on the grid. Meanwhile, the strikes on Russia's sanctions-evading shadow fleet squeeze both Crimea's fuel supply and Moscow's oil exports.
Ukraine's drone forces claim 11,010 Russian troop casualties in August
Brovdi also said the strikes killed or wounded 11,010 Russian soldiers over the month, about 355 a day — a figure that counts only losses the drone force attributes to its own strikes, not Russia's total casualties.
That daily rate was slightly below July's 374, down about 5 percent, even as the number of targets rose. Compared with January, the force said Russian personnel losses were up 17.3 percent.
Three campaigns inside the count
Most of the headline volume is small front-line targets, but three named operations account for the strategic hits. Under Operation "Milk", the force said it struck 54 shadow-fleet vessels in August, bringing the total to 260 since the campaign began on 6 July. Operation "PPOpad" — a play on the Ukrainian for air defense — hit 33 Russian air-defense elements in August and 263 across 2026.
The third, Operation "Crimean Switch Off", struck 168 energy nodes in August, bringing the total to 349 since early July. That campaign has been running for months, blacking out swaths of occupied Crimea.
Brovdi has argued that cutting power to stationary radars and other air-defense elements opens the airspace for deeper Ukrainian strikes. Months of these strikes have left occupied Crimea rationing fuel and living with rolling blackouts, and cut the Kerch ferry crossing's capacity by about three-quarters. All of the figures are the force's own, and Ukraine's military claims of Russian losses are not independently verified.

EU races to rethink Arctic policy as the global power grab continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:30:41 UTC
14:30:41 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is in Greenland to discuss the Arctic's growing importance among allies. The visit comes as Brussels is busy preparing a reviewed Arctic policy, with experts warning it must have security and defence at its core.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is completing her two-day whistlestop tour of the Greenlandic capital, Nuuk, on Monday to further European Union-Arctic relations — and gather intelligence as the European Union maps out a new Arctic Policy.
When the policy's first iteration was published in 2021, it made little reference to growing security threats. Instead, the then-EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell emphasised climate change, raw materials and geostrategic influence as central to the document.
But in the years since, the European Commission has admitted the policy needs an urgent revamp to address the changing security and defence environment in the region — a more militarised Russia, for one thing, as well as China's effort to expand its economic footprint as melting ice opens new Arctic Sea routes.
A European Commission spokesperson told Euronews that the updated document will aim to promote “peace, stability, and sustainable development in the region”, and that Brussels is committed to playing a constructive role in the territory.
They said the Arctic had gained “significant global attention” due to its unique environment and role in international dynamics.
“This update is necessary to maintain that the policy is relevant and effective in addressing the evolving challenges and opportunities in the Arctic region,” they said.
However, various people involved have told Euronews the publication of the policy has been “delayed”, and the Commission spokesperson was unable to provide a date.
As the wait continues, experts have warned Euronews there is much at stake if the EU executive does not get this new version right — particularly when it comes to security and defence.
Who is in the Arctic?
Russia and China have become increasingly active in the resource-rich High North. The United States and Canada are also present in the area, as are three EU member states: Finland, Sweden and Denmark.
“If you look at the Arctic, this is the place where all the superpowers meet,” Estonian MEP Urmas Paet told Euronews. Paet has drafted several high-profile reports regarding EU foreign policy, including one on the Arctic.
In a 2025 report, he strongly urged the European Commission to update its Arctic strategy, stressing that Russia’s militarisation and China’s Polar Silk Road have transformed the region into a major geopolitical flashpoint.
If the new strategy does not rise to the moment, he said, Europe will be “more and more” marginalised in the Arctic, with other superpowers potentially gaining the upper hand.
“The Americans, Chinese, and Russians will be more and more active, and well, Europe, less and less relevant,” he said.
Paet has urged Europe to work more closely with Greenlandic partners when it comes to critical raw materials and energy, and has called for the EU’s next long-term budget to earmark funds for a range of economic activities in the region, such as fishing, icebreakers, and infrastructure investments.
“The important point for this new strategy is that it clearly reflects adequately what is ongoing, and also shows the way how the European Union, also through its budget should react to all those changes we have witnessed."
The major issue now, Paet said, is publication. “They are very delayed,” he said.
What do these foreign powers want?
Arctic warmingis nearly four times the global average, with more than 10,000 cubic kilometres of sea ice lost in the region over the last 40 years. This continued warming has accelerated glacier melt, making the region increasingly attractive to countries by opening up new shipping routes in previously inaccessible areas.
In 2018, Chinese President Xi Jinping articulated his Polar Silk Road initiative. This is Beijing’s official vision to establish shipping infrastructure through the Arctic Ocean to link Europe and Asia.
In August, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov trumpeted the news that a container ship from China had arrived at the Russian city of Murmansk via a once-impassable Arctic route. He celebrated the development while outlining Russia’s plans to develop other international cooperation in the region.
Meanwhile, the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in February that given US President Donald Trump’s annexationist rhetoric toward Greenland, and these other geopolitical issues, the Arctic can no longer be considered a quiet corner of the map.
“It is the front line of the global power competition,” she said, while attending an Arctic-oriented conference in Tromsø, Norway.
Kallas warned that hybrid threats are growing in intensity and frequency in the region and are tied to Russia’s “enduring military build-up” in the High North.
“In response, European allies are stepping up on Arctic security, and the European Union is ready to do its part,” she said.
How do you secure the Arctic?
North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) Secretary-General Mark Rutte cautioned that in the face of China's growing interest in the High North and Russia's increased military activity, "it was crucial that we do more,” he said.
As a result, NATO launched Arctic Sentry in February. The multi-domain activity aims to strengthen the Alliance’s posture in the area by bringing together allies under one overarching operational strategy. A senior NATO official told Euronews the criteria for success would depend on how Russia and China respond to NATO’s increased footprint in the region.
Linda Solstrand Dahlberg, a senior representative of the Arctic University of Norway, told Euronews that the policy could incorporate a blueprint for greater EU and NATO coordination regarding the Arctic. This would safeguard subsea cables connecting Norway to mainland Europe, as well as coordination against the growing militarisation by foreign powers, such as Russia.
“A secure Arctic is inextricably linked with European security,” she said.
Dahlberg also suggested the document should explore the possibility of greater defence industry cooperation, which could benefit European countries looking for weather-tested capabilities.
“We've got competence and expertise in this area of the world, and we have stress testing capabilities for cold climates."
European Policy Centre defence analyst Maria Martisiute said the major shortcoming of the 2021 policy is that it does not mention military defence. She reiterated that the EU's geopolitical agenda has clearly changed since then, with Russa’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
But there have been developments outside of this, with Europe developing Security and Defence Partnerships with Canada, Iceland, Norway and the UK.
“These partnerships have to also be reflected in the new EU Arctic strategy,” Martisiute said.
Together, Martisiute and Dahlberg published a paper with dozens of recommendations for the EU's forthcoming policy. The most important thing that the European Commission must consider when finalising the document, according to them, is that they are cognisant that Arctic defence impacts European defence.
“The Arctic doesn’t exist in a vacuum,” Martisiute said. “It’s very closely integrated into the wider security landscape.”

Kim Jong Un commissioned a second nuclear destroyer
Kyiv • UNN
North Korea commissioned its second 5,000-ton-class destroyer at the port of Wonsan. Kim Jong Un linked the vessel to nuclear deterrence.
North Korea commissioned its second 5,000-ton-class destroyer in less than three months, continuing to build up its naval forces and nuclear capabilities. The ceremony, attended by Kim Jong Un, was held at the port of Wonsan amid Donald Trump’s efforts to resume talks with the North Korean leader. Bloomberg reports, UNN writes.
The new-generation destroyer is intended to deliver a deadly retaliatory strike against enemies, as it is a force incorporated into the state nuclear deterrence system
This came after North Korea commissioned its first 5,000-ton-class destroyer, "Choe Hyon," in June. Kim is stepping up efforts to strengthen the firepower of North Korea’s navy in the Yellow Sea to the west and in waters toward Japan to the east. At present, North Korea’s naval forces consist mostly of smaller vessels intended for coastal defense.
"The mere announcement of the commissioning of this ship, which is in fact an offensive destroyer, will be enough to convey our views and position to the world," Kim said. "We will exercise our legitimate right to self-defense and respond when necessary."
The commissioning of the destroyer comes amid Trump’s efforts to revive personal diplomacy with Kim that defined the first presidential term of the American leader. Although Kim has not yet publicly accepted Trump’s offers, South Korean intelligence said last week that a summit between the two leaders could take place "at any time."
Separately, the White House said that Trump remains ready to hold talks with Kim without preconditions.
The statement also came as the United States, South Korea, and Japan began five-day joint exercises on Monday in international waters near the South Korean resort island of Jeju. According to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, the exercises will involve the naval and air forces of the three countries to strengthen deterrence against threats from North Korea.
In his speech, Kim said that North Korea was implementing plans to strengthen its naval forces and that in eight months he would demonstrate this to the whole world. He did not specify what exactly would be presented then. Kim has said that North Korea plans to build two surface ships each year that are larger than the "Choe Hyon"-class vessel, including a cruiser with a displacement of 10,000 tons.

Putin backs proposal to allow volunteers with blindness, deafness, schizophrenia, and other severe medical conditions to serve in regional drone-defense units
Yevgeny Poddubny, a “war correspondent” for Russian state broadcaster VGTRK who heads United Russia’s electoral list, asked Vladimir Putin to allow volunteers with a Category D fitness classification to serve in regional units defending against Ukrainian drone attacks.
During a medical examination, conscripts and volunteers are assigned one of five fitness categories — A, B, V, G, or D — based on their health. Only people in Categories A and B may be called up for regular conscript service or alternative civilian service.
People in Category V are exempt from regular conscript service and assigned to the reserves. Category G grants a temporary deferment of up to one year, followed by another medical examination. Category D exempts people from military service entirely.
Poddubny claimed that wounded soldiers themselves were asking for the change.
“Of course, people in this category have severe medical conditions, but there are cases where […] people are capable of carrying out certain tasks — for example, serving in regional BARS units for air defense and destroying drones. Obviously, not everyone can. But there is a core group of volunteers who have assessed their own abilities and are pleading for an exception that would allow them to serve in regional units that protect facilities from drones. Obviously, this is not about the front line. Their own city, their own village, their own workplace,” Poddubny said.
Putin replied, “Zhenya, I support it.”
Poddubny made the proposal amid rumors that Russia will see another large-scale wave of mobilization this fall. Russian authorities deny having any such plans. Vladimir Putin has called the mobilization rumors “complete nonsense.”
Category D is assigned to people with severe, irreversible medical conditions, including blindness, deafness in both ears, and schizophrenia.

Explainer-Options for UK finance minister Healey to tax wealth in October's budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-07
05:22:04 UTC
14:22:04 KST

Explainer-Options for UK finance minister Healey to tax wealth in October's budget
LONDON, Sept 7 - British finance minister John Healey faces pressure to raise billions of pounds in tax at his first budget to offset higher borrowing costs and fund Prime Minister Andy Burnham's plans for expanded social care and more defence spending.
Following are some tax increase options for Healey, who is due to announce his first budget on October 28.
LOTS OF PLEDGES, NOT MUCH LEEWAY
Burnham said last year when he was mayor of Greater Manchester that Britain overtaxed workers and undertaxed wealth. He also pledged to keep Labour's commitment not to raise the rates of income tax, value-added tax, corporation tax or social security contributions.
Britain raised £1.1 trillion ($1.5 trillion) in tax in the 2025/26 financial year.
Budget forecasts in March showed the government had a relatively narrow £24 billion of leeway to meet its target of balancing day-to-day spending and tax revenue by 2029/30. Many economists think that headroom has narrowed sharply since.
CAPITAL GAINS TAX
Capital gains tax raised £24 billion in the 2025/26 tax year. Britain's previous finance minister, Rachel Reeves, increased the rate to 18% for basic-rate taxpayers and 24% for higher-rate taxpayers.
That is lower than income tax rates of 20% and 40% paid by basic and higher-rate tax payers. Earlier this year, Wes Streeting, then a potential challenger to Burnham and now defence minister, suggested CGT rates should match income tax.
The left-leaning Institute for Public Policy Research has made a similar proposal.
In August 2025, the University of Warwick's Centre for the Analysis of Taxation estimated that a comprehensive reform to CGT would raise an extra £11 billion a year.
As well as raising rates to the same level as income tax, this reform ends the exemption on CGT when someone dies but includes a new tax-free allowance to exempt normal investment returns. CGT would also be charged on unrealised gains when someone emigrates from Britain.
However, the sums raised from increasing CGT are disputed. In June 2025, Britain's tax office estimated that raising the higher CGT rate by 10 percentage points would lower revenue by up to £3.6 billion a year due to increased tax avoidance.
PROPERTY TAXES
Council tax, an annual levy paid by property occupiers, raises £54 billion a year while stamp duty on property purchases raises £17 billion.
Council tax is based on the relative values of properties in 1991. Up-to-date valuations would sharply increase payments in London and much of southern England and lower them elsewhere.
Most economists view stamp duty as an inefficient source of revenue as it discourages people from moving house to find work and older households from downsizing.
Last month, in an IPPR paper, University of Oxford Professor Ben Ansell proposed a 0.65% property value tax to replace revenue from council tax and stamp duty.
Before he was prime minister, Burnham was listed as a supporter of a proposal from the Fairer Share campaign group to merge both taxes into a single 0.48% levy on property values.
However, in July Burnham ruled out scrapping stamp duty or council tax at October's budget. He said he wanted to make tax "fairer" and backed plans announced last year which will charge extra council tax from 2028 on homes worth more than £2 million.
WEALTH TAX
Charity Oxfam and campaigners Tax Justice UK have called on Labour to introduce a 2% annual levy on assets over £10 million, which they say could raise £24 billion a year, extrapolating from a University of Warwick estimate.
Asked in a July podcast about the possibility of a "wealth tax ... on the super rich", Burnham said he wanted to take his time before making a decision but would not rule this out.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies said last year that annual wealth taxes were hard to implement, due to the difficulty of accurately valuing assets such as private businesses.
Most developed countries had abandoned wealth taxes due to the administrative burden and political pressure for exemptions which led to relatively little revenue being raised, it said.
Predicting how much a wealth tax would raise in Britain over the long term was hard due to the difficulty of knowing how many people would emigrate in response or find other ways to avoid it, the IFS added. REUTERS
